recall_advanced.x: DD Form 2579 documents small-business specialist coordination — the record that the set-aside analysis happened and who concurred. SF 1449 is the commercial award form; DD 1547 is weighted guidelines.

recall_advanced.q: Subcontracting plan thresholds?
recall_advanced.a: $900K; $2M construction.
d: $750K; $1.5M construction.
$1M; $2.5M construction.
The SAT; $1M construction.
recall_advanced.x: $900K standard, $2M construction — the thresholds where other-than-small primes owe a subcontracting plan. Small primes never owe one; the plan is how large business accounts for small-business opportunity below the prime level.

recall_advanced.q: Only one small business responds to your set-aside — now what?
recall_advanced.a: If the offer is fair-market priced, award — the Rule of Two tests the expectation, not the final count. Document what changed between research and offers.
d: Withdraw the set-aside and resolicit full-and-open.
Refer to the SBA for a certificate of competency before award.
Cancel and re-run the sources-sought — one offer defeats the set-aside.
recall_advanced.x: The Rule of Two tested your expectation — one responsive offer doesn't retroactively break it. If the price is fair-market, award, and document what changed between research and receipt. Withdrawing the set-aside because turnout disappointed is both unnecessary and protest bait.

recall_advanced.q: The requirement's been in the 8(a) program — can you compete it full-and-open now?
recall_advanced.a: Not unilaterally: once in 8(a), it stays unless SBA agrees to release it. That's the follow-on trap on 8(a) requirements.
d: Yes — each new requirement starts fresh; prior program history doesn't bind.
Yes, once the incumbent has graduated from the program.
Only the HCA can release it, with Competition Advocate concurrence.
recall_advanced.x: Once a requirement enters the 8(a) program, it stays unless the Small Business Administration (SBA) agrees to release it — the contracting officer (CO) can't unilaterally take the follow-on full-and-open, and incumbent graduation doesn't undo the program's hold. It's the classic 8(a) follow-on trap.

recall_advanced.q: When does 8(a) sole source need a justification and approval (J&A)?
recall_advanced.a: DoD: not below $100M. The program's statutory basis covers it — that's the 'authorized by statute' lane.
d: Above the SAT, like any other sole source.
Above $30M for DoD; $100M is the civilian line.
Never — 8(a) awards are exempt from J&As at every value.
recall_advanced.x: For DoD, 8(a) sole source needs no J&A below $100M — the program's statutory basis IS the competition exception ('authorized by statute'). The $30M figure is the civilian line; mixing the two is the standard miss.

recall_advanced.q: Recite the four SAMO carve-outs.
recall_advanced.a: SAP · statute · in-scope mods · orders under existing vehicles.
d: SAP · set-asides · urgent actions · commercial buys.
Statute · micro-purchases · options · GPC actions.
SAP · sole source · in-scope mods · bridge actions.
recall_advanced.x: SAMO: Simplified acquisition, Authorized by statute, in-scope Modifications, Orders under existing vehicles — the four lanes where the Competition in Contracting Act's (CICA) full-and-open machinery doesn't attach in the first place. Distinct from the seven exceptions, which excuse competition where it DOES attach.

recall_advanced.q: Name all seven RFO 6.103 exceptions, in any order.
recall_advanced.a: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/R&D · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest.
d: One source · urgency · follow-on · small business · statute · security · best value.
Sole source · emergency · mobilization · treaty · regulation · classification · agency head.
One source · urgency · logical follow-on · international agreement · statute · secrecy · economy.
recall_advanced.x: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/research and development (R&D) · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest. The distractors plant 'logical follow-on' and 'best value' — fair-opportunity and source-selection concepts that don't live in Part 6.

recall_advanced.q: Your justification and approval (J&A) is $18M — who approves? $95M (DoD)? $160M (DoD)?
recall_advanced.a: $18M → Competition Advocate; $95M DoD → HPA/PEO (DoD line is $150M); $160M DoD → SPE.
d: $18M → CO; $95M → Competition Advocate; $160M → HPA/PEO.
$18M → Competition Advocate; $95M → SPE; $160M → USD(A&S).
All three → HCA; the ladder applies only to fair-opportunity D&As.
recall_advanced.x: $18M → Competition Advocate (to $20M). $95M DoD → head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) (DoD tier runs to $150M). $160M DoD → senior procurement executive (SPE). The DoD $150M line is the tell — elsewhere the HPA tier tops at $90M.

recall_advanced.q: How long do you have to post a justification and approval (J&A) to SAM.gov after award? After an urgency award?
recall_advanced.a: 14 days; 30 days for urgency.
d: 30 days; 14 days for urgency.
10 days; 30 days for urgency.
14 days in both cases.
recall_advanced.x: 14 days after award standard; 30 for urgency — urgency is the one case where posting trails longer, because the buy couldn't wait. Reversing the pair is the classic error.

recall_advanced.q: Only one offer came in on your competitive solicitation — now what?
recall_advanced.a: If the solicitation allowed under 30 days for offers, consult the requiring activity and resolicit for at least 30. If interest was real but only one firm bid, find out why — get feedback, document it, and use it to open the next competition. The award can still be made if the price is fair and reasonable.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between full-and-open after exclusion of sources and other than full-and-open?
recall_advanced.a: Exclusion still competes — among a deliberately narrowed field (a set-aside is the everyday example). "Other than" means one or very few sources under an RFO 6.103 exception.
d: They're the same bucket — both require a J&A under RFO 6.103.
Exclusion is for security-driven narrowing only; 'other than' covers set-asides.
Exclusion needs SPE approval; 'other than' needs only the CO's certification.
recall_advanced.x: Exclusion (a set-aside is the everyday case) still COMPETES — among a deliberately narrowed field, no justification and approval (J&A) needed. 'Other than full and open' means one or few sources under an RFO 6.103 exception with a J&A. Same statute, entirely different burdens.

recall_advanced.q: Who approves your $40M justification and approval (J&A)? …and a $15M one?
recall_advanced.a: $40M → HPA/PEO. $15M → Competition Advocate. (Know your ladder cold — boards love the second ask.)
d: $40M → SPE. $15M → HPA/PEO.
$40M → Competition Advocate. $15M → CO.
Both → HCA — the DoD ladder starts at $50M.
recall_advanced.x: $40M → head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO); $15M → Competition Advocate. Boards ask the ladder twice in a row precisely to catch memorized-once answers — know the bands ($900K / $20M / $90M–$150M DoD / above), not just one rung.

recall_advanced.q: The program wants a bridge while the follow-on catches up. Fine?
recall_advanced.a: Only for a genuinely unforeseen cause — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory change. "We didn't plan" is never a valid basis, and repeat bridges escalate to higher approval each time.

recall_advanced.q: The three exchange types and the line between them.
recall_advanced.a: Clarifications (minor, no revisions) · communications (pre-range) · discussions (post-range, meaningful, all in range).
d: Clarifications (pre-range) · communications (post-range) · discussions (award stage).
Communications (minor fixes) · clarifications (pre-range) · negotiations (any time).
Clarifications (no limit) · discussions (pre-range) · debriefings (post-range).
recall_advanced.x: Clarifications: minor, no revisions. Communications: pre-competitive-range, to decide who's in — still no revisions. Discussions: post-range, must be meaningful, everyone in the range, revisions allowed. The revision line is what separates the lanes — cross it accidentally and you've opened discussions.

recall_advanced.q: Who evaluates, who decides, who runs the business side?
recall_advanced.a: SSEB · SSA · PCO.
d: SSA · SSEB · PCO.
SSEB · PCO · SSA.
SSAC · SSA · SSEB.
recall_advanced.x: Source selection evaluation board (SSEB) evaluates, source selection authority (SSA) decides, procuring contracting officer (PCO) runs the business side. Three roles, three accountabilities — and the SSA deciding is exactly why the evaluators and the business channel stay in their lanes.

recall_advanced.q: When can you award without discussions?
recall_advanced.a: Solicitation said so and initial proposals support it.
d: Whenever all offerors are technically acceptable.
Only under the SAT or on commercial actions.
When the SSA documents urgency in the SSDD.
recall_advanced.x: Award without discussions requires both halves: the solicitation preserved the right, AND the initial proposals support a clean award. 'Everyone was acceptable' isn't the test, and no dollar threshold or source selection authority (SSA) urgency finding substitutes.

recall_advanced.q: What must a post-award debrief include — and exclude?
recall_advanced.a: Include: evaluated result, significant weaknesses, ranking/rationale. Exclude: other offerors' proposal contents.
d: Include: all evaluator notes and scoresheets. Exclude: the award price.
Include: a point-by-point comparison with the winner. Exclude: past-performance sources.
Include: the SSDD verbatim. Exclude: the protester's own weaknesses.
recall_advanced.x: A debrief includes the offeror's own evaluated result, its significant weaknesses, and the ranking/rationale — and excludes other offerors' proposal contents. A good debrief answers questions; a defensive one provokes the protest it feared.

recall_advanced.q: Award without discussions — when is that OK?
recall_advanced.a: If the solicitation preserved it and the initial proposals support a clean award. On large, complex actions, discussions usually earn their keep — say you'd weigh it, not autopilot it.

recall_advanced.q: An evaluator wants to ping an offeror about an ambiguity before the range.
recall_advanced.a: That's a communication — through me, documented, no proposal revisions. The moment it invites a revision, it's discussions, and discussions have rules.
d: That's a clarification — the evaluator can send it directly.
Forbidden — no contact of any kind before the competitive range.
That's discussions — allowed pre-range if offered to every offeror.
recall_advanced.x: Pre-range contact to understand (not revise) a proposal is a communication — routed through the procuring contracting officer (PCO), documented. The moment the exchange invites a revision it becomes discussions, with all of discussions' obligations. Evaluators never freelance contact.

recall_advanced.q: Can price be a rating like technical?
recall_advanced.a: No — cost/price is evaluated (analysis, realism where applicable) but never adjectivally rated. It competes in the tradeoff as a number with analysis behind it.
d: Yes — price gets the same adjectival scale so the tradeoff is apples-to-apples.
Yes, but only in LPTA source selections.
No — price is considered only after the technical ranking is final.
recall_advanced.x: Cost/price is evaluated — analyzed, realism-checked where applicable — but never adjectivally rated. It enters the tradeoff as a number with analysis behind it. Rating price like technical is a protest-sustainable process error.

recall_advanced.q: What makes discussions 'meaningful'?
recall_advanced.a: Each offeror hears its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond — tailored, not generic, and even-handed across the range.
d: Every offeror receives the identical list of questions, verbatim.
At least two rounds with revised proposals after each.
The Government reveals its price objective so offerors can meet it.
recall_advanced.x: Meaningful = each offeror hears ITS OWN significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond — tailored, even-handed across the range. Identical question lists are the opposite of meaningful; revealing your price objective is a different violation entirely.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Current certified-data threshold, and the date line that changed it?
recall_advanced.a: $10M for actions entered after 30 Jun 2026 (FY26 NDAA §1804); $2.5M for earlier contracts and their mods.
d: $2.5M across the board until the RFO rulemaking finalizes.
$10M for everything — mods of older contracts included.
$5M after 30 Jun 2026; $2.5M before.
recall_advanced.x: $10M for actions entered after 30 June 2026 (FY26 the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) §1804); $2.5M for earlier contracts AND their mods. The date line matters more than the number — a mod to an old contract stays on the old trigger.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Recite CLAWM — and where do the exceptions live in the RFO?
recall_advanced.a: Commercial · Law/regulation · Adequate price competition · Waiver (HCA) · commercial Mods — RFO 15.403-2.
d: Competition · Law · Audit rights · Waiver · Market pricing — RFO 15.402-1.
Commercial · Low dollar · Adequate competition · Waiver (SPE) · Mods — RFO 15.403-4.
Catalog · Law/regulation · Award without discussions · Waiver (CO) · Mods — RFO 12.209.
recall_advanced.x: CLAWM: Commercial, Law/regulation set the price, Adequate price competition, Waiver (HCA), commercial Mods — at RFO 15.403-2. Run the exceptions BEFORE demanding certified data; most actions never need the certificate.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Which analysis is always required? When does cost realism apply?
recall_advanced.a: Price analysis, always (15.404-1); cost realism on competitive cost-type source selections (15.404-3).
d: Cost analysis, always; price analysis only when competition is adequate.
Price analysis above the SAT; realism on all fixed-price awards.
Both price and cost analysis, on every negotiated action.
recall_advanced.x: Price analysis always (15.404-1) — every action, every method. Cost realism applies on competitive cost-type source selections (15.404-3), where an unrealistically low estimate becomes the Government's overrun. Reversing 'always' onto cost analysis is the standard flip.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: All five elements of defective pricing.
recall_advanced.a: Was cost/pricing data · existed pre-agreement · not disclosed · relied upon · increased the price.
d: Certified data · post-award discovery · intent to deceive · materiality · Government harm.
Data existed · was requested · was withheld · caused overrun · exceeded threshold.
Cost data · pre-award · disclosed late · auditor flagged · price unreasonable.
recall_advanced.x: All five: it was cost/pricing data, it existed before agreement, it wasn't disclosed, the Government relied, the price increased. Intent is famously NOT an element — defective pricing is strict about facts, not motives. Each element the contractor can break defeats the remedy.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) fee ceilings for research and development (R&D), most others, architect-engineer (A&E).
recall_advanced.a: 15% R&D · 10% most others · 6% A-E under RFO 15.404-9. But for the Army, Navy and Air Force, R-DFARS 236.202-371 raises A-E to 10% of estimated construction cost — know which one your board is asking about.
recall_advanced.x: 15% R&D, 10% most others, 6% A&E — statutory CPFF fee ceilings. The A&E 6% rides on the design fee and is the one boards pull out when the first two come too easily.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between certified and other-than-certified cost or pricing data?
recall_advanced.a: The data can be identical — the certificate is the difference. Other-than-certified is what you request to determine price reasonableness when an exception applies; no certificate, no defective-pricing remedy.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: The contractor did a 'sweep' after agreement and found new data — now what?
recall_advanced.a: Sweeps are recommended, not required. Before award: incorporate — if the corrected price is lower, adjust down; if higher, the contractor generally eats it unless it's unreasonable, and you may reopen. After award: that's defective pricing — the Government is entitled to a price reduction plus interest; bring in Legal.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: The contractor refuses to provide further support during fact-finding.
recall_advanced.a: Document exactly what was requested and refused, use the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA)/the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) to press the field organization, elevate through the contractor's management — and remember I can't award without determining the price fair and reasonable. No data, no deal, and the file shows why.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: When would you get DCAA vs. DCMA support?
recall_advanced.a: Field pricing support scales with dollars and type — the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) forward-pricing rate support around $2.5M+ (fixed-price) / $10M+ (cost-type); the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) audit at $10M+ (fixed-price) / $100M+ (cost-type). Below those, my pricing office and I work it.

recall_advanced.q: Five type-selection factors.
recall_advanced.a: Requirement definition · estimate confidence · technical risk · competition · accounting system · acquisition history (any five).

recall_advanced.q: The point of total assumption (PTA) formula.
recall_advanced.a: PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Gov share + Target Cost.
d: PTA = (Ceiling − Target Cost) ÷ contractor share + Target Price.
PTA = Target Cost + (Ceiling − Target Cost) × Gov share.
PTA = Ceiling − (Target Profit ÷ Gov share).
recall_advanced.x: PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Government share + Target Cost. Past that point every cost dollar comes out of profit — the contractor is effectively on firm-fixed-price (FFP) to the ceiling. The distractors shuffle the same terms; write the formula once, correctly, and check the units.

recall_advanced.q: Two gates every cost-type contract must clear.
recall_advanced.a: Adequate accounting system; D&F.
d: DCAA pre-award audit; HCA approval.
Approved purchasing system; J&A.
EVMS certification; fee-ceiling waiver.
recall_advanced.x: Two gates, no exceptions: an adequate (approved) accounting system — because the Government pays incurred costs — and a determination and findings (D&F) justifying the type. Audits and earned value management system (EVMS) may follow on big programs, but they aren't the entry gates.

recall_advanced.q: E.O. 14402 justification thresholds — DoD and most agencies.
recall_advanced.a: DoD $100M; most agencies $10M.
d: DoD $50M; most agencies $10M.
DoD $100M; most agencies $25M.
DoD $150M; most agencies $35M.
recall_advanced.x: E.O. 14402: other-than-firm-fixed-price (FFP) needs justification above $100M for DoD, $10M for most agencies (DHS $25M, NASA $35M). The 10× DoD asymmetry is the memorable part — and the point: DoD buys more uncertainty than anyone.

recall_advanced.q: Walk me through the PTA.
recall_advanced.a: The point where the ceiling takes over: (ceiling price minus target price) divided by the Government's share, plus target cost. Past it, each cost dollar comes out of profit — the contractor is effectively on firm-fixed-price (FFP) from there to the ceiling.

recall_advanced.q: Why not firm-fixed-price (FFP) the development effort — doesn't it protect us?
recall_advanced.a: A contractor forced to price the unknowable pads the price or fails trying — both cost the Government more. FFP on high-uncertainty work is risk denial, not risk transfer.
d: It does — FFP always transfers cost risk; the objection is only fee-related.
Because cost-type contracts are cheaper to administer.
Because E.O. 14402 prohibits FFP on development above $10M.
recall_advanced.x: FFP on truly uncertain work doesn't transfer risk — it denies it. The contractor either pads the price (you pay for phantom certainty) or fails trying (you pay in schedule and litigation). Matching type to requirement definition IS the risk management.

recall_advanced.q: CPFF vs. CPIF in one sentence each?
recall_advanced.a: Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF): fee fixed at award regardless of cost outcome — buys effort under uncertainty. Cost-plus-incentive-fee (CPIF): fee slides with cost performance inside a min/max — buys cost discipline when a credible target exists.

recall_advanced.q: All six fair-opportunity exceptions.
recall_advanced.a: Urgency · only-one-capable · logical follow-on · minimum guarantee · statute · order-level small business set-aside.
d: Urgency · sole source · bridge · ceiling · statute · security.
Only-one-capable · follow-on · best value · minimum guarantee · SAP · set-aside.
Urgency · incumbent continuity · economy · guarantee · regulation · size status.
recall_advanced.x: Urgency, only-one-capable, logical follow-on, minimum guarantee, statute, and order-level small-business set-aside — the six fair-opportunity exceptions. Note what's absent: 'bridge,' 'incumbent continuity,' and 'best value' are not exceptions, however often they're pitched as one.

recall_advanced.q: Order-debrief breakpoint? The Government Accountability Office (GAO) order-protest thresholds?
recall_advanced.a: $7.5M; $35M DoD / $10M civilian (or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value).
d: $5.5M; $25M DoD / $10M civilian.
$7.5M; $10M DoD / $35M civilian.
$10M; $35M for both DoD and civilian.
recall_advanced.x: $7.5M starts order-level debriefing rights; GAO order protests start at $35M DoD / $10M civilian — except scope/period/ceiling growth protests, which land at any value. Three numbers plus the exception: that's the full answer.

recall_advanced.q: What document supports an over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) exception, and who approves at $12M?
recall_advanced.a: A D&A; $12M → Competition Advocate.
d: A J&A; $12M → HPA/PEO.
A D&F; $12M → the CO.
A D&A; $12M → HCA, non-delegable.
recall_advanced.x: Over-SAT fair-opportunity exceptions ride a determination and approval (D&A) (not a justification and approval (J&A) — different instrument, same ladder). $12M lands with the Competition Advocate. Instrument first, tier second: that order of answer shows you know both.

recall_advanced.q: What makes a follow-on 'logical' enough to use the exception?
recall_advanced.a: Genuine continuity economics — the original order was competed (or properly excepted), and switching performers mid-stream would cost duplication the Government can't recover. Used sparingly, documented hard, and it weakens every time you stack it.

recall_advanced.q: A holder complains the last three orders all went to one firm.
recall_advanced.a: They get the ombudsman, and I get a look in the mirror: consideration has to be real — rotating "considered but lost" paperwork isn't fair opportunity.
d: Complaints about order placement go to GAO like any protest.
Nothing is owed — fair opportunity ended when the IDIQ was awarded.
Refer them to the SBA size-protest process.
recall_advanced.x: Order-placement complaints go to the task-order ombudsman, not the Government Accountability Office (GAO) (below the protest thresholds). And the complaint is a mirror: consideration must be genuine — if the record shows rotation paperwork instead of real evaluation, the ombudsman will find it.

recall_advanced.q: Can you set aside an order for small business on a mixed vehicle?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — order-level set-asides are a recognized exception lane; document the Rule-of-Two logic among holders.
d: No — set-asides were decided at the vehicle level and can't reopen.
Only if the vehicle was awarded as a partial set-aside.
Yes, but it requires an SBA waiver and HCA approval.
recall_advanced.x: Yes — order-level set-asides are a recognized fair-opportunity exception lane. Document the Rule-of-Two logic among the vehicle's holders. No the Small Business Administration (SBA) waiver, no head of the contracting activity (HCA) approval, no vehicle-level bar: the analysis just moves down to the order.

recall_advanced.q: The exercise gates, all of them.
recall_advanced.a: Funds · existing need · most advantageous (fresh market/price look) · not excluded in SAM · performance considered.
d: Funds · CPARS above satisfactory · IGCE update · JA review · PM endorsement.
Need · funds · synopsis posted · price unchanged · contractor consent.
Funds · need · debrief complete · clearance approval · COR certification.
recall_advanced.x: Five gates, all of them: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous (a fresh market/price look), not excluded in SAM, and performance considered. The distractors swap in process artifacts — the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS) thresholds, judge advocate (JA) review, synopses — that aren't gates.

recall_advanced.q: What happens legally if the notice date passes?
recall_advanced.a: The unilateral right lapses — continuation is bilateral.
d: A 30-day grace period applies automatically.
The option self-exercises if funds were committed.
Nothing — notice dates are administrative, not binding.
recall_advanced.x: Miss the notice date and the unilateral right lapses — continuing becomes a bilateral negotiation where the contractor holds leverage. No grace period, no self-execution: the option's power was the calendar, and the calendar is unforgiving.

recall_advanced.q: The services duration rail and the extension-clause cap.
recall_advanced.a: ~5 years base+options; 6-month extension cap.
d: ~3 years base+options; 12-month extension cap.
~5 years base+options; 12-month extension cap.
~10 years base+options; 6-month extension cap.
recall_advanced.x: About 5 years base+options is the services rail; the extension-of-services clause adds at most 6 months. The pair works together: the rail bounds the structure, the clause bridges a transition — once.

recall_advanced.q: Three situations where you shouldn't use options at all.
recall_advanced.a: No realistic exercise chance · volatile pricing · full requirement already known and funded.
d: Incumbent performance concerns · multi-year funding · commercial items.
Under the SAT · sole source · severable services.
New contractors · cost-type work · congressional interest.
recall_advanced.x: Skip options when there's no realistic exercise chance (they still get evaluated and priced), when pricing is too volatile to hold, or when the full requirement is already known and funded (just buy it). Options are a tool for probable futures — not a default template.

recall_advanced.q: Market prices dropped 15% since award. Exercise anyway?
recall_advanced.a: Only if I can still call the option price the most advantageous path after an informal market check — otherwise the honest answer may be a new competition. The option price was reasonable then; the gate asks about now.

recall_advanced.q: You missed the notice window by a week.
recall_advanced.a: The unilateral right is gone. If continuing is still best, it's a bilateral agreement — negotiated, documented, and the contractor holds leverage. Then I fix the suspense system that let it slip.

recall_advanced.q: Performance is shaky — exercise and 'manage it'?
recall_advanced.a: The performance gate exists for exactly this. Options are leverage: a contractor renewed despite flags learns the flags don't matter. Decide with the record, not with inertia.
d: Exercise — continuity outweighs performance concerns inside the ordering period.
Exercise, but withhold fee until performance recovers.
Never exercise after any negative CPARS entry — the gate is absolute.
recall_advanced.x: The performance gate exists for exactly this moment. Exercising past known flags teaches the contractor the flags are decorative — options are leverage only if a shaky record can actually cost the renewal. Decide from the documented record, not from transition dread.

recall_advanced.q: Direct vs. assisted — the one-sentence difference and the document assisted requires.
recall_advanced.a: Direct: our CO orders on their vehicle; assisted: their shop buys for us — signed interagency agreement required.
d: Direct: they buy with our funds; assisted: we buy on their vehicle — MIPR required.
Direct: same-service orders; assisted: cross-service orders — D&F required.
Direct: under the SAT; assisted: over the SAT — Economy Act determination required.
recall_advanced.x: Direct: our contracting officer (CO) places orders on their vehicle under its terms. Assisted: their contracting shop buys FOR us — which is why a signed interagency agreement defining roles must exist before money moves. The military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) is how funds travel; the agreement is how accountability does.

recall_advanced.q: When does the Economy Act apply, and what paperwork rides with it?
recall_advanced.a: Only absent a more specific authority; MIPR + D&F (Government's interest, not better from private sector).
d: On every interagency order; just the MIPR.
Whenever DoD funds leave the Department; IAA + J&A.
Only for GSA schedule orders; the ordering-guide checklist.
recall_advanced.x: The Economy Act is the fallback — it applies only when no more specific authority (schedules, GWACs) covers the buy, and it rides with a military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus a determination and findings (D&F) finding it's in the Government's interest and not more cheaply available from the private sector.

recall_advanced.q: Does sending funds to another agency stop the fiscal clock?
recall_advanced.a: No — purpose, time, and amount rules travel with the money.
d: Yes — the receiving agency's fiscal rules take over at transfer.
Yes, for severable services under 12 months.
Only Time stops; Purpose and Amount stay with the sender.
recall_advanced.x: The fiscal clock never stops at the transfer: purpose, time, and amount rules travel WITH the money. Parking expiring funds at another agency doesn't extend their life — that's a bona fide need violation with extra steps.

recall_advanced.q: Why not just military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) it and let them worry about it?
recall_advanced.a: Because accountability doesn't transfer with the money — the requirement, the fiscal rules, and the outcome are still ours. The D&F exists to prove we chose this lane deliberately.
d: No reason not to — assisted acquisitions shift responsibility to the servicing agency.
Because MIPRs are capped at the SAT.
Because the Economy Act forbids assisted acquisitions for services.
recall_advanced.x: Accountability doesn't transfer with a MIPR — the requirement, the fiscal rules, and the outcome remain yours. The determination and findings (D&F) exists precisely to prove the lane was chosen deliberately, not to outsource a problem.

recall_advanced.q: Direct vs. assisted — who's the contracting officer?
recall_advanced.a: Direct: our CO places the order under their contract's terms. Assisted: their CO acts for us under the interagency agreement — which is why that agreement must define roles before a dollar moves.

recall_advanced.q: When is the Economy Act the wrong cite?
recall_advanced.a: Whenever a more specific authority exists — schedules and GWACs carry their own authority. Citing the Economy Act for a schedule order tells the board you memorized a name, not a framework.

recall_advanced.q: TPA — say what each letter tests.
recall_advanced.a: Time = availability + bona fide need; Purpose = appropriated use; Amount = ADA limits.
d: Time = fiscal-year end; Purpose = mission need; Amount = IGCE accuracy.
Time = obligation speed; Purpose = color match; Amount = ceiling compliance.
Time = period of performance; Purpose = CLIN structure; Amount = funded value.
recall_advanced.x: Time = period of availability plus bona fide need. Purpose = only what Congress appropriated it for. Amount = the Anti-Deficiency lines — never more than, never before, availability. Say what each letter TESTS and you've shown the framework, not the acronym.

recall_advanced.q: Colors and clocks: operation and maintenance (O&M), research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E), procurement.
recall_advanced.a: 1 · 2 · 3 years.
d: 1 · 3 · 5 years.
2 · 3 · 5 years.
1 · 2 · 5 years.
recall_advanced.x: O&M 1 year, RDT&E 2, Procurement 3 (MILCON 5). The 1-2-3 ladder decides which year's money a need belongs to — and every 'can we use this money?' question starts here.

recall_advanced.q: Severable vs. non-severable funding rules.
recall_advanced.a: Severable ≤12 months, may cross FYs, current funds; non-severable fully funded up front.
d: Severable fully funded up front; non-severable ≤12 months on current funds.
Both incrementally funded within the fiscal year of award.
Severable ≤24 months across FYs; non-severable funded by option year.
recall_advanced.x: Severable services: up to 12 months on current funds, may cross fiscal years. Non-severable: one end product, fully funded up front, can run long. Funding a non-severable effort incrementally is the violation this pair exists to catch.

recall_advanced.q: LoC vs. LoF — which contract, what notice?
recall_advanced.a: LoC on fully funded cost contracts, LoF on incremental — ~75% notice.
d: LoC on incremental, LoF on fully funded — ~85% notice.
LoC on fixed-price, LoF on cost-type — ~75% notice.
Both apply to every cost contract — ~50% notice.
recall_advanced.x: Limitation of Cost rides fully funded cost contracts; Limitation of Funds rides incrementally funded ones — both demand notice around 75%. The clause name follows the funding structure; the notice duty is the contractor's.

recall_advanced.q: The financing order of preference.
recall_advanced.a: Private → customary (PBP preferred) → unusual → advance payments.
d: Advance payments → progress payments → PBPs → private.
Customary → private → advance → unusual.
Private → unusual → customary → advance payments.
recall_advanced.x: Private financing first, then customary contract financing (PBPs preferred), then unusual, then advance payments — last, rare, and heavily approved. The order exists because each step moves Government money earlier than the work.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor blew past the ceiling without notice and wants more money.
recall_advanced.a: The limitation clause allocates that risk: no timely notice, no entitlement to overrun funding — the Government may fund, but doesn't have to. Facts first: when did they know, when did they tell.

recall_advanced.q: Why are performance-based payments preferred over progress payments?
recall_advanced.a: They pay for demonstrated events, not incurred cost — better incentive alignment, recoverable in default, and less administration on costs.
d: They pay faster — 30-day cycles instead of 45.
They're the only financing allowed on commercial contracts.
They avoid the Assignment of Claims Act entirely.
recall_advanced.x: PBPs pay for demonstrated events, not incurred costs — better incentive alignment, recoverable if the contractor defaults, and lighter administration. Progress payments finance effort; performance-based payments finance results.

recall_advanced.q: Can expired funds pay a claim on an old contract?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — within their 5-year expired window, for adjustments to obligations properly made when current. After cancellation, no.
d: No — expired means gone; claims need current-year funds.
Yes — expired funds stay available for claims indefinitely.
Only with an ADA waiver from the comptroller.
recall_advanced.x: Expired funds still pay adjustments to their own properly made obligations for 5 years — a claim on an old contract is exactly that. After cancellation, nothing: the account is gone for all purposes and current funds (with their own rules) are the only recourse.

recall_advanced.q: The three funding scenarios and the rights each produces.
recall_advanced.a: All Government $ → unlimited; mixed → GPR (converting to unlimited after the period); all private $ → limited (tech data)/restricted (software).
d: All Government $ → GPR; mixed → limited; all private $ → none.
All Government $ → unlimited; mixed → negotiated license only; private $ → GPR.
Funding doesn't drive rights — delivery and markings do.
recall_advanced.x: Funding source drives the license: all Government money → unlimited rights; mixed → Government Purpose Rights (converting to unlimited after the period); all private → limited (tech data) / restricted (software). Delivery and markings implement the rights — the money CREATED them.

recall_advanced.q: Who bears the burden of proving a restriction?
recall_advanced.a: The contractor.
d: The Government.
Whoever asserts in litigation first.
DCMA, as the administering office.
recall_advanced.x: The contractor asserting a restriction bears the burden of proving it — development at private expense, at the claimed component level. The Government doesn't have to disprove markings; it can challenge them and the assertion must survive.

recall_advanced.q: What may the Government do with Government purpose rights (GPR) data?
recall_advanced.a: Any Government purpose — including competitive reprocurement under protections; no commercial use.
d: Internal use only — no release outside the program office.
Anything, including licensing it commercially.
Emergency repair only, with the contractor's consent.
recall_advanced.x: GPR data serves any GOVERNMENT purpose — including handing it to competitors for a reprocurement under nondisclosure protections. What it can't do is go commercial. That's the entire design: competition enabled, market value protected.

recall_advanced.q: The challenge sequence, and what you must not do while it runs.
recall_advanced.a: Written challenge → contractor response (60 days) → CO final decision → appeal; honor the markings until resolved.
d: Verbal challenge → 30-day response → HCA decision; strip the markings pending outcome.
Written challenge → DCMA audit → SSA ruling; quarantine the data until resolved.
Notice of intent → 90-day response → board review; use the data freely meanwhile.
recall_advanced.x: Written challenge → contractor response (60 days) → contracting officer (CO) final decision → appeal. And through all of it: honor the markings. Using challenged data before resolution converts your challenge into their claim.

recall_advanced.q: Deliverables arrived unmarked. What rights do we have?
recall_advanced.a: Unmarked data delivered under the clause is effectively unrestricted in the Government's hands — but confirm through Legal before acting on it; the honest move is verifying, not pouncing.

recall_advanced.q: Can Government purpose rights (GPR) data go to a competitor for the sustainment request for proposals (RFP)?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — Government purposes include competitive reprocurement, with recipients under nondisclosure protections. That's exactly what GPR is for.
d: No — GPR bars release to any competitor until it converts to unlimited.
Only with the rights holder's written consent.
Yes, but doing so converts the data to unlimited immediately.
recall_advanced.x: Competitive reprocurement is precisely what GPR exists for — release to competitors under nondisclosure protections is a Government purpose. No consent needed, no conversion triggered. If GPR couldn't do this, it would be limited rights with better branding.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor says the whole system is proprietary because it 'integrates' their private-expense modules.
recall_advanced.a: Integration doesn't launder rights — map component by component. Mixed funding at the component level yields component-level rights, and the assertion list has to be that granular.
d: They're right — integration makes the system a single private-expense item.
The Government's funding of integration converts everything to unlimited.
Rights follow the majority: whoever funded most of the system owns it all.
recall_advanced.x: Integration doesn't launder rights. Rights attach component by component, following each component's funding — a private module stays restricted, the Government-funded integration doesn't 'absorb' it, and majority funding owns nothing. Demand the assertion list at that granularity.

recall_advanced.q: The four scope-test corners.
recall_advanced.a: Competition anticipation · contract type · period · cumulative cost.
d: Price · schedule · quality · quantity.
Anticipation · funding color · NAICS · clause changes.
Contract type · fee structure · option status · dollar delta.
recall_advanced.x: The scope test's four corners: what the competition anticipated, contract type, period, and cumulative cost. Price/schedule/quality is contract administration; the scope question is about the BARGAIN — what the original field of competitors signed up to compete for.

recall_advanced.q: Unilateral vs. bilateral — which actions belong to each?
recall_advanced.a: Unilateral: admin, in-scope change orders, option exercise; bilateral: substantive negotiated changes.
d: Unilateral: any change under the SAT; bilateral: everything above.
Unilateral: substantive changes; bilateral: admin and funding actions.
Unilateral: contractor-requested changes; bilateral: Government-directed ones.
recall_advanced.x: Unilateral: administrative changes, in-scope change orders, option exercises — the contracting officer (CO) acting alone under existing authority. Bilateral: substantive negotiated changes, both signatures. Dollar value doesn't pick the instrument; the nature of the change does.
recall_advanced.ref: RFO Part 43 pattern · Vol. 2, Mods & Scope

recall_advanced.q: Define constructive change and cardinal change in one sentence each.
recall_advanced.a: Constructive: Government conduct changes work without formal direction; cardinal: change so profound it exceeds what was competed — potential breach.
d: Constructive: a mod that builds on prior mods; cardinal: the first mod on a contract.
Constructive: contractor-initiated improvement; cardinal: CO-directed acceleration.
Constructive: a formal change order under the clause; cardinal: any change over $1M.
recall_advanced.x: Constructive: Government CONDUCT changes the work without formal direction — and may owe an equitable adjustment. Cardinal: change so profound it exceeds what was competed — potential breach that no Changes clause authorizes. One is an accident with a bill; the other is a boundary with consequences.

recall_advanced.q: Against what baseline is mod 100 judged?
recall_advanced.a: The original contract, all mods cumulative.
d: The contract as amended through mod 99.
The most recent bilateral modification.
The current-year funded value.
recall_advanced.x: Mod 100 is judged against the ORIGINAL contract with all mods cumulative — never against mod 99. Judging increment-to-increment is how scope creep launders itself: each step looks small while the total walks out of the competition.

recall_advanced.q: Who decides if it's in scope?
recall_advanced.a: The PCO, with Legal — documented. It's a judgment call with a test, not a vibe: anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost.
d: Legal alone — scope is a legal conclusion.
The requiring activity, since they own the requirement.
GAO, through the protest process — that's why you synopsize.
recall_advanced.x: The procuring contracting officer (PCO) decides scope, with Legal, documented — a judgment call with a four-corner test behind it. Not Legal alone (they advise), not the requiring activity (they want), and not the Government Accountability Office (GAO) (they review the record you built).

recall_advanced.q: A competitor found out about a big unpublicized mod and complained. Your answer?
recall_advanced.a: If my scope analysis is in the file and honest, I walk them (and my boss) through it. If the analysis was never done — that's the finding. Publicity follows scope: in-scope mods aren't competed or synopsized; new work is.

recall_advanced.q: PM directed extra testing verbally; contractor performed. What is that?
recall_advanced.a: A constructive change candidate — Government conduct changed the work. Contractor asserts its costs; I sort entitlement and get the direction channel fixed (all direction through the procuring contracting officer (PCO)).

recall_advanced.q: The default rule and the four-part exception test.
recall_advanced.a: Contractor furnishes; GFP only if best interest · benefit > burden · no substantial risk increase · not otherwise met — all four.
d: Government furnishes; contractor property only with a D&F.
Contractor furnishes; GFP if the PM certifies need — one part.
Contractor furnishes; GFP if cheaper · faster · safer — any one.
recall_advanced.x: Default: contractors furnish their own property. Government-furnished property (GFP) takes ALL FOUR: Government's best interest, benefit exceeding burden, no substantial risk increase, and no other way to meet the need. 'Any one' or a program manager (PM) certification is exactly the shortcut the test forbids.

recall_advanced.q: Who writes the Government-furnished property (GFP) justification?
recall_advanced.a: The requiring activity (PM), to the PCO.
d: The PCO, to the HCA.
The property administrator, to DCMA.
The contractor, in its proposal.
recall_advanced.x: The requiring activity (PM) writes the GFP justification to the procuring contracting officer (PCO) — they own the need, so they owe the case. The property administrator manages property after the decision; the contractor benefits from it and certainly doesn't author it.

recall_advanced.q: Name three clause functions that ride with the property clause.
recall_advanced.a: Marking/item unique identification (IUID) · loss reporting · property-system administration · disposal (any three).

recall_advanced.q: Consequence of delivering Government-furnished property (GFP) late or faulty?
recall_advanced.a: Government-caused delay — schedule/equitable-adjustment exposure.
d: None — GFP delivery dates are targets, not commitments.
T4D exposure for the contractor if they can't work around it.
An automatic 10% price reduction under the property clause.
recall_advanced.x: Late or faulty GFP is a GOVERNMENT-caused delay: schedule relief and equitable-adjustment exposure follow. Furnishing property puts the Government's own performance on the contract's critical path — the cost the four-part test makes you price in.

recall_advanced.q: Contractor reports a Government-furnished test set stolen.
recall_advanced.a: The loss-reporting clause machinery runs: report, investigate, determine liability under the risk allocation, and adjust the property record — with the property administrator carrying the process.

recall_advanced.q: Why not furnish property freely if it lowers proposed prices?
recall_advanced.a: Because price isn't the only ledger: administration, risk shift, and Government performance obligations all cost. The four-part test is that ledger.
d: No reason — a lower price always wins the tradeoff.
Because GFP is prohibited on competitive actions.
Because furnishing property converts the contract to cost-type.
recall_advanced.x: Lower proposed prices are one line of a longer ledger: administration burden, risk shifted to the Government, and Government performance obligations all cost money the price doesn't show. The four-part test forces the whole ledger onto the table.

recall_advanced.q: When is no justification needed?
recall_advanced.a: Property furnished for repair/modification/overhaul work — the property is the requirement there.
d: Under the SAT — the test applies only above it.
When the contractor requests it in writing.
On sole-source awards — competition concerns drop out.
recall_advanced.x: Repair, modification, and overhaul work needs no Government-furnished property (GFP) justification — the property IS the requirement; you can't overhaul an engine you don't furnish. Everywhere else, the four-part test applies at every dollar value.

recall_advanced.q: The obligation caps, before and after the qualifying proposal.
recall_advanced.a: 50% of NTE before; 75% after.
d: 75% of NTE before; 90% after.
25% of NTE before; 50% after.
50% of NTE before; 80% after.
recall_advanced.x: 50% of the not-to-exceed before the qualifying proposal, 75% after. The caps are the taxpayer's brake: an undefinitized contractor who wants more funded runway has to produce the proposal that starts real negotiation.

recall_advanced.q: The definitization clock and its other trigger.
recall_advanced.a: 180 days from qualifying proposal; also when obligations reach the caps.
d: 90 days from award; or when funds expire.
180 days from award; or at the contractor's request.
One year from the qualifying proposal; no other trigger.
recall_advanced.x: 180 days from the qualifying proposal — or when obligations hit the caps, whichever bites first. From the PROPOSAL, not award: that anchoring is what makes proposal slow-rolling a leverage play, and cap enforcement the counter.

recall_advanced.q: Two reasons that never justify an undefinitized contract action (UCA).
recall_advanced.a: Lack of planning; administrative convenience.
d: Urgency; industrial mobilization.
Funding uncertainty; protest risk.
Incumbent transition; requirement growth.
recall_advanced.x: Lack of planning and administrative convenience never justify a UCA. Real urgency can. If the 'emergency' traces to a requirement everyone saw coming, the UCA is the symptom and the finding writes itself.

recall_advanced.q: UCO vs. UCA in one sentence.
recall_advanced.a: UCO = unpriced unilateral change within an existing contract's scope; UCA = new undefinitized contract action.
d: UCO = undefinitized commercial order; UCA = its non-commercial twin.
UCO = an unpriced option; UCA = an unpriced change order.
They're interchangeable labels for the same instrument.
recall_advanced.x: UCO: an unpriced unilateral change WITHIN an existing contract's scope. UCA: a NEW undefinitized contract action. Same discipline (definitize fast, caps bite), different starting points — one modifies a bargain, the other opens one.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor is slow-rolling the qualifying proposal. Why might that be?
recall_advanced.a: Every month undefinitized is a month of cost-reimbursement-like comfort at negotiation leverage. My tools: the obligation caps bite, progress-payment posture tightens, and the definitization schedule is a contract term — enforce it.

recall_advanced.q: Why does fee usually come down at definitization?
recall_advanced.a: Weighted guidelines price risk. With actuals on the books, the cost risk the fee would have paid for has partly evaporated — fee follows the remaining risk, not the original unknowns.

recall_advanced.q: Do UCAs need clearance? A J&A?
recall_advanced.a: Clearance at definitization (award-stage clearance isn't the gate). And the circumstances driving an undefinitized contract action (UCA) usually drive a Part 6 exception too — urgency or one-source — so the justification and approval (J&A) rides in parallel.

recall_advanced.q: Business vs. contract clearance — what each approves.
recall_advanced.a: Business = release the solicitation / open negotiations; contract = the award/negotiated result.
d: Business = the acquisition strategy; contract = the clause structure.
Business = the negotiated result; contract = solicitation release.
Business = pre-award legal review; contract = post-award audit.
recall_advanced.x: Business clearance approves releasing the solicitation / opening negotiations — the strategy gate. Contract clearance approves the negotiated result — the deal gate. Two different failures get caught: a bad strategy well executed, and a good strategy badly landed.

recall_advanced.q: Why must the reviewer be independent?
recall_advanced.a: The selector can't approve the selection — independent senior review before commitment.
d: Because DCAA requires third-party validation of price.
To spread accountability across two offices.
Statute requires an SES reviewer on every action over the SAT.
recall_advanced.x: The selector can't approve the selection — independence is the entire value of the review. A reviewer inside the deal inherits its blind spots; the senior independent look before commitment is what catches them while they're still cheap.

recall_advanced.q: When does an undefinitized contract action (UCA) clear?
recall_advanced.a: At definitization.
d: At award of the undefinitized action.
At the qualifying proposal.
Twice — at award and again at definitization.
recall_advanced.x: UCAs clear at DEFINITIZATION — that's when there's finally a negotiated result to review. Award-stage clearance isn't the gate, because at award there was no price to bless. It's the exception that proves what clearance is for.

recall_advanced.q: Why two clearances instead of one?
recall_advanced.a: Because a sound strategy can still yield a bad deal, and a good deal can implement an unapproved strategy — the gates catch different failures.
d: Redundancy — either clearance can substitute for the other.
One is legal review; the other is fiscal certification.
Two clearances halve the protest window.
recall_advanced.x: Two gates catch two different failures: a sound strategy can still land a bad deal, and a good deal can execute an unapproved strategy. One clearance would have to be blind in one eye — the pair sees both.

recall_advanced.q: What does the clearance authority actually check?
recall_advanced.a: That the action implements the approved strategy · the price/result is fair and reasonable and supported · the file complies — statute, regulation, policy — before the Government commits.

recall_advanced.q: Clearance said no. Now?
recall_advanced.a: Fix what they flagged — position, support, or strategy — and return. Clearance friction is cheaper than any failure it prevents; treat the authority as a teammate with veto power.
d: Appeal to the SSA — clearance is advisory on competitive actions.
Award anyway and document the disagreement for the record.
Elevate to the HCA, who can override a clearance denial.
recall_advanced.x: Clearance said no → fix what they flagged and come back. There's no appeal-to-the-source selection authority (SSA), no award-anyway memo, no head of the contracting activity (HCA) override of an independent review. Clearance friction is cheaper than every failure it prevents — treat the authority as a teammate with veto power.

recall_advanced.q: The post-award stay rule, precisely.
recall_advanced.a: Stay if filed within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debrief, whichever is later.
d: Stay if filed within 5 days of award or 10 of the debrief, whichever is earlier.
Stay if filed within 10 days of award — the debrief has no effect.
Stay attaches to any protest filed before performance begins.
recall_advanced.x: Stay if filed within 10 days of award OR 5 days of the required debrief — whichever is LATER. Two branches, take the later one, and the debrief branch exists only when a required debrief was requested. That word 'later' decides real protests.

recall_advanced.q: Three venues and one distinguishing feature each.
recall_advanced.a: Agency — fastest/self-correcting; GAO — 100-day, automatic stay; COFC — binding, injunction instead of stay.
d: Agency — binding decision; GAO — injunction; COFC — automatic stay.
GAO — fastest; agency — 100-day clock; COFC — advisory opinion.
Agency — automatic stay; GAO — injunction; COFC — self-correcting.
recall_advanced.x: Agency: fastest, self-correcting. The Government Accountability Office (GAO): the 100-day clock and the automatic stay. The U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC): binding judgment, injunction instead of a stay. Venue choice is strategy — each offers a different weapon, and protesters pick accordingly.

recall_advanced.q: Who authorizes an override, and on what two bases?
recall_advanced.a: HCA, written: urgent & compelling circumstances, or best interests of the United States.
d: SPE, written: urgency, or mission degradation.
The CO, with JA concurrence: urgency, or contractor hardship.
GAO itself, on the agency's motion: either basis.
recall_advanced.x: Only the head of the contracting activity (HCA) authorizes an override, in writing, on two bases: urgent and compelling circumstances, or best interests of the United States. It's deliberately hard — the stay is the Competition in Contracting Act's (CICA) teeth, and overriding it casually invites the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) review.

recall_advanced.q: Task-order protest thresholds.
recall_advanced.a: $35M DoD / $10M civilian, or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value.
d: $25M DoD / $10M civilian, no exceptions.
$10M DoD / $35M civilian, or scope growth at any value.
$35M all agencies; growth protests go to the ombudsman.
recall_advanced.x: $35M DoD / $10M civilian for task-order protests at the Government Accountability Office (GAO) — plus the exception that eats the rule: ANY value when the protest alleges the order grew beyond the vehicle's scope, period, or ceiling. Quote the thresholds without the exception and you've given half the answer.

recall_advanced.q: Protest filed on day 9 after award, but the debrief was never requested. Stay?
recall_advanced.a: Day 9 is inside the 10-day award window — stay applies. The 5-day debrief branch only substitutes when a required debrief was requested and given later.
d: No stay — skipping the debrief forfeits it.
No stay — the clock ran from the unsuccessful-offeror notice.
Stay applies only if the protester requests it within 3 days.
recall_advanced.x: Day 9 sits inside the 10-day award window — the stay applies. The 5-day debrief branch only SUBSTITUTES when a required debrief was requested and given later; skipping the debrief doesn't forfeit the award-window branch.

recall_advanced.q: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendations are 'advisory' — so ignore one?
recall_advanced.a: Legally advisory, practically followed — non-compliance is reported to Congress and torches agency credibility. Treat a sustain as a to-do list with a deadline.
d: Yes — advisory means optional; document and proceed.
No — GAO decisions bind agencies like court judgments.
Only the COFC can excuse compliance with a GAO sustain.
recall_advanced.x: GAO recommendations are legally advisory and practically binding: non-compliance gets reported to Congress and torches the agency's credibility in every future protest. Treat a sustain as a to-do list with a deadline — because that's how your leadership will treat it.

recall_advanced.q: How do you protest-proof a source selection?
recall_advanced.a: You don't — you record-proof it: criteria stated and followed, evaluations contemporaneous and even-handed, meaningful discussions, a source selection decision document (SSDD) with real comparative reasoning, and a debrief that answers questions instead of provoking them.

recall_advanced.q: Four differences between an REA and a claim.
recall_advanced.a: Interest (claim only) · decision deadlines (claim) · prep costs (allowable REA / unallowable claim) · formality-certification.
d: Dollar cap (REA) · venue choice (claim) · JA review (claim) · time limits (REA).
Interest (REA only) · deadlines (REA) · prep costs allowable on both · certification (claim).
Writing required (claim only) · interest on both · appeal rights (REA) · certification (REA).
recall_advanced.x: Four seams between REA and claim: interest (claim only), decision deadlines (claim only), prep costs (allowable REA / unallowable claim), and formality-certification. The lanes carry different economics — which is why contractors choose deliberately and you classify by substance.

recall_advanced.q: Claim certification threshold and the accrual limit.
recall_advanced.a: $100K; 6 years from accrual.
d: $250K; 3 years from accrual.
$100K; 1 year from the final invoice.
The SAT; 6 years from award.
recall_advanced.x: $100K triggers claim certification; 6 years from accrual is the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) limitations period. Two numbers that anchor the whole disputes timeline — everything else (decisions, appeals) hangs off them.

recall_advanced.q: What is a deemed denial, and what does it start?
recall_advanced.a: CO silence past the decision deadline operates as denial — the appeal clock starts.
d: The contractor's withdrawal of a claim — it bars refiling.
A denial without a written decision — it voids the certification.
The Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction — it restarts the CO's clock.
recall_advanced.x: Contracting officer (CO) silence past the decision deadline operates as a denial — the 'deemed denial' — and it starts the contractor's appeal clock. Silence isn't neutral in the Contract Disputes Act (CDA): it's a decision with consequences, made by default.

recall_advanced.q: The two appeal routes and their clocks.
recall_advanced.a: Board of Contract Appeals, 90 days; COFC, 12 months.
d: Board, 12 months; COFC, 90 days.
GAO, 100 days; COFC, 6 months.
Board, 60 days; district court, 12 months.
recall_advanced.x: Board of Contract Appeals: 90 days. Court of Federal Claims: 12 months. Both run from receipt of the final decision. Miss the Board window and the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) remains; miss both and the decision is final forever.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor titled it 'request for equitable adjustment (REA)' but demands a sum certain, certified, 'decision requested.'
recall_advanced.a: Substance over label — that's functionally a claim, and the CDA machinery (interest, deadlines) may already be running. Classify with Legal, fast.
d: The title controls — treat it as an REA until refiled as a claim.
Reject it — a document can't be both an REA and a claim.
Hold it unprocessed until the contractor clarifies its intent.
recall_advanced.x: Substance over label: sum certain + certification + decision demanded = a claim, whatever the cover letter says — and the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) interest and deadlines may already be running. Classify with Legal fast; treating a functional claim as an REA doesn't stop the clock, it just means you missed it.

recall_advanced.q: Why would a contractor choose the request for equitable adjustment (REA) lane at all?
recall_advanced.a: Relationship preservation, allowable prep costs, speed, and settlement flexibility — the claim lane is leverage, but it burns goodwill and time.
d: Interest accrues faster on an REA.
REAs skip Legal review, so they settle quietly.
An REA preserves the right to protest at GAO.
recall_advanced.x: Contractors pick the REA lane for relationship preservation, allowable prep costs, speed, and settlement flexibility. The claim lane is leverage — interest and deadlines — at the price of goodwill. Knowing WHY they choose tells you how the negotiation will behave.

recall_advanced.q: What must a differing-site-conditions recovery show first?
recall_advanced.a: Notice — the clause requires prompt written notice before conditions are disturbed, so the Government can investigate. No notice, weakened recovery.
d: Causation — a geotechnical report proving the condition predated award.
Materiality — at least a 10% cost impact.
Fault — that the Government knew about the condition and stayed silent.
recall_advanced.x: Notice first: the clause requires prompt written notice BEFORE the condition is disturbed, so the Government can investigate the ground as found. Recovery weakens without it — causation and cost analysis come after, but notice is the gate.

recall_advanced.q: Termination for convenience (T4C) settlement contents — and the profit rule.
recall_advanced.a: Costs incurred + reasonable profit on work performed + settlement expenses; no anticipatory profit.
d: The full contract price, less amounts already paid.
Costs incurred only — profit never survives a termination.
Costs plus anticipated profit on the whole contract, discounted.
recall_advanced.x: T4C settlement: costs incurred on the terminated work + reasonable profit on work PERFORMED + settlement expenses — and never anticipatory profit on work never done. The Government buys its way out whole-ish, not generous.

recall_advanced.q: The termination for default (T4D) runway, in order.
recall_advanced.a: Cure notice → show cause → excusability analysis → T4D notice as final decision.
d: Show cause → cure notice → T4D notice → excusability review on appeal.
Cure notice → T4D notice → show cause → Board review.
Excusability analysis → show cause → cure notice → T4D.
recall_advanced.x: Cure notice → show cause → excusability analysis → T4D notice as the final decision. The order is the defense: each step builds the record that the failure was real, inexcusable, and fairly handled — skip one and the conversion risk is yours.

recall_advanced.q: Three classic excusable causes.
recall_advanced.a: Acts of God · sovereign/Government acts · fires/epidemics/similar events beyond control without fault.
d: Supplier bankruptcy · labor shortages · material price spikes.
Subcontractor default · weather delays · funding gaps.
Key-person loss · cyber incidents · shipping backlogs.
recall_advanced.x: Acts of God, sovereign/Government acts, and fires/epidemics/similar events beyond control without fault. The distractors — supplier trouble, labor shortages, price spikes — are ordinary business risk the contractor priced when it signed firm-fixed-price (FFP).

recall_advanced.q: What happens to a termination for default (T4D) later found wrongful?
recall_advanced.a: Converts to a T4C — settlement owed instead of costs recovered.
d: The contract revives and performance resumes.
It stands, but reprocurement costs are waived.
It becomes a no-cost cancellation by operation of law.
recall_advanced.x: A wrongful T4D converts to a termination for convenience (T4C): instead of collecting reprocurement costs, the Government owes a convenience settlement. That flip — from creditor to debtor — is why the excusability record precedes the notice, not the litigation.

recall_advanced.q: What does the contractor get in a termination for convenience (T4C) settlement?
recall_advanced.a: Costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on what was done, and settlement expenses — not the profit they hoped to earn on work never performed.
d: The full contract price, less the Government's reprocurement savings.
Costs incurred only; profit is forfeited at termination.
Anticipatory profit on the unperformed balance, capped at 10%.
recall_advanced.x: Costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on what was DONE, settlement expenses — never the profit they hoped to earn on the unperformed balance. 'Made whole for work performed' is the whole principle in six words.

recall_advanced.q: You defaulted them; the board later finds the failure excusable. Now?
recall_advanced.a: The T4D converts to a T4C — with the Government paying settlement instead of collecting reprocurement costs. That's why the excusability record precedes the notice.
d: The T4D stands; excusability affects only the reprocurement claim.
The contract is reinstated and the schedule equitably extended.
The contractor may re-compete but recovers nothing.
recall_advanced.x: Excusable failure → the termination for default (T4D) converts to a termination for convenience (T4C), and the Government pays a settlement instead of collecting reprocurement costs. The board isn't being generous; it's enforcing the clause. The excusability analysis you run BEFORE the notice is what prevents this ending.

recall_advanced.q: When would you skip the cure notice?
recall_advanced.a: A pure failure to deliver on time — the schedule was the cure period. But when facts are mixed, send it; a needless cure notice costs ten days, a missing one can cost the termination.
d: Never — the cure notice is jurisdictional for every default.
Whenever the contractor is in its first year of performance.
When the contract value is under the SAT.
recall_advanced.x: Pure late delivery needs no cure notice — the delivery schedule WAS the cure period. Mixed or murky facts: send it anyway. A needless cure notice costs ten days; a missing one can cost the entire termination on conversion.

recall_advanced.q: What makes broad agency announcement (BAA) evaluation lawful competition?
recall_advanced.a: Public announcement + stated criteria + independent scientific merit review — selection against the standard, not between offerors.
d: Head-to-head comparison of all proposals received each cycle.
A J&A covering the entire announcement period.
SSA source selection with a formal competitive range.
recall_advanced.x: A BAA is lawful competition because of three pieces: broad public announcement, stated evaluation criteria, and independent scientific merit review — selection against the standard, not between offerors. Miss a piece and it's just a sole source with a science vocabulary.

recall_advanced.q: The three Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) phases and Phase III's special property.
recall_advanced.a: I feasibility · II prototype · III production — no cap, sole-source eligible off competed early phases, SBIR rights persist.
d: I concept · II test · III fielding — capped at $50M with a J&A.
I feasibility · II prototype · III production — full-and-open required at Phase III.
I research · II development · III sustainment — rights expire at Phase III.
recall_advanced.x: Phase I feasibility, II prototype, III production — and Phase III is special: no dollar cap, sole-source eligible off competed early phases, SBIR data rights persist. The competition happened in Phases I/II; Phase III harvests it. Document the derivation.

recall_advanced.q: Two honest reasons to choose an Other Transaction (OT) — and one dishonest one.
recall_advanced.a: Honest: nontraditional participation; terms flexibility a prototype genuinely needs. Dishonest: "skipping the rules.".
d: Honest: speed; lower cost. Dishonest: nontraditional participation.
Honest: avoiding protests; fixed pricing. Dishonest: prototype flexibility.
Honest: classified work; foreign partners. Dishonest: follow-on production.
recall_advanced.x: Honest OT reasons: nontraditional participation, and terms flexibility a prototype genuinely needs. The dishonest one — 'skipping the rules' — is how OTs end up in hearings. The authority is a tool with a purpose, not an exit from oversight.

recall_advanced.q: How is funding one BAA proposal 'competition' without comparing proposals?
recall_advanced.a: The broad agency announcement (BAA) is a recognized competitive procedure: broad public announcement, stated criteria, independent merit review. The market competed by proposing; selection is merit against the standard, not against each other.

recall_advanced.q: Phase III Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) sole source — really no justification and approval (J&A)?
recall_advanced.a: The statutory program carries it when the work derives from competed Phase I/II — that's the authorized-by- statute lane. Document the derivation.
d: No — Phase III always needs a J&A above the SAT.
Correct, but only within five years of Phase II completion.
Correct — and derivation documentation is optional.
recall_advanced.x: Phase III sole source rides the SBIR statute itself — the 'authorized by statute' lane — when the work derives from competed Phase I/II. No J&A, but the derivation documentation is mandatory: the statute covers continuation, not anything wearing the vendor's logo.

recall_advanced.q: When would you steer away from an OT?
recall_advanced.a: Traditional performers, well-understood requirements, or when the flexibilities aren't actually needed — Other Transactions (OTs) trade a mature protections framework for agility; spend that trade only when it buys something.

recall_advanced.q: The two Miller-Act-style bonds and whom each protects.
recall_advanced.a: Performance bond — the Government's work; payment bond — subs/suppliers who can't lien Government property.
d: Performance bond — subs and suppliers; payment bond — the Government.
Bid bond — the Government; performance bond — the surety.
Payment bond — the prime's payroll; performance bond — the warranty period.
recall_advanced.x: Performance bond protects the Government's work; payment bond protects subs and suppliers — who can't lien Government property, so the bond replaces the lien they'd have on a commercial job. Knowing WHY the payment bond exists is what elevates the answer.

recall_advanced.q: The differing-site-conditions notice rule and its reason.
recall_advanced.a: Written notice before disturbing the condition, so the Government can investigate.
d: Notice within 30 days after discovery, to preserve the claim.
Verbal notice to the COR at the next site visit.
Notice at final inspection, documented in the punch list.
recall_advanced.x: Written notice BEFORE disturbing the condition — so the Government can investigate the site as found. Disturb first and the evidence is gone; the notice rule protects both parties' ability to know what was actually in the ground.

recall_advanced.q: The personal-services test in one sentence.
recall_advanced.a: Continuous Government supervision of contractor employees creates an employer-employee relationship — unlawful absent specific authority.
d: Contractor staff working on a Government installation triggers personal services.
Services lasting more than 12 continuous months become personal.
Any contract for individual experts is a personal-services contract.
recall_advanced.x: The test is continuous Government supervision of contractor employees — that's what creates the employer-employee relationship the law forbids without specific authority. Location, duration, and individual expertise are all red herrings; SUPERVISION is the trigger.

recall_advanced.q: Performance-based acquisition's (PBA) required elements.
recall_advanced.a: PWS (or SOO) · measurable standards · QASP · incentives where appropriate.
d: SOW · staffing plan · IGCE · award fee.
PWS · labor categories · wage determination · CPARS plan.
SOO · deliverables list · surveillance waiver · incentives.
recall_advanced.x: PBA requires: a performance work statement (PWS) (or statement of objectives (SOO)), measurable standards, a quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP), and incentives where appropriate. The set is a system — outcomes defined, measured, surveilled, and motivated. Drop one element and it's a staffing contract with aspirational adjectives.

recall_advanced.q: Why can't you pick the architect-engineer (A&E) firm on price like everything else?
recall_advanced.a: Statutory design: qualifications-based selection, then negotiate a fair price with the most qualified — design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee does.
d: You can — price competition is merely discouraged for A&E.
Because A&E work is always sole-source to the incumbent designer.
Union agreements set A&E fees, so price can't vary.
recall_advanced.x: A&E selection is qualifications-based by statute: rank on qualifications, then negotiate a fair price with the most qualified. The logic: design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than the design fee does — saving 1% on design that costs 10% in construction is bad math.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between a PWS and a SOO?
recall_advanced.a: Performance work statement (PWS): the Government defines outcomes and standards. Statement of objectives (SOO): the Government states objectives and offerors propose their own PWS — competition on approach, with the winning PWS becoming the yardstick.

recall_advanced.q: The COR is assigning daily tasks to contractor staff 'for efficiency.'
recall_advanced.a: That's the personal-services drift in action — direction flows to the contractor's manager against performance work statement (PWS) outcomes. Fix the practice, retrain the contracting officer's representative (COR), and check whether the PWS invites it.

recall_advanced.q: A bridge is on its third extension. What does each repeat do?
recall_advanced.a: Escalates approval higher each time — repeat bridges are a planning failure wearing an urgency costume.
d: Nothing — extensions inherit the original approval.
Resets the J&A posting clock.
Converts the bridge into a logical follow-on.
recall_advanced.x: Each repeat bridge escalates to higher approval — the system's way of making planning failures expensive. Extensions don't inherit the first approval; every one re-justifies against a bar that keeps rising.

recall_advanced.q: Why is apparent authority the trap in unauthorized commitment (UAC) cases?
recall_advanced.a: Because looking authorized isn't being authorized — the contractor can't rely on it, and neither can you.
d: Because apparent authority binds the Government retroactively.
Because it converts automatically to implied authority.
Because ratification cures it without any investigation.
recall_advanced.x: Apparent authority is the trap because it FEELS binding on the ground — a colonel said go — but binds nothing legally. The contractor can't rely on it and neither can you; only ratification by actual authority fixes what it breaks.

recall_advanced.q: Name the classic examples of source selection information.
recall_advanced.a: Proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate.
d: The synopsis, the PWS, and the wage determination.
CPARS ratings and SAM registration data.
The clause matrix and Section K representations.
recall_advanced.x: The classics: proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate. If it could hand an offeror an edge in THIS competition, treat it as SSI and control it.

recall_advanced.q: When must you spot an organizational conflict of interest (OCI) to have real options?
recall_advanced.a: Early — before solicitation; avoid, neutralize, and mitigate all work best pre-release.
d: At award — that's when the conflict legally attaches.
During discussions, once proposals are in.
At the debrief, when offerors raise it.
recall_advanced.x: OCI options exist before solicitation: you can still avoid (change the requirement), neutralize (restructure), or mitigate (firewall). After proposals arrive, most doors have closed and exclusion may be all that's left. Early is everything.

recall_advanced.q: Responsibility is decided as of when, on what evidence?
recall_advanced.a: At award, on the record before the CO — today's facts, documented.
d: At proposal receipt, on SAM status alone.
At solicitation release, on CPARS history.
Continuously — it's re-decided at each invoice.
recall_advanced.x: Responsibility is decided at award, on documented facts as they stand that day — not proposal-time snapshots, not continuous re-adjudication. A firm non-responsible today can be responsible next quarter; the determination is dated for a reason.

recall_advanced.q: Bundling rides on which research finding?
recall_advanced.a: Whether consolidating the requirement is necessary and justified — the research has to support it.
