No system, no cost-type award, whatever the mission pressure. That's why this scenario's accounting-system question comes before any structure conversation.

follow_ups.q: If they push T&M for the improvement work — what does the D&F have to say?
follow_ups.h: Five findings, and approval scales with dollars and years.
follow_ups.d: A T&M D&F addresses: market research was conducted; it's genuinely impossible to estimate the extent or duration of the work; no other contract type is appropriate; the contract minimizes T&M use; and the steps that will reduce T&M on future requirements. Approval: chief of the contracting office (COCO) to $10M, senior contracting official (SCO) above, head of the contracting activity (HCA) for periods over three years. T&M is the careful exception — a ceiling, active surveillance, and an exit plan, never a standing convenience.

scenarios.scenario: Calibration-services MA-indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ), two holders: a large business at $7.1M of its $7.5M ceiling, and a service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB) at $2.6M of its ceiling, both minimums satisfied, three ordering years left. A $260K Phase II repair requirement arrives; the customer wants it awarded to the large business "as a logical follow-on to their Phase I win." The SDVOSB was rated technically acceptable in the Phase I competition. The large business's BD lead has already emailed you a draft statement of work (SOW) "to save time."

facts.why: The "logical follow-on" would nearly exhaust the large holder's ceiling with three years left — steering an order into a nearly-full ceiling is bad vehicle management even before fairness enters.

facts.fact: SDVOSB rated acceptable in Phase I
facts.why: A capable second holder guts "only one capable" and weakens "logical follow-on" — fair opportunity (or an order-level set-aside) is available and defensible.
A holder writing the order's SOW is a biased-ground-rules organizational conflict of interest (OCI) in miniature — decline it, write our own, and note the contact in the file.
A $260K order competition between two holders costs days, not months — the time argument doesn't survive arithmetic.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd compete it between the holders — the SDVOSB proved capability in Phase I, so no exception honestly fits; and steering it would nearly max the large holder's ceiling anyway. The vendor-drafted SOW goes unused, and if the customer insists, the exception needs a D&A I don't think survives review.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) determinations and approvals (D&As), and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a D&A up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: The customer wants this order steered to the large holder as a logical follow-on. What would you do?
scenarios.script: This is a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507. My help: the vehicle's ordering guide, my Small Business Professional, and the Competition Advocate if an exception were real. The default: every holder gets a genuine chance at every order. Walking the facts: the SDVOSB proved capability in Phase I, so 'only one capable' fails; a logical follow-on has to stand on continuity economics, not preference — and it weakens every time it's stacked on a sole-source original. Steering this also nearly maxes the large holder's ceiling, which is just bad vehicle management. So I'd compete it between the holders, the vendor-drafted SOW goes unused, and if the customer insists, I'd tell them plainly: the exception needs an RFO 16.507-6 D&A, and I don't believe this one survives review.

follow_ups.q: What are ALL the exceptions to fair opportunity under RFO 16.507-6?
follow_ups.h: Six — urgency, uniqueness, follow-on, minimum, statute, and a set-aside lane.
follow_ups.d: RFO 16.507-6: (1) unacceptable delay in meeting an urgent need; (2) only one awardee is capable — unique or highly specialized circumstances; (3) logical follow-on to an order already competed under fair opportunity — use with caution, especially stacked; (4) necessary to satisfy the minimum guarantee; (5) authorized or required by statute; (6) order-level small business set-aside — which needs no D&A. Recite all six cold; it's the 16.5 counterpart to the seven the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) exceptions.

follow_ups.q: What does an over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) exception require, and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: Same ladder as the justification and approval (J&A), different document.
follow_ups.d: A Determination and Approval — structured like a J&A, riding the same tiers: chief of the contracting office (COCO) to $900K, Competition Advocate to $20M, head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) to $90M ($150M DoD), senior procurement executive (SPE) above — posted to SAM.gov (redacted) within 14 days, 30 for urgency. This $260K order sits below the SAT, so no D&A is required — but the fair-opportunity obligation itself never goes away; the file still shows genuine consideration.

follow_ups.q: What are the order-protest rules on this vehicle?
follow_ups.h: A dollar door and a growth door.
follow_ups.d: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) hears task-order protests over $35M for DoD ($10M civilian) — or at ANY value where the protest alleges the order exceeds the scope, period, or ceiling of the underlying contract. Below those doors, the lane is the task-order ombudsman, who reviews whether holders got fair consideration and can recommend corrective action. A steered $260K order can't reach GAO — but the SDVOSB absolutely gets the ombudsman, which is why the consideration record matters at every dollar value.

scenarios.scenario: A depot-support contract's option two is due; notice date in 21 days. The contracting officer's representative's (COR) file: two quality escapes, both closed with corrective action, the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS) "satisfactory." The contractor emails: they'll "need a 9% price adjustment to keep performing" because of wage pressure — "or we'd understand a no-cost mutual walk-away." The program manager (PM) says funding for the option year arrives in the new fiscal year, three weeks after the notice date.

facts.why: An option exercises at its priced terms — a contractor conditioning performance on a raise is refusing the option and inviting a negotiation. Exercise unilaterally at the option price, or don't; there's no "exercise at +9%."
The performance gate: documented, considered, and here probably passable — flags with completed corrective action are a judgment call to make on the record.

facts.fact: Funding arrives after the notice date
facts.why: Availability-of-funds mechanics exist for exactly this seam — align the exercise with the funds clause rather than obligating money that isn't there (the fiscal-law follow-up is coming).
That's the contractor negotiating against your leverage. The Government's alternatives — exercise, extend short, or recompete — get evaluated on their merits, not on the emailed menu.

scenarios.board_answer: The option exercises at its price or not at all — the 9% ask is a refusal dressed as a condition. I'd run the gates: performance is documented and arguably passes; the funding seam is handled through availability-of-funds mechanics; and if the contractor truly won't perform at the option price, my paths are a short extension while I recompete — with the record showing exactly why.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO Part 17 gates: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous check, SAM exclusions, performance considered — with timely written notice, or the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: Notice is due in 21 days and the contractor wants 9% to keep going. Do you exercise?
scenarios.script: This is an options question — the RFO Part 17 exercise gates, applied to today. My help: financial management (FM) on funds, the COR's record, and Legal on the contractor's letter. The rule: an option exercises at its evaluated, awarded price or not at all — the unilateral right is exactly what we bought. The 9% demand is a refusal dressed as a condition. So I run the gates on the record: performance is documented — two escapes, closed, CPARS satisfactory — arguably passing; funds ride availability-of-funds mechanics across the fiscal seam; need continues. If the contractor truly won't perform at the option price, I don't negotiate the option — my paths are a short extension while I recompete, with the record showing exactly who declined what, and when.

follow_ups.q: Recite every gate you clear before exercising an option.
follow_ups.h: Seven checks, then a timely signature.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 17: price still fair and reasonable — a fresh market look; funds available; the option serves an existing need and is the best method for it; the option was synopsized or is exempt; the contractor isn't excluded in SAM; performance has been considered; and written notice by the date in the contract. Miss the notice date and the unilateral right dies — continuation becomes a bilateral negotiation.

follow_ups.q: What duration limits cap a services structure?
follow_ups.h: Five, ten, and six months.
follow_ups.d: Service contracts: five years total, base plus all options (DFARS 217.204). DoD task and delivery order contracts: ten years without a Head of Agency determination, senior procurement executive (SPE) approval beyond that. The extension-of-services clause adds at most six months — a transition bridge, not a strategy. And any period bought with the extension clause counts against the honest answer to 'why wasn't the recompete ready?'

follow_ups.q: The contractor flatly refuses to perform at the option price. What are your lawful paths?
follow_ups.h: You can't negotiate an option — but you can bridge and recompete.
follow_ups.d: An option exercises at its evaluated, awarded price or not at all — 'exercise plus 9%' is a new agreement, not an option, and it forfeits the competitive pricing the option preserved. Paths: exercise anyway if they're bluffing (refusal to perform an exercised option is anticipatory repudiation with termination for default (T4D) exposure); or don't exercise, use a short justified extension for continuity, and recompete immediately — with the record showing exactly who refused what. Either way, the refusal enters their performance record.

scenarios.scenario: September 12th. A program manager (PM) arrives with a signed military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) for $1.9M of current-year operation and maintenance (O&M) to a civilian agency's assisted-acquisition shop for a "12-month analytics support task" — award expected "by December, they're backed up." The PM says the funds "are good because we're sending them before September 30th," and there's no interagency agreement on file yet, "but they say their standard one covers everything."

facts.why: Sending expiring funds cross-agency doesn't extend their life — the bona fide need and obligation rules follow the money. A December award of FY-expiring O&M for services starting then is the parking scheme fiscal lawyers feast on.

facts.fact: "Good because we send them before Sep 30"
facts.why: Transfer isn't obligation. The clock runs until a qualifying obligation exists — moving money to another agency's account doesn't stop it.
Assisted acquisition requires the signed agreement — roles, terms, fees — before performance. "Their standard one covers everything" is not an agreement in our file.

facts.fact: Over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), non-DoD servicing agency
facts.why: The best-procurement-approach determination and findings (D&F) is required — and "they're backed up until December" is evidence against this being the best approach.

scenarios.board_answer: Three problems: the funds question — expiring O&M doesn't gain life by traveling, so a December award likely fails bona fide need; the missing interagency agreement, which must be signed before we proceed; and the D&F, which has to honestly conclude a backed-up shop is our best approach. As written, I'd pull the MIPR back and either buy it ourselves or fix all three on the record.

coach.qtype: an interagency question — RFO Part 17 interagency acquisition and the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. 1535): direct vs. assisted, and whose rules travel with the money.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) (the fiscal rules travel with the funds), Legal, and the servicing agency's contracting office.
coach.rule: Pick the lane deliberately: direct (our contracting officer (CO) orders on their vehicle) vs. assisted (their CO buys for us under a signed agreement). The Economy Act applies only absent a more specific authority — military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus determination and findings (D&F).

scenarios.ask: The MIPR is signed and the PM says the funds are safe because they're 'committed.' What do you tell him?
scenarios.script: This is an interagency question — RFO Part 17 and the Economy Act, 31 U.S.C. 1535 — wearing a fiscal-law hat. My help: financial management (FM) first — the fiscal rules travel with the money — then Legal, then the servicing agency's shop. Three problems, in order: Time — expiring O&M doesn't gain life by traveling; a December award by a backed-up shop likely fails bona fide need, and 'committed' isn't 'obligated.' Second, assisted acquisition requires a signed interagency agreement defining roles before we proceed — there isn't one. Third, the best-procurement-approach D&F has to honestly conclude that a shop advertising a three-month backlog is our best path — it can't. As written, I'd pull the MIPR back and either buy it ourselves or fix all three, on the record.

follow_ups.q: Direct versus assisted acquisition — define both, and the paperwork each requires.
follow_ups.h: Who places the order decides the lane and the documents.
follow_ups.d: Direct: the requesting agency places the order itself against the servicing agency's contract — no written interagency agreement required, but the best-approach analysis is documented. Assisted: the servicing agency awards and administers on your behalf — a written interagency agreement signed by both parties, defining roles and unique terms, before funds move. And for any order against a non-DoD agency's contract over the SAT, a best-procurement-approach D&F: alternatives analyzed, schedule and performance weighed, the servicing agency's authority verified.

follow_ups.q: When does the Economy Act apply, and what rides with it?
follow_ups.h: It's the fallback authority — with a MIPR and a finding.
follow_ups.d: 31 U.S.C. 1535 applies only when no more specific authority — schedules, GWACs — covers the buy. It rides on a MIPR plus a D&F finding the interagency acquisition is in the Government's best interest and the supplies or services can't be obtained as conveniently or cheaply from a private source, with at least one qualifying circumstance (their existing contract, their expertise, or specific statutory authorization). Citing the Economy Act for a schedule order tells the board you memorized a name, not a framework.

follow_ups.q: Does money change color or clock when it travels to another agency?
follow_ups.h: T-P-A rides in the MIPR envelope.
follow_ups.d: No. Time, Purpose, and Amount travel with the funds — expiring O&M doesn't gain life at another agency, the bona fide need is still judged by the requesting agency's need in the appropriation's period, and the purpose statute follows the dollars. Parking expiring funds with a servicing agency to 'save' them is a Time violation with postage. Unobligated balances come home as what they are.

scenarios.scenario: A cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) software-integration contract runs 1 March to 28 February, funded with one year's operation and maintenance (O&M). On 12 February the contractor emails: costs will hit the ceiling in ten days because Government-furnished test rigs "were down for repairs half the year" — they request additional funds and note "we already told the contracting officer's representative (COR) about the rigs back in June." The program manager (PM) wants to add this year's O&M "since the work slid into this year anyway."

facts.fact: Notice on 12 Feb for a ceiling 10 days out
facts.why: The limitation clause's 75% rhythm exists to prevent exactly this ambush. Late notice weakens any entitlement to more funds — establish what they knew and when.

facts.fact: Faulty Government-furnished property (GFP) "reported to the COR in June"
facts.why: Defective GFP can ground a legitimate equitable adjustment — but telling the COR isn't notifying the contracting officer (CO), and a request for equitable adjustment (REA) has its own lane. It doesn't convert into "send money" at the ceiling.

Which year's need is this? Work performed against last year's requirement is last year's bona fide need — funding it with this year's O&M is a Time violation. Expired funds from the proper year handle proper adjustments.

scenarios.board_answer: Three lanes, kept separate: the limitation-of-cost mechanics — late notice means no automatic entitlement; the GFP issue — a potential REA, evaluated on its own record; and the money — any adjustment funds from the appropriation that bore the need, likely the prior year's expired O&M, not this year's. And the contractor isn't obligated to perform past funding while we sort it.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: Ten days from the ceiling, the contractor wants more money and blames Government test rigs. What do you instruct the PM and the contractor?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-finance question — the RFO Part 32 limitation clauses with an RFO Part 45 GFP thread — and the discipline is keeping three lanes separate. My help: financial management (FM), Legal, and the property administrator. Lane one, the limitation-of-cost mechanics: notice was due around 75%, and a ten-day warning at the ceiling means no automatic entitlement to overrun funding — the Government may fund, but doesn't have to. Lane two, the GFP: faulty Government-furnished rigs are a potential REA — Government-caused delay — evaluated on its own record, not waved through as ceiling relief. Lane three, the money: any adjustment comes from the appropriation that bore the need — likely prior-year expired O&M, not this year's. And the contractor isn't obligated to perform past funding while we sort it — I'd say that plainly to both of them.

follow_ups.q: LoC versus LoF versus LOGO — which clause on which contract, and what trigger?
follow_ups.h: Fully funded, incremental, and the fixed-price cousin.
follow_ups.d: Limitation of Cost — fully funded cost-type contracts: notice when costs will reach 75% of the estimate within the coming 60 days. Limitation of Funds — incrementally funded cost-type: the same 75% trigger applied to the allotted amount. LOGO — incrementally funded fixed-price contract line item numbers (CLINs): notice within 90 days of hitting 85% of the CLIN amount. In every case the notice is the contractor's duty, the contractor isn't obligated to perform past funding, and a ten-day warning at the ceiling means no automatic entitlement.

follow_ups.q: Recite the financing order of preference.
follow_ups.h: Private first, advance payments last.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 32: private financing; then customary contract financing — where performance-based payments are preferred (events, not costs; recoverable in default) and progress payments run at the clause and current class-deviation rates; then loan guarantees (rare); then unusual financing, requiring higher approval; and advance payments last — least preferred, most heavily approved, commercial advances capped at 15% of price.

follow_ups.q: Which year's money pays whatever adjustment comes out of this?
follow_ups.h: The appropriation that bore the need — and its expired window.
follow_ups.d: The adjustment charges the appropriation that funded the original need — likely the prior year's O&M, now expired. Expired funds remain available for five years for exactly this: adjustments to obligations properly made when they were current — claims, terminations, equitable adjustments. After cancellation they're gone for every purpose. Reaching for this year's money because it's handy is a Time violation dressed as convenience.

scenarios.scenario: Sustainment planning for a mission-planning suite. The development contract file shows: module A built under the contract with program funds; module B adapted from the contractor's commercial product; module C built "on contractor independent research and development (IR&D), matured on contract" per the contractor. Deliverables: binaries only — source "available under a separate license, price on request." The assertion list from award names only module B. The program manager (PM) proposes just emailing the whole package to two potential competitors "under nondisclosure agreement (NDA), to gauge interest."

facts.fact: Assertion list names only module B
facts.why: Restrictions live or die on the assertion list. Module C's "IR&D then matured on contract" story was never asserted — the Government's default position on C is strong, and the burden of proving otherwise is theirs.
Entirely Government-funded → unlimited rights. That's the clean core of any competition package.
The commercial base rides its customary license; the adaptation's rights follow the adaptation's funding. Component-level mapping, not system-level slogans.

Rights without deliverables are theoretical — if source and build artifacts weren't contract deliverables, competing sustainment may require buying them now. That's negotiating posture, budget, and schedule.
Not until the rights map is settled — releasing B or C prematurely hands the contractor a claim and the competition a taint.

scenarios.board_answer: Component by component: A is unlimited — Government-funded; B rides its commercial license with the adaptation's rights following its funding; and C was never asserted, so the contractor carries the burden if they want restrictions now. Before anything leaves the building, we settle that map — and the real constraint may be deliverables, since rights to source we never took delivery of don't compete a sustainment contract.

coach.qtype: a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: the funding source drives the license.
coach.smes: Legal (IP counsel), the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertion administration.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 227: who paid for development answers most of it — Government funds → unlimited, mixed → Government purpose rights (GPR), private → limited/restricted. The contractor proves the restriction (the 252.227-7017 assertion list); honor the markings until a challenge resolves.

scenarios.ask: The program executive officer (PEO) wants sustainment competed and the contractor says the Government's rights are narrow. What rights do we actually have — and what do you do about it?
scenarios.script: This is a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: funding source drives the license, component by component. My help: IP counsel in Legal, the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertions. The rule: Government funds → unlimited; mixed → Government Purpose Rights; private → limited or restricted — and integration never launders any of it. Walking the map: module A is Government-funded, unlimited. Module B rides its commercial license, with the adaptation's rights following the adaptation's funding. Module C was never asserted — the contractor carries the burden if they want restrictions now. Before anything leaves the building we settle that map in writing. And the real constraint may be deliverables: rights to source code we never took delivery of don't compete a sustainment contract.

follow_ups.q: Recite the rights levels for technical data.
follow_ups.h: Three levels, funding-driven, one converts on a clock.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 227: unlimited rights — development entirely at Government expense; use, modify, release to anyone for any purpose. Government Purpose Rights — mixed funding; any Government purpose including competitive reprocurement under nondisclosure protections, no commercial use, converting to unlimited after the period (five years standard). Limited rights — entirely private expense; internal Government use and emergency repair or overhaul only.

follow_ups.q: And for computer software?
follow_ups.h: One level swaps names, and Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) runs long.
follow_ups.d: Unlimited and Government Purpose Rights mirror the technical-data levels. The private-expense level becomes restricted rights — use on one computer at a time, tight copying limits. And SBIR data rights protect for twenty years under current policy, transitioning afterward. Remember the definitional split: technical data is recorded scientific/technical information; computer software is programs and code — and you can't reverse-engineer software you hold under restriction.

follow_ups.q: Walk the marking-challenge sequence — and the discipline while it runs.
follow_ups.h: Written, sixty days, decision, appeal — and hands off meanwhile.
follow_ups.d: Written challenge stating the grounds; the contractor has 60 days to justify the assertion with records — the burden of proof is theirs; unresolved, the contracting officer (CO) issues a final decision; the contractor may appeal within 90 days. Challenges can issue up to three years after contract completion. The discipline: honor the markings until every appeal resolves — using challenged data as if unrestricted converts your challenge into their claim.

scenarios.scenario: A firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract delivers 120 vehicle-mounted jammers. Mod history: mod 3 added winterization kits (+$1.8M), mod 7 upgraded the power amplifier (+$4.2M), mod 11 added 20 units (+$6M). Now the program manager (PM) wants mod 14: swap the jamming waveform suite for a new-generation library the vendor "already developed for another customer" (+$9.5M on an original $38M). "Each mod passed scope review individually," the file notes. The contractor hints that if mod 14 is competed instead, "the request for equitable adjustment (REA) for disruption will be substantial."

facts.why: The test is cumulative against the original: $38M has become $59.5M+ with materially different capability. Individually-blessed mods don't immunize the sum.

Anticipation test: did the original competition's offerors bid expecting a next-gen capability swap? A vendor-proprietary library "from another customer" reads like new work other vendors could compete.
The tightest scope perimeter of all types — cumulative drift on FFP is judged harshly.
A disruption REA is priced and defended on its merits — it isn't a toll that buys out competition. Decisions made to avoid asserted REAs are decisions made for you.

scenarios.board_answer: Cumulatively this contract has grown more than half again and is about to change capability generations — judged against the original award, mod 14 is out-of-scope new work. It gets competed or carried on a real justification and approval (J&A); and the REA threat gets evaluated as an REA, not as leverage over my scope call.

coach.qtype: a scope question — RFO Part 43: a modification, or a new procurement in disguise.
coach.smes: Legal, the procuring contracting officer (PCO) chain, and the original competition record itself.
coach.rule: The test is what the original competitors reasonably anticipated — judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative. In scope: modify under RFO Part 43. Beyond it: compete it or justify it under RFO Part 6.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants mod 14 executed and the contractor hints at an REA if you compete instead. How do you rule?
scenarios.script: This is a scope question — RFO Part 43: is this a modification or a new procurement in disguise? My help: Legal and the original competition record itself. The test: what the original competitors reasonably anticipated at award, judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative — never against mod 13. Walking it: this contract has already grown more than half again, and mod 14 changes capability generations — a new-generation waveform suite is not what the original field competed for. That's out-of-scope new work: it gets competed or carried on a real RFO 6.103 J&A at the right tier. And the REA threat gets evaluated as an REA, on its own facts — it doesn't get a vote on my scope call.

follow_ups.q: What are the four elements of the scope assessment?
follow_ups.h: Anticipation, type, period, and the cumulative ledger.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 43: scope of the competition — would the original offerors have reasonably anticipated this change at award; contract type — FFP carries tighter scope than cost-type; period of performance — a reasonableness standard; and contract cost or price — the cumulative impact of ALL modifications, never just the one in front of you. Mod 14 is judged against the original award with mods 1 through 13 on the scale.

follow_ups.q: Define the modification types for me.
follow_ups.h: Two signatures' worth, plus the two accidents and the boundary.
follow_ups.d: Unilateral — signed only by the contracting officer (CO): administrative changes, in-scope change orders, option exercises, termination notices; the contractor keeps its REA right. Bilateral (supplemental agreement) — both parties; preferred for anything substantive. Directed change — a formal change order under the Changes clause. Constructive change — Government conduct alters the work without formal direction; equitable adjustment, asserted within 30 days of incurring costs. Cardinal change — beyond the original competition entirely: potential breach, and the Changes clause cannot authorize it.

follow_ups.q: What does the Changes clause actually cover — and what does it NOT?
follow_ups.h: Three things per contract family — and two famous exclusions.
follow_ups.d: Supply contracts: drawings, designs, or specifications; method of shipment or packaging; place of delivery. Service contracts: description of services; time of performance; place of performance. Time-and-materials (T&M) adds Government-furnished property (GFP). What it does NOT cover: period-of-performance changes — those go by mutual agreement — and Government property changes, which ride the GFP clause. Reaching for the Changes clause outside its list is how in-scope theories quietly die.

scenarios.scenario: Mid-way through a cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) sensor-integration effort, the contractor requests the Government furnish a $700K calibrated antenna range "like the one we let them use informally last year through the lab." The program manager (PM) supports it: "we own one that's idle, it obviously saves the contract money." The lab chief mentions the informal arrangement ended after "some damage nobody ever sorted out."

facts.why: Savings speaks to best-interest — one of four. Burden, risk, and can't-otherwise-be-met still need answers on the record, from the requiring activity.
Property in contractor hands without contract coverage is the anti-pattern: no clause, no risk allocation, no accountability. Whatever happens next happens on contract.
Exhibit A for why informality fails — and a live input to the risk prong of the four-part test now.

scenarios.board_answer: Possibly yes — but properly: the PM documents all four justifications, the property goes on contract with the full clause set and marking, condition is baselined on delivery, and the old damage gets resolved first — because the last informal loan ended with damage nobody owned, which is exactly what the clause machinery exists to prevent.

coach.qtype: a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception.
coach.smes: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the program manager (PM) — who owes the written justification.
coach.rule: RFO Part 45: contractors furnish property. Government-furnished property (GFP) only when all four parts hold — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, not otherwise satisfiable — and furnishing it puts the Government's own performance on the schedule.

scenarios.ask: The PM says furnishing the antenna range 'obviously saves money.' Do you furnish it, and on what terms?
scenarios.script: This is a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception. My help: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the PM, who owes the written justification. The default: contractors furnish their own property. Government-furnished property (GFP) takes all four findings — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, no other way to meet the need — documented by the requiring activity, not asserted in a meeting. Possibly the answer is yes here — but properly: the range goes on contract with the full property clause set, marking and item unique identification (IUID), condition baselined on delivery, and the damage from last year's informal loan resolved first. Because that informal loan — damage nobody owned — is exactly what the clause machinery exists to prevent.

follow_ups.q: Recite the four-part GFP justification test.
follow_ups.h: Interest, ledger, risk, and no alternative — all four.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 45: (1) furnishing the property is in the Government's best interest; (2) the overall benefit significantly outweighs the increased administrative cost; (3) it does not substantially increase the Government's risk; and (4) the requirement cannot otherwise be met. All four must hold, documented by the requiring activity — the PM — in a memorandum for record (MFR) to the procuring contracting officer (PCO). The exception needing no justification: property furnished for repair, modification, or overhaul, where the property IS the requirement.

follow_ups.q: What clauses ride with Government property?
follow_ups.h: The foundational clause brings a six-pack with it.
follow_ups.d: FAR 52.245-1, Government Property — the foundational clause — plus Use and Charges, and the DFARS set that always travels with it: IUID registry reporting, tagging/labeling/marking, loss reporting, property-management-system administration, and reporting/reutilization/disposal. All required whenever the property clause is in. That clause architecture is exactly what last year's informal loan skipped — which is why the damage had no owner.

follow_ups.q: The range gets damaged mid-contract — who determines liability, and on what standard?
follow_ups.h: A process, an administrator, and a risk allocation.
follow_ups.d: The loss/damage machinery under the property clause: the contractor reports and investigates, the property administrator manages the process, and the contracting officer (CO) determines liability under the contract's risk allocation — on a cost-type effort the contractor typically bears loss only where managerial personnel were at fault or the property system failed. Condition baselined at delivery is what makes any of that adjudicable — undocumented condition is how disputes become coin flips.

scenarios.scenario: Day 210 after qualifying proposal on an urgent airfield-defense undefinitized contract action (UCA). Obligations sit at 72% of NTE. Negotiations stalled over overhead rates; the contractor proposes "rolling the remaining scope into a follow-on UCA to keep momentum" and notes their proposed fee "shouldn't move — we took all the risk when we started without a price." The program manager (PM) asks you to obligate "the last 28% now" so the funding doesn't expire.

facts.why: The 180-day clock is blown — this is now a reportable discipline failure. Definitization becomes the commanding priority, with any extension papered deliberately, not assumed.
Chaining UCAs to avoid negotiating is the exact abuse the limits exist for — a second UCA needs its own justification and senior approval, and "we couldn't close the first one" isn't it.

facts.fact: "Fee shouldn't move — we took all the risk"
facts.why: Backwards: with 72% obligated and actuals visible, the remaining cost risk is small — weighted guidelines should price the risk that remains, which argues fee down.
The 75% post-proposal cap says no — and obligating to rescue expiring funds is a Time problem stacked on a cap violation.

scenarios.board_answer: We're past the definitization clock, so closing the negotiation is now the mission — no follow-on UCA, no obligations past the 75% cap, and no year-end money parked in an unpriced action. On fee, the actuals cut the other way: risk already burned down, and the weighted guidelines will show it.

coach.qtype: an undefinitized contract action (UCA) question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying negotiation leverage.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the clearance authority, and Legal; the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for actuals once performance starts.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 217.74 makes UCAs the exception: 50% obligation cap (75% after the qualifying proposal), definitize within 180 days, clearance at definitization — and neither poor planning nor administrative convenience ever justifies one.

scenarios.ask: Day 210, obligations at 72%, and the contractor proposes a follow-on UCA. What's your position going into this negotiation?
scenarios.script: This is a UCA question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying leverage. My help: my pricing office, the clearance authority, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on the actuals. The rules I anchor on: definitization was due at 180 days, obligations stop at the 75% cap, and neither timeline is negotiable leverage for the contractor. So my position: closing this negotiation is now the mission. No follow-on UCA — that's rewarding delay with a second undefinitized comfort period. No obligations past the cap, and no year-end money parked in an unpriced action. And on fee, the actuals cut against them: months of incurred costs mean the risk their fee would have priced has already burned down — weighted guidelines will show it, and the number comes down.

follow_ups.q: Recite the UCA obligation caps and the definitization clock.
follow_ups.h: Two percentages, one deadline, one extension.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 217.74: obligations capped at 50% of the not-to-exceed price before the qualifying proposal, up to 75% after it. Definitization within 180 days of the qualifying proposal — or when obligations hit the caps, whichever comes first — extendable 90 days if the head of the contracting activity (HCA) finds it in the Government's interest. Obligate only consistent with the contractor's spend plan; no spend plan, no payment.

follow_ups.q: When is a UCA justified in the first place?
follow_ups.h: Three conditions — and two disqualifiers everyone tries anyway.
follow_ups.d: Only when there's no time for negotiations, a binding agreement is needed so work can begin immediately, and waiting would cause genuine harm. Lack of planning and administrative convenience are never valid. Approval sits with the HCA, delegable (no lower than chief of the contracting office (COCO) under $50M), and the circumstances driving a UCA usually drive a Part 6 exception in parallel — urgency or one-source — so the justification and approval (J&A) rides alongside.

follow_ups.q: Why does fee come down at definitization?
follow_ups.h: Weighted guidelines price risk — and months of actuals retired some.
follow_ups.d: The weighted-guidelines fee prices the cost risk the contractor carries. By definitization, months of performance have converted unknowns into actuals — the risk the fee would have compensated has partly evaporated, so the fee follows the risk actually remaining. Pricing the performed portion on estimates when facts exist would pay a risk premium for risk already retired. Say it exactly that way; it's a favorite probe.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiations on a $40M sole-source engine-overhaul action closed Thursday, $2.1M above the Government's objective. The program manager (PM) wants award signed Monday "since we already had business clearance and the delta is only 5%." Your price negotiation memorandum (PNM) draft explains the movement in two sentences: "positions converged after productive discussion; price determined fair and reasonable."

facts.why: Business clearance authorized opening negotiations — the result needs contract clearance. Two gates, two purposes; the first doesn't waive the second.
Movement from the objective is precisely what the PNM must explain — what changed, what facts emerged, why the final position is still fair and reasonable.
"Productive discussion" documents nothing. The PNM tells the negotiation's full story — that draft wouldn't survive the clearance meeting, and shouldn't.

scenarios.board_answer: Monday isn't the gate — contract clearance is. And before I take it there, the PNM has to actually explain the $2.1M: which cost elements moved, on what new facts, and why the result is still fair and reasonable. Business clearance opened the negotiation; it doesn't bless the deal.

coach.qtype: a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before the Government commits.
coach.smes: the clearance authority itself, your chief, and Legal on any compliance flags.
coach.rule: Two gates catching two failures: business clearance blesses the strategy before release; contract clearance blesses the negotiated result before award. The selector never approves the selection.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants award signed Monday since business clearance is done and the delta is 'only 5%.' What do you tell him?
scenarios.script: This is a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before the Government commits. My help: the clearance authority itself and my chief. The rule: business clearance approved opening the negotiation; it does not bless the result — contract clearance does, and no award moves before it. And before I take this deal there, my PNM has to actually explain the $2.1M movement: which cost elements moved, on what new facts, and why the outcome is still fair and reasonable — 'the delta is only 5%' is arithmetic, not analysis. Monday isn't the gate; the review is. Treat the clearance authority as a teammate with veto power, because that's what they are — and this file isn't ready for them yet.

follow_ups.q: Business versus contract clearance — what does each approve, and where do undefinitized contract actions (UCAs) fit?
follow_ups.h: Strategy gate, deal gate, and one deliberate exception.
follow_ups.d: Business clearance approves releasing a competitive solicitation or opening sole-source negotiations — the strategy gate. Contract clearance approves the negotiated result — the award, the deal gate. In competitive selections it attaches to the source selection authority's (SSA) decision points. UCAs are the deliberate exception: no clearance at award — there's no price to bless yet — clearance comes at definitization.

follow_ups.q: Walk the clearance approval thresholds.
follow_ups.h: Six rungs from the procuring contracting officer (PCO) to the Secretariat.
follow_ups.d: Under $10M: the PCO. $10M to $75M: three levels below the senior contracting official (SCO). $75M to $200M: two below. $200M to $500M: one below — the OSF. $500M to $1B: the SCO. Over $1B: SAF/AQC. This $40M action clears three levels below the SCO — and no calendar, quarter-close, or handshake moves the gate.

follow_ups.q: What must the PNM tell the clearance reviewer?
follow_ups.h: The whole story — especially where the number moved.
follow_ups.d: The purpose of the negotiation, the acquisition and the parties, contractor systems status, any certified-data exception, what data the contracting officer (CO) relied on, the Government's objectives versus the negotiated result — with every significant movement explained on facts — the profit or fee basis, and the statement that the price is fair and reasonable. A PNM that explains a $2.1M move in two sentences isn't a record; it's a request to take your word for it.

scenarios.scenario: Award posted Monday for a base-communications recompete. The incumbent — who lost — requests a debrief Tuesday; you hold it the following Monday. Wednesday after the debrief, they file at the Government Accountability Office (GAO). The program manager (PM) erupts: "That's day 9 after award for a required debrief held day 7 — they missed the 5-day window, right? Keep the new contractor working." Meanwhile the awardee offers to "keep going unpaid until it sorts out, as a good-faith gesture." Your Legal advisor is TDY until Friday.

facts.fact: Debrief held day 7, protest filed 2 days later
facts.why: The rule is 10 days from award or 5 from the required debrief — whichever is later. Two days post-debrief is timely; the stay attaches. The PM's arithmetic uses the wrong rule.
Performance is performance — paid or not, it violates the stay and taints the corrective-action space. Direct a stop in writing.
The stay isn't optional pending counsel's return — execute it now, reach whatever Legal coverage exists, and start the agency-report clock.

scenarios.board_answer: The protest is timely — five days from the required debrief controls, not ten from award — so I stop performance in writing today, awardee's goodwill notwithstanding. Then notifications, the agency report, and my statement of facts; and if the fielding schedule genuinely can't absorb 100 days, the head of the contracting activity (HCA) override gets considered on real urgency facts, not frustration.

coach.qtype: a protest question — RFO Part 33 and the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA): venue, stay math, and the record you built months earlier.
coach.smes: Legal drives; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) counsel through Legal; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any override decision.
coach.rule: Know the RFO 33.105 machinery cold — the 10-day/5-day stay rule, three venues with different powers — and remember the real defense was built earlier: criteria stated, followed, and documented.

scenarios.ask: The PM says the protest is late — day 9 versus a debrief 'held too long after award.' Is it timely, and what do you do right now?
scenarios.script: This is a protest question — the RFO 33.105-3 stay math first, feelings second. My help: Legal drives, AFLOA/JAQ represents us at GAO, and the HCA owns any override. The rule: the stay attaches if the protest lands within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debrief — whichever is later. They requested a required debrief and filed within five days of it, so this protest is timely — the debrief branch controls, and the award-date math the PM is doing doesn't. So today, in writing: stop performance, awardee's goodwill notwithstanding. Then notifications, the agency report, my statement of facts. If the fielding schedule genuinely can't absorb GAO's 100 days, the HCA override gets considered on real urgency facts — not on frustration.

follow_ups.q: Recite the post-award stay rule precisely — and how it's overridden.
follow_ups.h: Two windows, take the later; override is written and high.
follow_ups.d: At GAO, a post-award protest triggers the automatic stay if filed within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debriefing — whichever is later. Override requires written HCA authorization on one of two bases: urgent and compelling circumstances, or the best interests of the United States — and for a post-award override, within 30 days. Pre-award protests stay the award itself upon GAO's notice.

follow_ups.q: Compare the three protest venues for me.
follow_ups.h: Fast, structured, and judicial.
follow_ups.d: Agency-level: fastest and least formal, roughly a 35-day target, self-correcting — and the protester can still go elsewhere after. GAO: the 100-day statutory clock, the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) automatic stay, recommendations that are legally advisory but followed in practice — non-compliance is reported to Congress. The U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC): full judicial proceedings, binding and appealable decisions, no automatic stay — the protester must win a preliminary injunction.

follow_ups.q: What are your responsibilities while the GAO protest runs?
follow_ups.h: Notify, assemble, state the facts, then implement.
follow_ups.d: Notify everyone concerned including the source selection authority (SSA); coordinate with Legal immediately; assemble the agency report; prepare the contracting officer's (CO) Statement of Facts; support the Memorandum of Law; and if GAO sustains, implement the recommendations within 60 days — including paying protest costs where warranted. And if counsel finds a real defect mid-protest, voluntary corrective action beats riding to a sustain: faster, cheaper, and you control the remedy.

scenarios.scenario: A services contractor submits a certified "claim" for $128K: $67K for extra reporting a departed Government analyst "required weekly for five months," $38K for a two-week facility-access lockout during an exercise, and $23K in "claim preparation and outside counsel fees." The contracting officer's representative (COR) "vaguely remembers the reports being briefed." The program manager (PM) wants to "pay the access piece to make it go away and deny the rest verbally."

facts.why: Over $100K and certified — the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) clock and interest are running. This gets a written contracting officer (CO) final decision, not a verbal anything.

Constructive-change candidate: unauthorized direction, performed, arguably benefiting the Government. Entitlement analysis (who directed, was it beyond the performance work statement (PWS)) before any quantum talk.
Government-caused suspension of access is classic delay entitlement — evaluate honestly; it may be the strongest element.
In the claim lane those costs are unallowable — the element fails as pleaded.

facts.fact: "Pay one piece, deny the rest verbally"
facts.why: Piecemeal cash without findings plus a verbal denial = interest still running and no appealable decision. One written final decision (or a negotiated global settlement with release) closes it.

scenarios.board_answer: It's a certified CDA claim, so interest is running and my output is a written final decision — or a settlement. Element by element: the lockout has real entitlement; the reports need a constructive-change analysis; the prep and counsel fees are unallowable in the claim lane. I'd negotiate a global resolution with a release if the facts support it, and decide formally what doesn't settle.

coach.qtype: a disputes question — the Contract Disputes Act and RFO Part 33: request for equitable adjustment (REA) lane or CDA claim, and substance beats the label.
coach.smes: Legal early, financial management (FM) on funding the outcome, and the contracting officer's representative (COR)/program manager (PM) for the facts record.
coach.rule: Classify by substance under the CDA: a sum certain, certified, with a decision demanded is a claim — interest and decision deadlines already running. The machinery doesn't care what the cover letter says.
coach.cite: Contract Disputes Act · RFO Part 33 · Vol. 2, REAs & Claims

scenarios.ask: The contractor's certified claim is on your desk. How do you handle it — and what's your answer on each piece?
scenarios.script: This is a disputes question — a certified CDA claim, so the machinery is already running: interest from receipt, decision deadlines, and my output is a written final decision or a settlement. My help: Legal early, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) or the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) on the numbers, the COR's record for the facts. Element by element, the way the panel wants it: the facility lockout has real entitlement — Government-caused, documented. The extra weekly reports need a constructive-change analysis — who directed them, with what authority. The prep and counsel fees are unallowable in the claim lane — that's the request for equitable adjustment (REA)/claim seam. I'd negotiate a global resolution with a release if the facts support one, and formally decide whatever doesn't settle — by certified mail, with appeal rights stated.

follow_ups.q: REA versus claim — give me the four differences.
follow_ups.h: Interest, clocks, prep costs, formality.
follow_ups.d: Interest: accrues on a claim from receipt; none on an REA. Decision deadlines: the CDA puts the CO on a clock for claims; REAs have none. Preparation costs: allowable as contract administration for an REA; unallowable for a claim. Formality: claims are written, demand a sum certain, carry appeal rights, and require certification over $100K — plus DoD's separate REA certification above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT). Substance controls the label.

follow_ups.q: Walk the claim clocks.
follow_ups.h: Six years back, sixty days to answer, two appeal doors.
follow_ups.d: Submission within 6 years of accrual. Certification over $100K. For claims over $100K the CO issues a decision within 60 days or states when it will issue; silence becomes a deemed denial and starts the appeal clock. Appeals: the Board of Contract Appeals within 90 days, or the Court of Federal Claims within 12 months. Over $500K, coordinate alternative dispute resolution (ADR) potential — and every decision goes by certified mail with appeal rights stated.

follow_ups.q: Which pieces of a mixed claim like this one actually settle, and how do you close it?
follow_ups.h: Element by element, then one document that ends it.
follow_ups.d: Evaluate entitlement element by element — the lockout has clear Government causation; the extra reports need the constructive-change analysis; prep and counsel fees are unallowable in the claim lane and come out. Then negotiate a global settlement where the facts support one, and paper it as a bilateral modification with a release of claims — the release is what makes the settlement final. Whatever won't settle gets a written final decision, certified mail, appeal rights stated.

scenarios.scenario: A grounds-keeping contractor has missed quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP) standards three months running. The contracting officer's representative's (COR) log is thorough. The program manager (PM) demands "default them today — we have it all documented." The contract runs seven more months; the next-best source's rates are 22% higher; and the contractor's owner calls you personally: her equipment was destroyed in a hangar fire last month — "give me six weeks and a schedule adjustment and I'll be back on my feet." The fire is confirmed; the performance failures predate it by two months.

facts.fact: Three documented months of QASP failure
facts.why: Real grounds — but for a performance-failure default the runway is cure notice first, not "today." The documentation makes the cure notice strong; it doesn't replace it.
An excusable cause — for what it actually caused. It explains the last month, not the two before it. Slice the failure timeline in the analysis.
Reprocurement economics inform the business judgment (and excess-cost recovery math) — they don't decide excusability or entitlement to default.
Compassion isn't a contract action — but a cure notice with a realistic cure period is lawful, humane, and strategically sound all at once.

scenarios.board_answer: Cure notice today — the documented failures support it — with a cure period that acknowledges the fire's genuine impact on recent weeks. If performance doesn't recover, show cause, excusability analysis slicing pre-fire from post-fire failure, then the default decision with Legal. And the 22% figure waits for the reprocurement math, where it belongs.

coach.qtype: a termination question — RFO Part 49 (or the commercial clause under RFO 12.403): fault drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (mandatory), your termination contracting officer channel, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on settlement.
coach.rule: Who's at fault decides what's owed under RFO Part 49: termination for convenience (T4C) makes the contractor whole for work done, no anticipatory profit; termination for default (T4D) demands the full runway — cure, show cause, excusability — because a wrongful default converts to a T4C.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants them defaulted today, and the record looks strong. What's your move?
scenarios.script: This is a termination question — RFO Part 49: fault drives the remedy, and process protects the outcome. My help: Legal, mandatory, plus the termination CO channel and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on any settlement math. The rule: termination for default (T4D) is a remedy of last resort with a runway — cure notice, show cause, excusability analysis, then the decision. So: cure notice today — the documented QASP failures support it — with a cure period that honestly acknowledges the fire's impact on recent weeks. If performance doesn't recover, show cause, then the excusability analysis slicing pre-fire failure from post-fire failure — because a default that ignores excusable causes converts to a convenience termination later, with us paying. And the 22% reprocurement figure waits for the reprocurement math, where it belongs.

follow_ups.q: Walk the T4D runway, in order.
follow_ups.h: Cure, show cause, excusability, final decision.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 49: cure notice — Government's intent, the failures, 10 days to cure (not required for pure late delivery; when in doubt, send it); show cause — demand the contractor explain why the contract shouldn't be terminated; excusability analysis — documented before the decision, not after; then the T4D notice as the CO's final decision, hard copy, with the required contents: the failures, liability for excess reprocurement costs, non-excusability, reserved rights, appeal rights.

follow_ups.q: Name the classic excusable causes.
follow_ups.h: Beyond control, without fault — three families.
follow_ups.d: Acts of God; acts of the Government in its sovereign capacity; and fires, epidemics, strikes, unusually severe weather — events beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence. A subcontractor's failure excuses the prime only if the cause was beyond the control and without the fault of BOTH prime and sub, and substitute performance wasn't reasonably available. The fire here is why the excusability record gets built before any notice goes out.

follow_ups.q: And if your default is later found wrongful?
follow_ups.h: The remedy flips sides.
follow_ups.d: The T4D converts to a termination for convenience: instead of collecting excess reprocurement costs, the Government pays a settlement — costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on work performed, and settlement expenses. That conversion risk is the entire reason for the runway: every skipped step is a step the board of contract appeals will walk back through, with the Government paying for the shortcut.

scenarios.scenario: A lab team wants to "broad agency announcement (BAA)" a requirement to build 40 ruggedized sensor pods "to the attached ICD, delivered within 14 months, evaluated on price and past performance." Separately, they want to hand a Phase III production contract to a firm whose Phase II was performed for another service — "Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) is SBIR, right?" — and a colonel asks why you can't "just Other Transaction (OT) the whole thing since OTs skip the rules."

facts.fact: "BAA... to the attached ICD, price and past performance"
facts.why: That's a production buy with a spec and comparative factors — a request for proposals (RFP) wearing a BAA nametag. BAAs buy research toward broadly stated objectives with merit review; this gets the Part 15 treatment it actually is.

facts.fact: Phase III off another service's Phase II
facts.why: Phase III derives from the work, not the agency — a competed Phase I/II anywhere in the program can carry Phase III. Verify the derivation and document it.

OTs exchange the FAR framework for negotiated terms — they don't suspend fiscal law, ethics, or the need for disciplined agreements; and their best use case (nontraditionals, prototypes) has to actually be present.

scenarios.board_answer: Three answers: the pod buy is a specification-driven production requirement — that's an RFP, not a BAA; the Phase III is likely fine because derivation follows the SBIR work, not the sponsoring service — we verify and paper it; and OTs don't skip rules, they trade frameworks — I'd use one where nontraditional participation genuinely needs it, not as a bypass.

coach.qtype: a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35, the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) statute, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 Other Transactions (OTs): the right instrument for genuine uncertainty.
coach.smes: your agreements officer channel, Legal, and the science and technology (S&T) program office.
coach.rule: Pick the authority for a reason: RFO Part 35 broad agency announcements (BAAs) compete proposals against a published standard, SBIR Phase III carries statutory sole-source off competed early phases, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 OTs trade the mature protections framework for agility — 'skipping the rules' is never the reason.
coach.cite: RFO Part 35 · SBIR statute · 10 U.S.C. 4022 · Vol. 2, R&D

scenarios.ask: The lab wants a BAA for the pods, a handshake Phase III, and 'an OT to skip the FAR.' Take each one.
scenarios.script: This is a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35, the SBIR statute, and 10 U.S.C. 4022: the right instrument for each piece of work. My help: the agreements officer channel, Legal, and the science and technology (S&T) program office. Three answers, in order. The pod buy: forty units to a spec on a schedule, evaluated on price — that's a production requirement; it takes an RFP, not a BAA, because BAAs compete ideas against a published standard, not deliverables against a spec. The Phase III: likely legitimate — eligibility follows derivation from the competed SBIR work; we verify the derivation chain and paper it, no justification and approval (J&A) needed. The OT: OTs don't skip rules — they trade a mature protections framework for agility. I'd use one where nontraditional participation genuinely needs it, and say no where it's just a bypass.

follow_ups.q: What makes BAA evaluation lawful competition?
follow_ups.h: Announcement, criteria, independent review — against a standard.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 35: broad public announcement; stated evaluation criteria; and independent scientific or engineering merit review — with each proposal evaluated against the published standard, not compared head-to-head. The market competed by proposing. The Government can fund all, part, or none, and award a contract or an assistance instrument. What a BAA cannot do is buy production units to a spec — that's an RFP wearing a lab coat.

follow_ups.q: Walk the SBIR phases — and Phase III's special properties.
follow_ups.h: Feasibility, prototype, production — and the third has no cap.
follow_ups.d: Phase I, feasibility — small, short, typically firm-fixed-price (FFP). Phase II, prototype — larger, longer. Phase III, production — funded outside the SBIR set-aside, no dollar cap, no J&A required when it derives from competitively awarded Phase I/II work (the statutory 'authorized by statute' lane), and SBIR data rights persist. Document the derivation chain — and note: SBIR authorization has lapsed and been in flux recently, so verify the current program status before building a strategy on new starts.

follow_ups.q: When would you steer AWAY from an OT?
follow_ups.h: The trade only pays when it buys something.
follow_ups.d: Traditional performers, well-understood requirements, or flexibilities nobody actually needs. A 10 U.S.C. 4022 OT trades the mature protections framework — competition rules, cost principles, disputes machinery — for agility and nontraditional participation. Spend that trade only when it buys something real: a commercial tech company that won't take a FAR contract, prototype-speed terms a real schedule demands. 'Skipping the rules' is the dishonest reason, and boards can smell it.

scenarios.scenario: Week three of a $900K taxiway-repair contract: the contractor's excavator uncovers a buried debris field of old construction rubble not on any drawing, keeps digging "to stay on schedule," and a week later submits a $210K request for equitable adjustment (REA) with photos. Meanwhile your facilities customer, thrilled with the same contractor's site crew, asks you to "add a clause so their foreman can take daily direction from our shop lead on small stuff — it'll save everyone emails."

facts.fact: Kept digging, notice a week later
facts.why: The differing-site-conditions clause demands notice before disturbance so the Government can verify. Late notice doesn't automatically kill recovery, but it damages it — and the photos don't substitute for the investigation we never got to do. Entitlement analysis with that lens.
A genuine Type-condition candidate — materially different from the indications. The merits may be real even while the notice failure discounts them.
That clause would write personal services into the contract — Government supervision of contractor employees. Direction goes to the contractor's foreman through the contract's terms, period.

scenarios.board_answer: Two answers: the REA gets an honest differing-site-conditions analysis — real merits, discounted by the notice failure that cost us our investigation; and no, we don't write a daily-direction clause — that's personal services. The shop lead's needs route through the performance work statement (PWS) and the contractor's own supervisor.

coach.qtype: a construction/services question — RFO Parts 36 and 37, with RFO Part 28 bonds: specialized statutory machinery.
coach.smes: Legal, the labor advisor on wage determinations, and the installation civil engineers.
coach.rule: Construction and services run on their own rails: RFO Part 28 bonds over $150K, written notice before disturbing a differing site condition (RFO Part 36), qualifications-based architect-engineer (A&E) selection, and no personal-services drift (RFO Part 37).
coach.cite: RFO Parts 36/37 · Part 28 bonds · Vol. 2, Construction

scenarios.ask: The contractor's $210K REA is in, and the facility chief wants direct tasking authority added. Answer both.
scenarios.script: This is a construction question — RFO Part 36 — with an RFO Part 37 services trap attached. My help: Legal, the labor advisor, and civil engineering. On the REA: the differing-site-conditions clause exists for exactly this — a latent condition materially different from the drawings — but the clause demands written notice before disturbing the site, and he kept digging for a week. So the analysis is honest on merits and discounted for the notice failure that cost the Government its investigation. Real entitlement, reduced recovery — negotiated on that record. On the tasking request: no — daily direction of contractor employees is personal services without authority. The shop lead's needs route through the PWS and the contractor's own supervisor, and I'd fix that expectation now, in writing.

follow_ups.q: What does the differing-site-conditions clause require before recovery — and why?
follow_ups.h: Paper before shovels.
follow_ups.d: Written notice before the condition is disturbed, so the Government can investigate the site as found — that's the clause's bargain. A Type I condition differs materially from what the contract documents indicated; keep digging for a week and the evidence is gone, which is why the notice failure discounts recovery even when the entitlement is real. Honest merits, reduced by the investigation the Government lost.

follow_ups.q: What's the legal test for personal services?
follow_ups.h: Supervision, not location.
follow_ups.d: Whether Government personnel exercise relatively continuous supervision and control over contractor employees — the employer-employee pattern: assigning daily tasks, directing how work is done, approving leave. That relationship is unlawful without specific statutory authority (RFO Part 37). Proximity and embedded seating don't create it; supervision does. The fix is always structural: direction flows through the PWS and the contractor's own management.

follow_ups.q: What bonds and protections ride a construction contract at this value?
follow_ups.h: Two bonds over $150K, and damages that must be forecasts.
follow_ups.d: Over $150K: a performance bond at 100% of the contract price protecting the Government's work, and a payment bond — no smaller — protecting subs and suppliers who can't lien Government property, plus a bid guarantee at solicitation. Liquidated damages, where used, must be a documented forecast of probable actual delay costs — punitive rates collapse as penalties. And the solicitation discloses the magnitude range, never the estimate.

scenarios.scenario: You inherit a services contract supporting a munitions test range: three-year base, two one-year options, option year one begins in 60 days. The contracting officer's representative (COR) emails you: performance has been "shaky since spring" — two missed surveillance reports and a near-miss safety writeup — but the PM "already told the contractor we're picking up the option, since re-competing would take a year." Meanwhile the contractor's program manager mentions on a call that they've been "doing a little extra environmental monitoring the range officer asked for back in March — we'll square up the cost later."

frameworks.why: Before exercising: price still fair and reasonable · funds available · option still meets the need and is the best method · contractor eligible in SAM · performance considered. Two missed reports and a safety writeup go straight into that determination — an option is a unilateral right, never an obligation.

Document the deficiencies now, engage the COR's surveillance records against the QASP, consider a letter of concern or cure path — the record you build is what makes any downstream decision (option, extension, termination) defensible.

The range officer had no authority to direct new work. The Government isn't bound — this is ratification territory: investigate, get the facts and a statement from whoever directed it, confirm funds were and are available, and route to the ratifying authority. Train the range officer — direction flows through the PCO only.
"Already told the contractor" binds nothing — only the PCO commits the Government. But it does create a communication problem you now manage deliberately.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO Part 17 gates: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous check, SAM exclusions, performance considered — with timely written notice, or the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: Option year one starts in 60 days. Do you exercise — and what do you do about the 'extra monitoring'?
scenarios.script: Two questions wearing one scenario: an RFO Part 17 options question and an RFO 1.405 unauthorized-commitment question. My help: the COR's record, Legal, and financial management (FM). On the option: it's a unilateral right with gates — and performance is a gate. Two missed surveillance reports and a safety near-miss go straight into the determination; the PM's promise to the contractor binds nothing, and I'd correct that channel today. If the record supports exercise, notice goes out on time; if not, my honest paths are a short extension or recompete. On the 'extra monitoring': work directed by a range officer with no authority is a UAC candidate — stop the practice in writing, sort entitlement through the ratification or constructive-change lane, and retrain everyone who touched it.

follow_ups.q: Recite the option-exercise gates.
follow_ups.h: Seven checks and a deadline.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 17: price still fair and reasonable on a fresh look; funds available; the option serves an existing need and is the best method; synopsized or exempt; contractor not excluded in SAM; performance considered — which is where the missed reports and the near-miss live; and written notice by the contract's date. The PM's verbal promise satisfies none of them and binds nothing.

follow_ups.q: The 'extra monitoring' — ratification lane or constructive change? Sort it for me.
follow_ups.h: New work versus changed work.
follow_ups.d: Sort by what happened: work OUTSIDE the contract's scope that someone without authority commissioned is an unauthorized commitment — the RFO 1.405 ratification lane, six elements, chief of the contracting office (COCO) or head of the contracting activity (HCA) approval by dollars. Government conduct that CHANGED existing in-scope work is a constructive change — equitable adjustment through the Changes clause via a request for equitable adjustment (REA). Environmental monitoring the contract never contained points toward ratification; either way, the practice stops in writing today.

follow_ups.q: Can you even exercise the option with an open UAC investigation on the same contract?
follow_ups.h: The gates don't pause — but one of them absorbs it.
follow_ups.d: Yes, if the gates honestly pass — there's no rule suspending options during a ratification investigation. But the performance-considered gate absorbs the whole picture: the surveillance failures, the safety near-miss, and a contractor performing unpriced work on a range officer's say-so. Document the option decision on that complete record. If the record says extend, extend with corrective expectations in writing; if it says compete, a year is exactly enough time to start now.

scenarios.scenario: A lab complex needs custodial and preventive-maintenance support for the next five years, starting this October. Financial management (FM) says the requirement will be funded annually with operation and maintenance (O&M). The facility manager wants "one award covering all five years so we never re-do this," and suggests obligating the first two years now "since this year's money is healthy."

frameworks.why: Recurring custodial/PM support is severable — benefit delivered as performed. Annual O&M funds a period generally ≤12 months; two years of obligation from one year's O&M fails Time.

The five-year need is met by a base year plus four one-year options (services rail: base+options ≈ 5 years), each option exercised with the 17.204-1 gates and funded by its own year's money — continuity without violating the appropriation clock.
Healthy money isn't the test; bona fide need of the appropriation's period is.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: The facility manager wants one five-year award funded two years deep today. How do you structure and fund this?
scenarios.script: This is a fiscal-law question with an RFO Part 17 structure answer. My help: FM first and always, then Legal. The rules: custodial and preventive maintenance is severable — benefit delivered as performed — and severable services on annual O&M fund up to 12 months, may cross fiscal years, but never two years off one appropriation. Obligating two years now fails Time, period. The structure that lawfully meets the five-year need: a base year plus four one-year options on the services rail — one award, one competition, renewed by exercise, each year funded by its own money. The facility manager gets exactly what he wants — 'never re-do this' — without a single fiscal violation. That's the answer: structure solves what funding can't.

follow_ups.q: Severable versus non-severable — define both and fund both.
follow_ups.h: Benefit as performed, or one product at the end.
follow_ups.d: Severable services deliver benefit as they're performed — custodial, maintenance, help desk: fundable with annual money for a period up to 12 months, which may cross fiscal years. Non-severable services produce a single end product — one study, one overhaul: a bona fide need of the award year, fully funded up front, and they may run past a year. Fund a non-severable effort incrementally and you've violated Time and Amount at once.

follow_ups.q: What duration limits cap the structure you just proposed?
follow_ups.h: The services rail and the emergency spare.
follow_ups.d: Base plus all options can't exceed five years on service contracts (DFARS 217.204) — so base-plus-four is exactly the ceiling. The extension-of-services clause holds six more months in reserve for a transition emergency, and DoD task/delivery-order contracts run to ten years only with a Head of Agency determination. The five-year rail is why 'one award forever' was never on the table.

follow_ups.q: Could you obligate year-two money at award using the availability-of-funds mechanism?
follow_ups.h: That clause times an exercise; it doesn't advance an appropriation.
follow_ups.d: No. Availability-of-funds language lets the Government exercise an option on time subject to funds, with the obligation attaching when the appropriation arrives — it preserves the unilateral right across the fiscal seam.
