What it cannot do is obligate money Congress hasn't appropriated or stretch this year's O&M across next year's severable period. Each option year gets funded by its own year's money, exercised through its own gates.

scenarios.scenario: You solicited a $1.7M simulator-maintenance requirement full-and-open, 30-day response period, healthy industry-day attendance. One proposal arrives — from Meridian Support Group, priced 6% under the independent Government cost estimate (IGCE). The program manager (PM) is delighted: "award it before they change their mind."

frameworks.framework: Competition — one offer after full and open
frameworks.why: The competition was full and open — one responsive offer doesn't undo that. Find out why the field passed (debrief the no-bids informally; the answers improve the next solicitation) and document it.

With one offer, "adequate price competition" needs care — price analysis against the IGCE, history, and market data carries the fair-and-reasonable determination. At $1.7M, no certified data (under threshold, and it's a competitive solicitation); other-than-certified data if the analysis needs it.
Speed is fine — skipping the price-reasonableness record isn't.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: One offer came back. The PM says award it today. How do you proceed?
scenarios.script: This is a competition-and-pricing question — RFO Part 6 posture, RFO 15.404-1 price analysis. My help: my pricing office and the no-bid field itself. The rule: the competition was full and open — one responsive offer doesn't undo that; what changes is my pricing burden. First, find out why the field passed: informal debriefs of the no-bids — the answers either reveal a solicitation defect worth fixing or confirm the market is thin, and both belong in the file. Then price the single offer on evidence: 6% under the IGCE is a good sign, but I'd support it with prior-buy history and catalog comparisons before calling it fair and reasonable. If the record holds, award — documented single-offer awards are perfectly defensible. What's not defensible is 'they might change their mind' as price analysis.

follow_ups.q: Does one offer defeat 'adequate price competition'?
follow_ups.h: The exception is about expectation and the price you can prove.
follow_ups.d: Not automatically — the competition was full and open, and one responsive offer received under competitive expectations can still support the exception. But with one offer, the pricing burden rises: support fair-and-reasonable with the IGCE, prior-buy history, catalog and market comparisons, and document why the price stands on its own evidence. If the support isn't there, request data other than certified and analyze — the count of offers never substitutes for price analysis.

follow_ups.q: What would you actually ask the no-bids — and why does it matter?
follow_ups.h: The answers either fix your solicitation or clear your file.
follow_ups.d: Why they passed: requirement shaped wrong, period too short, bundling too big, terms too risky, incumbency assumed unbeatable? Informal, documented conversations. The answers matter twice — they either reveal a solicitation defect worth fixing before award, or they confirm the competition was genuinely open and the field chose not to play, which is exactly the record that defends a single-offer award and improves the next cycle.

follow_ups.q: Where would certified cost or pricing data enter this picture?
follow_ups.h: Check the threshold and the exceptions before asking.
follow_ups.d: At $1.7M this action sits below the certified-data trigger, so certification never enters — and even above it, you'd run the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions first, where adequate price competition may still apply to a competitively solicited single offer. What you can always demand is data other than certified sufficient to price the action. Know the ladder: threshold, then exceptions, then the data ask sized to what the file actually needs.

scenarios.scenario: A fixed-price contractor is 45 days late delivering deployable generator sets. Three weeks ago the contracting officer's representative (COR) emailed the contractor "keep at it — we need these units." The contractor now says the delay stems from a subcontractor's plant fire, "so it's excusable," and adds that since the Government "told us to keep working, you can't default us anyway." The program manager (PM) wants them terminated today and the units bought elsewhere.

frameworks.framework: Terminations — default posture after late delivery
frameworks.why: Late delivery on FP supplies supports T4D without a cure notice — but the intervening "keep at it" message raises schedule waiver. Re-establish a firm delivery date in writing (show cause framing) before any default.
Fires can be excusable if beyond control and without fault at both prime and sub tiers — test whether the prime could have mitigated (second sources, schedule buffer). Slice entitlement by timeline.

frameworks.framework: Authority — the COR's email — bait, with teeth
frameworks.why: The COR can't modify the schedule — but the Government's conduct (through any agent) can still create waiver facts. Both things are true; fix the record.
If T4D holds, excess reprocurement costs are recoverable — buy the replacement reasonably and mitigate.

coach.qtype: a termination question — RFO Part 49 (or the commercial clause under RFO 12.403): fault drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (mandatory), your termination contracting officer channel, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on settlement.
coach.rule: Who's at fault decides what's owed under RFO Part 49: termination for convenience (T4C) makes the contractor whole for work done, no anticipatory profit; termination for default (T4D) demands the full runway — cure, show cause, excusability — because a wrongful default converts to a T4C.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants them terminated today. The contractor claims excusable delay and waiver. What's your move?
scenarios.script: This is a termination question — RFO Part 49 — complicated by our own conduct. My help: Legal, mandatory, before any notice moves. The rules in play: late delivery on fixed-price supplies supports default without a cure notice — the schedule was the cure period — but the COR's 'keep at it' message three weeks ago raises schedule waiver, which means the original date may no longer be enforceable. So first, with Legal, I re-establish a firm delivery date in writing — show-cause framing — restoring an enforceable schedule. In parallel, the excusability analysis on the subcontractor's fire: fires can be excusable if beyond control and without fault, and that record gets built before, not after, any default. Terminate today and we buy the conversion to convenience later.

follow_ups.q: When is a cure notice NOT required?
follow_ups.h: Three cases — and a default instinct when unsure.
follow_ups.d: Pure failure to deliver on time — the delivery schedule was the cure period; defaults based on a contract clause that doesn't require notice; and construction under its own default clause. When facts are mixed — like performance failures alongside lateness — send it: a needless cure notice costs ten days, a missing one can cost the termination on conversion. Here the complication isn't the notice; it's the waiver.

follow_ups.q: How exactly does the COR's 'keep at it' email change your posture?
follow_ups.h: Encouragement after a missed date can waive the schedule.
follow_ups.d: Post-delinquency encouragement to continue performing — from someone the contractor reasonably heard as the Government — can waive the delivery schedule, making the original date unenforceable. The cure: re-establish a firm, reasonable delivery date in writing, show-cause framing, restoring an enforceable schedule before any default posture. And the channel lesson rides along: CORs don't direct, and every 'keep going' from now on comes from the CO in writing.

follow_ups.q: Walk the excusability test on the subcontractor's plant fire.
follow_ups.h: Beyond control and without fault — counted twice.
follow_ups.d: A sub's failure excuses the prime only when the cause was beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of BOTH the prime and the subcontractor, AND the supplies weren't obtainable from another source in time. So: was the fire genuinely beyond the sub's control? Did the prime manage the risk — second sources, inventory, diligence? Could substitute generators have been had? Build that record before choosing between default, waiver-repair, or riding out the delay.

scenarios.scenario: A cyber vulnerability in runway-lighting controllers must be patched fleet-wide "within 60 days" per an operational order. One holder on your five-vendor infrastructure MA-indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) built the original controller firmware; the other four have never touched it. The program wants a $1.4M direct task order to the builder today, and asks whether you can "skip the paperwork given the threat."

frameworks.why: Two candidate exceptions: urgency (unacceptable delay in meeting the 60-day order) and only one capable (unique firmware knowledge). Pick the one the facts actually support — probably both braid together here — and write the D&A (over SAT), approved at the right tier ($1.4M → Competition Advocate), posted.
The exception is the paperwork lane — a D&A takes hours, not weeks, when the facts are real. Skipping it converts a defensible urgent award into a finding.
Confirm cyber-patch work is within the IDIQ's scope — an out-of-scope order is a new procurement no exception can save.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) determinations and approvals (D&As), and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a D&A up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: Can you place the $1.4M order directly with the builder — and what paperwork actually stands between you and award?
scenarios.script: This is a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507 — under real urgency. My help: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO), Legal, and the Competition Advocate — because at $1.4M, that's the determination and approval (D&A) approval tier. The default is fair opportunity to all five holders; the exceptions that fit are urgency — the 60-day operational order — and only-one-capable, the original firmware knowledge. The facts braid both, and the D&A gets written on whichever the evidence actually supports, approved at the CA tier and posted. Here's what I'd stress: the paperwork isn't the delay — a same-week D&A is entirely achievable. 'Skip the paperwork' is the only path that actually risks the schedule, because an undocumented direct award invites the ombudsman complaint or protest that stops everything.

follow_ups.q: What are the exceptions to fair opportunity under RFO 16.507-6?
follow_ups.h: Six — and two of them are braided into this scenario.
follow_ups.d: (1) Unacceptable delay in meeting an urgent need; (2) only one awardee capable — unique or highly specialized circumstances; (3) logical follow-on to a fairly competed order; (4) satisfying the minimum guarantee; (5) authorized or required by statute; (6) order-level small business set-aside, which needs no D&A. This scenario braids the first two — the 60-day operational order and the original firmware authorship — and the D&A gets written on whichever the evidence actually carries.

follow_ups.q: Approval and posting for your $1.4M D&A?
follow_ups.h: Same ladder as a justification and approval (J&A) — find the rung.
follow_ups.d: The D&A rides the J&A tiers: contracting officer (CO) to $900K, Competition Advocate above $900K to $20M, head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) to $90M ($150M DoD), senior procurement executive (SPE) above. At $1.4M: the Competition Advocate. Post the redacted D&A to SAM.gov within 14 days of the order — 30 under urgency. A same-week D&A at this tier is entirely achievable, which is the honest answer to 'skip the paperwork.'

follow_ups.q: Why does 16.507 govern here instead of a the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) urgency exception?
follow_ups.h: Orders under existing vehicles are a CICA carve-out.
follow_ups.d: Task and delivery orders under existing IDIQs are one of the lanes where CICA doesn't attach — the SAMO carve-outs: simplified acquisition procedures (SAP), statutory authorities, in-scope mods, and orders under existing vehicles. Competition discipline for orders lives in RFO 16.507 fair opportunity instead — same values, different machinery. Citing 6.103-2 urgency for a task order tells the board you know a name; explaining why 16.507 governs tells them you know the architecture.

scenarios.scenario: During a source selection for base network services, your cost analyst mentions at a staff meeting — with two support contractors in the room — that "the incumbent's past-performance rating came back weaker than expected." Four days later, the incumbent's capture lead emails the program manager (PM) asking to "discuss addressing any performance concerns before final proposal revisions (FPRs)." The PM forwards it to you with: "harmless, they obviously heard nothing specific."

frameworks.why: A past-performance evaluation in an active selection is source selection information; saying it in front of support contractors is a disclosure. Legal now · facts · affidavits on what was heard and where it went · MFR from the analyst · written impact determination.
Evidence the information may have reached an offeror — that's the high-impact branch of the determination (and their "discuss before FPRs" ask is itself an improper exchange to decline in writing).

Impact is determined on the record, not presumed by the PM. If the selection is compromised, the HCA decides the path — and unequal-information problems can force reopened discussions or corrective action.

coach.qtype: a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104: protected information and what its movement does to the competition.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) immediately; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) channel if the procurement is impacted.
coach.rule: RFO 3.104 protects two classes — source selection information and contractor bid/proposal data. Contain first, document everything; the written record closes the incident, not a reply email.

scenarios.ask: The PM says the leak was harmless. Is this a PIA problem, and what do you do about the capture lead's email?
scenarios.script: This is a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104 — and a disclosure has already happened. Legal comes in now; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) channel stands by depending on impact. The facts: a past-performance rating in an active selection is source selection information, and saying it in front of two support contractors is a disclosure — 'harmless' isn't a determination the PM gets to make. Then the email: the capture lead asking to 'address performance concerns before FPRs' is evidence the information may have reached an offeror — the serious branch. So: affidavits on what was heard and where it went, a memorandum for record (MFR) from the analyst, containment, and my written impact determination. If it reached the offeror, the HCA decides how — and whether — this selection proceeds.

follow_ups.q: Walk your response steps, in order.
follow_ups.h: Legal, facts, containment, affidavits, MFR, determination.
follow_ups.d: Notify Legal immediately. Gather the facts and documents — who was in the room, what exactly was said. Contain: the support contractors' firms confirm no further dissemination, with signed affidavits and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs). Get an MFR from the analyst who disclosed. Notify affected parties as Legal advises. Then the written determination: does this disclosure impact the procurement? No impact — the record goes forward for concurrence and the selection proceeds. Impact — the HCA decides: proceed, investigate, cancel, or disqualify.

follow_ups.q: Is a past-performance rating really source selection information?
follow_ups.h: It's an evaluation result in an active selection.
follow_ups.d: Yes. Evaluation results — including past-performance ratings — in an active source selection are squarely protected: information that could give an offeror a competitive edge. That's why every source-selection document carries the SSI cover sheet, why distribution runs through the procuring contracting officer (PCO) as conduit, and why 'it was just one sentence at a staff meeting' doesn't change the analysis. The venue made it a disclosure; the email four days later made it evidence of impact.

follow_ups.q: What obligations attach to the incumbent now that they may hold protected information?
follow_ups.h: Mirror image of the Government's containment.
follow_ups.d: Stop, safeguard, report, and don't use. An offeror that receives protected information must not act on it — and the capture lead's email seeking to 'address performance concerns before FPRs' looks like acting on it, which compounds the violation. Their conduct after receipt becomes evidence in the impact determination: an offeror that reports promptly may survive with mitigation; one that exploits the leak volunteers itself for the disqualification analysis.

scenarios.scenario: A program manager (PM) has $6M of this year's research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E) and wants to start a four-year, ~$40M sensor-fusion prototype effort immediately. Her plan: award the whole effort now, fund it incrementally "as money shows up," and if RDT&E runs short in the out-years, "operation and maintenance (O&M) can cover integration and test since that's kind of operations." She wants the strategy meeting tomorrow.

frameworks.framework: Purpose — the O&M plan fails now
frameworks.why: Development integration and test is development — RDT&E work can't ride O&M "later." Kill that branch in the strategy meeting, on the record.

frameworks.framework: Structure — incremental funding on a cost-type development
frameworks.why: A cost-type effort can be incrementally funded with Limitation of Funds discipline — but the award must match honest funding expectations, and unfunded out-years are program risk to surface, not paper over.
A prototype producing a single outcome leans non-severable — check whether discrete fundable phases (design → build → test) can structure the effort honestly instead.
Hope is not a funding profile — the strategy documents what's programmed, and the contract's ceiling and clauses reflect it.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: Strategy meeting is tomorrow. What do you tell the PM about her funding plan and the award structure?
scenarios.script: This is a fiscal-law question — Purpose under 31 U.S.C. 1301 and the Anti-Deficiency Act — dressed as an acquisition strategy. My help: financial management (FM) and Legal before the meeting, not after. Two rules kill two branches of her plan. Purpose: development integration and test is development — RDT&E work can't ride O&M 'later'; that branch dies in the meeting, on the record. Time and Amount: awarding a four-year, forty-million-dollar effort against six million in hand is an Anti-Deficiency exposure unless the structure honestly matches the money. The lawful shape: a cost-type development effort, incrementally funded under Limitation of Funds discipline, with the contract ceiling and funding schedule stated honestly — or phased awards matched to real appropriations. She can start now; she just can't promise money that doesn't exist yet.

follow_ups.q: Which colors of money, and what clocks run on each?
follow_ups.h: 1, 2, 3, 5 — then five more expired years.
follow_ups.d: O&M — one year for new obligations. RDT&E — two years. Procurement — three. Military construction (MILCON) — five. After the window, funds expire: no new work, but available five more years for adjustments to properly made obligations — claims, terminations, equitable adjustments. Then cancelled: gone for every purpose. Her $6M of current RDT&E has two years of obligational life — the plan's problem is the out-years, not the start.

follow_ups.q: Can integration and test ride O&M in years four and five?
follow_ups.h: Purpose follows the work, not the calendar.
follow_ups.d: No. Integration and test of a developmental system is development — RDT&E work under the Purpose Statute, 31 U.S.C. 1301: funds only for the purposes Congress appropriated. Calling late-stage development 'kind of operations' is a misappropriation exposure, and knowing obligation of the wrong color invites the Anti-Deficiency analysis behind it. That branch of her plan dies in the strategy meeting, on the record — kindly, but dead.

follow_ups.q: So how do you lawfully structure a $40M effort with $6M in hand?
follow_ups.h: Incremental funding with the right clause — and honest ceilings.
follow_ups.d: A cost-type development contract, incrementally funded under Limitation of Funds discipline: the ceiling stated honestly, funding allotted as appropriations arrive, the contractor's 75% notice machinery running, and no obligation ever ahead of or above the money — that's the Antideficiency Act (ADA) guardrail. Or phase the effort into separately funded awards matched to real appropriations. She can start immediately with $6M of honest scope; what she can't do is promise $40M the Treasury hasn't produced.

scenarios.scenario: A $780K interior-renovation contractor opens a wall and finds friable asbestos wrap on piping — none of the specs or drawings mention it. He stops work, photographs everything, notifies you in writing the same day, and states he "cannot finish the job at this price and wants to be paid for work done and released." The customer asks if you can "just make the scope smaller so he finishes the safe rooms and we call it complete."

frameworks.why: Immediate written notice before further disturbance: textbook. The condition (latent, materially different from the documents) supports an equitable adjustment for the changed work — abatement, schedule, price.

A DSC entitles him to an adjustment, not to walk away — performance continues under the adjusted terms once directed. If the Government's need truly changed, we hold the T4C/partial-termination pen, not him.

frameworks.framework: "Shrink the scope, call it complete" — bait, partially
frameworks.why: Descoping is legitimate — as a deliberate partial termination for convenience or deductive change, priced and papered — not as an informal handshake that leaves asbestos in the walls and entitlements unresolved.

coach.qtype: a construction/services question — RFO Parts 36 and 37, with RFO Part 28 bonds: specialized statutory machinery.
coach.smes: Legal, the labor advisor on wage determinations, and the installation civil engineers.
coach.rule: Construction and services run on their own rails: RFO Part 28 bonds over $150K, written notice before disturbing a differing site condition (RFO Part 36), qualifications-based architect-engineer (A&E) selection, and no personal-services drift (RFO Part 37).
coach.cite: RFO Parts 36/37 · Part 28 bonds · Vol. 2, Construction

scenarios.ask: The contractor wants to be paid and released; the customer wants the scope quietly shrunk. What's your ruling on each?
scenarios.script: This is a differing-site-conditions question — the RFO Part 36 clause machinery — and for once, the contractor did everything right. My help: Legal, civil engineering, and the labor advisor on abatement requirements. The rule: a latent condition materially different from the contract documents, with written notice before further disturbance — textbook Type I. That entitles him to an equitable adjustment — abatement, schedule, price — not to walk away; a DSC is not a termination right, and I'd negotiate the adjustment on the documented record. On the customer's idea: quietly descoping to 'call it complete' is a constructive termination for convenience wearing a modification costume — if the Government genuinely wants less work, we do a partial T4C with a proper settlement, honestly labeled. The clause machinery exists so nobody improvises.

follow_ups.q: Type I versus Type II differing site conditions?
follow_ups.h: Differs from the documents, or differs from the ordinary.
follow_ups.d: Type I: subsurface or latent physical conditions differing materially from what the contract documents indicated — asbestos the specs never mentioned, exactly this case. Type II: unknown physical conditions of an unusual nature, differing materially from what's ordinarily encountered in work of this character, even if the documents were silent. Type I turns on the documents; Type II on the ordinary. Both require the written notice before disturbance — which this contractor nailed.

follow_ups.q: What does a DSC actually entitle the contractor to — and what not?
follow_ups.h: An adjustment, not an exit.
follow_ups.d: An equitable adjustment — the cost and time consequences of the changed condition: abatement, resequencing, schedule relief — negotiated on the documented record. It is not a termination right: the contractor continues performing as directed while the adjustment is worked. 'Pay me for work done and release me' is a convenience-termination outcome, and that decision belongs to the Government, not to the discovery.

follow_ups.q: The customer's 'just shrink the scope' idea — what is it really, and how would you do it honestly?
follow_ups.h: Deleting work the Government still wants finished elsewhere has a name.
follow_ups.d: Descoping the contaminated rooms to 'call it complete' is a partial termination for convenience wearing a modification costume — the Government is ending part of the work for its own reasons. Done honestly: a partial T4C with a proper settlement — costs incurred on the terminated portion, reasonable profit on work performed, settlement expenses — or a deductive change honestly negotiated if the work is genuinely no longer needed. The label matters because the settlement machinery and the record follow it.

scenarios.scenario: A wing exercise ends with leadership directing that a contractor-run 'innovation cell' be stood up within 90 days. The program manager (PM) has a vendor in mind ('they briefed us at the symposium'), no requirements document, and asks you to 'start the contract paperwork while we figure out the details.'
baits: The 90-day directive implies urgency that hasn't been tested
'Vendor in mind' before any requirement exists
key_moves: No paperwork starts before a requirement definition — push for the need, outcomes, and an IGCE
Symposium familiarity is not market research — run a real capability look
Directed timelines don't create a competition exception; plan backward from 90 days with the real process

follow_ups.q: What belongs in the requirements conversation?
follow_ups.h: Start with what the Government must hand you before any strategy exists — the thing the seven-step loop begins with.
follow_ups.d: The requirements conversation produces the inputs everything else rides on: what outcomes the cell must deliver, how much of it, by when, measured how — captured in a performance work statement (PWS) or statement of objectives (SOO) — plus an IGCE so price has a yardstick. Without those, there's no market research target, no competition strategy, and no defensible file. A directed vendor and a deadline are inputs to none of it.

follow_ups.q: When would urgency legitimately shortcut competition?
follow_ups.h: Urgency has a legal definition — think about what a 6.103-2 justification must actually quantify.
follow_ups.d: Urgency legitimately shortcuts competition only when the Government would suffer serious harm — mission failure, safety, unacceptable delay quantified in the justification and approval (J&A) — not when leadership set an ambitious date. A self-imposed 90-day goal is planning pressure, not statutory urgency; and even a real urgency J&A requires soliciting as many sources as practical and is limited in duration.

coach.qtype: an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning built on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture, timing, and what the file must prove.
coach.smes: the program manager (PM)/requiring activity, Legal (JA), the Competition Advocate, and your pricing office.
coach.rule: Strategy precedes paper: no solicitation, bridge, or justification and approval (J&A) before the rights-deliverables-market inventory is done — and lack of advance planning never justifies skipping it (RFO Part 6).

scenarios.ask: Leadership wants the innovation cell stood up in 90 days and the PM has a vendor picked. Where do you start?
scenarios.script: This is an acquisition-planning question — RFO Part 7, built on RFO Part 10 research. My help: the PM and requiring activity on outcomes, Legal, and my Small Business Professional once research starts. The default: strategy precedes paper — no vendor conversations, no timeline promises, until a requirement exists. So my first move is the requirements conversation: outcomes, quantities, measures, an independent Government cost estimate (IGCE). Then real market research — a symposium briefing isn't research, it's marketing. On the 90 days: a directed timeline doesn't create urgency under 6.103-2 — urgency is quantified mission harm, and self-imposed deadlines don't qualify. If the date matters, the honest answer is a right-sized initial capability competed quickly, not a sole source justified by the calendar we set ourselves.

scenarios.scenario: A services contract's final option year ends in 10 months. The program office says the follow-on 'will just be the same thing again' and asks you to hold off on strategy work until the new program manager (PM) arrives in the spring — roughly 5 months out.
baits: 'Same thing again' minimizes the strategy work needed
Waiting for the new PM feels reasonable but burns the runway
key_moves: Start now — fresh market research, set-aside look, and requirement scrub take months
A bridge caused by waiting for personnel is a planning failure, not an unforeseen cause
Document the timeline so the record shows deliberate planning

follow_ups.q: What makes a bridge justification valid?
follow_ups.h: Bridges need a cause the Government couldn't foresee. Is a staffing gap one?
follow_ups.d: A valid bridge justification stands on genuinely unforeseen causes — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory shift. Waiting for a new PM to arrive is a staffing choice, fully within the Government's control: a bridge born of it is a planning failure documented in real time, and repeat bridges escalate approval each round. The Decision Memorandum has to name the cause honestly — and 'we waited' won't survive review.

follow_ups.q: What could have changed since last award that invalidates 'the same thing'?
follow_ups.h: Think about everything a fresh strategy would re-test — market, size standards, requirement shape.
follow_ups.d: Since last award: the market may have new entrants (or lost the incumbent's competitors), small-business capability may now satisfy the Rule of Two, thresholds and program rules changed in 2025-2026, the requirement itself may have drifted — new systems, new volumes, changed standards. 'The same thing again' assumes five years of stasis; fresh research and a requirement scrub are how you find out, and both take months you only have if you start now.

coach.qtype: an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning built on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture, timing, and what the file must prove.
coach.smes: the program manager (PM)/requiring activity, Legal (JA), the Competition Advocate, and your pricing office.
coach.rule: Strategy precedes paper: no solicitation, bridge, or justification and approval (J&A) before the rights-deliverables-market inventory is done — and lack of advance planning never justifies skipping it (RFO Part 6).

scenarios.ask: The program says wait five months for the new PM. What do you tell them — and what starts today?
scenarios.script: This is acquisition planning — RFO Part 7 — with an RFO Part 17 options rail. My help: the requiring activity as it stands today, my Small Business Professional, and financial management (FM). The rule I'd anchor: strategy work starts now — ten months is barely enough for research, a set-aside look, and a requirement scrub, and none of it needs the new PM to begin. Waiting five months manufactures a bridge, and a bridge born of waiting for staff is a planning failure, not an unforeseen cause — it won't justify. So today: fresh sources-sought, requirement validation with the current team, timeline documented so the record shows diligence. The new PM inherits a strategy in motion instead of a crisis with his name on it.

scenarios.scenario: A deployed civil engineer emails a portable-generator vendor 'we accept your quote, ship ASAP' to beat a storm window. The units arrive and work perfectly. The vendor invoices $65K. The engineer says exigency justified it and points out the base commander verbally concurred at the time.
baits: Genuine urgency and a good outcome make it feel excusable
Commander concurrence sounds like authority
key_moves: Neither engineers nor commanders hold contracting authority — this is an unauthorized commitment regardless of outcome
Government benefited and price may be fair → ratification package: statement, fund availability at the time, Legal
$65K ≤ SAT → COCO-level ratification; then train the unit on the emergency-buy channels that DO exist

follow_ups.q: Which ratification element most often fails?
follow_ups.h: Six elements — which one turns on money that may or may not have been there in the storm window?
follow_ups.d: The element that most often fails is funds availability — then and now. Benefit is usually obvious (the Government used the generators), the price is often supportable, and the proper-if-a-CO-had-done-it test usually passes. But if no funds were available at the time of the commitment, ratification cannot cure it — that's an Anti-Deficiency problem wearing a UAC costume, and it escalates rather than resolves.

follow_ups.q: What lawful rapid-buy tools existed for the storm?
follow_ups.h: The storm didn't require an unauthorized email — what lawful fast lanes existed?
follow_ups.d: Real rapid tools existed: the Government Purchase Card (GPC) up to the micro-purchase threshold (MPT) for fragments genuinely under it, an oral/letter authorization through an actual CO on emergency footing, existing blanket purchase agreements (BPAs) or indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) vehicles with same-day ordering, and — for true operational exigency — the contingency thresholds. The lesson the panel wants: speed never requires bypassing authority; it requires knowing which lawful fast lane fits before the storm, which is a training point for that unit.

coach.qtype: an authority question — RFO 1.402 warrant authority and the RFO 1.405 ratification lane: who can bind the Government, and what happens when someone who can't, did.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) first, your chief of the contracting office (COCO)/flight chief, and financial management (FM) for the funds picture.
coach.rule: Only a warranted contracting officer (CO) binds the Government (RFO 1.402). Apparent authority binds nothing — an unauthorized commitment stays unratified until an official with actual authority runs all six RFO 1.405 elements.

scenarios.ask: The vendor wants $65K and the engineer says exigency covers it. Is the Government bound — and what now?
scenarios.script: This is an authority question — an RFO 1.405 unauthorized commitment with good intentions. My help: Legal first, financial management (FM) on the funds timeline, then the ratifying official. The rule: engineers don't hold contracting authority, and exigency doesn't create it — the Government isn't bound until an official with actual authority ratifies. The path: stop anything ongoing, gather the record — the engineer's statement, the storm timeline, receipt and use of the units — then run the elements: proper if a contracting officer (CO) had done it, benefit received, fair and reasonable price, and the one that decides most cases: funds available then and now. At $65K, ratification sits at the chief of the contracting office (COCO) level. Then prevention: that unit gets trained on the lawful rapid-buy tools they actually had.

scenarios.scenario: Reviewing invoices, you find a contractor billing 15% over the award for 'verbal expansions approved by the site lead' across six months — small additions each time, all documented in the contractor's notes but never in a mod. The site lead says 'that's how we've always flexed the work.'
baits: 'How we've always done it' normalizes the violation
Small increments hide the cumulative problem
key_moves: Site leads don't direct work — stop the practice in writing immediately
Sort what happened: unauthorized new work (ratification lane) vs. Government-directed changes to existing work (constructive change/REA lane)
Fix the channel: all direction through the PCO, and brief both the site and the contractor

follow_ups.q: How do you distinguish ratification from constructive change here?
follow_ups.h: One lane is for brand-new work nobody authorized; the other is for Government conduct that changed existing work.
follow_ups.d: Ratification handles unauthorized NEW work — a commitment someone without authority made that the Government must now decide to adopt. Constructive change handles Government CONDUCT that altered existing contract work without formal direction — entitlement flows through the Changes clause via an REA. Here, each 'expansion' gets sorted: additions outside the contract's scope go down the ratification lane; directed alterations to in-scope work are constructive-change candidates. The sorting determines who approves what and which money pays.

follow_ups.q: What does the cumulative 15% do to your scope analysis?
follow_ups.h: Small changes, judged one at a time, are how contracts drift — what's the cumulative test?
follow_ups.d: Scope is judged against the original contract with all changes cumulative — not increment by increment. Fifteen percent growth through undocumented verbal direction may still be in scope, but it's unexamined scope: the four corners (competition anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost) have to be run on the total. And the process failure is its own finding: changes that never became mods mean the contract file no longer describes the contract being performed.

coach.qtype: an authority question — RFO 1.402 warrant authority and the RFO 1.405 ratification lane: who can bind the Government, and what happens when someone who can't, did.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) first, your chief of the contracting office (COCO)/flight chief, and financial management (FM) for the funds picture.
coach.rule: Only a warranted contracting officer (CO) binds the Government (RFO 1.402). Apparent authority binds nothing — an unauthorized commitment stays unratified until an official with actual authority runs all six RFO 1.405 elements.

scenarios.ask: Fifteen percent of unbilled 'verbal expansions' just surfaced. How do you sort this out?
scenarios.script: This is an authority-and-scope question — RFO 1.405 ratification sorted against RFO Part 43 constructive change. My help: Legal, the site's chain, and the contractor's own records — which, notably, are better than ours. First move: stop the practice in writing today — site leads don't direct work, and every future need routes through me. Then sort six months of history into its lanes: unauthorized new work goes down the ratification path; Government-directed changes to existing work are constructive-change candidates handled as requests for equitable adjustment (REAs). Then the scope check: fifteen percent cumulative growth gets tested against the original award, all four corners. The contractor performed in good faith and documented everything — that helps them and shames us. The fix is channel discipline and a file that matches reality again.

scenarios.scenario: During proposal evaluations, a source selection evaluation board (SSEB) member's spouse posts on LinkedIn congratulating her company — one of the offerors — on 'great momentum on the base network bid.' The evaluator swears he's never discussed the source selection at home and offers to keep evaluating 'since nothing actually leaked.'
baits: 'Nothing actually leaked' — unproven and not his call
The post may be innocent, making inaction feel safe
key_moves: Report to Legal now — the question is what protected information was accessible and whether any moved
The evaluator's continued participation is a decision for the PCO/SSA with Legal, not a self-assessment
Document the facts and the determination whichever way it lands

follow_ups.q: What's protected under 3.104?
follow_ups.h: Two categories, RFO 3.104 — one belongs to the Government, one to the offerors.
follow_ups.d: Protected classes: source selection information — rankings, evaluation results, the source selection plan, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate — and contractor bid and proposal information. The spouse's post suggests offeror awareness of momentum, which is why the question isn't the evaluator's intent but what information was accessible in his position and whether any of it could have moved. The PIA reaches attempts and appearances, not just proven leaks.

follow_ups.q: When does an appearance problem become a disqualification problem?
follow_ups.h: Recusal instincts are personal; disqualification decisions are institutional.
follow_ups.d: An appearance problem becomes a disqualification problem when a reasonable observer, knowing the facts, would doubt the integrity of the process — a spouse employed by an offeror, posting about the very competition, sits close to that line. The evaluator doesn't get to self-assess; the procuring contracting officer (PCO) and SSA, with Legal, decide his continued participation based on documented facts: what he accessed, when the spouse's role began, what controls existed. Document the decision either way — the record is the defense.

coach.qtype: a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104: protected information and what its movement does to the competition.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) immediately; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) channel if the procurement is impacted.
coach.rule: RFO 3.104 protects two classes — source selection information and contractor bid/proposal data. Contain first, document everything; the written record closes the incident, not a reply email.

scenarios.ask: The evaluator swears nothing was discussed. Does he stay on the SSEB — and who decides?
scenarios.script: This is a Procurement Integrity question — RFO 3.104 — about appearance and access. My help: Legal now, and the source selection authority (SSA) on team composition. The rule: protected information includes evaluation results and rankings, and the Procurement Integrity Act (PIA) cares about access and appearances, not just intent — his sincerity isn't the test. So: report it, establish the facts — what he accessed, when the spouse's employment began, whether any protected information could have moved — and make the participation decision at my level with the SSA and Legal, not his. If the appearance can't be cured, he comes off the board and evaluations he touched get reviewed. And the team gets re-briefed: the next LinkedIn post shouldn't be how we find out.

scenarios.scenario: A week before award, an offeror's VP calls your chief of the contracting office (COCO): 'We heard we're rated second on past performance — we'd like to submit supplemental references.' Nobody outside the team should know any ratings. The COCO wants to 'just decline the references and move on quietly.'
baits: Declining the references feels like it contains the problem
'Move on quietly' avoids schedule pain
key_moves: The call itself is evidence protected information leaked TO an offeror — the serious branch of PIA
Legal immediately; trace the leak; written impact determination — quiet handling creates the protest AND the scandal
Decline the references in writing as an improper exchange, but that's the smallest part of the response

follow_ups.q: Who decides whether the procurement proceeds?
follow_ups.h: Impact on the procurement moves this above the procuring contracting officer's (PCO) desk.
follow_ups.d: The PCO owns the investigation and the written impact determination — but when a disclosure has reached an offeror and may have compromised the competition, the proceed/cancel/disqualify decision belongs to the HCA, with Legal driving the analysis. Quiet local handling is exactly how a curable incident becomes a sustained protest: the venue for 'does this competition survive' is above the person who ran it.

follow_ups.q: What are the offeror's obligations when it receives protected info?
follow_ups.h: The offeror holding Government information has duties too — think mirror image of the Government's containment.
follow_ups.d: An offeror that receives protected information must stop, safeguard it, report the receipt, and not use it — continuing to act on it (like sending supplemental references shaped by a known rating) compounds the violation. Their conduct after receipt becomes evidence: an offeror that reported promptly may survive with mitigation; one that exploited the leak has volunteered itself for disqualification analysis.

coach.qtype: a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104: protected information and what its movement does to the competition.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) immediately; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) channel if the procurement is impacted.
coach.rule: RFO 3.104 protects two classes — source selection information and contractor bid/proposal data. Contain first, document everything; the written record closes the incident, not a reply email.

scenarios.ask: An offeror just told your COCO their own second-place rating. What has to happen before this award can proceed?
scenarios.script: This is the serious branch of an RFO 3.104 Procurement Integrity question — protected information reached an offeror. My help: Legal immediately; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns the big decision. The facts: ratings are source selection information, and the VP's call is evidence of a leak — declining the references doesn't un-ring it. So: containment and tracing — who knew that rating, who talked; affidavits; the offeror gets written direction on its obligations — safeguard, don't use, report. Then my written impact determination, and because this reached an offeror, the proceed-or-not decision goes to the HCA with the full record. What I won't do is handle it quietly — quiet handling converts a recoverable incident into the protest that ends the program.

scenarios.scenario: Your engineering-support contractor is helping the program office draft test criteria for an upcoming production competition. You learn the contractor's parent company just acquired one of the likely production bidders. The contractor proposes a firewall memo: separate teams, separate buildings, no shared drives.
baits: The firewall sounds robust and proactive
The acquisition just happened — 'nothing improper occurred yet'
key_moves: Test criteria authorship for a competition your affiliate will enter = biased ground rules — the hardest OCI to mitigate
Firewalls address information flow, not ground rules already being shaped — likely remedy is removing the contractor from the criteria work or excluding the affiliate
PCO decides, Legal advises, before the solicitation moves

follow_ups.q: Why don't firewalls fix biased ground rules?
follow_ups.h: A firewall controls where information goes. What did the conflicted work already shape?
follow_ups.d: Firewalls address information FLOW — unequal access. Biased ground rules is a different disease: the requirement itself has been shaped by a party with a stake in the outcome, and no wall un-writes test criteria already drafted. The influence is baked into the documents every competitor will be measured against, which is why exclusion, not mitigation, is the usual outcome — and why the panel calls it the hardest OCI type.

follow_ups.q: What would a valid path look like if the Government wants the affiliate to compete?
follow_ups.h: Fixing this means changing who authored what — or what gets authored.
follow_ups.d: A valid path re-establishes untainted ground rules: remove the contractor from criteria work now, have the Government (or a conflict-free party) independently develop or scrub the test criteria, document what the affiliate's people touched, and only then let the affiliate compete on requirements it demonstrably didn't shape. If the criteria can't be untangled from the conflicted authorship, exclusion stands — the waiver lane (HCA, non-delegable) exists but is for cases where the benefit demonstrably outweighs the taint.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any waiver, non-delegable.
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written.

scenarios.ask: The contractor proposes a firewall and the affiliate wants to bid. What's your call?
scenarios.script: This is an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5 biased ground rules, the hardest type. My help: Legal, the organizational conflict of interest (OCI) review chain, and the head of the contracting activity (HCA) if anyone breathes the word waiver. The rule: type drives remedy. A firewall manages information flow — it does nothing about test criteria the contractor is drafting for a competition its new affiliate will enter; that influence is already in the documents. So: the contractor comes off the criteria work now, the Government independently develops or scrubs what they touched, and the record documents exactly what their people authored. If the affiliate wants to compete, it competes on ground rules it provably didn't shape. And the final decision on any mitigation plan is mine as the procuring contracting officer (PCO) — panels advise, I own it.

scenarios.scenario: On your advisory and assistance services (A&AS) multiple-award indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ), Holder A's analysts maintain the program's requirements database. A new task order competition opens to all five holders — and Holder A's proposal cites specific unfunded requirements from that database as 'anticipated growth' no other holder mentions.
baits: Holder A did nothing overtly wrong — they used what they knew
The insight makes their proposal genuinely better
key_moves: Unequal access to non-public information — no bad act required; the imbalance is the conflict
Options: neutralize (share the same data with all holders and allow revisions) or address Holder A's access in the evaluation, with Legal
Fix the structure: database-support roles need OCI clauses and data walls before the next competition

follow_ups.q: Can you cure this mid-competition? How?
follow_ups.h: Mid-competition cures level the field — what levels information?
follow_ups.d: Yes — the classic cure for unequal access is equal access: release the same database extract (scrubbed appropriately) to all five holders, extend the response date, and allow proposal revisions so everyone competes on the same picture. Alternatives: neutralize Holder A's advantage by excluding the tainted content from evaluation, or in a bad case exclude Holder A from this order. Document whichever cure you pick and why it restores fairness — the record is what survives the ombudsman.

follow_ups.q: What contract language prevents this on support task orders?
follow_ups.h: The fix for next time lives in the support task order's own terms.
follow_ups.d: Support task orders should carry OCI clauses tailored to the access the work creates: firewall and nondisclosure obligations, restrictions on using program information in the holder's own proposals, screening or recusal duties when competitions open, and — where the access is structural — an agreed mitigation plan as a condition of the support work. The time to price and paper those terms is when the support order is placed, not when the first tainted proposal arrives.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any waiver, non-delegable.
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written.

scenarios.ask: Holder A's proposal is quoting the requirements database it maintains. Can this competition proceed?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 9.5 organizational conflict of interest (OCI) question inside an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity competition — unequal access to nonpublic information. My help: Legal and the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO). The rule: the imbalance is the conflict — Holder A citing unfunded requirements from a database it maintains for the Government is competing on information the other four holders can't see. No bad act required. The cure that keeps the competition alive: give everyone the same picture — release the scrubbed data to all holders, extend the clock, allow revisions. If the taint runs deeper, neutralize or exclude, documented. And going forward, the support order itself gets OCI terms — firewalls, use restrictions, screening duties — because this conflict was foreseeable the day we let a holder run the requirements database.

scenarios.scenario: Your apparent awardee on a $700K paving contract lists an office address that turns out to be a mailbox store, has no equipment in its own name ('we lease everything per job'), and its listed superintendent also appears full-time on another company's website. Price is excellent and references check out by phone.
baits: Good references and price pull toward award
Leasing equipment is legitimately common in construction
key_moves: Run the standards on facts: organization, equipment access, key personnel actually available — a pre-award survey fits here
Leasing is fine IF the lease commitments are real — ask for them
If it nets to non-responsible and they're small: SBA referral for the CoC decision, not a quiet pass-over

follow_ups.q: Which of the seven standards are in play?
follow_ups.h: Map each fact to a standard: organization, equipment, personnel.
follow_ups.d: In play: adequate organization and experience (a mailbox office and no visible operation), necessary equipment and facilities or the ability to obtain them (leasing is legitimate — IF lease commitments exist for this job), and key personnel actually available (a superintendent already employed full-time elsewhere fails the availability test unless there's a real transition plan). None of these facts is disqualifying alone; each demands verification. A pre-award survey is the right tool at this dollar value and doubt level.

follow_ups.q: What does a CoC do to your determination?
follow_ups.h: The referral is mandatory; the certificate is conclusive.
follow_ups.d: If the offeror is small and you determine non-responsibility, the referral to SBA is mandatory — and a Certificate of Competency, if SBA issues one, conclusively establishes responsibility: you award. The contracting officer's (CO) protection then shifts to administration — surveillance, milestones, early engagement. Appeal paths exist in a dollar band (roughly $100K to $25M) but are worked through channels with Legal and SBA, not unilaterally.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Mailbox address, leased-everything, moonlighting superintendent. Award, or not — and on what?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards on today's documented facts. My help: my chain, a pre-award survey, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) if this goes where it might. The rule: doubt cuts in the Government's favor, but doubt must stand on facts, so I verify before I judge: demand the equipment lease commitments for this job, the superintendent's actual availability and transition plan, and evidence of an operating organization behind the mailbox. Leasing is a legitimate model — undocumented leasing is not. If the facts hold up, award. If they don't, non-responsibility on the standards — and because they're small, mandatory referral to SBA, whose Certificate of Competency, if issued, I honor and then protect the Government through hard-nosed administration.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor you terminated for default eight months ago is the apparent low offeror on a new solicitation — bidding through a newly formed LLC with the same owners, same address, and a fresh Commercial and Government Entity (CAGE) code. Your evaluator says 'new entity, clean slate, we can't hold the past against them.'
baits: 'New entity' formalism
Fear that considering history is prejudice
key_moves: Responsibility looks through paper: same owners and operations means the performance and integrity record follows them
The T4D is exactly the kind of documented history the standards exist to weigh — considering it is the job, not prejudice
Document the affiliation facts; if small and heading to 'no,' SBA referral still applies

follow_ups.q: What distinguishes a legitimate fresh start from evasion?
follow_ups.h: What separates reorganization from costume change?
follow_ups.d: A legitimate fresh start shows substantive change: new capital, new management, corrected root causes of the failure, and a track record — however short — under the new structure. Evasion shows continuity wearing new paper: same owners, same operations, same address, new CAGE code. Responsibility looks through the paper to the people and the operation; a shell that exists to shed a default record is itself an integrity fact under the standards.

follow_ups.q: What system checks reveal the connection?
follow_ups.h: The systems are built for exactly this connection — think beyond a clean SAM search on the new name.
follow_ups.d: FAPIIS and CPARS searched by the principals, not just the entity; SAM exclusion records checked against owners and key individuals (exclusions attach to people too); state incorporation records showing officers and addresses; and the prior contract file itself. A new CAGE code resets none of it. Over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), the FAPIIS review is mandatory — and the connection this scenario hands you is precisely what that review exists to surface.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the Small Business Administration (SBA) — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Same owners, new LLC, low offer. Does the default history follow them?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — RFO 9.104 — about continuity. My help: Legal and the record systems — the Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System (FAPIIS), the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS), SAM, searched by the people, not just the new entity. The rule: responsibility looks through paper. Same owners, same address, same operations means the performance and integrity record follows them — my own termination for default (T4D) eight months ago is exactly the documented history the standards exist to weigh. 'New entity, clean slate' is true for the CAGE code and false for the humans. So: evaluate the fresh-start claim on substance — new capital, new management, root causes fixed — and if it's a costume, determine non-responsibility on documented facts. If they're small, the Small Business Administration (SBA) referral follows. What doesn't happen is the low price laundering the history.

scenarios.scenario: For a niche electronic-warfare training service, your sources-sought draws zero responses. The program manager (PM) takes it as proof only the incumbent can perform and asks you to start the justification and approval (J&A). The notice ran 10 days over a holiday period, used the program's internal acronym in the title, and posted under a generic North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).
baits: Zero responses looks like market absence
The PM's conclusion matches what the program wants anyway
key_moves: Zero responses to a badly shaped notice proves nothing — fix the title, NAICS, period, and do direct outreach
A J&A built on defective research is protest bait — the market-research section is its spine
Document round two either way; absence must be demonstrated, not inferred

follow_ups.q: What makes a sources-sought effective?
follow_ups.h: A notice nobody qualified could find proves what, exactly?
follow_ups.d: An effective sources-sought is findable and answerable: right NAICS and product service code (PSC) codes, a title that says what the work is, a response window that doesn't die over a holiday, a description with enough substance to let a capable firm self-identify, and direct outreach to the firms research already suggests. Zero responses to a mis-coded, badly-timed notice measures the notice, not the market — and a J&A whose market-research section rests on it inherits the defect.

follow_ups.q: How much research is enough for a $10M sole source?
follow_ups.h: Scale the evidence to a $10M sole-source claim.
follow_ups.d: For a $10M sole source, the research has to support the strongest claim in contracting: nobody else can do this. That means a properly shaped notice AND direct industry outreach, trade channels, adjacent-NAICS sweeps, other services' experience, and documented conversations — an effort a competitor's lawyer will read line by line. The J&A's market-research section is its spine; thin research is the number-one way sole-source justifications die at review or protest.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's subject-matter experts (SMEs), your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, request for informations (RFIs), industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001 treats it as current for 18 months.

scenarios.ask: Zero responses, and the PM wants the J&A started. Is the market really empty?
scenarios.script: This is a market-research question — RFO Part 10 — and the evidence doesn't say what the PM thinks it says. My help: my Small Business Professional, industry channels, and the requiring activity to fix the requirement description. The rule: research is the evidence; the J&A is a conclusion the evidence must earn. Zero responses to a notice with the wrong codes, a holiday window, and a vague title proves the notice failed — not that the market is empty. So: reshape and rerun it — right NAICS, real title, adequate window — plus direct outreach to plausible performers. If genuine absence emerges, the J&A writes itself on solid ground. If competition surfaces, we just avoided a protest. Either way, the file shows we measured the market, not our own noise.

scenarios.scenario: The program wants a custom-built environmental test chamber and has written a 40-page spec. Your research finds three commercial chamber makers whose catalog units meet every parameter except one vibration profile — which two vendors say they routinely add as a factory option.
baits: The 40-page spec presumes custom development
'Except one parameter' feels like disqualification
key_moves: Research exists to reshape requirements: a catalog unit plus a routine factory option is likely a commercial product with minor modification
Rewrite toward performance terms; a commercial determination unlocks Part 12 streamlining
Document the comparison analysis — it becomes the CID's core

follow_ups.q: What makes a modification 'minor'?
follow_ups.h: Minor is measured against form, fit, and function — not against effort.
follow_ups.d: A modification is minor when it doesn't alter the item's essential form, fit, or function — the chamber still does what commercial chambers do, in the same envelope, the same way. A factory-offered vibration option two vendors already sell is close to definitionally minor: it's within the product line's normal configuration space. The determination is a facts-and-engineering call documented in the CID, not a gut call — and 'we wrote a 40-page spec' doesn't make an item noncommercial.

follow_ups.q: What does Part 12 change about this buy?
follow_ups.h: Part 12 changes the data you can demand, the clauses, and the termination machinery.
follow_ups.d: Commercial procedures mean: no certified cost or pricing data (price on market evidence — catalogs, competition among the three makers), streamlined commercial terms with a firm-fixed-price (FFP) preference, customary commercial data rights only, and termination under the commercial clause rather than Part 49. Under the $9M streamlined ceiling this buy moves fast. The trade: less Government-unique protection — which is exactly right for a catalog product with three competing makers.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's subject-matter experts (SMEs), your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, request for informations (RFIs), industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001 treats it as current for 18 months.

scenarios.ask: Three catalog makers cover everything but one vibration profile. Custom build, or commercial with a mod?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 10 market-research question that becomes an RFO 2.101 commerciality call. My help: the program engineers, my pricing office, and the commercial item determination (CID) approver one level up. The rule: research exists to reshape requirements, not just to document them. Three catalog makers cover every parameter but one vibration profile — and two offer that profile as a factory option. That's a commercial product with a minor modification: form, fit, and function unchanged. So I'd push the requirement toward performance terms, write the CID on the comparison analysis, and compete it among the three makers under commercial procedures — market pricing, no certified data, fast. The 40-page custom spec buys a slower, costlier chamber and a thinner industrial base. The catalog buys the mission.

scenarios.scenario: A unit orders custodial supplies monthly from a commercial e-commerce site using the Government Purchase Card (GPC) because 'it's cheaper than the mandatory source and delivery is faster.' Annual spend across the unit: about $140K, in individual orders that never top $3K.
baits: Each swipe is legitimately under the MPT
Cheaper-and-faster feels like good stewardship
key_moves: Mandatory sources (AbilityOne procurement-list items especially) aren't price-optional — check what's actually covered
$140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing 50 swipes — structure it (BPA/consolidated buy) through the source ladder
Fix the unit's process, not just this order

follow_ups.q: Walk the supplies priority ladder
follow_ups.h: Walk it: what the Government owns, then statute, then schedules, then market.
follow_ups.d: Supplies ladder, in order: existing Government inventory; excess from other agencies; Federal Prison Industries (UNICOR); AbilityOne procurement-list items; wholesale sources; mandatory Federal Supply Schedules; then the commercial market. Each rung is checked and documented before moving past it — and for procurement-list items, AbilityOne isn't a suggestion. Price alone never unlocks the next rung; fit and availability problems are worked through the program channels, on the record.

follow_ups.q: When does GPC use become splitting?
follow_ups.h: Fifty swipes, one predictable annual demand — what's the requirement, really?
follow_ups.d: Splitting happens whenever a known requirement is fragmented to stay under a threshold — intent to evade isn't required for the pattern to be a violation. $140K of predictable custodial demand is one annual requirement; buying it as 50 GPC swipes both evades the MPT and bypasses the mandatory sources. The structural fix: a BPA or purchase-order arrangement against the right source, sized to the real annual demand, with the GPC reserved for genuine micro-purchases.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries) program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The unit says the e-commerce site is cheaper and faster than the mandatory source. What do you fix, and how?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 8 required-sources question compounded by RFO Part 13 splitting. My help: the GPC program coordinator, the AbilityOne program office, and my policy shop. Two rules: the supplies ladder is mandatory and runs in priority order — and price alone doesn't unlock the open market; if these items sit on the procurement list, AbilityOne is the source, cheaper e-commerce notwithstanding. Second: $140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing fifty swipes — that's splitting, and it evades both the micro-purchase threshold (MPT) and the mandatory sources. The fix: structure the real demand into a blanket purchase agreement (BPA) or purchase orders against the correct source, retrain the unit's cardholders, and document the transition. Faster delivery is a requirement to work through the program — not a license to shop.

scenarios.scenario: Your customer wants specific network switches 'exactly like the General Services Administration (GSA) Advantage shows, from Vendor Q's schedule listing, $290K.' A quick eBuy check shows four other schedule holders carry the same original equipment manufacturer (OEM) line, two with published prices 6-9% lower.
baits: 'GSA already negotiated the price' — schedule fair-and-reasonable ≠ order fair-and-reasonable
The customer's vendor preference
key_moves: On schedules, the ordering CO still determines the order price fair and reasonable — compare holders, seek discounts
Four holders with the same line = easy comparison; document the quotes and the basis
Vendor preference without a differentiator is steering

follow_ups.q: What does GSA's determination actually cover?
follow_ups.h: GSA priced the schedule; who prices the order?
follow_ups.d: GSA's determination establishes schedule-level ceiling prices as fair and reasonable — for the schedule, not for your order. The ordering contracting officer (CO) independently determines the ORDER price fair and reasonable: comparing holders carrying the same line, seeking discounts (schedule prices are ceilings, discounts are expected), and documenting the comparison. Four holders with published prices 6-9% apart is a comparison begging to be run.

follow_ups.q: When can you limit consideration to one schedule holder?
follow_ups.h: Limiting sources on a schedule buy has its own justification lane.
follow_ups.d: An order can be limited to one schedule holder only on a documented basis — a logical follow-on to a schedule order, urgency, only-one-holder-carries-it, or an item peculiar to one vendor — written and kept in the file (the schedule equivalent of a brand-name justification). 'The customer likes Vendor Q's listing' isn't a basis. When multiple holders carry the same OEM line, competition among them is both the default and the easiest path to a defensible price.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries) program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The customer wants Vendor Q's listing bought as-is at $290K. What does a defensible schedule order look like?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 8 schedules question about what GSA's pricing actually covers. My help: the schedules' eBuy tools and my own comparison file. The rule: GSA established schedule-level prices as fair and reasonable — the order-level determination is mine, and it doesn't come free with the listing. Four holders carry the same OEM line, two visibly cheaper. So: request for quotations (RFQ) among the holders, seek discounts — schedule prices are ceilings, not floors — and document the comparison as my price analysis. If the customer wants Vendor Q specifically, that takes a written justification naming a real basis, and 'we liked their listing' isn't one. Ten minutes of eBuy competition is the difference between a defensible order and a $290K habit.

scenarios.scenario: A vendor proposes its 'commercially available' logistics-analytics platform for $4.2M. Digging in: the platform has one prior sale — to a foreign navy — and the proposal's 'catalog' was created last month. The vendor stresses the underlying database engine is genuinely commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) with millions of users.
baits: The genuinely-COTS engine launders the whole platform
A 'catalog' document exists
key_moves: Commerciality is determined at the level of what you're buying — the platform, not its ingredients
One military sale + a fresh catalog ≠ sold to the general public; the assertion likely fails
Component-level analysis may still except real COTS pieces; the rest needs data to price

follow_ups.q: What evidence establishes 'of a type' sold commercially?
follow_ups.h: 'Of a type' still needs a market — whose purchases prove one exists?
follow_ups.d: Evidence that establishes commerciality: actual sales, leases, or licenses to the GENERAL PUBLIC — commercial customers, at market prices, in ordinary volumes — or an item evolved from such a product and available in time. Catalogs corroborate; they don't substitute. One sale to a foreign navy is a government sale, and a catalog created last month for this proposal is advocacy, not evidence. The determination is the Government's, made on the record the vendor supplies — and the burden of supporting the assertion sits with the vendor.

follow_ups.q: What data can you demand if it's non-commercial?
follow_ups.h: Non-commercial at $4.2M sole source — what does the pricing lane become?
follow_ups.d: If the item is non-commercial, the Part 12 shortcuts fall away: at $4.2M the action is above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) but below the certified-data trigger, so you demand data other than certified cost or pricing data — cost element detail, sales history, supporting quotes — sufficient for a fair-and-reasonable determination, with price analysis always and cost analysis as needed. The vendor's refusal to provide adequate data becomes its own answer: no data, no deal.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the commercial item determination (CID), and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: One foreign military sale and a month-old catalog. Does the commercial assertion survive — and what happens to the buy either way?
scenarios.script: This is a commerciality question — RFO 2.101 — and the Government makes the call, not the proposal. My help: my pricing office, Legal, and the commercial item determination (CID) approver one level up. The rule: commercial means sold, leased, or licensed to the general public — or evolved and available in time. One sale to a foreign navy is a government sale; a catalog created last month is a prop. On these facts the assertion likely fails, and my CID says so with the comparison analysis written down. Then the buy continues honestly: non-commercial, $4.2M, sole source — I demand data other than certified sufficient to price it, run price analysis plus cost analysis as needed, and if the vendor won't support its own price, that refusal is my answer. No data, no deal.

scenarios.scenario: A commercial-items contract for fleet telematics is going badly — units fail in cold weather. The program manager (PM) asks you to 'send a cure notice and start the termination for default (T4D) like we did on the radar contract.' The contract was awarded under Part 12 with the standard commercial clause.
