baits: The radar-contract playbook feels transferable
'Cure notice / T4D' vocabulary is muscle memory
key_moves: Part 49 machinery doesn't run commercial contracts — the commercial clause's termination-for-cause framework does
Rights and remedies come from the clause: notice, opportunity, cause standards — with Legal on the specifics
The performance record and re-procurement logic still matter; the procedure differs

follow_ups.q: How does termination-for-cause differ from T4D in effect?
follow_ups.h: Same failure, different clause — what machinery actually runs a Part 12 contract?
follow_ups.d: Termination for cause under the commercial clause reaches the same destination as T4D — the Government doesn't pay for nonconforming performance and can pursue reprocurement exposure — but the road differs: rights and procedures come from the commercial clause itself (notice, opportunity consistent with commercial practice), not Part 49's cure/show-cause machinery. Citing 49.x procedures on a commercial contract invites the conversion argument that the termination itself was procedurally defective.

follow_ups.q: What does the Government owe on a commercial convenience termination?
follow_ups.h: Commercial convenience settlements are narrower than Part 49's.
follow_ups.d: On a commercial termination for convenience, the Government owes the percentage of work performed at the contract price plus reasonable charges resulting from the termination — a leaner formula than Part 49's cost-plus-settlement machinery, with no anticipatory profit either way. The contractor's records support the charges. Knowing the two formulas apart — and which contract carries which — is precisely the seam this scenario tests.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the commercial item determination (CID), and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: The PM wants a cure notice and a T4D 'like the radar contract.' What's different here?
scenarios.script: This is a terminations question on a commercial contract — RFO 12.403 territory, not RFO Part 49 — and the seam is the whole answer. My help: Legal before any notice, and the contracting officer's representative's (COR) cold-weather failure record. The rule: Part 49 doesn't run Part 12 contracts. The commercial clause's own framework does — termination for cause for the failures, with notice consistent with its terms, or convenience under its leaner settlement formula. So: document the cold-weather failures against the requirement, give the clause's notice honestly, and if we terminate for cause, do it under the right authority with the right words — because citing 49.x machinery on a commercial award hands the contractor a procedural-defect argument. Same destination as the radar contract; different road, and the road matters.

scenarios.scenario: An exercise planner needs 30 days of portable toilets, fencing, and light towers across three sites — about $120K total. A staff sergeant already collected one quote per item from 'the companies we used last year' and asks you to cut three POs today so setup can start Monday.
baits: Pre-collected single quotes feel like completed legwork
Monday deadline
key_moves: The band is small-business reserved — confirm the vendors' size or solicit competitors
One quote per item at $120K needs price-reasonableness support: add quotes or comparison evidence fast
SAP can absolutely hit Monday — done properly it's hours, not weeks

follow_ups.q: How many quotes is 'enough' under SAP?
follow_ups.h: SAP wants promoting competition 'to the maximum extent practicable' — what does that mean at $120K?
follow_ups.d: There's no statutory quote count — the standard is promoting competition to the maximum extent practicable and, always, a supportable price-reasonableness determination. At $120K, one quote per item from last year's vendors is thin: solicit at least a few capable sources per item (the band is small-business reserved), or support the single quotes with real comparison evidence — history, catalogs, independent Government cost estimate (IGCE). The documentation, not a magic number, is what defends the award.

follow_ups.q: Could a BPA serve the recurring exercise cycle?
follow_ups.h: Same sites, same gear, every exercise cycle — what structure fits recurring demand?
follow_ups.d: Yes — a BPA against the recurring exercise cycle: negotiated up front with one or more small-business sources, priced terms, then each exercise's needs placed as fast calls without re-soliciting. It converts an annual fire drill into an account with discipline — and the calls stay inside the BPA's scope and the band's rules. The structural fix is what prevents next year's staff sergeant from collecting one quote per item under deadline.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your Government Purchase Card (GPC) program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and chief of the contracting office (COCO).
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: One quote per item, award by Friday. What does this buy actually need?
scenarios.script: This is a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13. My help: my Small Business Professional and the exercise planners on the real recurring demand. The rules: the micro-purchase threshold (MPT)-to-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) band is reserved for small business — so the first check is the vendors' size status — and price reasonableness rides on evidence, not on Friday. One quote per item at $120K is thin: I'd quickly solicit competitors or support the quotes with history and catalog comparisons; simplified acquisition procedures (SAP) is streamlined, not standard-free. Then the structural answer: this same requirement recurs every exercise cycle, so it belongs on a blanket purchase agreement (BPA) — negotiated once, called quickly forever after. That's how Friday deadlines stop producing one-quote files.

scenarios.scenario: September 28th. A flight has $47K of expiring operation and maintenance (O&M) and a wish list: two years of software licenses ($22K), a training course occurring in November ($9K), and 'stocking up' on toner and cables ($16K). 'Just get it obligated by Friday.'
baits: Everything is under the SAT so it feels easy
Use-or-lose framing
key_moves: Two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — current-year period only
November training: bona fide need analysis (when does the need arise?) with FM
Reasonable stock replenishment is fine; hoarding isn't — document the consumption basis

follow_ups.q: When can a current-year obligation serve next-year performance?
follow_ups.h: The question is when the need arises, not when the money dies.
follow_ups.d: A current-year obligation serves next-year performance only when the need is bona fide to the current year: severable services within their 12-month window may cross fiscal years; delivery lead times can justify ordering now for later arrival; reasonable stock replenishment is current-year need. What never works: obligating simply because money expires — for a November course, the analysis is when the training need genuinely arises, worked with FM, not the color of September's calendar.

follow_ups.q: What's the severability of a license term?
follow_ups.h: A license term is a service period — measure it like one.
follow_ups.d: Software licenses are generally severable services measured by their term: a 12-month license on current-year O&M works (and may cross fiscal years); a 24-month term on one-year money fails Time — the second year is next year's need bought with this year's appropriation. The lawful shapes: buy the one-year term now and next year's separately, or structure a base-plus-option that lets each year's money fund each year's term.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your Government Purchase Card (GPC) program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and chief of the contracting office (COCO).
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: It's September 28th with $47K expiring. What survives the fiscal test, and what doesn't?
scenarios.script: This is a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, applied item by item. My help: financial management (FM) first and always — the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references behind every call here. The wish list, sorted: two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — buy the 12-month term, structure the rest; the November course gets a bona fide need analysis — when does the need actually arise? — worked with FM rather than assumed; and reasonable toner-and-cable replenishment is legitimate current-year need, while 'stocking up' beyond reasonable levels is next year's need wearing this year's money. And I'd say the quiet part: expiring funds create urgency, never authority. The test is the need's year — not the money's expiration date.

scenarios.scenario: Market research for a $3.1M cyber-hygiene assessment shows five interested firms: three small (one 8(a), one woman-owned small business (WOSB), one plain small) and two large incumbents from predecessor work. The customer worries small firms 'can't handle the clearances' — though all three hold facility clearances per DISS.
baits: The clearance worry is asserted, and disproven, in the same breath
Incumbent gravity
key_moves: Rule of Two is met on documented capability — set-aside required posture, and check the socioeconomic programs before the plain set-aside
The clearance objection died in DISS; record it as resolved
Wrong-direction pressure gets answered with the file, DD 2579 coordinated

follow_ups.q: Order of precedence among 8(a)/HUBZone/service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB)/WOSB and total set-asides?
follow_ups.h: The socioeconomic programs get their look before the plain set-aside.
follow_ups.d: Before a total small-business set-aside, consider the socioeconomic lanes — 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB — against their program conditions and caps; the plain set-aside is the default posture once the Rule of Two is met, and the program lanes are checked in coordination with your Small Business Professional (DD 2579). There's no universal mandatory ranking among the programs — what's mandatory is considering them deliberately and documenting the path chosen.

follow_ups.q: What breaks a Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately?
follow_ups.h: The expectation breaks on evidence, not anxiety.
follow_ups.d: A Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately breaks when documented research shows fewer than two capable small businesses likely to offer at fair market prices — capability gaps proven against the actual requirement, not presumed from size; past small-business failure on THIS work; or market changes since research. Customer nervousness, clearance myths, and incumbent preference break nothing. If the expectation stands, the set-aside posture is required — and the file carries the evidence either way.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA) PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: Five interested firms, three of them small, and a nervous customer. What's your set-aside call?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business question — the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two on documented capability. My help: my Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA), with the DD 2579 papering the coordination. The rule: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices means set-aside — and three interested small firms with relevant past performance is a textbook expectation. The customer's clearance worry died in the facility-clearance database; I'd record it as resolved, not let it haunt the strategy. Before the plain set-aside, the program lanes get their look — 8(a), WOSB — against their conditions. Then we compete it small, and the record carries any protest. Nervousness isn't evidence; the research is.

scenarios.scenario: An 8(a) firm has performed your base's grounds maintenance for six years across two competed-in-8(a) awards. The follow-on estimate is $5.8M. The district the Small Business Administration (SBA) office is slow answering emails, and the program manager (PM) suggests 'just doing it full-and-open this time — more competition is always better, right?'
baits: 'More competition is always better' sounds virtuous
SBA slowness invites unilateral action
key_moves: Once in 8(a), the requirement stays unless SBA releases it — full-and-open without release is a program violation, not extra competition
$5.8M exceeds the competitive-threshold family → competitive 8(a) is the likely lane
Chase the release question through channels, documented

follow_ups.q: When is release from 8(a) appropriate to request?
follow_ups.h: Release is SBA's call — when would the Government even ask?
follow_ups.d: Requesting release from 8(a) is appropriate when the requirement has genuinely outgrown the program's purpose — mandatory sources changed, the requirement transformed, or long-term strategy (like consolidations) needs the flexibility — and SBA weighs the program's development interest in the incumbent community. It's a deliberate, documented request through your Small Business Professional and the district office — not a workaround for slow email, and never a unilateral contracting officer (CO) decision.

follow_ups.q: Competitive vs. sole-source 8(a) — what sets the line?
follow_ups.h: Find the line the $5.8M estimate crosses.
follow_ups.d: Competitive 8(a) begins at $8.5M for manufacturing and $5.5M for everything else. At $5.8M, this services follow-on exceeds the competitive threshold — so it competes among eligible 8(a) firms rather than going sole source. Sole-source 8(a) below the thresholds needs no justification and approval (J&A) (DoD's statutory lane runs to $100M); above them, competition inside the program is the design. Know the family: $8.5M/$5.5M is the same pair that caps HUBZone and woman-owned small business (WOSB) sole source.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the Small Business Administration (SBA) PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: SBA is slow and the PM wants it competed full-and-open. What controls this follow-on?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business programs question — RFO 19.8, the 8(a) follow-on trap. My help: my Small Business Professional and the SBA district office, escalated past the slow inbox. The rule: once a requirement enters 8(a), it stays unless SBA agrees to release it — six years and two in-program awards make this unmistakably an 8(a) requirement, and full-and-open without a release letter is a program violation, not extra competition. At $5.8M we're over the $5.5M services line, so the lawful path is competitive 8(a) among eligible firms. If the program genuinely wants out of 8(a) someday, that's a deliberate release request with a rationale — not a decision made by an unanswered email.

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs original equipment manufacturer (OEM)-proprietary calibration of 12 test stands. The OEM quotes $480K. Your predecessor's file contains three identical annual justifications and approvals (J&As) citing 'only one responsible source,' each noting 'the Government intends to develop organic capability' — which never happened.
baits: Three approved J&As feel like precedent
The OEM lock may be genuinely real
key_moves: Repetition weakens, not strengthens: each J&A promised barrier-removal actions that never occurred — this year's must address that honestly
Attack the barrier: data/licensing for organic or third-party calibration priced as a line of effort
If the lock is real this year, the J&A can still be truthful — about the failure too

follow_ups.q: What does 6.104-1 require about overcoming barriers?
follow_ups.h: The J&A has a required section about knocking the barrier down — read the last three.
follow_ups.d: A one-source justification must describe the actions the agency will take to overcome the barriers to competition — data purchases, qualification of second sources, organic capability. When three consecutive J&As promised the same actions and nothing happened, this year's justification must confront that record honestly: what was promised, why it didn't occur, and what concrete funded steps change it now. Reviewers and protesters both read the file backward — a fourth copy-paste is where sole-source cases go to die.

follow_ups.q: Who approves at $480K?
follow_ups.h: $480K sits in a specific rung of the ladder.
follow_ups.d: At $480K the J&A is above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) and below $900K — approval by the contracting officer's certification at the chief of the contracting office (COCO) tier (the CO's certification constitutes approval in the lowest band). Know the whole ladder anyway, because the panel will climb it: CA to $20M, head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) to $90M ($150M DoD), senior procurement executive (SPE) above. Tier questions are the board's favorite second ask.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: Three identical J&As in the file and a fourth on your desk. What does this year's have to say?
scenarios.script: This is a competition question — RFO 6.103-1 — about repetition. My help: Legal, the Competition Advocate's office, and the program on the barrier itself. The rule: each J&A must be true when written — and repetition weakens rather than grandfathers it. Three identical justifications each promised barrier-removal that never happened; a fourth copy-paste is protest bait. So this year's J&A confronts the record: what was promised, why it didn't happen, and the funded, dated plan that actually attacks the barrier — buying the calibration data or licensing, qualifying a second source, or building organic capability. At $480K the approval sits low, but the credibility question sits high. The OEM can win this year honestly; the Government just can't keep buying the same excuse.

scenarios.scenario: A lab wants to award a $2M 'study extension' to the university that just finished a basic-research grant, sole source, 'to preserve research continuity.' The work statement reads like applied development with deliverable prototypes. The lab argues grants don't need justifications and approvals (J&As) so neither should this.
baits: Grant history blurs the instrument question
'Continuity' as an all-purpose justification
key_moves: Name the instrument first: prototype deliverables for Government benefit = acquisition (contract), not assistance — competition rules attach
Continuity can support a 6.103-1 case only with market research showing unique capability
If it's genuinely basic research, a BAA or assistance lane may fit — but the SOW says otherwise

follow_ups.q: Acquisition vs. assistance — the test?
follow_ups.h: Who principally benefits — the public purpose or the Government's own need?
follow_ups.d: The test is principal purpose: assistance instruments (grants, cooperative agreements) transfer support for a public purpose — the Government stimulates research it doesn't primarily consume. Acquisition (a contract) obtains supplies or services for the Government's direct benefit. Deliverable prototypes serving a Government capability need are acquisition, whatever the paperwork was last time — and acquisition brings CICA, competition, and Part 6 with it.

follow_ups.q: Could a BAA have covered this from the start?
follow_ups.h: The BAA's lane is ideas competed against a standard — could this work have started there?
follow_ups.d: Yes — applied research with varying technical approaches is the BAA's home turf: broad announcement, stated criteria, independent scientific merit review, proposals evaluated against the standard rather than head-to-head. A BAA from the start would have made every award competitive by design, including follow-on phases within its scope. The lesson to say out loud: instrument choice at the beginning determines the competition posture years later.

coach.qtype: a competition question — the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a justification and approval (J&A) approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: A sole-source 'study extension' that reads like prototype development. What instrument — and what process?
scenarios.script: This is a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35 against the assistance instruments — name the instrument before anything else. My help: Legal, the agreements officer channel, and the lab's program office. The test: principal purpose. Deliverable prototypes for a Government capability need are acquisition — a contract — no matter how the last award was papered; and acquisition means the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) attaches. So the $2M 'extension' either competes or stands on a real RFO 6.103-1 justification with market research behind it — 'research continuity' is an argument, not an authority. Going forward, I'd point the lab at the broad agency announcement (BAA) lane: applied research with varied approaches competed against a published standard is exactly what BAAs exist for, and starting there makes the follow-on question disappear.

scenarios.scenario: Mid-evaluation on a trade-off selection, the source selection evaluation board (SSEB) discovers every offeror misread an ambiguous performance work statement (PWS) paragraph the same way — pricing 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. The source selection authority (SSA) wants to 'just evaluate what they offered and fix it with the winner after award.'
baits: Uniform misreading feels evaluable ('same playing field')
Fixing post-award avoids schedule slip
key_moves: A materially defective solicitation isn't cured by consistent confusion — amend, and give offerors a chance to revise
'Fix it with the winner' = negotiating scope after award: pricing shifts, protest exposure, scope questions
Amendment now costs weeks; the alternative costs the competition

follow_ups.q: When does an amendment require proposal revisions?
follow_ups.h: Materiality decides between a clarifying answer and an amendment with revisions.
follow_ups.d: An amendment requires proposal revisions when it changes what offerors priced or how they'd technically respond — a materially different coverage requirement is exactly that. Minor clarifications that don't affect price or approach can be answered without revisions. Here, every offeror priced 24/7 coverage the Government doesn't want: the amendment changes the deal, so offerors get the amendment and the chance to revise — anything less evaluates proposals against a requirement nobody was asked to meet.

follow_ups.q: What if the ambiguity surfaced after award instead?
follow_ups.h: Post-award, the same fix becomes a scope-and-competition problem.
follow_ups.d: If the ambiguity surfaced after award, the 'fix' becomes a modification reducing coverage — a price-relevant change the losers never got to compete. That invites the descoping protest ('we'd have bid differently at 12-hour coverage') and a scope analysis with an honest consideration adjustment. The comparison is instructive for the panel: pre-award, an amendment cures it cleanly; post-award, the same facts become protest exposure plus a negotiated mod. Timing is everything — which is why you fix it now.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications, communications, discussions — and make discussions meaningful.

scenarios.ask: Every offeror priced coverage the Government never wanted. The SSA says evaluate as-is and fix it with the winner. Your call?
scenarios.script: This is a source-selection question — RFO Part 15 — about a defective solicitation. My help: Legal and the SSA — who I'd respectfully redirect. The rule: proposals are evaluated against the solicitation as written, and this solicitation misstates the requirement — every offeror priced 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. Consistent confusion doesn't cure a defect; it proves it. 'Fix it with the winner' is negotiating scope after award: the price shifts, the losers protest, and they'd be right. So: amend the solicitation, state the real coverage requirement, and give all offerors the chance to revise. It costs two weeks now. The alternative costs a sustained protest, a descoping mod, and the program's credibility later.

scenarios.scenario: After award, the losing offeror's debrief question list includes: their own weaknesses (fine), the winner's proposed staffing plan, the winner's price broken out by contract line item number (CLIN), and 'all evaluator notes mentioning our company.' The program manager (PM) wants to 'give them everything so they feel heard and don't protest.'
baits: Generosity as protest-avoidance strategy
'Feeling heard' conflated with disclosure
key_moves: Debriefs disclose the requester's own evaluation, the evaluated award result and rationale — never the winner's proposal details or CLIN pricing
Over-disclosure creates the next problem (winner's proprietary data released)
A quality debrief is thorough about THEM — that's what actually prevents protests

follow_ups.q: What must a post-award debrief include?
follow_ups.h: The debrief discloses their evaluation and the outcome's rationale — whose proposal stays sealed?
follow_ups.d: A post-award debrief must include: the requester's own evaluation — significant weaknesses and deficiencies — the overall evaluated cost/price and technical rating of requester and awardee, past-performance conclusions on the requester, rankings where used, the award rationale, and answers to reasonable questions about whether procedures were followed. It's a real accounting of THEIR result and WHY the winner won — described at the level of the source selection decision document's (SSDD) reasoning, not the winner's papers.

follow_ups.q: What's releasable about the awardee?
follow_ups.h: The winner's information has an owner.
follow_ups.d: About the awardee, releasable: identity, total evaluated price, overall ratings, and the comparative rationale for selection. Not releasable: their staffing plan, technical approach, CLIN-level pricing, or anything revealing proposal content — that's contractor bid and proposal information, protected, and over-disclosure creates the next integrity problem (the winner's own protest, or a the Procurement Integrity Act (PIA) issue). The discipline: explain the decision, guard the proposals.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications, communications, discussions — and make discussions meaningful.

scenarios.ask: The loser wants the winner's staffing plan and CLIN prices. What does their debrief contain?
scenarios.script: This is a debrief question — RFO Part 15's disclosure lines — and a good debrief is protest prevention, not a document fight. My help: Legal on the disclosure lines, the source selection evaluation board (SSEB) record for the substance. The rule: the loser gets a full, honest accounting of their own evaluation — weaknesses, deficiencies, their ratings and evaluated price, the rankings, and the rationale for the award — plus the winner's identity, total evaluated price, and overall ratings. What they don't get: the winner's staffing plan, approach, or CLIN pricing — that's protected proposal information, and releasing it trades one protest for another. So I'd run the debrief generously inside those lines: answer questions, show the process was fair, take feedback. Offerors protest mysteries far more often than they protest explanations.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a $16M sole-source sustainment mod (awarded July 2026), the contractor certifies its data. Three weeks after agreement on price — before the mod is signed — their sweep surfaces a vendor quote 22% below the one in the proposal for a major material item.
baits: 'We already agreed on price'
The sweep feels like good faith that shouldn't be punished
key_moves: Pre-award discovery: use the corrected data — adjust the price downward before signature
The certificate speaks as of the date of agreement; incorporating the correction protects both sides
Document the adjustment in the PNM; good-faith sweeps are exactly why the process works

follow_ups.q: Same facts discovered 6 months after award — what changes?
follow_ups.h: Six months post-award, the same quote becomes a different animal with a remedy attached.
follow_ups.d: Discovered after award, that undisclosed quote is defective pricing: the certified data wasn't accurate, complete, and current at agreement. The Government becomes entitled to a price reduction plus interest (and profit on the delta) through the defective-pricing clause — with Legal driving, and a unilateral mod if the contractor won't settle. Same facts, different timing: before signature it's a correction; after award it's a remedy. That contrast is the whole lesson.

follow_ups.q: All five defective-pricing elements?
follow_ups.h: Run the five elements against these exact facts.
follow_ups.d: The five: (1) the vendor quote is cost or pricing data — yes; (2) it existed before agreement on price — yes, the sweep found it in their files; (3) it wasn't disclosed to the contracting officer (CO) — yes; (4) the Government relied on the data submitted — yes, the negotiation priced the higher quote; (5) reliance increased the price — yes, by the delta. All five hold, which is what makes the pre-signature correction so valuable: it resolves cleanly what would otherwise be a textbook defective-pricing case.

coach.qtype: a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on what data you're owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for field pricing and rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) for audit, and Legal on defective-pricing exposure.
coach.rule: Price analysis always (RFO 15.404-1). Certified data only past the threshold with the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions checked first — and no award without a documented fair-and-reasonable determination.

scenarios.ask: The sweep surfaced a 22% cheaper vendor quote after agreement but before signature. What happens to the price?
scenarios.script: This is a pricing question — the 10 U.S.C. §§3701–3708 certified-data machinery at the sweep seam. My help: my pricing office and Legal on the exposure math. The rule: the certificate speaks as of the date of agreement on price, and we haven't signed — so the corrected data gets used now. The price adjusts downward for the 22% quote before signature, the price negotiation memorandum (PNM) is updated to tell the true story, and the certificate is executed against accurate, complete, current data. I'd also credit the contractor's sweep — that's the system working. And I'd say the contrast out loud for the panel: caught today, it's a correction; caught six months after award, it's defective pricing — price reduction plus interest, with Legal. Same quote, different day, very different meeting.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor offers to 'save everyone time' on a $14M sole-source development action: they'll accept firm-fixed-price (FFP) if the Government skips 'the whole certified data exercise,' arguing the fixed price transfers all risk so the data doesn't matter.
baits: Risk-transfer logic sounds economically clever
Everyone loves skipping the exercise
key_moves: Contract type is not a CLAWM exception — over threshold, sole source, non-commercial = certified data, period
An FFP priced without data analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — risk transfer at an unknown premium
Separately evaluate whether FFP even fits development-grade uncertainty

follow_ups.q: Recite CLAWM
follow_ups.h: Recite the exceptions — is contract type on the list?
follow_ups.d: CLAWM: Commercial items; prices set by Law or regulation; Adequate price competition; Waiver by the head of the contracting activity (HCA); commercial-item Modifications. That's the list. Contract type appears nowhere on it — FFP is a risk allocation, not a data exception. Over the threshold, sole source, non-commercial: certified cost or pricing data is required regardless of type, and offering FFP doesn't buy out of it.

follow_ups.q: Why is unanalyzed FFP worse than analyzed cost-type here?
follow_ups.h: What does the fixed price actually lock in if nobody analyzed the number?
follow_ups.d: An unanalyzed FFP locks in an unanalyzed number — if it's padded 30%, the Government pays the padding with certainty, every unit, no remedy. Analyzed cost-type at least buys visibility: costs are auditable, fee is negotiated on known risk, and overruns are seen as they happen. Risk transfer only has value when the price transferring the risk was priced right — which is precisely what the data exists to establish. 'FFP protects us' without analysis protects the contractor's margin.

coach.qtype: a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on what data you're owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for field pricing and rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) for audit, and Legal on defective-pricing exposure.
coach.rule: Price analysis always (RFO 15.404-1). Certified data only past the threshold with the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions checked first — and no award without a documented fair-and-reasonable determination.

scenarios.ask: FFP in exchange for skipping certified data — 'the fixed price transfers all the risk anyway.' Deal?
scenarios.script: This is a pricing question wearing a contract-type disguise. My help: my pricing office, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on rates, Legal if this gets creative. The rule: RFO 15.403-2's CLAWM — commercial, law, adequate competition, waiver, commercial mods — and contract type is not on the list. A $14M sole-source, non-commercial development action over the threshold requires certified cost or pricing data whatever the type. And I'd dismantle the pitch itself: an FFP priced without analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — if it's padded, we pay the padding with certainty. Risk transfer has value only when the transferring price was priced right. So: certified data comes in, we analyze, we negotiate — and then FFP may well be the right answer, at a defensible number.

scenarios.scenario: A program manager (PM) wants cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) for a follow-on production lot of 200 proven units, 'because the contractor says material prices are volatile and won't hold a firm price.' Cost history from three prior firm-fixed-price (FFP) lots is extensive and stable except for two commodity metals.
baits: Contractor preference presented as necessity
Real-but-narrow volatility inflated into type-wide uncertainty
key_moves: Mature production with deep cost history is FP territory — the named risk is two commodities, not the effort
FFP with economic price adjustment scoped to those indices prices the actual risk
CPFF on stable production shifts all cost risk to the Government for no reason — and check the E.O. 14402 justification implications of going non-FFP

follow_ups.q: How does an EPA clause get structured?
follow_ups.h: An EPA clause prices a named risk — name it, index it, bound it.
follow_ups.d: A defensible EPA clause: identifies the specific cost elements exposed (the two volatile commodities), ties adjustment to named published indices, sets a trigger band so routine noise doesn't adjust anything, applies ceilings and floors, and defines the adjustment math and timing. It surgically prices the actual risk while everything else stays firm — protecting both parties from the named volatility without converting the whole lot to cost-plus.

follow_ups.q: When would production legitimately be cost-type?
follow_ups.h: When would production honestly need cost-type?
follow_ups.d: Rarely — and only when genuine cost uncertainty pervades the effort: first articles after major redesign, production restart after a long break with a broken supplier base, or configuration instability that makes quantities and processes honestly unpriceable. Mature, stable, repeatedly-priced production is the opposite of that. The type question always returns to requirement definition: uncertainty you can name and bound gets priced with an instrument; uncertainty that pervades gets cost-type. Two commodities have names.

coach.qtype: a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and why.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the program manager (PM) on requirement certainty, and your reviewing chain for the determination and findings (D&F).
coach.rule: RFO Part 16 matches risk to definition: firm-fixed-price (FFP) when the work prices firmly; cost-type (approved accounting system + D&F) when it can't. Forcing FFP onto the unknowable is risk denial, not risk transfer — and E.O. 14402 makes other-than-FFP a justified decision (RFO 16.104).

scenarios.ask: CPFF for a proven production lot because 'material prices are volatile.' What type does this work actually take?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: match the type to where the risk actually lives. My help: my pricing office and the cost history from three prior lots. The facts: mature production, deep stable actuals, and the named risk is two commodities — not the effort. That's fixed-price territory: FFP with an economic price adjustment clause scoped to those two indices — named elements, published indices, trigger bands, ceilings. CPFF would hand back the entire cost risk of a proven production line to cure a problem two indices can carry — and the accounting-system and determination and findings (D&F) gates would have to be cleared for a type the work doesn't need. Price the real risk surgically; keep the rest firm. The contractor's volatility concern is legitimate; their prescription isn't.

scenarios.scenario: On a fixed-price incentive (firm target) (FPIF) negotiation — target cost $20M, target profit $1.6M, ceiling 125%, share 80/20 — the contractor's final position quietly moves the ceiling to 135% 'to reflect supply-chain reality' while leaving everything else unchanged. The program manager (PM) thinks that's harmless 'since we only pay actuals plus profit anyway.'
baits: 'We only pay actuals' misunderstands FPIF
One parameter moving 'quietly' among four
key_moves: The ceiling is the Government's hard protection — raising it moves the PTA and extends Government exposure by $2M
Run the PTA math both ways and show the delta; price any real supply-chain risk explicitly instead
Every FPIF element is negotiated geometry; nothing moves 'quietly'

follow_ups.q: Compute PTA before and after
follow_ups.h: Run PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Gov share + Target Cost, both ways.
follow_ups.d: Target price is $21.6M (target cost $20M + target profit $1.6M). At a 125% ceiling ($25M): PTA = (25 − 21.6) ÷ 0.8 + 20 = $24.25M. At 135% ($27M): PTA = (27 − 21.6) ÷ 0.8 + 20 = $26.75M. The quiet edit moved the point of total assumption $2.5M to the right and raised the Government's maximum exposure by $2M — the contractor stays on the shared-risk gravy longer before bearing full cost risk. Run the math at the board; the delta IS the argument.

follow_ups.q: What happens to contractor behavior past PTA?
follow_ups.h: After PTA, whose money funds each additional dollar of cost?
follow_ups.d: Past the PTA, every additional cost dollar comes out of the contractor's profit until the ceiling, where the contractor bears everything — effectively firm-fixed-price (FFP) from PTA to ceiling. That's why PTA placement drives behavior: a contractor operating below PTA shares overruns with the Government (20 cents on the dollar here); past it, cost discipline suddenly gets personal. Raising the ceiling delays that discipline — which is exactly why they proposed it quietly.

coach.qtype: a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and why.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the program manager (PM) on requirement certainty, and your reviewing chain for the determination and findings (D&F).
coach.rule: RFO Part 16 matches risk to definition: firm-fixed-price (FFP) when the work prices firmly; cost-type (approved accounting system + D&F) when it can't. Forcing FFP onto the unknowable is risk denial, not risk transfer — and E.O. 14402 makes other-than-FFP a justified decision (RFO 16.104).

scenarios.ask: The contractor quietly moved the ceiling from 125% to 135%. What did that change, and what's your response?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-type question — RFO Part 16 FPIF mechanics, and the ceiling is the Government's hard protection. My help: my pricing office, with the PTA math on one page. The move: raising the ceiling from 125% to 135% shifts the PTA from $24.25M to $26.75M and adds $2M of Government exposure — the contractor rides the 80/20 share longer before cost discipline gets personal. 'Supply-chain reality' may be genuine, but the cure isn't a quiet ceiling raise — if there's a real, nameable risk, we price it explicitly: adjust the target cost on evidence, or scope an economic price adjustment (EPA)-style protection to the named exposure. My response: the ceiling stays, the math goes on the table, and any real risk gets priced in daylight.

scenarios.scenario: On a 4-holder engineering indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ), the program shapes a new task order around a proprietary modeling tool that only Holder C owns — the requirement literally names the tool. Asked why, the program manager (PM) says 'their engineer demoed it and it's exactly what we need.'
baits: Naming the tool feels like precision, not steering
The demo genuinely was impressive
key_moves: A requirement written around one holder's proprietary product is steering wearing a spec costume — restate to performance terms
If only the tool truly satisfies the need, that's an 'only one capable' exception argument — made honestly in a D&A, not smuggled in
Fair opportunity means the other three get a real shot at the actual need

follow_ups.q: What belongs in the D&A if the tool is genuinely unique?
follow_ups.h: The D&A for a genuinely unique tool still has required content — evidence, not enthusiasm.
follow_ups.d: A defensible only-one-capable D&A documents: the performance need the tool satisfies, the market check across the OTHER holders (what they were asked, what they answered), why alternatives genuinely can't meet the need in time, the price-reasonableness plan absent competition, and — like a justification and approval (J&A) — what the Government will do to open future orders. Approved at the tier the dollars demand, posted. 'Their engineer demoed it and it's exactly what we need' appears nowhere in that outline.

follow_ups.q: How does this differ from a brand-name justification in open competition?
follow_ups.h: Same disease, different venue — how does the open-market version of this get justified?
follow_ups.d: In open competition, naming a product is a brand-name justification: a documented explanation of the particular feature-need only that product meets, with market research behind it, approved and made public with the solicitation. The fair-opportunity D&A is its vehicle-level cousin — narrower field, same discipline. The shared lesson: requirements stated as performance outcomes preserve competition in both venues; requirements stated as product names must earn the restriction in writing.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) determinations and approvals (D&As), and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a D&A up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: The order names Holder C's proprietary tool by name. How do you handle the requirement — and the demo-driven enthusiasm?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity question — a requirement written around one holder's product. My help: the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO), Legal, and the program engineers on what the mission actually needs. The rule: fair opportunity is the default, and a spec that names Holder C's tool is steering wearing a requirements costume. First move: restate the requirement in performance terms — what must the modeling produce, to what fidelity, by when — and ask all four other holders the capability question directly. If the honest answer is that only the tool satisfies the need in time, then the exception is real: an only-one-capable determination and approval (D&A) on evidence, approved at tier, posted. The demo enthusiasm goes in a drawer; the performance requirement and the market answers go in the file.

scenarios.scenario: A $9M task order for logistics software support is at month 30 of 36. The program wants to add data-migration work for a completely different system owned by another program executive officer (PEO) — 'the vehicle's ceiling has room and the contractor is willing.'
baits: Ceiling room framed as authority
Contractor willingness framed as feasibility
key_moves: Ceiling is capacity, not scope — test the new work against the IDIQ's scope and this order's
Another PEO's unrelated system is a new requirement: fair opportunity on this vehicle (if in scope) or a new procurement (if not)
Out-of-scope orders are protestable at any dollar value as improper sole-source awards

follow_ups.q: Who protests an out-of-scope order and where?
follow_ups.h: An improper order is a competition someone was denied — who complains, and to whom?
follow_ups.d: An out-of-scope order is effectively a sole-source award of new work: the other vehicle holders (denied fair opportunity) complain to the task-order ombudsman at any dollar value — and at the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an order that exceeds the scope, period, or ceiling of the underlying contract is protestable at ANY value, by holders or even by contractors outside the vehicle whose competitive universe was bypassed. Scope growth is the exception that unlocks GAO's door below the dollar thresholds.

follow_ups.q: What analysis documents an in-scope conclusion?
follow_ups.h: The in-scope memo has two layers — the vehicle's four corners and this order's.
follow_ups.d: The analysis documents both levels: does the work fit the IDIQ's scope statement (the enterprise every holder signed up to compete within), and does it fit THIS order's scope (what this order's competition anticipated)? Corners: nature of the work versus the scope statement, period, cumulative value, and what the original order competition reasonably anticipated. A different PEO's unrelated system fails at both levels — and writing the honest analysis now is cheaper than writing the protest response later.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.507: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's procuring contracting officer (PCO) and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) determinations and approvals (D&As), and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.507-2 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions (16.507-6) ride a D&A up the same approval ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As), and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: Ceiling room exists and the clock is running. Can the migration work ride this task order?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO 16.507 fair-opportunity question about scope — and ceiling is capacity, not permission. My help: the vehicle procuring contracting officer (PCO) and Legal on the scope analysis. The test runs at two levels: does data migration for a different PEO's unrelated system fit the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity's (IDIQ) scope statement, and does it fit this order's own scope? On these facts it fails both — it's a new requirement, not growth of this one. So the lawful paths: compete it among the vehicle's holders as a new order if the vehicle's scope truly covers it, or take it to its proper vehicle or a new competition if it doesn't. Riding the ceiling because 'the contractor knows our environment' is a sole source without a justification — and out-of-scope orders are protestable at any dollar value. That's a door I'm not opening.

scenarios.scenario: Exercising option year 2 of a lab-services contract, you discover the option contract line item number (CLIN) was never priced at award — the schedule says 'TBD, to be negotiated.' The contracting officer's representative (COR) has already emailed the contractor that 'the option is being picked up' and performance continues seamlessly in three weeks.
baits: Seamless continuity pressure
The COR's email creating apparent momentum
key_moves: An unpriced 'option' isn't an option — there's no unilateral right to exercise; it's a negotiation (and its competition posture needs Legal now)
The COR email binds nothing but complicates the negotiation — correct it in writing
Bridge honestly if needed while the real path (negotiate/compete) is worked

follow_ups.q: What made the option invalid at award — evaluation or pricing?
follow_ups.h: An option's power comes from what happened at award — what has to have happened?
follow_ups.d: A real option was priced at award and evaluated in the source selection — that's what makes later exercise a unilateral right and shields it from being a new sole-source procurement. 'TBD, to be negotiated' fails the pricing half: there's nothing to exercise, only something to negotiate. And a negotiated continuation with the incumbent is a new procurement action wearing an option's label — its competition posture needs Legal immediately.

follow_ups.q: What are the Government's lawful continuity tools here?
follow_ups.h: Continuity tools exist — each with its own clock and justification.
follow_ups.d: The lawful kit: negotiate a bilateral extension with the incumbent supported by an honest justification and price analysis; use the extension-of-services mechanism (up to 6 months) if the clause is in the contract; or bridge via a properly justified short sole-source while competing the follow-on. In parallel: start the recompete NOW, because every continuity tool is a rented month, not a strategy — and document why the defective option wasn't caught at award, because that finding is coming.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO Part 17 gates: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous check, SAM exclusions, performance considered — with timely written notice, or the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: The option CLIN says 'TBD.' The COR already promised exercise. Where does this leave you?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 17 options question where the option turns out not to exist. My help: Legal, immediately, and financial management (FM) on the continuity gap. The rule: an option is a unilateral right because it was priced and evaluated at award — a 'TBD' CLIN was never an option, just an agreement to negotiate later. So there's nothing to exercise: continuing with the incumbent is a negotiation, and its competition posture has to be sorted with Legal before anything is signed. The COR's email binds nothing — but I correct that channel today in writing. Then continuity honestly: a justified bilateral extension or the extension-of-services clause buys months, the recompete starts now, and the award-time failure that let 'TBD' through gets documented so it never recurs.

scenarios.scenario: An option must be exercised by 15 September for a performance period starting 1 October. Financial management (FM) says the new fiscal year's funds obviously don't exist yet, and the program manager (PM) concludes 'so we legally can't exercise until October — the contractor will just have to gap two weeks.'
baits: The fiscal logic sounds airtight
A two-week gap normalized as inevitable
key_moves: The availability-of-funds mechanism exists for exactly this: exercise subject to availability, obligation upon funds
Missing the 15 September date kills the unilateral right — that's the real risk in the room
Coordinate the clause mechanics with FM now; no gap required

follow_ups.q: What does the funds-availability clause actually promise the contractor?
follow_ups.h: The clause promises obligation when funds arrive — what does it let you do before?
follow_ups.d: The availability-of-funds mechanism lets the Government exercise on time, subject to availability — the exercise preserves the unilateral right and the contractor's obligation to perform, while the Government's obligation attaches when funds become available. It exists precisely for option cycles straddling the fiscal seam. The notice says what it must: exercised subject to availability, obligation upon funds — and FM coordinates the funding document the moment the appropriation lands.

follow_ups.q: What if funds never materialize?
follow_ups.h: If the appropriation never comes, what protects each party?
follow_ups.d: If funds never materialize, the Government isn't obligated — that's the clause's core protection; no Anti-Deficiency exposure, and the contractor was on notice from the exercise language. The contractor's protection is honesty and speed: prompt notice if availability fails, so it isn't holding capacity for a ghost. The Government then faces the real consequences — no option year, a continuity gap, possibly a termination for convenience (T4C) of the exercised period — which is why availability exercises ride actual appropriation expectations, not hope.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) for funds, the contracting officer's representative (COR) and program manager (PM) on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO Part 17 gates: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous check, SAM exclusions, performance considered — with timely written notice, or the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: Exercise is due 15 September; the money arrives 1 October. Is the PM right that you're stuck?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 17 options question at the fiscal seam — and the PM has it backwards. My help: FM on the funding mechanics and Legal on the notice language. The rule: missing the 15 September date kills the unilateral right — after that, continuation is a bilateral negotiation where the contractor holds the leverage. The seam is exactly what the availability-of-funds mechanism exists for: exercise on time, expressly subject to availability, with the obligation attaching when the new year's money arrives. So: run the gates, issue the notice by the 15th with the availability language, and have FM ready to obligate on 1 October. Waiting for the money to feel real is how the Government converts its own right into the contractor's negotiation.

scenarios.scenario: An outfit wants to send $3.2M to another agency's 'rapid-tech marketplace' office, which promises award in 30 days through 'pre-competed innovation vehicles.' The one-page flyer doesn't identify the underlying contracts, the fee is 6%, and the program manager (PM) says 'everyone at the symposium uses them.'
baits: Speed and social proof
'Pre-competed' as a magic word
key_moves: Identify the actual vehicles and authority before a dollar moves — 'marketplace' is marketing, not analysis
Over SAT to a non-DoD shop → best-procurement-approach D&F: alternatives, fee scrutiny, servicing agency's track record
Assisted acquisition needs the signed interagency agreement; our fiscal rules travel with the money

follow_ups.q: What makes the 6% fee acceptable or not?
follow_ups.h: A fee buys services — which ones, at what value?
follow_ups.d: The fee question is answered by the D&F's analysis: what does 6% buy — real acquisition expertise, vehicle access, administration — and is that value reasonable against alternatives, including buying it ourselves? A fee isn't inherently improper; an unexamined fee is. If the marketplace's value is speed we could achieve in-house, the fee fails the best-procurement-approach test; if it's genuine capability we lack on a real timeline, it can pass — documented, not assumed.

follow_ups.q: Direct vs. assisted here — which is this?
follow_ups.h: Who awards the eventual contract decides which lane you're in.
follow_ups.d: This is assisted acquisition: the marketplace office would award and administer on our behalf — which triggers the written interagency agreement (roles, responsibilities, unique terms) signed before funds move, plus the D&F for non-DoD orders over the SAT. Direct acquisition would be our contracting officer (CO) placing orders on their vehicles ourselves — no agreement required, but then their office isn't doing the work. The flyer's vagueness about who actually awards is itself the first question to resolve.

coach.qtype: an interagency question — RFO Part 17 interagency acquisition and the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. 1535): direct vs. assisted, and whose rules travel with the money.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) (the fiscal rules travel with the funds), Legal, and the servicing agency's contracting office.
coach.rule: Pick the lane deliberately: direct (our contracting officer (CO) orders on their vehicle) vs. assisted (their CO buys for us under a signed agreement). The Economy Act applies only absent a more specific authority — military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus determination and findings (D&F).

scenarios.ask: $3.2M to a 'rapid-tech marketplace' promising 30-day awards. What has to be true before that military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) moves?
scenarios.script: This is an interagency question — RFO Part 17 assisted acquisition — and a one-page flyer isn't an acquisition strategy. My help: financial management (FM), Legal, and the servicing office itself, on the record. Before a dollar moves: identify the actual underlying vehicles and their authority — 'marketplace' is marketing, and I can't verify scope, competition posture, or fee reasonableness against a brochure. Then the lane: they'd award for us, so it's assisted acquisition — written interagency agreement, signed, defining roles, before funds transfer. Over the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) to a non-DoD shop, the best-procurement-approach determination and findings (D&F) has to honestly conclude they beat our alternatives — schedule, cost including the 6% fee, and compliance. If the vehicles are real and the analysis holds, fine, we proceed with eyes open. If it's a flyer and a fee, we just bought ourselves a finding.

scenarios.scenario: Last September your office MIPRed $1.5M of operation and maintenance (O&M) to a servicing agency for a training-support task. It's now July; their contracting officer (CO) reports $410K will go unspent when the task ends next month, and their program office suggests 'rolling the remainder into a follow-on task so the funds don't go to waste.'
baits: 'Don't go to waste' — the eternal siren
The servicing agency's helpfulness
key_moves: Unobligated MIPR balances come home — they don't become the servicing agency's seed corn
The FY25 O&M is expiring; a new follow-on task is a new (current-year) need
Recover the funds, close the agreement cleanly, fund any follow-on properly

follow_ups.q: What happens to the recovered funds now?
follow_ups.h: Whose money is it once the task ends?
follow_ups.d: Unobligated MIPR balances return to the requesting agency — they don't become the servicing agency's working capital. And the returning funds keep their identity: FY25 O&M, now expiring or expired, available only for adjustments to the original obligations, not for new work. 'Rolling it forward' converts prior-year money into a new-year need — a Time violation dressed as efficiency. Recover the balance, report it to FM, and let the new need compete for current-year funds honestly.

follow_ups.q: Who tracks interagency balances — and how often should you?
follow_ups.h: This surprise was avoidable — what does routine interagency management look like?
follow_ups.d: The requesting agency tracks its own interagency balances: the agreement should require periodic financial reporting; the procuring contracting officer (PCO) or program office reconciles obligation and expenditure status quarterly at minimum (monthly near year-end), asks for burn-rate data, and triggers early recovery of excess. Discovering $410K in July for an August-ending task means nobody was watching for three quarters — the finding isn't the balance, it's the silence.

coach.qtype: an interagency question — RFO Part 17 interagency acquisition and the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. 1535): direct vs. assisted, and whose rules travel with the money.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM) (the fiscal rules travel with the funds), Legal, and the servicing agency's contracting office.
coach.rule: Pick the lane deliberately: direct (our contracting officer (CO) orders on their vehicle) vs. assisted (their CO buys for us under a signed agreement). The Economy Act applies only absent a more specific authority — military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) plus determination and findings (D&F).

scenarios.ask: $410K will go unspent, and the servicing agency suggests 'rolling it into' a new task. Your answer?
scenarios.script: This is an interagency-fiscal question — 31 U.S.C. 1535 machinery — and the money comes home. My help: financial management (FM) immediately, and the servicing agency's CO for the reconciliation. The rules: unobligated military interdepartmental purchase request (MIPR) balances return to us, and they return as what they are — FY25 O&M, expiring, good for adjustments to the original task and nothing new. A 'rolled' follow-on task is a new need, and new needs take current-year money; the suggestion fails Time no matter how efficient it sounds. So: recover the $410K now, reconcile the task's final costs, and if the follow-on is real, fund it properly and compete it properly. Then I'd fix the process — quarterly balance reconciliation in the agreement — because finding this in July means we weren't watching.

scenarios.scenario: A small business on a firm-fixed-price (FFP) production contract asks for progress payments, then mid-year requests the rate be raised 'to the max allowed' and asks whether the Government can also pay for a materials stockpile it wants to pre-buy against future orders that aren't on contract yet.
baits: Small-business sympathy
'Max allowed' framed as an entitlement
key_moves: Progress payments follow the clause rates; customary financing is fine — but payments attach to THIS contract's performance
Financing a stockpile for hoped-for future orders isn't contract financing — it's an advance against nothing
If cash flow is the real issue, performance-based payments or delivery scheduling may honestly help

follow_ups.q: Order of preference for financing methods?
follow_ups.h: Walk the ladder — where do progress payments sit and what outranks them?
follow_ups.d: Order of preference: private financing first; then customary contract financing — where progress payments and performance-based payments live, approvable by the contracting officer (CO) in the normal course; then unusual financing (requires higher approval); and advance payments last, the least preferred, most heavily approved. PBPs are preferred over cost-based progress payments where events can be defined. The rates themselves come from the clause and current class deviations — they're set, not negotiated upward on request.

follow_ups.q: What protects the Government in progress payments (title, liquidation)?
follow_ups.h: The Government pays early — what does it hold in exchange?
follow_ups.d: Two protections: title — under the progress-payments clause, title to work-in-process, materials, and inventory allocable to the contract vests in the Government as payments are made; and liquidation — progress payments are recovered by liquidation against delivery invoices, so the financing unwinds as performance completes. Both attach to THIS contract's performance, which is exactly why financing a stockpile for hoped-for FUTURE orders doesn't fit: no contract, no allocability, no title, no liquidation path.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: Max progress-payment rates plus financing for a stockpile 'for future orders.' What do you approve?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-finance question — RFO Part 32 customary financing, at clause rates, for this contract's work. My help: financial management (FM), the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on the payment administration, and the clause itself. The rules: progress payments ride the clause and the current class deviation — as a DoD small business they already get the favorable rate; 'raise it to the max' isn't a negotiation, the rate is the rate. The stockpile ask fails differently: progress payments finance costs allocable to this contract, with title vesting and liquidation against deliveries. Materials for hoped-for future orders have no contract, no allocability, no title path — that's asking the Government to bank speculation. If cash flow is the real issue, performance-based payments on defined events are the preferred structure — and I'd offer to build exactly that.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor delivers the final technical data package for a missile-handling trailer — every drawing stamped with limited-rights legends, including drawings the Government watched them create under this fully Government-funded contract. 'Standard company template,' their data manager shrugs, offering to 'sort it out during sustainment.'
baits: 'Template' minimization
Deferral to sustainment (when leverage is gone)
key_moves: Government-funded development = unlimited rights; the legends are nonconforming markings — challenge/correct now, in writing
'Sort it later' means competing sustainment against markings you accepted silently
The assertion list from award is the yardstick — unasserted restrictions carry the contractor's burden

follow_ups.q: The marking-challenge sequence?
follow_ups.h: Challenge in writing, honor the markings meanwhile — walk the clock.
follow_ups.d: The sequence: written challenge notice stating the grounds; contractor has 60 days to respond with justification; unresolved, the contracting officer (CO) issues a final decision; contractor may appeal (COFC or the Board, 90 days). Challenges can issue up to 3 years after contract completion. Critical discipline: until appeals resolve, honor the markings — using challenged data as if unrestricted converts your challenge into their claim. The Government's leverage is the process, not self-help.

follow_ups.q: What if some drawings genuinely mixed in private-expense heritage?
follow_ups.h: Mixed heritage doesn't rescue a blanket stamp.
follow_ups.d: If some drawings genuinely mix private-expense heritage, rights resolve at the component level: the contractor identifies which elements derive from private development — with records proving it, since the burden of supporting restrictions is theirs — and those elements carry limited rights while Government-funded portions stay unlimited. The blanket stamp fails precisely because it asserts nothing specific: an assertion list with evidence, drawing by drawing, is what the challenge process forces into existence.

coach.qtype: a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: the funding source drives the license.
coach.smes: Legal (IP counsel), the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertion administration.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 227: who paid for development answers most of it — Government funds → unlimited, mixed → Government purpose rights (GPR), private → limited/restricted. The contractor proves the restriction (the 252.227-7017 assertion list); honor the markings until a challenge resolves.

scenarios.ask: Every drawing arrived stamped limited-rights — including ones we watched them create on contract. What now?
scenarios.script: This is an R-DFARS 227 data-rights question — nonconforming markings on Government-funded work. My help: IP counsel in Legal and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertions administration. The rule: development funded entirely by the Government yields unlimited rights, and legends don't rewrite funding history — but the remedy is process, not self-help. So: written challenge now, stating the grounds — this was Government-funded development under this contract; the contractor gets their 60 days to justify with records, because the burden of proving any restriction is theirs. Where genuine private-expense heritage exists at the component level, those pieces get their proper legends; everything else gets corrected. And until it resolves, we honor the markings — because sorting this at sustainment competition time means competing against our own paid-for drawings.

scenarios.scenario: A small firm's Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase II produced a promising power-management module. Years later, your program wants the design data to second-source production. The firm asserts SBIR data rights; your engineer argues 'the protection must be expired by now,' and the program manager (PM) suggests just reverse-engineering it from delivered units.
baits: 'Must be expired' — assumed, not verified
Reverse-engineering framed as a clean workaround
key_moves: SBIR protection runs long — verify the actual window from the contract and delivery dates before anyone acts
Reverse-engineering has its own legal limits and practical costs; it's a Legal conversation, not a shop decision
The durable fix is negotiating rights or a license priced against the second-source business case

follow_ups.q: What do SBIR rights protect during the period?
follow_ups.h: During the protection window, what can the Government do with SBIR data?
follow_ups.d: During the SBIR protection period, the Government holds SBIR rights — it can use the data for Government purposes within the Government, but cannot release it for competitive procurement or disclose it outside without the firm's permission. The window is long (20 years under current policy) and runs from defined trigger dates in the contract. It exists to let small firms commercialize without the Government handing their innovation to competitors — that's the program's bargain.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the rights when the window closes?
follow_ups.h: When the window closes, the default rights story resumes.
follow_ups.d: After the SBIR period ends, the Government's rights transition toward the ordinary framework — the protection lapses and the Government's license broadens per the clause. Verify the actual window and trigger dates from the contract and delivery records before planning anything. And the planning lesson: if second-sourcing was foreseeable, the time to negotiate specially-tailored rights or buy a license was when the Government had leverage — at Phase III award — not years later at the sustainment cliff.

coach.qtype: a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227: the funding source drives the license.
coach.smes: Legal (IP counsel), the program engineers on the component map, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on assertion administration.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 227: who paid for development answers most of it — Government funds → unlimited, mixed → Government purpose rights (GPR), private → limited/restricted. The contractor proves the restriction (the 252.227-7017 assertion list); honor the markings until a challenge resolves.

scenarios.ask: SBIR rights on the module, and your engineer wants to 'just reverse-engineer it.' What's your counsel?
scenarios.script: This is a data-rights question — R-DFARS 227 SBIR rights, the long-protection species. My help: IP counsel and the contract file for the actual trigger dates. The rules: SBIR protection runs long — verify the real window from the contract before anyone acts on a guess — and during it, the Government can't release the data for competitive reprocurement without the firm's agreement. On reverse-engineering: it has its own legal limits and real costs, and 'engineering around' data we hold under restriction is litigation bait — that path gets sized honestly with counsel, not tossed off in a meeting. The constructive paths: negotiate a license or specially-tailored rights with the firm — they may sell what we can't take — or plan the second source for when the window actually closes. Leverage lives at award time; we spend what's left of it deliberately.

scenarios.scenario: A firm-fixed-price contract delivers training courseware in English. Partway through, the customer asks to add Spanish and Portuguese versions — roughly 40% more content-hours — and the contractor cheerfully offers a 'no-cost mod' in exchange for a 10-month period extension and relief from two quality metrics.
baits: 'No-cost' hides the real price (time + quality relief)
Contractor cheerfulness
key_moves: Nothing about this is no-cost — schedule and metric relief ARE consideration; price the exchange honestly
New-language versions at +40% effort: run the four-corner scope test; this may be out-of-scope new work
If out of scope: competition or a justified exception — a mod can't carry it

follow_ups.q: What counts as consideration in a mod?
follow_ups.h: Consideration isn't only money — price what the Government is giving up.
follow_ups.d: Consideration is anything of value exchanged: schedule extensions, relaxed performance metrics, waived remedies — all are Government givings with real value. A 'no-cost' mod that trades 40% more work for schedule and metric relief is a priced exchange with the price hidden. Papering it honestly means valuing both sides: what the added work is worth, what the relief costs the Government, and whether the exchange is fair — documented, so the file shows a bargain, not a favor swap.

follow_ups.q: How does the anticipation test apply to added languages?
follow_ups.h: Would the original competitors have bid differently on a three-language contract?
follow_ups.d: The anticipation test asks what the original competition reasonably contemplated. A courseware contract competed in English, growing 40% in content-hours to add two languages, is at least at the scope boundary: translation and localization could change who would have bid and how they'd have priced. Run the four corners — competition anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost — and if the honest answer is 'this is new work,' it competes or rides a justification. The contractor's cheerfulness doesn't move the scope line.

coach.qtype: a scope question — RFO Part 43: a modification, or a new procurement in disguise.
coach.smes: Legal, the procuring contracting officer (PCO) chain, and the original competition record itself.
coach.rule: The test is what the original competitors reasonably anticipated — judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative. In scope: modify under RFO Part 43. Beyond it: compete it or justify it under RFO Part 6.

scenarios.ask: Forty percent more content for 'no cost' — in exchange for schedule and metric relief. How do you paper this?
