scenarios.script: This is a modifications question — RFO Part 43: scope first, then honest consideration. My help: Legal on the scope analysis and my pricing office on valuing the exchange. Two rules: nothing here is 'no cost' — schedule relief and relaxed metrics ARE consideration, and the exchange gets priced and papered as the bargain it is. And scope: 40% more content-hours adding two languages gets the four-corner test against the original competition — would the field have bid differently on a trilingual contract? If it's in scope, we negotiate a bilateral mod that values both sides honestly. If it's beyond, it's new work: competed or justified, not absorbed. Cheerful offers deserve the same analysis as hostile ones — sometimes more.

scenarios.scenario: During a base network upgrade, the Government's fiber-conduit maps prove wrong in six buildings — the contractor reroutes on the fly at the contracting officer's representative's (COR) verbal 'keep moving, we'll square up.' Four months later a consolidated $340K request for equitable adjustment (REA) arrives. The program manager (PM) objects: 'they never got a mod authorizing any of that.'
baits: 'No mod = no entitlement' — exactly backwards here
The consolidated lump obscures per-building facts
key_moves: Government-caused changes (bad maps + directed continuation) are constructive changes — the missing mod is the Government's paperwork failure, not the contractor's entitlement bar
Evaluate entitlement building-by-building, then quantum with technical support
Settle bilaterally with a release; and fix the direction channel

follow_ups.q: REA vs. claim consequences if this stalls?
follow_ups.h: If this stalls unresolved, which lane's consequences attach?
follow_ups.d: As a certified claim, the CDA machinery runs: interest accrues from receipt, the CO owes a written final decision on a statutory clock (or a deemed denial arises), and appeal rights follow — Board in 90 days, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) in 12 months. If it had stayed an REA, none of those clocks run and prep costs are allowable. Once converted, delay costs the Government interest and initiative — which is why working entitlement promptly beats hoping it goes away.

follow_ups.q: Who had authority to say 'keep moving' — and what does that change?
follow_ups.h: Authority analysis changes the theory, not the entitlement.
follow_ups.d: The COR lacked authority to direct changes — but Government conduct is bigger than one email: defective Government-furnished maps plus continued direction to perform is a constructive-change theory that doesn't depend on the COR's warrant. The authority failure changes the Government's internal story (channel discipline broke) more than the contractor's entitlement. What the COR's role does affect: your prevention plan — direction flows through the CO, and that gets fixed in writing regardless of how the claim resolves.

coach.qtype: a scope question — RFO Part 43: a modification, or a new procurement in disguise.
coach.smes: Legal, the procuring contracting officer (PCO) chain, and the original competition record itself.
coach.rule: The test is what the original competitors reasonably anticipated — judged against the original contract with all mods cumulative. In scope: modify under RFO Part 43. Beyond it: compete it or justify it under RFO Part 6.

scenarios.ask: Bad Government maps, a COR's 'keep moving,' and a $310K consolidated claim. How do you work it?
scenarios.script: This is a disputes question — the Contract Disputes Act — built on our own paperwork failure. My help: Legal early, the COR's records, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) if the quantum needs support. The frame: defective Government maps plus 'keep moving' direction is a constructive-change case — the missing mods are the Government's failure, not the contractor's entitlement bar. As a certified claim, interest is already running and my output is a final decision or a settlement. So: entitlement element by element — the reroutes trace to the bad maps; quantum gets a real technical and cost review rather than resentment; and I'd negotiate hard toward a global settlement with a release. Then the internal fix: direction flows through the CO, in writing, and the mapping failure gets reported where it can't recur. The contractor did the work; the Government does the honest math.

scenarios.scenario: Closing out a five-year research and development (R&D) contract, the property report lists 212 Government-furnished items; the contractor can locate 168. Of the missing 44, they say 30 were 'consumed in testing years ago' (no records), 9 are 'probably at the subcontractor,' and 5 are simply unknown. They propose closing out now and 'reconciling later.'
baits: 'Consumed in testing' as an unverifiable catch-all
Closeout momentum
key_moves: No closeout with an open property reconciliation — the leverage ends at closeout
Loss/damage/destruction process per the clause: investigation, liability determination under the risk allocation, records
Subcontractor-held property is still the prime's accountability

follow_ups.q: Who adjudicates property loss — and on what standard?
follow_ups.h: The clause has a process and a standard — who runs it and against what?
follow_ups.d: Property loss runs through the clause machinery: the contractor reports and investigates each loss; the property administrator manages the process; and the contracting officer (CO) determines liability under the contract's risk allocation — on a cost-type contract the contractor typically bears loss only where its managers were at fault or the property system failed. 'Consumed in testing, no records' isn't an outcome — it's an unproven claim the investigation either substantiates or converts into liability.

follow_ups.q: What does the contractor's property-management-system status change?
follow_ups.h: The property system's approval status shifts the burden.
follow_ups.d: An approved property management system creates confidence records exist and losses were managed — individual determinations proceed against a working system. A disapproved or deficient system flips the posture: systemic recordkeeping failure is itself contractor fault, supporting broader liability and corrective demands. Forty-four unaccounted items out of 212 suggests the system, not just the items, needs the look — and DCMA's property specialists are the ones to give it.

coach.qtype: a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception.
coach.smes: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the program manager (PM) — who owes the written justification.
coach.rule: RFO Part 45: contractors furnish property. Government-furnished property (GFP) only when all four parts hold — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, not otherwise satisfiable — and furnishing it puts the Government's own performance on the schedule.

scenarios.ask: 212 items furnished, 168 found, and the contractor wants closeout. What happens first?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 45 Government-property question at the worst possible moment — closeout, where the leverage ends. My help: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency's (DCMA) property specialists, and Legal on liability. The rule: no closeout with an open property reconciliation. Each of the 44 missing items runs the clause machinery — report, investigate, liability determination under the contract's risk allocation. 'Consumed in testing, no records' gets tested against the property system's records, and if the system itself failed, that failure is contractor fault with broader consequences. Scrap sold 'to offset costs' without authorization is disposal outside the process — its own liability. Closeout happens when the record is reconciled and liabilities are resolved — not when the contractor is tired of the contract.

scenarios.scenario: To help a struggling firm-fixed-price (FFP) contractor meet schedule, the program manager (PM) wants to lend them a Government CNC machine 'for a few months, informally — putting it on contract takes too long and they only need it for one part run.'
baits: Informality justified by brevity
Helping-the-schedule urgency
key_moves: No informal property loans — on contract with the property clause set or not at all
Furnishing property to an FFP contractor shifts risk and may found an REA if it's late or faulty — price/paper the arrangement deliberately
The four-part GFP justification still applies, brief or not

follow_ups.q: What happens if the informal machine breaks mid-run?
follow_ups.h: Mid-run failure with no clause set — trace where every cost lands.
follow_ups.d: If the informal machine breaks mid-run: no property clause allocates the loss, so the Government and contractor litigate ownership of the damage from a paperwork vacuum; the contractor claims Government-caused delay on the FFP schedule (the machine was the Government's, informally provided); the part run stops; and nobody's insurance clearly answers. The 'few months informal' loan becomes a request for equitable adjustment (REA), a property dispute, and a schedule slip — all purchasable for the price of one modification.

follow_ups.q: How does Government-furnished property (GFP) alter FFP's risk story?
follow_ups.h: GFP hands the Government a role in an FFP story it wasn't supposed to have.
follow_ups.d: FFP's clean allocation — contractor bears cost risk, Government pays the price — assumes the contractor controls its means of production. Furnish property and the Government joins the performance path: late, faulty, or broken GFP is Government-caused delay and REA exposure, and the four-part justification plus clause set exists to make that trade deliberate. Helping a struggling FFP contractor with Government property can be right — but it's a priced, papered decision, because it moves risk back to the Government that FFP had transferred away.

coach.qtype: a Government-property question — RFO Part 45: the default rule and the four-part exception.
coach.smes: the property administrator, the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), and the program manager (PM) — who owes the written justification.
coach.rule: RFO Part 45: contractors furnish property. Government-furnished property (GFP) only when all four parts hold — best interest, benefit over burden, no substantial risk shift, not otherwise satisfiable — and furnishing it puts the Government's own performance on the schedule.

scenarios.ask: An informal loan of a Government CNC machine 'for a few months.' What do you tell the PM?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 45 Government-property question — and 'informal' is the problem, not the timeline. My help: the property administrator and the PM, who owes the justification if we do this at all. The rule: no informal property loans, ever — on contract with the full clause set, or not at all. If lending the CNC machine is genuinely in the Government's interest, the PM documents the four findings, the machine goes on contract with marking, condition baselined, and the property clauses allocating risk. And I'd tell the PM what the shortcut actually costs: furnishing property to an FFP contractor moves schedule risk back to us — if that machine breaks mid-run with no clause set, we own a dispute, a delay claim, and a stopped part run simultaneously. The mod takes days. The vacuum takes a year.

scenarios.scenario: An undefinitized contract action (UCA) for aircraft battle-damage repair was issued at a $30M not-to-exceed (NTE). The qualifying proposal arrives at $41M with a letter explaining 'actual damage exceeded initial survey.' The contractor requests the NTE be raised to match 'so definitization can proceed on real numbers.'
baits: 'Real numbers' framing makes the raise sound like accuracy
Definitization urgency used as leverage
key_moves: The NTE is the Government's liability ceiling — it doesn't float up to meet proposals
Is the extra damage in-scope growth (negotiate within/adjust deliberately with approvals) or new work (new action, new approvals)?
Definitize what was ordered; obligations stay inside the caps meanwhile

follow_ups.q: What approvals would an NTE increase require?
follow_ups.h: An NTE increase is a deliberate Government decision with a chain — whose?
follow_ups.d: Raising a UCA's NTE isn't a negotiating concession — it's a formal Government decision requiring the UCA approval authority's action (HCA delegable to senior contracting official (SCO); lower for smaller actions), supported by a documented scope analysis: is the 'extra damage' in-scope growth of this repair or new work needing its own action and justification? Funds must exist for any increase, and the definitization schedule presses on regardless. The contractor's proposal doesn't move the ceiling; the Government's deliberate process might.

follow_ups.q: How do the 50/75% caps apply during this fight?
follow_ups.h: The caps ride the NTE — run the arithmetic through the fight.
follow_ups.d: The obligation caps key to the NTE: 50% before the qualifying proposal, 75% after. On a $30M NTE, that's $15M and $22.5M — and they don't float with the contractor's $41M number. If actual in-scope work genuinely exceeds the NTE, the Government's deliberate increase would move the caps with it; until then, obligations stay inside the existing arithmetic, which is precisely the leverage that makes the contractor negotiate rather than perform indefinitely on an open tab.

coach.qtype: an undefinitized contract action (UCA) question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying negotiation leverage.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the clearance authority, and Legal; the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for actuals once performance starts.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 217.74 makes UCAs the exception: 50% obligation cap (75% after the qualifying proposal), definitize within 180 days, clearance at definitization — and neither poor planning nor administrative convenience ever justifies one.

scenarios.ask: The proposal came in at $41M against a $30M NTE, and the contractor wants the ceiling raised. What's your negotiating position?
scenarios.script: This is a UCA question — R-DFARS 217.74: the NTE is the Government's liability ceiling, and it doesn't float. My help: my pricing office on the actuals, the UCA approval authority, and Legal on scope. The position: the qualifying proposal starts definitization; it doesn't reprice the ceiling. First, scope: is the 'extra damage' growth of this repair — negotiable within a deliberately, formally increased NTE if the evidence supports it — or new work needing its own action? Second, the caps hold: 75% of thirty million, not of forty-one. Third, the actuals cut our way on fee — months of incurred cost mean burned-down risk, and weighted guidelines will show it. We definitize on evidence, on schedule, at a ceiling the Government chooses deliberately — not one proposed to us.

scenarios.scenario: Definitizing a 9-month-old undefinitized contract action (UCA), the contractor proposes forward rates for the remaining work but resists providing actual incurred costs for the months already performed — 'the certified proposal covers everything going forward, and actuals would just confuse the comparison.'
baits: 'Certified forward proposal' sounds complete
'Confuse the comparison' — the confusion is the point
key_moves: Work performed has actuals — they're exactly what definitization pricing must use for the performed portion
Certified data spans the action; incurred costs are cost or pricing data
Fee reflects the burned-down risk in weighted guidelines — actuals are how you see it

follow_ups.q: Why does fee typically drop at definitization?
follow_ups.h: Definitization prices two different time zones — which one has facts instead of estimates?
follow_ups.d: Fee drops at definitization because weighted guidelines price RISK, and months of performance burned much of it down: the cost uncertainty the fee would have compensated has partly become known actuals. Pricing the performed portion on estimates when facts exist would pay risk premium for risk already retired. The forward work keeps its honest risk pricing; the performed work gets priced on what happened — that split is the intellectual core of definitizing a mature UCA.

follow_ups.q: What audit support fits here?
follow_ups.h: Match the audit tool to the dollars and the dispute.
follow_ups.d: For incurred-cost visibility on a UCA definitization: DCMA field pricing support for rates and forward-pricing positions, DCAA for incurred-cost and proposal audits at the dollar thresholds — and the contractor's resistance itself is a flag worth an auditor's attention. The ask is targeted: actuals for the performed months, current rate agreements, and reconciliation of the proposal's forward estimates against the performance record to date. No visibility, no agreement — and the caps hold while they decide.

coach.qtype: an undefinitized contract action (UCA) question — R-DFARS 217.74: undefinitized work and decaying negotiation leverage.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the clearance authority, and Legal; the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) for actuals once performance starts.
coach.rule: R-DFARS 217.74 makes UCAs the exception: 50% obligation cap (75% after the qualifying proposal), definitize within 180 days, clearance at definitization — and neither poor planning nor administrative convenience ever justifies one.

scenarios.ask: The contractor resists providing incurred costs — 'the certified proposal covers everything going forward.' What do you require?
scenarios.script: This is a UCA-pricing question — R-DFARS 217.74 meeting RFO 15.403: actuals versus estimates. My help: the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on rates, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) if the audit thresholds or the resistance warrant, my pricing office throughout. The rule: certified cost or pricing data spans the whole action, and incurred costs for nine months of performed work ARE cost or pricing data — 'the proposal covers going forward' is a scope argument against their own certificate. So I require the actuals: the performed portion gets priced on facts, the remaining work on honestly-priced estimates, and fee follows the risk actually remaining — which the actuals will show has burned down. If they won't open the books, the caps hold, the definitization clock presses, and no agreement happens on estimates where facts exist. That's not hardball; that's what definitization means.

scenarios.scenario: Your negotiation team reaches a handshake deal Friday on a $60M sole-source action — inside the objective. The contractor's CEO emails Monday asking to 'paper it this week before our quarter closes.' Clearance is scheduled in twelve days. The program manager (PM) asks if you can sign now and 'ratify through clearance after.'
baits: Deal inside the objective feels pre-blessed
CEO/quarter pressure
key_moves: No award before contract clearance — the review is the approval, not a receipt
'Ratify after' inverts the design: independent eyes before commitment
Ask the clearance shop to accelerate on merits; that's the lawful fast path

follow_ups.q: What does the clearance authority review in the PNM?
follow_ups.h: The PNM is the reviewer's window — what story must it tell?
follow_ups.d: The clearance authority reads the PNM for the whole negotiation: objectives versus outcome and why they moved, the facts behind each significant position change, price analysis supporting fair-and-reasonable, profit basis, data relied on, and compliance. A handshake inside the objective still needs the story told — 'we did well' isn't documentation. The PNM is finished and honest BEFORE clearance, because the review is of the record, not the vibe.

follow_ups.q: What if clearance directs a position change after your handshake?
follow_ups.h: A directed change after handshake tests your professionalism, not your loyalty.
follow_ups.d: If clearance directs a position change, the handshake yields — the deal was always subject to approval, and the negotiation reopens on the directed point with the contractor told honestly that final Government approval required it. This is why you never let a contractor believe a handshake is an award: manage that expectation up front ('agreement subject to clearance'), and the CEO's quarter-close pressure becomes his planning problem, not your integrity problem.

coach.qtype: a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before the Government commits.
coach.smes: the clearance authority itself, your chief, and Legal on any compliance flags.
coach.rule: Two gates catching two failures: business clearance blesses the strategy before release; contract clearance blesses the negotiated result before award. The selector never approves the selection.

scenarios.ask: Handshake Friday, CEO wants it papered this week, clearance is 12 days out. What do you tell everyone?
scenarios.script: This is a clearance question — the Department of the Air Force (DAF) clearance procedures: independent review before commitment, and a calendar can't override it. My help: the clearance authority's shop, my chief, and a finished price negotiation memorandum (PNM). The rule: no award before contract clearance — the review is the approval, not a receipt stamp. And a handshake was always 'agreement subject to Government approval'; I'd confirm the contractor understood that Friday. What I can do honestly: ask the clearance shop to accommodate an earlier review if the file is truly ready — the PNM telling the full story, inside-objective or not. What I won't do is invert the design and paper first, ratify later. The CEO's quarter is real; so is the reason an independent set of eyes comes before the Government commits sixty million dollars.

scenarios.scenario: Day 40 of a the Government Accountability Office (GAO) protest on your IT award, agency counsel concludes the evaluation record has a genuine defect — one factor was scored against an unstated standard. GAO's decision is 60 days away; the program manager (PM) wants to 'ride it out since we might still win.'
baits: 'Might still win' gambling with a known defect
Sunk-cost momentum
key_moves: Voluntary corrective action on a real defect beats a sustain: faster, cheaper, and you control the remedy scope
Riding out a known defect risks paying protester's costs on top of losing
Define the correction precisely (re-evaluate the factor, revised SSDD) — not a panicked full redo

follow_ups.q: What corrective actions are available?
follow_ups.h: Corrective action is the Government prescribing its own remedy — what's on the menu?
follow_ups.d: The menu scales to the defect: reopen the evaluation and re-score against stated criteria; amend the solicitation and take revised proposals if the criteria themselves were defective; reopen discussions if they were flawed; terminate the award and re-award if the outcome changed. The Government chooses the narrowest action that genuinely cures the defect — controlled, scoped, and documented — versus a sustain where GAO recommends and the agency implements under a deadline anyway.

follow_ups.q: How does GAO treat corrective action taken mid-protest?
follow_ups.h: GAO's response to mid-protest correction is the system working.
follow_ups.d: When the agency takes corrective action addressing the protest's core, GAO typically dismisses the protest as academic — the remedy is happening without a decision. Timing matters for costs: correcting promptly after the defect became clear avoids reimbursing protest costs; riding a known defect to a sustain invites paying the protester's costs and attorney fees on top of the same corrective action. Early, honest correction is both cheaper and faster — and it keeps the remedy in the agency's hands.

coach.qtype: a protest question — RFO Part 33 and the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA): venue, stay math, and the record you built months earlier.
coach.smes: Legal drives; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) counsel through Legal; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any override decision.
coach.rule: Know the RFO 33.105 machinery cold — the 10-day/5-day stay rule, three venues with different powers — and remember the real defense was built earlier: criteria stated, followed, and documented.

scenarios.ask: Day 40, real defect found, decision 60 days away. Ride it out or act — and how?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 33 protest question where our own record failed. My help: agency counsel — who found it — plus the source selection authority (SSA) and the evaluation team for the fix. The math: riding out a known defect for 60 more days buys a probable sustain, GAO-directed remedy on GAO's terms, protest costs on top, and a program 60 days later than honest correction would put it. So: voluntary corrective action now — scoped to the actual defect. One factor was scored against an unstated standard, so we reopen that evaluation and re-score against the stated criteria, amending only if the criteria themselves were the problem. GAO dismisses as academic, we control the remedy, and the program moves. The PM's 'we might win' is hope arguing with a record — and the record already told us who wins.

scenarios.scenario: A holder on your MA-indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) emails a formal-looking 'protest' of a $4M task order award (DoD), citing unfair evaluation. It's below the Government Accountability Office (GAO) order-protest threshold and doesn't allege scope growth. The contractor CCs your senior contracting official (SCO) and threatens 'escalation to GAO and the Court' within five days.
baits: Formal formatting and CC-intimidation
The five-day ultimatum
key_moves: Under $35M with no scope allegation: GAO lacks jurisdiction — the lane is the task-order ombudsman
Treat it seriously anyway: review the order file, respond through the ombudsman process
No stay attaches; performance continues while the complaint is worked

follow_ups.q: What DOES get an order to GAO?
follow_ups.h: Two doors to GAO for orders — dollars, or growth.
follow_ups.d: A task or delivery order reaches GAO two ways: value over the threshold ($35M DoD / $10M civilian), or an allegation that the order exceeds the scope, period, or maximum value of the underlying contract — the growth theory, protestable at any dollar value because it alleges work escaped the vehicle's competed boundaries. This complaint alleges neither growth nor crosses the threshold, so GAO's door is closed — which makes the ombudsman the lane, not a loophole.

follow_ups.q: What does the ombudsman actually do?
follow_ups.h: The ombudsman is review, not decoration.
follow_ups.d: The task-order ombudsman — senior, independent of the procuring contracting officer (PCO) — reviews complaints that holders weren't afforded fair opportunity: examines the order file, the evaluation, and the consideration record, and can recommend corrective action to the contracting activity. It's the deliberate substitute Congress built for order-level GAO protests. Engage it seriously: a real review with a documented response either fixes an actual fairness failure or creates the record that ends the complaint.

coach.qtype: a protest question — RFO Part 33 and the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA): venue, stay math, and the record you built months earlier.
coach.smes: Legal drives; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) counsel through Legal; the head of the contracting activity (HCA) owns any override decision.
coach.rule: Know the RFO 33.105 machinery cold — the 10-day/5-day stay rule, three venues with different powers — and remember the real defense was built earlier: criteria stated, followed, and documented.

scenarios.ask: A $4M order 'protest' lands, below GAO's threshold, CC'd to your SCO. How do you handle it?
scenarios.script: This is a protest-jurisdiction question — the RFO 16.508 order-protest rules — and the answer is a lane, not a shrug. My help: Legal, the vehicle's ombudsman, and my own order file. The rule: under $35M with no scope-growth allegation, GAO lacks jurisdiction over a DoD task-order complaint — the lane Congress built is the task-order ombudsman. So I'd respond in writing, correctly and respectfully: naming the right lane, committing to a genuine ombudsman review, and meaning it — the order file, the evaluation, the consideration record all get an honest look, because if fair opportunity actually failed, I want to fix it before the ombudsman tells me to. The SCO on copy gets a heads-up from me first with the facts. Jurisdiction answers the venue question; it doesn't answer the fairness question — I owe both.

scenarios.scenario: A contractor's $85K request for equitable adjustment (REA) for Government-caused test-range delays has sat in your predecessor's inbox for seven months unanswered. The contractor's new letter converts it to a certified claim 'for $85K plus interest from the original submission' and demands a final decision in 60 days.
baits: Interest 'from the original submission' — check the actual trigger
Seven months of silence feels indefensible (it is, but it's not entitlement)
key_moves: Interest runs from receipt of the certified CLAIM, not the earlier REA — correct the math while owning the delay
Under $100K certification isn't required, but as submitted the decision clock is real: decide or settle within the window
Evaluate entitlement on the delay facts now — the merits didn't age out

follow_ups.q: Deemed denial — when and what follows?
follow_ups.h: Silence past the decision deadline is itself a decision — what starts?
follow_ups.d: For claims over $100K, the contracting officer (CO) must decide within 60 days or state when the decision will issue; failure to respond becomes a deemed denial — silence operating as a denial — and the contractor's appeal clock starts: Board within 90 days, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC) within 12 months. A deemed denial surrenders the Government's chance to shape the outcome. The lesson in this file: the seven silent months were free only in appearance; the machinery was always going to start, with or without us.

follow_ups.q: How does the 6-year accrual limit interact with the seven months?
follow_ups.h: The six-year clock runs from accrual — where do seven months fit?
follow_ups.d: The CDA's six-year limit runs from claim accrual — when the events fixing liability occurred — not from REA submission or conversion. Seven months of administrative silence consumes calendar inside that window but doesn't threaten it here. What the delay does cost: goodwill, negotiating position, and now interest from the certified claim's receipt. Accrual math matters most on old, slow-developing disputes — know where the clock started before assuming how much remains.

coach.qtype: a disputes question — the Contract Disputes Act and RFO Part 33: request for equitable adjustment (REA) lane or CDA claim, and substance beats the label.
coach.smes: Legal early, financial management (FM) on funding the outcome, and the contracting officer's representative (COR)/program manager (PM) for the facts record.
coach.rule: Classify by substance under the CDA: a sum certain, certified, with a decision demanded is a claim — interest and decision deadlines already running. The machinery doesn't care what the cover letter says.
coach.cite: Contract Disputes Act · RFO Part 33 · Vol. 2, REAs & Claims

scenarios.ask: A seven-month-old REA just converted to a claim demanding interest back to the REA. What's right, and what's owed?
scenarios.script: This is a disputes question our own silence made worse. My help: Legal now, and the file my predecessor left. First, the classification: as submitted — certified, sum certain, decision demanded — it's a the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) claim, and the machinery runs regardless of the seven embarrassing months. Second, the math: interest runs from receipt of the certified CLAIM, not the earlier REA — I'd correct that respectfully while owning the delay honestly. Under $100K the certification wasn't required, but they've certified it and the substance controls. Then I work it on merits: Government-caused test-range delays have real entitlement; quantum gets an honest review; and I'd move fast toward settlement or a written final decision — because this file has already demonstrated what silence costs.

scenarios.scenario: After a partial termination for convenience (T4C) removed one of three sites from a custodial contract, the contractor's settlement proposal includes: costs at the terminated site (fine), 'unabsorbed overhead' spread across the surviving sites, anticipated profit on the cancelled option years, and $12K in settlement-proposal preparation costs.
baits: The plausible-sounding mix of allowable and not
Option-year profit smuggled into a convenience settlement
key_moves: Costs incurred + reasonable profit on work PERFORMED + settlement expenses = the frame; prep costs are generally allowable here
Anticipated profit on unperformed work (cancelled options especially) is out
Unabsorbed overhead is a real doctrine with strict proof — DCAA support, Legal on the standard

follow_ups.q: Why are settlement prep costs treated differently than claim prep costs?
follow_ups.h: Settlement expenses ride a different rule than claim prep — why?
follow_ups.d: T4C settlement proposal costs — accounting, legal, preparation — are generally allowable as settlement expenses: the Government chose convenience, and making the contractor whole includes the cost of unwinding. The Contract Disputes Act (CDA) claim prep costs are unallowable because the claim is adversarial litigation posture, not performance or settlement of the Government's own choice. Same invoice category, different lane, opposite answers — a favorite board seam.

follow_ups.q: What proof supports unabsorbed overhead?
follow_ups.h: Unabsorbed overhead is a real theory with a real proof burden.
follow_ups.d: Unabsorbed overhead compensates fixed costs that continued while the terminated work no longer absorbed its share. The proof: the termination actually idled capacity (not backfilled by other work), the overhead pools and allocation bases showing the under-absorption, and a causal link to the partial termination — auditable accounting, not assertion. DCAA support fits here. It can be allowable when proven; it's routinely claimed and rarely proven well.

coach.qtype: a disputes question — the Contract Disputes Act and RFO Part 33: request for equitable adjustment (REA) lane or CDA claim, and substance beats the label.
coach.smes: Legal early, financial management (FM) on funding the outcome, and the contracting officer's representative (COR)/program manager (PM) for the facts record.
coach.rule: Classify by substance under the CDA: a sum certain, certified, with a decision demanded is a claim — interest and decision deadlines already running. The machinery doesn't care what the cover letter says.
coach.cite: Contract Disputes Act · RFO Part 33 · Vol. 2, REAs & Claims

scenarios.ask: The partial-T4C settlement asks for unabsorbed overhead, lost anticipated profit, and prep costs. What survives?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 49 terminations-settlement question — the frame decides every line item. My help: the termination contracting officer (CO) channel, the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) on the overhead math, Legal throughout. The frame: costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on work PERFORMED, plus settlement expenses — never anticipatory profit on work the convenience termination cancelled. So: the terminated site's costs, fine. Settlement prep costs, generally allowable — the Government chose convenience and pays for the unwinding. Anticipated profit on the cancelled balance: no, categorically. Unabsorbed overhead: a real theory with a real burden — prove the idle capacity, the pools, the causation, with DCAA's help; assertion isn't absorption. We negotiate the honest package and paper it with a release.

scenarios.scenario: A key-supplier bankruptcy leaves your avionics contractor unable to deliver for at least nine months. They propose novating 'the whole contract' to a competitor who bought the supplier's assets — or, alternatively, ask the Government to termination for convenience (T4C) them 'so nobody's record gets hurt.' Units are needed in six months.
baits: T4C offered as a courtesy to their CPARS
Novation floated casually
key_moves: Bankruptcy upstream may be excusable delay — analyze before any termination posture
T4C isn't a record-laundering service; the decision follows the Government's interest, honestly recorded
Novation runs its own legal process (successor-in-interest, through Legal); meanwhile mission needs may drive reprocurement of the six-month quantity

follow_ups.q: Excusable vs. not for subcontractor failure?
follow_ups.h: Subcontractor failure is excusable only through a specific chain of proof.
follow_ups.d: A subcontractor's failure excuses the prime only when the cause was beyond the control and without the fault of BOTH prime and sub — and the prime couldn't obtain the supplies elsewhere in time. A supplier bankruptcy may qualify; the analysis asks whether the prime managed the risk (second sources, inventory, diligence) and whether substitute performance was truly unavailable. Excusable delay defeats default; it doesn't create entitlement to Government rescue.

follow_ups.q: What does a termination for default (T4D) require if delay proves non-excusable?
follow_ups.h: A non-excusable nine-month slip still demands the full runway.
follow_ups.d: If the delay proves non-excusable, T4D still requires the record: for this anticipatory failure, a demand for adequate assurances / show-cause posture, the excusability analysis documented, Legal engaged, and the final-decision notice with its required contents. Skipping steps because the outcome seems obvious is how defaults convert to convenience terminations on appeal — with the Government paying settlement instead of collecting reprocurement costs.

coach.qtype: a termination question — RFO Part 49 (or the commercial clause under RFO 12.403): fault drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (mandatory), your termination contracting officer channel, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on settlement.
coach.rule: Who's at fault decides what's owed under RFO Part 49: termination for convenience (T4C) makes the contractor whole for work done, no anticipatory profit; termination for default (T4D) demands the full runway — cure, show cause, excusability — because a wrongful default converts to a T4C.

scenarios.ask: Novate to the asset buyer, or T4C 'so nobody looks bad'? What actually governs?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 49 terminations question with a novation offer riding shotgun. My help: Legal, mandatory, and the novation office for the corporate side. Order of operations: first, the excusability analysis — an upstream bankruptcy may excuse the delay if it was beyond the control and without the fault of both prime and sub, and no substitute existed; that record gets built before any termination posture. Second, the novation: a transfer to the asset buyer is a deliberate Government decision — successor capability, responsibility, terms — not a rescue reflex. Third, the 'T4C so nobody looks bad' idea dies on contact: convenience isn't a record-laundering service; the termination decision follows the Government's interest, honestly labeled. Nine months of non-delivery deserves a real analysis, not a face-saving exit.

scenarios.scenario: Two months into a $2M roofing contract, the contractor's crews stop showing up; calls go unanswered for three weeks; the bonding company writes that the firm 'has ceased operations.' The program manager (PM) asks whether you still have to send a cure notice to an empty office before defaulting.
baits: Process formalism ('must cure-notice a ghost?')
Ignoring the surety's role
key_moves: Ceased operations = anticipatory failure; document the abandonment record (attempts, surety letter) with Legal — the notice posture follows the facts
The performance bond is now the story: demand on the surety to complete or fund completion
Move fast; weather and schedule are running against an unmanned roof

follow_ups.q: What does the surety owe under the performance bond?
follow_ups.h: The performance bond exists for this exact morning.
follow_ups.d: Upon default, the surety's obligations under the performance bond activate: it can complete the work itself, finance the contractor's completion, or pay the Government's cost to complete up to the penal sum (100% of the original contract price on construction). Notify the surety formally and early — their letter already signals engagement — and coordinate the completion path through them, because the bond is the Government's primary financial protection on this job now.

follow_ups.q: How do excess reprocurement costs work with a surety in play?
follow_ups.h: Excess costs and the surety's checkbook meet in the completion math.
follow_ups.d: Excess reprocurement costs — the delta between the defaulted contract price and the completion cost — are the defaulted contractor's liability, and on bonded construction the surety stands behind that liability up to the penal sum. Document the reprocurement diligently (competed or justified, mitigated, reasonable) because the surety scrutinizes completion costs like the adversary it partially is. The Government's job: honest completion at a defensible cost, papered for two audiences.

coach.qtype: a termination question — RFO Part 49 (or the commercial clause under RFO 12.403): fault drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (mandatory), your termination contracting officer channel, and the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) on settlement.
coach.rule: Who's at fault decides what's owed under RFO Part 49: termination for convenience (T4C) makes the contractor whole for work done, no anticipatory profit; termination for default (T4D) demands the full runway — cure, show cause, excusability — because a wrongful default converts to a T4C.

scenarios.ask: Crews gone, phones dead, surety says the firm ceased operations. Do you still owe a cure notice — and what next?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 49 termination question where the contractor already answered it. My help: Legal, the surety, and a documented abandonment record. On the cure notice: abandonment — crews gone, three weeks of silence, the surety's own ceased-operations letter — is anticipatory failure; the notice posture follows the facts, and with Legal I'd move on a show-cause/final-decision footing built on the documented record of attempts to reach them. When in doubt, send the notice — it costs days and forecloses arguments. Then the real machinery: formal notice to the surety, whose RFO Part 28 performance bond now owns completion — they finish it, fund it, or pay our cost to complete. Reprocurement gets documented like the surety will audit it, because they will. The roof gets built; the record gets built with it.

scenarios.scenario: An open broad agency announcement (BAA) topic on autonomous logistics draws a white paper from a nontraditional startup — genuinely novel approach, weak cost volume, and a note that they 'won't sign anything giving the Government our IP.' The lab wants them badly and asks whether an Other Transaction (OT) fixes everything.
baits: 'OT fixes everything' — flexibility ≠ magic
Enthusiasm outrunning the rights conversation
key_moves: An OT can tailor IP terms — but the Government still needs SOMETHING durable: define minimum-essential rights against the transition plan
Weak cost volume gets fixed in negotiation regardless of instrument
Write the follow-on production pathway into the prototype OT now if you ever want it

follow_ups.q: What makes a performer 'nontraditional'?
follow_ups.h: Nontraditional has a definition, not a vibe.
follow_ups.d: A nontraditional defense contractor is one that hasn't performed (for a defined preceding period) work subject to full cost accounting standards coverage — the startups, commercial firms, and labs the OT authority exists to attract. Verify status rather than assume it: the OT's justification often rides on nontraditional participation (or cost share, or exceptional circumstances), so the definition is load-bearing, not paperwork.

follow_ups.q: What rights floor would you hold for a transition-bound prototype?
follow_ups.h: Prototype rights are negotiated — what's the floor the transition plan demands?
follow_ups.d: An OT can tailor IP terms freely — that's its power — but the Government still needs rights sufficient for the prototype's PURPOSE: enough license to evaluate, integrate, test, and — critically — transition to production or sustainment per the transition plan. The floor is defined by the roadmap: what the Government must be able to do with the design, data, and interfaces at the next phase. 'You get nothing' fails the floor; 'we take everything' kills the deal the authority exists to enable. Negotiate to the plan.

coach.qtype: a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35, the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) statute, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 Other Transactions (OTs): the right instrument for genuine uncertainty.
coach.smes: your agreements officer channel, Legal, and the science and technology (S&T) program office.
coach.rule: Pick the authority for a reason: RFO Part 35 broad agency announcements (BAAs) compete proposals against a published standard, SBIR Phase III carries statutory sole-source off competed early phases, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 OTs trade the mature protections framework for agility — 'skipping the rules' is never the reason.
coach.cite: RFO Part 35 · SBIR statute · 10 U.S.C. 4022 · Vol. 2, R&D

scenarios.ask: A novel white paper, a weak cost volume, and an IP ultimatum. Does the OT lane fit — and on what terms?
scenarios.script: This is a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — the 10 U.S.C. 4022 OT lane, used for its actual purpose. My help: the agreements officer, Legal, and the lab on the transition plan. The fit: a genuinely novel approach from a nontraditional performer is exactly what OT authority exists for — verify their nontraditional status, because the justification rides on it. The weak cost volume gets fixed in negotiation, not held against the science. On IP: an OT can tailor terms, but 'the Government gets nothing' isn't tailoring — it's failing the transition plan. So we negotiate to the floor the roadmap defines: rights sufficient to evaluate, integrate, and transition the prototype. Flexibility is the OT's gift; purpose is its discipline. We use both.

scenarios.scenario: A program office wants to award a Phase III Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) production contract to a firm — but the firm was acquired last year by a large defense prime, and a competitor argues Phase III 'is a small business program, so they're ineligible now.'
baits: 'Small business program' intuition misapplied to Phase III
Competitor advocacy shaping the analysis
key_moves: Phase III has no size requirement and no dollar cap — eligibility follows derivation from the competed SBIR work, which survives acquisition
Verify the derivation chain and document it; the sole-source basis is the statute
SBIR data rights also survived the acquisition — relevant to everyone's expectations

follow_ups.q: What documents the derivation?
follow_ups.h: The derivation chain is the eligibility document.
follow_ups.d: Document the derivation: the competed Phase I/II awards, the technology developed under them, and how the Phase III work derives from, extends, or completes that SBIR effort — a traceable technical lineage in the file. That derivation is what carries the statutory sole-source basis ('authorized by statute'), so it's written like it will be challenged: because as this competitor demonstrates, it will be.

follow_ups.q: What happens to SBIR rights post-acquisition?
follow_ups.h: The rights were earned during SBIR — what does the acquisition change?
follow_ups.d: SBIR data rights attach to the data developed under the SBIR awards and survive corporate transactions — the acquiring prime steps into the rights the small firm earned, for the protection period the contract defines. What changes with acquisition: future SBIR participation (size matters for new Phase I/II awards), not the earned rights or Phase III eligibility of work already derived. Verify the specific window and scope from the contracts rather than assuming either extreme.

coach.qtype: a research and development (R&D)-authorities question — RFO Part 35, the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) statute, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 Other Transactions (OTs): the right instrument for genuine uncertainty.
coach.smes: your agreements officer channel, Legal, and the science and technology (S&T) program office.
coach.rule: Pick the authority for a reason: RFO Part 35 broad agency announcements (BAAs) compete proposals against a published standard, SBIR Phase III carries statutory sole-source off competed early phases, and 10 U.S.C. 4022 OTs trade the mature protections framework for agility — 'skipping the rules' is never the reason.
coach.cite: RFO Part 35 · SBIR statute · 10 U.S.C. 4022 · Vol. 2, R&D

scenarios.ask: Phase III to a firm now owned by a large prime — the competitor says the program is small-business-only. Who's right?
scenarios.script: This is an SBIR-statute question — Phase III mechanics under new ownership. My help: Legal, the SBIR program office, and the contract file for the derivation record. The rule the competitor missed: Phase III has no size requirement and no dollar cap — eligibility follows DERIVATION from the competed Phase I/II work, and that eligibility survives acquisition. The competition happened in the early phases; Phase III harvests it, by statute, no justification and approval (J&A). So my job is the record: document the derivation chain — awards, technology, lineage to this production work — like it will be challenged, because it just was. And the SBIR data rights the firm earned ride through the acquisition for their defined window. The competitor gets a courteous, correct answer; the file gets the proof.

scenarios.scenario: A design-bid-build project for a maintenance hangar comes in: independent Government cost estimate (IGCE) $8.4M. The draft solicitation announces 'estimated value $8.4M' verbatim, requires only a payment bond 'to save the contractor money,' and sets liquidated damages at $25K/day because 'that will motivate them.'
baits: Transparency instinct (publishing the estimate)
'Motivational' LDs
key_moves: Disclose the magnitude RANGE, never the estimate — protects the Government's negotiating position
Over the bonding threshold both performance AND payment bonds are required
LDs must be a genuine pre-estimate of daily harm — punitive rates are unenforceable

follow_ups.q: How is an LD rate derived defensibly?
follow_ups.h: An LD rate survives review when it estimates something.
follow_ups.d: Liquidated damages must be a reasonable forecast of the Government's probable ACTUAL costs of late completion — extended inspection and administration, alternate facility costs, mission impacts — computed and documented per day. Punitive rates ('high to motivate') are legally unenforceable as penalties: the contractor attacks the rate, and an unsupported number can collapse entirely. The derivation memo in the file is what makes the clause collectible.

follow_ups.q: Who is the payment bond actually for?
follow_ups.h: Follow who can't lien a federal building.
follow_ups.d: The payment bond protects subcontractors and suppliers — who cannot place mechanics' liens on Government property, so the bond replaces the security a lien would give them on a commercial job. It's not protection for the Government or a cost to 'save' the contractor; it's what lets subs extend credit on federal construction at all. Dropping it above the threshold isn't kindness — it's unlawful, and it dries up the very subcontractor base the project needs.

coach.qtype: a construction/services question — RFO Parts 36 and 37, with RFO Part 28 bonds: specialized statutory machinery.
coach.smes: Legal, the labor advisor on wage determinations, and the installation civil engineers.
coach.rule: Construction and services run on their own rails: RFO Part 28 bonds over $150K, written notice before disturbing a differing site condition (RFO Part 36), qualifications-based architect-engineer (A&E) selection, and no personal-services drift (RFO Part 37).
coach.cite: RFO Parts 36/37 · Part 28 bonds · Vol. 2, Construction

scenarios.ask: The draft solicitation discloses the $8.4M IGCE, drops the performance bond, and sets LDs 'high to motivate.' Fix it.
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 36 construction question — three fixes before this solicitation moves. My help: civil engineering on the LD math, Legal, and the labor advisor. One: never disclose the estimate — the solicitation states the magnitude RANGE; publishing $8.4M verbatim hands every offeror our negotiating position. Two: over the RFO Part 28 bonding threshold, performance AND payment bonds are both required — the payment bond protects subs who can't lien Government property; dropping it is unlawful, not thrifty. Three: liquidated damages must forecast probable actual costs of delay — computed, documented, per day; 'high to motivate' is a penalty, and penalties don't survive review. Construction runs on specialized rails. This draft missed three of them; that's what review is for.

scenarios.scenario: Six months into a base operations support contract, the contractor's site manager quits. Rather than wait for a replacement, the squadron 'temporarily' assigns tasking through the Government flight chief — daily standups, direct assignments, leave approvals for contractor staff. Everyone agrees it's working great.
baits: Temporary-and-working normalizes the arrangement
Leave approvals buried in the list (the loudest red flag)
key_moves: Government supervision of contractor employees — down to leave approval — is personal services without authority; stop it now
The contract requires the contractor to manage its people: demand the replacement manager under the key-personnel terms
Document the interim fix that routes direction through the contractor's structure

follow_ups.q: What's the legal test for personal services?
follow_ups.h: The test is the relationship, not the location.
follow_ups.d: Personal services exist when Government personnel exercise relatively continuous supervision and control over contractor employees — the employer-employee pattern: assigning daily tasks, directing how work is done, approving leave. That relationship requires specific statutory authority the contract doesn't have. Proximity, embedded seating, and long duration don't create the violation; supervision does — and daily standups with leave approval is supervision by any definition.

follow_ups.q: What does the key-personnel clause let you demand?
follow_ups.h: The contract already has a lever for the manager gap.
follow_ups.d: The key-personnel clause lets the Government demand what the vacancy actually requires: a qualified replacement for the departed site manager within the clause's timeline, Government approval rights over the substitution, and interim management arrangements THE CONTRACTOR provides. The gap that invited the drift is a contractor performance obligation — enforce it as one, rather than back-filling with Government supervision that violates the services statute.

coach.qtype: a construction/services question — RFO Parts 36 and 37, with RFO Part 28 bonds: specialized statutory machinery.
coach.smes: Legal, the labor advisor on wage determinations, and the installation civil engineers.
coach.rule: Construction and services run on their own rails: RFO Part 28 bonds over $150K, written notice before disturbing a differing site condition (RFO Part 36), qualifications-based architect-engineer (A&E) selection, and no personal-services drift (RFO Part 37).
coach.cite: RFO Parts 36/37 · Part 28 bonds · Vol. 2, Construction

scenarios.ask: The flight chief is running the contractor's crew — standups, tasking, even leave approval. What's broken, and how do you fix it?
scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 37 services question — personal-services drift, in full bloom. My help: Legal and the squadron's leadership, because the fix is behavioral. The test: continuous Government supervision of contractor employees creates an employer-employee relationship that's unlawful without specific authority — and daily tasking plus leave approval is textbook. So, today, in writing: the flight chief stops directing the crew; all tasking flows through the performance work statement (PWS) and the contractor's own management. Then enforce the contract: the key-personnel clause demands a qualified site-manager replacement on the clause's timeline — the vacancy is the contractor's obligation to cure, not the Government's invitation to supervise. And I'd check whether the PWS itself invites this drift, because clauses don't fix what habits recreate weekly.

scenarios.scenario: An audit flags that a unit paid a contractor twice for the same invoice eight months ago — $38K. The contractor never mentioned it. The program manager (PM) suggests 'just deducting it from next month's invoice quietly' to avoid the paperwork of a formal demand.
baits: Quiet netting feels efficient
Eight months of contractor silence goes unremarked
key_moves: Overpayments are Government debts with a process: written demand, interest rules, FM coordination — not informal netting
The contractor's duty to report duplicate payments matters; note it in the record
Fix the payment-review breakdown that let it happen

follow_ups.q: When can you offset against invoices — and how formally?
follow_ups.h: Offset is a real tool with formal clothes.
follow_ups.d: The Government can offset — but through the debt process, not informal netting: a written demand establishing the debt, the contractor's opportunity to respond, interest per the debt rules, FM and the payment office executing formally so both ledgers reconcile. A quiet deduction leaves the debt unestablished, the interest uncollected, the accounting records false, and invites a dispute over an 'unexplained' short payment. Same money, lawful clothes.

follow_ups.q: What does the contractor's silence do to the relationship record?
follow_ups.h: Silence about known overpayments is a data point about the partner.
follow_ups.d: Contractors have obligations to report known overpayments — eight months of silence on a $38K windfall goes to integrity and business ethics, and belongs in the relationship record: raised with the contractor directly, documented, and weighed in future responsibility and past-performance contexts. One quiet windfall isn't debarment material, but the pattern it might reveal is exactly what the integrity standard exists to catch.

coach.qtype: a fiscal-law question — Time, Purpose, Amount under the appropriations statutes, with RFO Part 32 carrying the financing side.
coach.smes: Financial management (FM)/Comptroller first and always, then Legal; the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Red Book and DoD FMR are the references.
coach.rule: Run T-P-A on every dollar: the right-year money for a bona fide need of that period, the appropriated purpose (31 U.S.C. 1301), within the available amount — Anti-Deficiency violations are the serious, reportable kind.
coach.cite: RFO Part 32 · GAO Red Book / DoD FMR · Vol. 2, Fiscal

scenarios.ask: A $38K double payment, eight months quiet, and a PM proposing quiet deduction. What's the lawful path?
scenarios.script: This is a fiscal question — Government debt collection under 31 U.S.C. 3711 — with an integrity thread. My help: financial management (FM) first — this is their machinery — plus Legal and the payment office. The rule: an overpayment is a Government debt with a process: written demand establishing the $38K, interest per the debt rules, and recovery by payment or formal offset — executed so both sides' books reconcile. The PM's quiet deduction fails audit, forfeits interest, and manufactures a dispute. Separately, the contractor's eight months of silence on a known double payment is an integrity data point: I'd raise it directly, document the conversation, and let it inform the relationship record. Recover the money formally; remember the silence professionally.

scenarios.scenario: On a competitive cost-type source selection, one offeror's proposed labor rates run 30% below the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA)-recognized rates for their own facility. Their technical volume is strong. An evaluator suggests scoring them down on technical 'to reflect the pricing games.'
baits: Punishing price problems in the technical score
'Games' assumed rather than analyzed
key_moves: The lane for low cost-type pricing is cost realism: adjust to a most-probable-cost for evaluation — the proposal competes at what it will really cost
Technical scores reflect technical merit; cross-lane punishment is protest fuel
Document the realism adjustments and their basis (DCMA rates)

follow_ups.q: Probable cost vs. proposed cost in the source selection decision document (SSDD)?
follow_ups.h: The SSDD compares offers at the cost the Government will actually pay.
follow_ups.d: On cost-type competitions, the source selection authority's (SSA) tradeoff uses most-probable cost — the Government's realism-adjusted estimate of what each offeror will actually cost — not the proposed number. Proposed cost is the offeror's claim; probable cost is the evaluation's finding; the delta between them is itself a risk signal documented in the record. An SSDD trading off against lowball proposed numbers compares fictions — and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reads SSDDs for exactly this.

follow_ups.q: When does realism apply on fixed-price competitions?
follow_ups.h: Fixed-price flips who owns the overrun — what's left to evaluate?
follow_ups.d: On firm-fixed-price (FFP) competitions, cost realism isn't used to adjust price — the contractor owns any overrun, so the price stands as proposed. Realism analysis may still appear for a different purpose: assessing whether an unrealistically low price reflects misunderstanding of the requirement or performance risk (documented in risk ratings, responsibility analysis) — but the evaluated price doesn't move. Know both regimes; the panel loves the contrast.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications, communications, discussions — and make discussions meaningful.

scenarios.ask: An offeror's rates run 30% under their own DCMA-recognized rates. Score them down, or something else?
scenarios.script: This is a source-selection pricing question — RFO 15.404-3 cost realism, not ratings. My help: my pricing office, DCMA's rate data, and the source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chair on keeping lanes clean. The rule: on a competitive cost-type selection, unrealistically low cost gets a cost-realism adjustment — we evaluate at most-probable cost, because on cost-type the Government eats the overrun. Rates 30% under the offeror's own DCMA-recognized rates get adjusted upward on that evidence, and the proposal competes at what it will actually cost. Technical ratings stay technical — scoring merit down to punish pricing corrupts both records. If the strong technical volume survives the honest cost picture, they can still win. They just can't win with arithmetic we know is fiction.

scenarios.scenario: You are the contracting officer on a competitive tradeoff source selection for 3,000 widgets, Government estimate $16.5M. Three proposals arrive. Offerors A and C are priced within 10% of the estimate, but both drew initial technical ratings of Marginal — neither demonstrated an adequate approach to the requirements. Offeror B is priced 40% above the estimate with an initial technical rating of Unacceptable: a deficiency-riddled proposal that is unawardable as written.
scenarios.ask: How would you proceed?

frameworks.why: The range comprises the most highly rated proposals — a formal PCO determination, SSA-approved, documented in the CRDD with reasons for inclusion and exclusion.

Nobody is cleanly awardable, so discussions are how the Government gets to an award: each offeror in the range must hear its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond.

baits: "Award without discussions to the least-bad offeror" — no initial proposal supports a clean award
"Keep B in the range out of caution" — an unawardable proposal priced 40% high has to earn inclusion, not inertia
key_moves: No proposal supports award as submitted — establish a competitive range and open discussions
Include A and C (Marginal is fixable through meaningful discussions); document B's exclusion in the CRDD on ratings AND price
Conduct meaningful discussions with A and C — each hears its own weaknesses and deficiencies, tailored, even-handed
Request FPRs after discussions close, re-evaluate, and select on the stated criteria

follow_ups.q: Offeror B demands to stay in — 'you can't eliminate us before discussions.' Can you?
follow_ups.h: The range is the most highly rated proposals — is B among them on any honest reading?
follow_ups.d: Yes, you can exclude B. The competitive range comprises the most highly rated proposals — an unawardable technical rating combined with a price 40% above the estimate keeps B out on both dimensions, documented in the CRDD signed by the CO and SSA. B is entitled to a pre-award debrief explaining its exclusion; it is not entitled to discussions the range determination lawfully denied it.

follow_ups.q: During discussions, Offeror A asks how their price compares to the competition. What can you say?
follow_ups.h: Discussions address their weaknesses — whose information would a price comparison reveal?
follow_ups.d: You can tell A their price appears high or low relative to the Government's analysis if that's a documented concern — but never reveal other offerors' prices, rankings, or relative standing. Discussions are about each offeror's own proposal. Disclosing competitive standing crosses into conduct that taints the selection: it's source selection information, and sharing it invites both a the Procurement Integrity Act (PIA) problem and a protest from whoever the disclosure disadvantaged.

scenarios.script: This is an RFO Part 15 source-selection question — the competitive-range decision. My help: the source selection evaluation board's (SSEB) documented evaluations, Legal, and the source selection authority (SSA) who approves the range. The rule: no initial proposal supports award — two Marginals and an Unacceptable — so award without discussions is off the table even if the solicitation preserved it. I'd establish the competitive range on the most-highly-rated standard: A and C are in — Marginal with fixable weaknesses is exactly what meaningful discussions exist to cure; B is out on ratings and price together, documented in the CRDD. Then discussions with A and C — each hears its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies, tailored and even-handed — followed by final proposal revisions (FPRs), re-evaluation, and a tradeoff decision on the stated criteria. The panel wants the sequence: range, discussions, FPRs, award — each step on the record.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the source selection authority (SSA), your source selection evaluation board (SSEB) chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications, communications, discussions — and make discussions meaningful.

scenarios.scenario: A board member leans back and asks: "What can Air Force Contracting do to combat the threat of China catching up to — and in some areas surpassing — USAF capabilities?"
scenarios.ask: There's no framework to recite here — the panel wants your perspective as a business leader. What do you say?
key_moves: Speed as a weapon: every month cut from acquisition lead time is capability fielded sooner — use the streamlined authorities we already own (commercial procedures, OTs, CSOs, the RFO's trimmed process) instead of defaulting to the long way
Broaden the base: nontraditionals, commercial tech, and small business bring the innovation velocity the threat demands — the tools exist; the habit is what's missing
Buy like a portfolio: data rights and modular strategies that keep competition alive across a system's life, so we're never hostage to one vendor's pace
Develop people: COs who know the full toolkit make speed decisions confidently; training and warrants are combat capability
Protect the industrial base and supply chain — know where the single points of failure are before the crisis finds them

follow_ups.q: Which one of those would you actually change first in your own office, and how?
follow_ups.h: Pick something inside a procuring contracting officer's (PCO) actual authority — not policy you'd wish for.
follow_ups.d: Strong answers pick a lever the speaker actually controls: defaulting to commercial procedures and existing vehicles before building bespoke contracts; setting internal cycle-time standards for routine actions; pre-negotiating blanket purchase agreements (BPAs) and ordering structures against recurring demand; or building the office's OT/CSO muscle through one deliberate pilot. The panel is testing whether your strategic view survives contact with your own signature block — answer with something you could start Monday.

follow_ups.q: Which acquisition authorities do you see as underused today — and what's the risk of overusing them?
follow_ups.h: Name the agility lanes, then show you know their discipline.
follow_ups.d: Underused: commercial-first determinations, existing vehicles before bespoke contracts, OTs and CSOs for genuinely nontraditional work, and the RFO's streamlined procedures used as designed. The overuse risk is the mirror image: agility lanes used to dodge discipline — an OT to skip competition, a CSO stretched past its purpose — which burns the authority for everyone when it fails review. The board wants both halves: eagerness to use the toolkit, and the judgment that every authority survives scrutiny only when used for its actual purpose.

scenarios.script: This is a perspective question — the panel is testing whether I think like a business leader, not whether I can recite. I'd anchor on speed and breadth. Speed: our adversary's advantage is decision-to-fielding velocity, and contracting owns a controllable slice of that timeline — so my office defaults to the fastest lawful lane: commercial procedures, existing vehicles, Other Transactions (OTs) and commercial solutions openings (CSOs) where they genuinely fit, and the RFO's streamlined process used as designed. Breadth: the innovation we need lives partly outside the traditional base — nontraditionals and small business come in through the authorities built for them. Underneath both: data rights and modular strategies that keep competition alive for a system's whole life, and people trained to use the full toolkit confidently. China isn't out-regulating us — it's out-pacing us. Contracting's contribution to the fight is tempo.

coach.qtype: a perspective question — the panel is testing how you think as a business leader, not what you can recite.
coach.smes: Nobody to phone — this one is yours. Anchor on your own experience, your office, and what you actually control.
coach.rule: Answer in your own voice with a definition, a concrete plan, and one example — and show the judgment to know where the boring answer is the right one.
coach.cite: Your own experience — verify anything you cite at acquisition.gov/far-overhaul

scenarios.scenario: The board president asks: "What does innovation mean to you — and how will you push innovative practices into your programs once you're an Unlimited procuring contracting officer (PCO)?"
scenarios.ask: Answer in your own voice — the panel wants your working definition and your concrete plan, not a poster slogan.
key_moves: Define it operationally: innovation is fielding a better outcome faster — a business-process result, not a technology buzzword
Name your tools: commercial preference, OTs and CSOs where they fit, performance-based requirements that buy outcomes instead of tasks, modular strategies that keep options open
Make risk explicit: innovation means taking deliberate, documented business risk — the file explains the judgment, and my warrant exists to sign for it
Push it downward: train the team to bring me options, not just compliance — the question 'what would faster look like?' asked on every strategy
One concrete habit: every new requirement gets a genuine commercial-first and existing-vehicle look before anyone drafts a bespoke solicitation

follow_ups.q: Give the panel one example where innovation would be the WRONG answer.
follow_ups.h: Think about where the boring tool is the right tool — mature requirements, stable markets.
follow_ups.d: Strong answers show judgment about fit: a mature, stable, well-priced production requirement wants an FFP contract and disciplined administration, not a novel instrument; a routine severable service wants the base-plus-options rail. Innovation spent where a proven tool fits adds risk without return — the discipline is matching the instrument to the uncertainty, and 'boring on purpose' is often the most professional answer in the room. Panels reward candidates who know when NOT to reach for the shiny authority.

follow_ups.q: How do you create room for your people to take smart risks?
follow_ups.h: Cover, documentation, and what happens after a miss.
follow_ups.d: Three moves: give cover — the PCO owns the decision, so the team knows a defensible judgment call won't be re-litigated onto them; demand documentation — the file tells the story of the judgment, which converts 'risk' into 'reasoned decision'; and debrief misses without blame — a documented, reasonable call that didn't work is training material, not a career event. Innovation dies in offices where the only safe answer is the slowest one; it lives where judgment is expected, papered, and defended.

scenarios.script: This is a perspective question, and I'd answer it as a definition plus a plan. My definition: innovation in contracting is fielding a better outcome faster — it's a business result, not a gadget. The plan, as an Unlimited PCO: first, defaults — every requirement gets a real commercial-first and existing-vehicle look before anyone builds bespoke; second, the right authorities used for their actual purpose — Other Transactions (OTs) and commercial solutions openings (CSOs) where nontraditional participation or prototype speed genuinely needs them, never as rule-avoidance; third, requirements shaped as outcomes so industry can propose the how. And underneath it: deliberate, documented risk-taking — my warrant exists so someone can sign for professional judgment, and my file will always show the judgment. The other half of the answer is knowing when innovation is wrong: mature production wants boring, disciplined firm-fixed-price (FFP). Matching the tool to the uncertainty — that's the craft.

coach.qtype: a perspective question — the panel is testing how you think as a business leader, not what you can recite.
coach.smes: Nobody to phone — this one is yours. Anchor on your own experience, your office, and what you actually control.
coach.rule: Answer in your own voice with a definition, a concrete plan, and one example — and show the judgment to know where the boring answer is the right one.
coach.cite: Your own experience — verify anything you cite at acquisition.gov/far-overhaul

scenarios.scenario: A panel member notes: "The rules are changing faster than they ever have — the RFO rewrite, class deviations landing monthly, thresholds moving, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) sections taking effect mid-year. What's right one day is wrong the next." She asks how you, as a contracting officer, stay current — and how you keep your team from acting on stale guidance.
scenarios.ask: What are some concrete things you do to stay abreast of changes that affect your acquisitions?
key_moves: Primary sources on a rhythm: the live RFO text and class deviation lists at acquisition.gov, DPC memos, and the Federal Register — checked on a schedule, not when convenient
Never quote a threshold or citation from memory — verify against the current text before it goes in a document; the reg you memorized may have moved

Structured team mechanisms: a recurring policy touchpoint in staff meetings, routing significant changes with a one-line 'what this changes for us,' and updating office templates the week a change lands
Your network as an early-warning system: policy shop, Legal, peer COs across the enterprise — most changes announce themselves in conversation before they bite in a file
Treat currency as a professional obligation: the appendix of every guide rots — the habit of verification is what doesn't

follow_ups.q: A change lands mid-acquisition — the threshold your strategy relied on moved. What do you actually do with the active file?
follow_ups.h: Effective dates and applicability rules decide — which actions does the change actually reach?
follow_ups.d: First, read the change's own applicability terms: most changes apply to actions initiated (or contracts awarded) after an effective date, and many expressly grandfather in-flight actions — the answer is usually in the deviation or rule itself. Then document the analysis in the file: which version governs this action and why. If the change genuinely reaches your acquisition, adjust the strategy deliberately — amend the solicitation, re-approve at the right tier — rather than hoping nobody notices. The file that explains its own regulatory baseline survives every audit that follows a rule change.

follow_ups.q: A teammate cites a threshold from memory in a justification and approval (J&A) draft — what do you do?
follow_ups.h: The habit is the finding, not the number.
follow_ups.d: Verify the number against the live RFO text before the document moves — most thresholds shifted in October 2025, so memory is a known-bad source. Fix the document, then coach the habit: every number in every document gets verified at acquisition.gov against the current text and deviations, no exceptions. And check the office templates, because a stale template reproduces the same wrong number faster than any individual can. The specific threshold matters less than the discipline — that's what the panel is really asking about.
