scenarios.script: This is a professional-habits question, and I'd answer with my actual system. Primary sources on a rhythm: the live RFO text and the class-deviation list at acquisition.gov, DPC policy memos, and the Federal Register — on my calendar, not left to chance. A personal rule the current environment demands: I never quote a threshold or citation from memory; every number gets verified against the live text before it enters a document, because what I memorized last quarter may have moved. For the team: a standing policy touchpoint in staff meetings, significant changes routed with one line on what they change for us, and templates updated the week a change lands — stale templates are how offices act on dead guidance. And my network — policy shop, Legal, peer COs — is the early-warning system; most changes announce themselves in conversation before they bite a file. The rules will keep moving. The habit of verification is what stays.

thresholds.q: Micro-purchase threshold?
thresholds.x: $15,000 since the 1 Oct 2025 adjustment. $10K is the legacy figure old guides still print; contingency operations carry higher MPTs. Below it: Government Purchase Card (GPC) lane, fair distribution, no formal competition file.

thresholds.q: Simplified Acquisition Threshold?
thresholds.x: $350,000 since 1 Oct 2025 ($250K is the pre-adjustment reflex). The SAT is the biggest fork: above it, the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) and formal procedures; the micro-purchase threshold (MPT)-to-SAT band is auto-reserved for small business.

thresholds.q: Certified cost or pricing data — DoD actions entered after 30 Jun 2026?
thresholds.a: $10,000,000 — DoD only (10 U.S.C. 3702 as amended by FY26 NDAA §1804(c); R-DFARS 215.403-3). Civilian agencies stayed at $2.5M; Title 41 was never amended.
d: $2,000,000 (unchanged by the FY26 NDAA)
thresholds.x: FY26 the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) §1804 raised the trigger to $10M for actions entered after 30 June 2026. The statute controls even where printed regulation text still shows the old figure — know which side of the date line your action sits on.

thresholds.q: Certified cost or pricing data — contracts entered on/before 30 Jun 2026 and their mods?
thresholds.a: $2,500,000 — and still the figure for every civilian agency regardless of date. $950,000 for prime contracts awarded before 1 Jul 2018.
thresholds.x: Contracts entered on or before 30 June 2026 — and their modifications — keep the $2.5M trigger. A mod to an old contract doesn't graduate to the new $10M line; the contract's entry date governs.

thresholds.q: Certified data prohibited at or below…?
d: the MPT ($15,000)
thresholds.x: At or below the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) ($350K), requiring certified data is prohibited — not optional. Between the SAT and the trigger you work with data other than certified when the market evidence is thin.

thresholds.q: Commercial streamlined procedures ceiling (RFO 12.201-1)?
thresholds.x: $9M is the streamlined-commercial ceiling at RFO 12.201-1 — the lane that lets commercial buys move on simplified acquisition procedures (SAP)-like speed well above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT). Confusable with the $7.5M market-research and debrief lines; keep the three apart.

thresholds.q: When is market research required? (RFO 10.001)
thresholds.a: Before developing new requirements documents; before soliciting over the SAT ($350,000); and before awarding a task or delivery order over the SAT. Documentation carries no dollar threshold — suit it to the size and complexity of the buy.
d: $9,000,000; research current within 12 months
$5,000,000; research current within 24 months
the SAT ($350,000); research current within 18 months
thresholds.x: Over $7.5M non-commercial, documented market research is required, and research is treated as current for 18 months. Two numbers, one card: the dollar trigger and the shelf life.

thresholds.q: Justification and approval (J&A) approval — up to $900K?
d: The Competition Advocate
One level above the CO
The HCA (delegable)
thresholds.x: Up to $900K the CO's own certification on the J&A is the approval — no separate signature needed. The ladder starts above that: Competition Advocate to $20M.

thresholds.q: Justification and approval (J&A) approval — $5M? $15M?
d: The contracting officer (certification = approval)
HPA/PEO (tier runs to $150M DoD)
The SPE — everything above $900K
thresholds.x: Both $5M and $15M sit in the Competition Advocate's band, which runs from above $900K to $20M. Boards love asking two values inside one tier to see if you know the band, not just a number.

thresholds.q: Justification and approval (J&A) approval — $60M (DoD)?
thresholds.a: Head of the Procuring Activity / PEO (tier to $150M DoD)
d: Competition Advocate (tier to $90M DoD)
Senior Procurement Executive (everything above $20M)
The HCA, non-delegable, at any value over $50M
thresholds.x: $60M sits in the HPA/program executive officer (PEO) tier, which for DoD runs from above $20M to $150M. The $150M DoD line (vs. $90M elsewhere) is the detail that separates the prepared from the guessing.

thresholds.q: Justification and approval (J&A) approval — $200M (DoD)?
d: Head of the Procuring Activity / PEO (no upper limit)
USD(A&S) — above $100M DoD
Competition Advocate with SPE concurrence
thresholds.x: Above $150M (DoD) the J&A goes to the Senior Procurement Executive. There's no USD(A&S) tier in this ladder — SPE is the top rung.

thresholds.q: Justification and approval (J&A) posting to SAM.gov — standard? urgency?
thresholds.a: 14 days after award; 30 days for urgency
d: 30 days after award; 14 days for urgency
10 days after award; 20 days for urgency
Before award in all cases — that's the point of posting
thresholds.x: 14 days after award is the standard posting window; urgency awards get 30 — the one exception where posting trails longer, because the buy couldn't wait for paperwork. Posting before award isn't the rule.

thresholds.q: 8(a) sole source without justification and approval (J&A) — DoD? civilian?
d: $50M DoD; $25M civilian
$100M DoD; $10M civilian
$150M DoD; $30M civilian
thresholds.x: 8(a) sole source without a J&A runs to $100M for DoD, $30M civilian — the program's statutory basis covers it below those lines. The $10M/$25M-style figures belong to other ladders.

thresholds.q: Competitive 8(a) begins at…?
d: $7M manufacturing / $4M other
$10M manufacturing / $5M other
$8.5M across all industries
thresholds.x: Competitive 8(a) begins at $8.5M manufacturing / $5.5M other — above those, requirements in the program compete among 8(a) firms. Same numbers as the HUBZone/woman-owned small business (WOSB) caps; that's not a coincidence, it's the pattern.

thresholds.q: HUBZone / woman-owned small business (WOSB) sole-source caps?
d: $7.5M manufacturing / $4.5M other
$8.5M manufacturing / $5M other
$10M manufacturing / $6.5M other
thresholds.x: HUBZone and WOSB sole-source caps: $8.5M manufacturing / $5.5M other. The service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB) 'other' cap is $5M — half a million lower — which is exactly the confusion this card exists to kill.

thresholds.q: Service-disabled veteran-owned small business (SDVOSB) sole-source caps?
d: $8.5M manufacturing / $5.5M other
$7M manufacturing / $4M other
$10M manufacturing / $5.5M other
thresholds.x: SDVOSB: $8.5M manufacturing / $5M other. The $5M (not $5.5M) 'other' figure is the odd one out among the program caps — the detail that catches people who memorized one pair.

thresholds.q: Subcontracting plan trigger?
d: $750K ($1.5M construction), non-small primes
$1M ($2.5M construction), all primes
the SAT ($350K), non-small primes
thresholds.x: Subcontracting plans trigger at $900K ($2M construction) for other-than-small primes. Small businesses never owe one — the plan is how large primes account for small-business opportunity.

thresholds.q: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) task-order protest floor — DoD? civilian?
thresholds.a: $35M DoD / $10M civilian (any value if the order grows scope, period, or ceiling)
d: $25M DoD / $10M civilian (no exceptions)
$35M for both DoD and civilian
$10M DoD / $5M civilian (any value for scope growth)
thresholds.x: GAO hears task-order protests at $35M+ (DoD) / $10M+ (civilian) — but at ANY value when the protest says the order grew beyond the vehicle's scope, period, or ceiling. That exception is the half everyone forgets.

thresholds.q: Indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) order debriefing rights begin at… (RFO 16.507)?
d: the SAT ($350K)
thresholds.x: Order-level debriefing rights begin at $7.5M under RFO 16.507. Below that, unsuccessful holders get brief explanations, not the full debrief machinery.

thresholds.q: Fair-opportunity exception determination and approval (D&A) approval tiers?
thresholds.a: Same ladder as J&As: ≤$900K CO · ≤$20M CA · ≤$90M/$150M-DoD HPA-PEO · above SPE
d: One flat tier: the fair-opportunity ombudsman approves all D&As
The head of the contracting activity at every value — non-delegable
One level above the CO at any value, per the CID pattern
thresholds.x: Fair-opportunity exceptions ride a D&A up the same ladder as justifications and approvals (J&As): contracting officer (CO) to $900K, Competition Advocate to $20M, head of the procuring activity (HPA)/program executive officer (PEO) to $90M ($150M DoD), senior procurement executive (SPE) above. One ladder, two documents — learn it once, cite it twice.

thresholds.q: The Contract Disputes Act (CDA) claim certification required over…?
thresholds.x: Claims over $100,000 must be certified — accuracy, good faith, and authority to bind. It's a CDA requirement, distinct from the DoD request for equitable adjustment (REA) certification that starts at the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT).

thresholds.q: The Contract Disputes Act (CDA) claim must be brought within…?
d: 3 years of accrual
1 year of the CO's final decision
10 years of contract closeout
thresholds.x: Six years from accrual — the CDA statute of limitations. It runs from when the claim accrued (events fixing liability), not from award, invoice, or closeout.

thresholds.q: Claim appeal windows — Board? The U.S. Court of Federal Claims (COFC)?
d: 12 months Board / 90 days COFC
60 days Board / 6 months COFC
90 days for both venues
thresholds.x: 90 days to the Board of Contract Appeals, 12 months to the Court of Federal Claims — from receipt of the contracting officer's (CO) final decision. Miss the Board window and COFC is the only door left.
thresholds.ref: Contract Disputes Act · Vol. 2, REAs & Claims

thresholds.q: Request for equitable adjustment (REA) certification (DoD) kicks in above…?
d: $100,000 — same as the claim certification
all REAs regardless of value
thresholds.x: The DoD REA certification kicks in above the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) ($350K) — an R-DFARS requirement, and a different certification from the Contract Disputes Act (CDA) claim cert at $100K. Two certs, two thresholds, two purposes.

thresholds.q: Undefinitized contract action (UCA) obligation cap before qualifying proposal? after?
d: 75% of NTE; 90% after
50% of NTE; 80% after
25% of NTE; 50% after
thresholds.x: 50% of the not-to-exceed before the qualifying proposal; 75% once it's in. The caps are the Government's leverage — an undefinitized contractor runs out of funded runway unless the proposal shows up.

thresholds.q: Undefinitized contract action (UCA) definitization deadline?
thresholds.a: 180 days from the qualifying proposal (or when obligations hit the caps)
d: 90 days from the qualifying proposal
180 days from award, regardless of proposal
One year from the undefinitized award
thresholds.x: 180 days from the qualifying proposal — or earlier if obligations hit the caps. The clock runs from the proposal, not from award; that's what makes slow-rolling the proposal a leverage play.

thresholds.q: Construction performance + payment bonds required over…?
thresholds.x: Performance and payment bonds are required for construction over $150,000 — the Miller Act pattern. Payment bonds exist because subs and suppliers can't lien Government property.

thresholds.q: Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) fee ceilings — research and development (R&D)? most others? Architect-engineer (A&E)?
thresholds.a: 15% R&D · 10% most others · 6% A-E (RFO 15.404-9). For the Army, Navy and Air Force, A-E is 10% — R-DFARS 236.202-371 overrides the 6%.
thresholds.x: CPFF fee ceilings: 15% R&D, 10% most other work, 6% A&E. Statutory lids, not negotiation targets — and the A&E 6% applies to the design fee, a favorite board follow-up.

thresholds.q: E.O. 14402 other-than-firm-fixed-price (FFP) justification — DoD? most agencies?
d: $50M DoD; $10M most agencies (RFO 16.104)
$100M DoD; $25M most agencies (RFO 16.104)
$150M DoD; $35M most agencies (RFO 16.104)
thresholds.x: E.O. 14402 requires justification for other-than-FFP above $100M for DoD and $10M for most agencies (DHS $25M, NASA $35M). The DoD line being 10× the default is the memorable asymmetry.

thresholds.q: Ratification approval — over simplified acquisition threshold (SAT)? at/under?
thresholds.a: HCA (delegable) over SAT; COCO level at/under
d: HCA (non-delegable) at every value
SPE over SAT; HCA at/under
The CO who discovers it, with JA concurrence
thresholds.x: Ratification approval sits with the head of the contracting activity (HCA) (delegable) over the SAT, and at the chief of the contracting office (COCO) level at or under it. It never belongs to the person who made the commitment — that's the point.

thresholds.q: Post-award protest stay window at the Government Accountability Office (GAO)?
thresholds.a: 10 days from award or 5 days from the required debrief — whichever is later
d: 5 days from award or 10 days from the debrief — whichever is later
10 days from award, full stop — the debrief has no effect
30 days from award or 10 days from the debrief — whichever is earlier
thresholds.x: The Competition in Contracting Act (CICA) stay attaches if the protest is filed within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debrief — whichever is LATER. 'Later' is the word that decides real cases; the debrief branch only exists when a required debrief was requested.

thresholds.q: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) protest decision deadline? Agency-protest target?
d: 60 days GAO; ~30 days agency
100 days GAO; ~65 days agency
120 days GAO; ~45 days agency
thresholds.x: GAO must decide within 100 days by statute; agency protests target roughly 35. The 100-day certainty is why agencies take GAO seriously — the clock never slips.

thresholds.q: Services extension-of-services clause cap?
d: 3 months
12 months
90 days
thresholds.x: The extension-of-services clause buys at most 6 months of continuation — a bridge for transition, not a strategy. Reaching for it twice on the same contract is a planning finding wearing a clause number.

thresholds.q: Services base + options duration rail?
d: About 3 years
About 7 years
No limit, if priced at award
thresholds.x: About 5 years, base plus options, is the standard services rail. Longer structures exist but need authority and justification — the 5-year instinct keeps you honest.

thresholds.q: Severable services funded with annual money can run…?
thresholds.a: Up to 12 months, may cross fiscal years
d: Up to 12 months, within one fiscal year only
Up to 24 months, may cross fiscal years
Through 30 September only, then new-year funds
thresholds.x: Severable services on annual money: up to 12 months, and they MAY cross fiscal years — the crossing is legal, the 13th month isn't. Non-severable work follows a different rule entirely (fully funded, single product).

thresholds.q: Colors of money — operation and maintenance (O&M)? Research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E)? Procurement?
d: 1 year · 3 years · 5 years
2 years · 3 years · 5 years
1 year · 2 years · 5 years
thresholds.x: O&M lives 1 year, RDT&E 2, Procurement 3 (MILCON 5). After the window funds expire (adjustments only, 5 more years), then cancel. The 1-2-3 ladder is the fiscal skeleton under every funding question.

thresholds.q: Limitation of Cost / Funds notice trigger?
thresholds.a: ~75% of the estimate (LoC) or allotted amount (LoF)
d: ~50% of the estimate or allotted amount
~85% of the estimate or allotted amount
~90% of the estimate (LoC) or 75% (LoF)
thresholds.x: Both limitation clauses require notice around 75% — of the total estimate (Limitation of Cost, fully funded) or of the allotted amount (Limitation of Funds, incremental). The notice is the contractor's duty; missing it forfeits overrun entitlement.

thresholds.q: Expired funds remain usable for adjustments for…?
thresholds.a: 5 years, then cancelled (gone for all purposes)
d: 3 years, then cancelled
5 years, then returned to Treasury but recoverable
1 year, then cancelled
thresholds.x: Expired funds pay adjustments to their own obligations for 5 years, then the account cancels and the money is gone for every purpose. 'Expired' and 'cancelled' are different states — one adjusts, the other is dead.

thresholds.q: Small business set-aside band (automatic posture)?
d: Everything at or under the SAT ($350K)
Between $25K and $500K
Above the SAT, up to $1M
thresholds.x: The automatic small-business reservation covers the band between the micro-purchase threshold (MPT) ($15K) and simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) ($350K) — when the Rule of Two is met. The reservation comes from the dollar band itself, not from using simplified acquisition procedures (SAP) procedures.

thresholds.q: Cure notice rhythm before a performance-failure termination for default (T4D)?
thresholds.a: 10 days to cure (not required for pure late delivery)
d: 30 days to cure, required in every default
10 days to cure, required in every default
5 days to cure (not required for late delivery)
thresholds.x: The cure notice gives 10 days to fix a performance failure before T4D — but it's NOT required for a pure failure to deliver on time; the delivery schedule was the cure period. Mixed facts? Send it anyway: it costs ten days, not the termination.

combination.def: The boundary of the bargain — modifications live inside it or become new procurements.
A written demand for payment as a matter of right — certified over $100K, and the clocks start running.
Acceptance of an offer — the moment the Government is bound.
A response the Government can accept to form a binding contract — quotes aren't one.
What analysis must prove fair and reasonable — on every single action.
The examination of contractor records that backs up cost analysis on the big ones.
Performance and payment protection — required on construction over $150,000.
Information, not an offer — the Government's order is the offer; the vendor can still walk.
Excusable or not — the fork that decides whether a default termination survives.
No money, no contract — obligation without appropriation is an Antideficiency Act problem.
Giving up a known right — like the HCA waiving certified cost or pricing data.
The clauses that allocate risk — read them before the contractor does.
Allowable, allocable, and reasonable — a cost must clear all three to be paid.
The contracting officer's final decision — the document that starts every appeal clock.
Best value — the basis of every source selection, tradeoff or lowest-price-technically-acceptable.
Who owns the property — it passes by the clause, not by who paid.
The Board of Contract Appeals — 90 days from the final decision, or 12 months to the COFC.
Only a warranted agent binds the United States — apparent authority binds nothing.
A task or delivery order — fair opportunity governs who gets it.
Exclusion from Government contracting — check SAM before every award.
Trade agreements open foreign sources above their thresholds — Buy American below.
Small-business participation targets — the subcontracting plan carries them past $900K.
Procurement integrity's hard edge — report it, never negotiate around it.
Describe the need, not the vendor — restrictive specifications kill competition.
Service and construction labor standards — wage determinations ride the contract.
Labor-hour and T&M contracting — the ceiling and surveillance are the safeguards.
Firm-fixed-price — one price, whatever it costs; the contractor owns the risk.
Assistance, not acquisition — if the purpose is public benefit, it isn't a contract at all.
Limitation of Cost and Funds — the ~75% notice that keeps cost-type work funded.
Economic price adjustment rides a published index — protection, not speculation.
The share ratio — how incentive contracts split every dollar of overrun and underrun.
'Brand name or equal' — the salient characteristics define what equal means.
The cure notice gives 10 days to fix a failure — skip it only for pure late delivery.
A novation moves the contract when companies do — the Government must recognize the successor.
The GPC holder's lane — micro-purchases to $15K, spread fairly, never split.
DPAS-rated orders jump the queue — DO and DX ratings are mandatory to accept.
Data rights follow the money — who funded development decides what the Government may do.
Multiyear and options stretch a contract — about five is the services rail.
The bona fide need — this year's money buys this year's requirement.
The CICA stay — file at GAO within 10 days of award or 5 of debrief, and performance stops.
Think before you buy — the written strategy that lines up requirement, market, and schedule before a dollar moves.
Rent or buy? The lease-versus-purchase analysis you run before committing the government to owning something.
Float it before you fix it — the pre-solicitation version you circulate so industry can sharpen the requirement.
The legal reason you're competing less than fully — one of the named exceptions, each carrying its own justification.
How evaluation turns judgment into a rating — adjectival, color, or number, but always tied to the factors you published.
The short list after the first cut — the offerors still realistically in the running, the ones you hold discussions with.
One determination covering a whole category of actions, so you don't re-justify the same thing buy after buy.
You're buying the effort, not a deliverable — a set level of labor aimed at a broadly stated task.
Who bears the cost of the unknown — fixed-price puts it on the contractor, cost-reimbursement on the government.
The split that decides how much of an overrun or underrun each side eats — the heart of an incentive arrangement.
Labor and indirect rates — the multipliers that turn hours into a bill, and exactly what DCAA shows up to audit.
The paperwork endgame — final invoice paid, property disposed, releases signed, file closed.
Money the contractor owes back — overpayments, unliquidated advances, financing the government will collect.
Where the protest goes — the agency, GAO, or the Court of Federal Claims, each with its own forum and clock.
The Court of Federal Claims — where a contractor can take a claim instead of, or after, the board of contract appeals.
The one holding the contract with the government — every subcontractor below flows their work up through them.
What you can't accept from someone doing business with the government — the line between a courtesy and a bribe.
The quiet sibling of fraud and abuse — not criminal, just money spent with nothing to show for it.
Sealed bidding — price only, no negotiation: bids come in sealed, open in public, and the low responsive bidder wins.
Changed the requirement mid-solicitation? Amend it — in writing, to every offeror, before proposals are due.
Best value is about worth, not just price — what the government actually gets for the money, tradeoffs and all.
How R&D gets picked — scientific and technical merit through a Broad Agency Announcement, not lowest price.
A binding contract needs a contracting officer with actual authority — without it you have an unauthorized commitment, not a deal.
Wages the government makes you pay — Service Contract Labor Standards set the floor for the people doing the work.
You can't lien federal property, so payment bonds stand in — the surety pays the subs and suppliers a prime stiffs.
Splitting one requirement into smaller buys to duck a threshold or competition — a classic prohibited move.
'Brand name or equal' — when only a specific product will do, and the written justification that unlocks it.
The third of fraud-waste-abuse — authority or resources bent to the wrong ends, even when no crime is charged.

sat.q: Before signing any contract, what two assurances must the contracting officer make?
sat.a: That the contract meets all requirements of law, Executive orders, regulations, and applicable procedures (including clearances and approvals), and that funds are available for obligation.

cite.quote: Ensuring it meets all requirements of law, Executive orders, regulations, and all other applicable procedures, including clearances and approvals; and (2) Ensuring funds are available for obligation

sat.q: What standard of treatment does a contracting officer owe offerors and contractors?
sat.a: Impartial, fair, and equitable treatment.

cite.quote: Ensuring offerors and contractors receive impartial, fair, and equitable treatment

sat.q: How is a contracting officer appointed?
sat.a: In writing, on a Standard Form 1402, Certificate of Appointment — and the certificate must state any limits on the contracting officer's authority beyond those already in law or regulation. Individuals given micro-purchase authority are also appointed in writing, but an SF 1402 is not required for them. For DoD the certificate rides on statutory qualifications: under 10 U.S.C. 1724 (R-DFARS 201.403-1), serving with authority above the simplified acquisition threshold requires completion of the required contracting courses, at least 2 years of experience in a contracting position, and a baccalaureate degree — with narrow exceptions for legacy pre-2001 incumbents, the contingency contracting force, and 3-year developmental positions.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must be appointed in writing, using a Standard Form (SF) 1402, Certificate of Appointment. The certificate must state any limitations placed on the contracting officer’s scope of authority, other than limitations contained in applicable law or regulation.

sat.q: What must a person have to qualify as a DoD contracting officer with authority above the SAT?
sat.a: Under 10 U.S.C. 1724: completion of all contracting courses required for the grade, at least 2 years of experience in a contracting position, and a baccalaureate degree — plus any additional requirements the Secretary of Defense sets based on dollar value and complexity. The degree requirement does not reach legacy pre-2000 incumbents, the contingency contracting force, or 3-year developmental appointees.

cite.quote: In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 1724, in order to qualify to serve as a contracting officer with authority to award or administer contracts for amounts above the simplified acquisition threshold, a person must— (i) Have completed all contracting courses required for a contracting officer to serve in the grade in which the employee or member of the armed forces will serve; (ii) Have at least 2 years experience in a contracting position; (iii) Have received a baccalaureate degree from an accredited educational institution;

sat.q: May a contracting officer's representative commit the Government to a change in contract terms?
sat.a: No. A COR has no authority to make any commitments or changes affecting price, quality, quantity, delivery, or other terms and conditions of the contract. DoD adds an eligibility rule: a COR must be a Government employee — military or civilian (or foreign-government, NATO, or coalition-partner personnel) — and contractor personnel must never serve as CORs.

cite.quote: A COR has no authority to make any commitments or changes that affect price, quality, quantity, delivery, or other terms and conditions of the contract.

sat.q: What is an unauthorized commitment?
sat.a: An agreement that is not binding solely because the Government representative who made it lacked the authority to enter into it on behalf of the Government.

cite.quote: Unauthorized commitment means an agreement that is not binding solely because the Government representative who made it lacked the authority to enter into that agreement on behalf of the Government.

sat.q: Who may ratify an unauthorized commitment, and how far down may that authority be delegated?
sat.a: The head of the contracting activity; agencies may delegate the authority, but never below the chief of the contracting office.

cite.quote: Agencies cannot delegate this authority below the level of the chief of the contracting office.

sat.q: Can an unauthorized commitment be ratified if funds were not available at the time the commitment was made?
sat.a: No. Funds must be available now and must also have been available when the unauthorized commitment was made.

cite.quote: Funds are available and were available at the time the unauthorized commitment was made.

sat.q: What does the simplified acquisition threshold become for acquisitions supporting a contingency operation?
sat.a: $1 million for a contract awarded and performed, or purchase made, inside the United States; $2 million outside the United States. The same tiers apply to the other categories in that exception — defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack; international disaster assistance; and response to an emergency or major disaster — and all of them turn on a head-of-agency determination. Do not confuse this with the separate humanitarian or peacekeeping operation tier in the same definition, which is $650,000 and only for contracts awarded and performed outside the United States (10 U.S.C. 3015).

cite.quote: $1 million for any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, inside the United States; and (ii) $2 million for any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, outside the United States

sat.q: What does the micro-purchase threshold become for acquisitions supporting a contingency operation?
sat.a: $25,000 for a contract awarded and performed, or purchase made, inside the United States; $40,000 outside the United States — on a head-of-agency determination. The carve-out matters: the increase does not reach construction subject to the Wage Rate Requirements (Construction) statute, so covered construction stays at the $2,000 micro-purchase threshold no matter how urgent the contingency.

cite.quote: $25,000 in the case of any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, inside the United States; and (ii) $40,000 in the case of any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, outside the United States

sat.q: The micro-purchase threshold is $15,000 — when is it actually lower?
sat.a: Two labor-standards sub-tiers: $2,000 for construction subject to the Wage Rate Requirements (Construction) statute, and $2,500 for services subject to Service Contract Labor Standards. Miss the sub-tier and a $10,000 construction buy you treated as a micro-purchase was really a simplified acquisition owing labor-standards clauses.

cite.quote: Micro-purchase threshold means $15,000, except it means- (1) For acquisitions of construction subject to 40 U.S.C. chapter 31, subchapter IV, Wage Rate Requirements (Construction), $2,000; (2) For acquisitions of services subject to 41 U.S.C. chapter 67, Service Contract Labor Standards, $2,500;

sat.q: Which acquisitions does RFO part 13 cover?
sat.a: Noncommercial products and services valued at or below the SAT. Commercial acquisitions use the part 12 procedures instead.

cite.quote: This part implements simplified procedures for the acquisition of noncommercial products and services valued at or below the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT)

sat.q: Before you reach for part 13 simplified procedures, what two checks gate their use?
sat.a: First, no commercial product or service can satisfy the need — commercial buys run under part 12. Second, the supplies or services are not available from a required source under part 8. Only when both checks clear are part 13 procedures on the table.

cite.quote: The procedures in this part may be used only if— (1) There are no commercial products or commercial services that can satisfy the agency’s needs (see part 12); and (2) The supplies or services are not available from a required source (see part 8).

sat.q: May you split a requirement into smaller pieces to stay under the SAT?
sat.a: No. Requirements whose aggregate value exceeds the SAT must not be divided merely to permit use of simplified procedures.

cite.quote: Do not divide requirements, the aggregate value of which exceeds the SAT, merely to permit use of the procedures in this part.

sat.q: What document supports soliciting from only one source under simplified procedures?
sat.a: A determination and findings (subpart 1.5) that only one source is reasonably available — for example urgency, exclusive licensing agreements, brand-name, or industrial mobilization.

cite.quote: Contracting officers may solicit from a single source based on a determination and findings (see subpart 1.5) that only one source is reasonably available (e.g., urgency, exclusive licensing agreements, brand-name or industrial mobilization).

sat.q: Does a quotation bind the vendor? Does the purchase order bind the Government?
sat.a: Neither forms a contract by itself. A quotation is not an offer, and the purchase order is only the Government's offer to buy.

cite.quote: Neither a quotation nor the purchase order issued by the Government in response to a quotation form a binding contract. The purchase order is the Government’s offer to a supplier to buy certain products or services upon specified terms and conditions.

sat.q: When is a binding contract formed under RFQ and purchase-order procedures?
sat.a: When the supplier accepts the Government's offer — by written acceptance of the purchase order or by substantial performance.

cite.quote: A binding contract is formed when the supplier accepts the Government’s offer, either by written acceptance of the purchase order or substantial performance of the purchase order.

sat.q: When soliciting quotations directly from suppliers at or below the SAT, how many sources must you solicit?
sat.a: At least three — and whenever practicable, two sources not included in the previous solicitation.

cite.quote: Solicit quotations from at least three sources; and (iii) Whenever practicable, solicit quotations from two sources not included in the previous solicitation.

sat.q: On what should price reasonableness be based when awarding under part 13?
sat.a: Competitive quotations, whenever possible.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must determine the price to be fair and reasonable. Whenever possible, base price reasonableness on competitive quotations.

sat.q: What is the cap on each individual purchase under a blanket purchase agreement?
sat.a: It depends on which part the BPA lives under. A part 12 commercial BPA caps each individual purchase at the simplified-procedures ceiling in 12.201-1(a) — $9 million, or the increased ceiling under 12.001(c) ($15 million for contingency, cyber/CBRN, international disaster assistance, or emergency/major disaster support). A part 13 (noncommercial) BPA is tighter: 13.201 caps the maximum value of each individual purchase under a BPA at the SAT. Quoting the SAT as the cap on a commercial BPA leaves real headroom on the table.

cite.quote: The dollar limitation for each individual purchase under the BPA, which may not exceed the threshold for use of simplified procedures at 12.201-1(a) (including the increased threshold at 12.001(c)

sat.q: Must micro-purchases be competed?
sat.a: No. They may be awarded without soliciting competitive quotations if the price is considered reasonable.

cite.quote: Micro-purchases may be awarded without soliciting competitive quotations if the contracting officer or individual appointed in accordance with 1.403-2(b) considers the price to be reasonable.

sat.q: What is the primary method for making micro-purchases?
sat.a: The Governmentwide commercial purchase card — authorized for purchases of supplies, services, or construction, and only for purchases authorized by law or regulation. Purchase orders are the other primary method. DoD goes further: use the purchase card as the method of purchase and/or payment for everything at or below the MPT unless a 212.403 exception applies.

cite.quote: The Governmentwide commercial purchase card is authorized for use in making purchases of supplies, services, or construction.

sat.q: When may you use an SF 44, Purchase Order-Invoice-Voucher?
sat.a: It is a pocket-size form for on-the-spot, over-the-counter buys away from the purchasing office or at isolated activities — and only when every condition holds: the agency authorizes it, the amount is at or below the MPT (or an agency-set ceiling for urgency or contingency support), the supplies or services are immediately available with one delivery and one payment, and it beats the purchase card on economy and efficiency. In DoD the purchase card is the mandated micro-purchase method, so an SF 44 rides on a 212.403 exception — a Standard Form 44 purchase for aviation fuel is the listed example.

cite.quote: The SF 44, Purchase Order-Invoice-Voucher, is a multipurpose pocket-size purchase order form designed primarily for on-the-spot, over-the-counter purchases of supplies and nonpersonal services while away from the purchasing office or at isolated activities.

sat.q: When must a contract be set aside for small business (the Rule of Two)?
sat.a: For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, when there is a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small business concerns that are competitive on fair market prices, quality, and delivery. The test does not apply to purchases at or below the MPT or to purchases from required sources under part 8. Note the separate, categorical rule for noncommercial buys: under 13.102 an acquisition above the MPT but at or below the SAT must be set aside, with no expectation analysis. For DoD, R-DFARS 219.104-1 applies FAR 19.104-1(a) and (b) to construction (including maintenance and repairs) under $3.5 million, dredging under $2 million, and architect-engineer services for military construction or family housing under $1 million, and excepts supplies developed and financed in whole or in part by Canadian sources under the U.S.-Canadian Defense Development Sharing Program.

cite.quote: For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, the contracting officer must set the contract aside for small business if there is a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers— (1) From two or more responsible small business concerns; and (2) That are competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery.

sat.q: For a noncommercial acquisition between the micro-purchase threshold and the SAT, when must it be set aside for small business?
sat.a: Always. Under 13.102 the set-aside is categorical in that band — no Rule-of-Two expectation analysis. Do not generalize it past part 13: part 13 covers noncommercial products and services only. A commercial buy in the same dollar band runs under part 12, which points to part 19, where 19.104-1's Rule of Two governs and requires the reasonable-expectation-of-two-offers judgment.

cite.quote: Acquisitions of supplies or services that have an anticipated dollar value above the MPT, but at or below the SAT, must be set aside for small business concerns (see part 19).

sat.q: What must a prospective contractor demonstrate to be found responsible?
sat.a: Adequate financial resources (or the ability to obtain them); ability to meet the delivery or performance schedule given all existing commitments; a satisfactory performance record — though never nonresponsible solely for lacking one; a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; the necessary organization, experience, controls, and technical skills; the necessary equipment and facilities; and otherwise qualified and eligible under law. DoD adds one for cost-type, incentive, and progress-payment work: the accounting system and internal controls must give reasonable assurance the cost data are reliable.

cite.quote: To demonstrate responsibility, a prospective contractor must— (a) Have adequate financial resources to perform the contract, or the ability to obtain them (see 9.104-3(a));

sat.q: When must an agency buy commercial?
sat.a: Whenever the agency determines commercial products or services are available to meet its needs.

cite.quote: Agencies must acquire commercial products or commercial services when the agency determines that they are available to meet the agency’s needs (see part 10).

sat.q: A customer insists on a brand-name item at or below the SAT. What documentation does restricting competition require?
sat.a: Document the decision that only one source is available and the basis for the decision. (Over the SAT it takes a written justification approved under 6.104.) DoD reads brand-name more strictly: under R-DFARS 212.102-70, implementing section 888(a) of the FY 2017 NDAA, the 12.102 documentation is required even for brand-name-or-equal descriptions and for proprietary specifications and standards — allowing an equal product does not excuse the paperwork.

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued at or below the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), document the decision that only one source is available and the basis for the decision.

sat.q: Up to what value do the commercial simplified procedures (RFQ followed by a purchase order) apply?
sat.a: $9 million.

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued up to $9 million, issue a request for quotations (RFQ) followed by a purchase order.

sat.q: When is market research required?
sat.a: Appropriate to the circumstances, before developing new requirements documents and before soliciting offers or awarding task or delivery orders valued over the SAT. DoD adds triggers: conduct market research before issuing any solicitation with tiered evaluation of offers, and use the results to make the part 19 set-aside call and to inform price reasonableness.

cite.quote: Agencies must conduct market research appropriate to the circumstances before— (1) Developing new requirements documents; (2) Soliciting offers for acquisitions with an estimated value over the simplified acquisition threshold; or (3) Awarding a task or delivery order over the simplified acquisition threshold.

sat.q: When must you post a presolicitation notice, and what lets a SAT-level buy skip it?
sat.a: Post a presolicitation notice to the GPE for any proposed contract action expected to be greater than $20,000. At or below the SAT you may skip it if the solicitation itself will be posted to the GPE under 5.201 and the public can respond to it electronically.

cite.quote: For proposed contract actions expected to be greater than $20,000, post a presolicitation notice to the GPE unless an exemption in paragraph (b) applies.

sat.q: What defines a firm-fixed-price contract?
sat.a: A price not subject to any adjustment on the basis of the contractor's cost experience in performing the contract — the contractor bears the cost risk.

cite.quote: A firm-fixed-price contract provides for a price that is not subject to any adjustment on the basis of the contractor’s experience in performing the contract.

sat.q: When may a cost-reimbursement contract be used?
sat.a: Only when the requirements cannot be sufficiently defined for a fixed-price type contract, or performance uncertainties do not permit costs to be estimated accurately enough for any fixed-price type. Clearing that gate is not enough — 16.301-3 adds four hard prerequisites: a written acquisition plan approved at least one level above the contracting officer; the agency head's approval of a justification for other than fixed-price if 16.104 requires one; a contractor accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate contract costs; and sufficient Government resources, including a designated COR, to award and manage a non-firm-fixed-price contract. Cost-reimbursement is also barred outright for commercial products and services.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must use cost-reimbursement contracts only when- (a) The requirements cannot be sufficiently defined to allow for a fixed-price type contract (see part 7); or (b) Uncertainties involved in contract performance do not permit costs to be estimated with sufficient accuracy to use any type of fixed-price contract.

sat.q: May a cost-reimbursement contract be used to buy commercial products or services?
sat.a: No — it is not allowed. DoD stacks a second hard stop on the same section: for military construction or military family housing projects, cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-award-fee, and cost-plus-incentive-fee types are barred — even under a declaration of war or national emergency.

cite.quote: The use of cost-reimbursement contracts is not allowed for the purchase of commercial products and commercial services (see part 12).

sat.q: How must a termination be communicated to the contractor?
sat.a: Only by written notice, stating the reason (convenience or default), the effective date, the extent, and any special instructions.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must terminate contracts only with a written notice to the contractor.

sat.q: What is the contractor's first duty after receiving a convenience termination notice?
sat.a: Stop work immediately on the terminated portion and stop placing subcontracts for that work — then terminate related subcontracts and promptly submit a settlement proposal.

cite.quote: Stop work immediately on the terminated portion of the contract and stop placing subcontracts for that work

sat.q: What should a convenience-termination settlement pay the contractor for?
sat.a: Work completed, preparations made for the terminated portion, and a reasonable profit amount.

cite.quote: Settlements should pay contractors fairly for— (1) Work they have completed; (2) Preparations they made for terminated portions of the contract; and (3) A reasonable profit amount.

sat.q: Is profit paid on work the contractor never performed?
sat.a: No. No profit is paid for unperformed work, settlement costs, or consequential damages.

cite.quote: Do not pay profit for- (i) Settlement costs (the costs of working out the final payment); (ii) To cover the profit amount the contractor expected to make on work they never did; or (iii) Consequential damages.

sat.q: When should a contracting officer not bother terminating for convenience?
sat.a: When the remaining work is worth less than $5,000.

cite.quote: Contracting officers should not terminate a contract for convenience when the remaining work is worth less than $5,000.

sat.q: What makes a delay excusable under a commercial purchase order?
sat.a: Nonperformance caused by an occurrence beyond the contractor's reasonable control and without its fault or negligence.

cite.quote: The Contractor shall be liable for default unless nonperformance is caused by an occurrence beyond the reasonable control of the Contractor and without its fault or negligence.

sat.q: What are the two types of differing site conditions?
sat.a: Two categories, known in practice as Type I and Type II — the clause itself doesn't use those labels. The first: latent or subsurface conditions at the site differing materially from those indicated in the contract. The second: unknown physical conditions of an unusual nature, differing materially from those ordinarily encountered and generally recognized as inhering in that kind of work.

cite.quote: (1) Latent physical conditions or subsurface conditions at the site which differ materially from those indicated in this contract; or (2) Unknown physical conditions at the site, of an unusual nature, which differ materially from those ordinarily encountered and generally recognized as inherent in work of the character provided for in the contract.

sat.q: When must a contractor give notice of a differing site condition?
sat.a: Promptly, in writing, and before the conditions are disturbed.

cite.quote: The Contractor shall promptly, and before the conditions are disturbed, give a written notice to the Contracting Officer

sat.q: What happens if the contractor disturbs a differing site condition without giving the written notice?
sat.a: No equitable adjustment is allowed under the clause without the required written notice — and none at all after final payment.

cite.quote: No request for an equitable adjustment to the contract under this clause will be allowed, unless the Contractor has given the written notice required.

sat.q: May contractors perform inherently governmental functions?
sat.a: No. Contracts must not be used to perform inherently governmental functions — the non-exclusive list includes awarding contracts, approving contractual documents, administering and terminating contracts, and serving as a voting member on a source selection board. For DoD, the written determination FAR 7.503(e) requires must be prepared using DoD Instruction 1100.22 and must also determine that none of the functions are exempt from private sector performance; contracting for the closely-associated functions at 7.503(d) carries its own 10 U.S.C. 4508 gate.

cite.quote: Contracts must not be used to perform inherently governmental functions.

sat.q: A flight chief wants a contractor employee in the office taking daily tasking under his direct supervision. What is the key indicator that this is a prohibited personal services arrangement?
sat.a: The Government exercising relatively continuous supervision and control over contractor personnel — making them appear, in effect, Government employees. Personal services contracts are barred unless specifically authorized by statute.

cite.quote: The Government exercising relatively continuous supervision and control over multiple contractor personnel is frequently a key indicator of a personal services contract.

sat.q: What is the difference between a latent and a patent defect?
sat.a: Latent defect (2.101) — a defect that exists at the time of acceptance but cannot be discovered by a reasonable inspection. Patent defect (46.101) — any defect that exists at the time of acceptance and is not a latent defect. The distinction is what decides whether Government acceptance is still open to challenge.

cite.quote: Latent defect means a defect that exists at the time of acceptance but cannot be discovered by a reasonable inspection.

sat.q: Is Government acceptance final?
sat.a: Generally conclusive — except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided in the contract.

cite.quote: Acceptance shall be conclusive, except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided in the contract.

sat.q: What inspection does the Government normally perform for contracts at or below the SAT?
sat.a: Inspection at destination, and only for type and kind; quantity; damage; operability (if readily determinable); and preservation, packaging, packing, and marking. DoD reinforces it from the other side: do not require quality assurance at source at or below the SAT unless the 246.402 criteria are met.

cite.quote: the Government must inspect contracts at or below the simplified acquisition threshold at destination and only for type and kind; quantity; damage; operability (if readily determinable); and preservation, packaging, packing, and marking, if applicable.

sat.q: What is a claim?
sat.a: A written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter of right, payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief arising under or relating to the contract. Two carve-outs travel with the definition: a contractor demand for money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim until certified, and a routine, undisputed voucher or invoice is not a claim — though it can become one if it is later disputed as to liability or amount, or is not acted on in a reasonable time.

cite.quote: Claim means a written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter of right, the payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief arising under or relating to the contract. However, a written demand or written assertion by the contractor seeking the payment of money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim under 41 U.S.C. chapter 71, Contract Disputes, until certified as required by the statute. A voucher, invoice, or other routine request for payment that is not in dispute when submitted is not a claim.

sat.q: At what dollar value must a contractor certify a claim?
sat.a: Over $100,000 — a money demand exceeding $100,000 is not even a claim under the Disputes statute until certified.

cite.quote: a written demand or written assertion by the Contractor seeking the payment of money exceeding $100,000 is not a claim under 41 U.S.C. chapter 71 until certified

sat.q: How long does the contracting officer have to decide a contractor claim?
sat.a: For claims of $100,000 or less: if the contractor requests a decision in writing, render it within 60 days of the request. For certified claims over $100,000: within 60 days, either decide the claim or tell the contractor the date by which the decision will be made.

cite.quote: For Contractor claims of $100,000 or less, the Contracting Officer must, if requested in writing by the Contractor, render a decision within 60 days of the request. For Contractor-certified claims over $100,000, the Contracting Officer must, within 60 days, decide the claim or notify the Contractor of the date by which the decision will be made.

sat.q: A contractor threatens to stop work until a dispute is resolved. What does the Disputes clause require?
sat.a: The contractor must proceed diligently with performance pending final resolution, and comply with the contracting officer's decision.

cite.quote: The Contractor must proceed diligently with performance of this contract, pending final resolution of any request for relief, claim, appeal, or action arising under the contract.

sat.q: Who may execute contract modifications?
sat.a: Only contracting officers acting within the scope of their authority. Other Government personnel must not act in a way that makes the contractor believe they can bind the Government.

cite.quote: Only contracting officers acting within the scope of their authority may execute contract modifications on behalf of the Government.

sat.q: What is the difference between a bilateral and a unilateral modification?
sat.a: Bilateral (supplemental agreement) — signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer, e.g., negotiated equitable adjustments. Unilateral — signed only by the contracting officer, e.g., administrative changes, change orders, termination notices.

cite.quote: A bilateral modification (supplemental agreement) is a contract modification that is signed by the contractor and the contracting officer.

sat.q: Does an in-scope modification require a new competition?
sat.a: No. Part 6 competition requirements do not apply to modifications within the scope of the contract, including exercising priced options evaluated in the original competition.

cite.quote: Contract modifications that are within the scope of the contract, including exercising priced options that were evaluated as part of the original competition (see part 17)

sat.q: Before exercising an option, what must the contracting officer determine about the price?
sat.a: That the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and that exercising the option is in the Government's best interest — after written notice to the contractor and confirming funds are available. For DoD, R-DFARS 217.204-170 adds pre-exercise gates — an active, accurate SAM record and current SPRS entries (a NIST SP 800-171 assessment score and a CMMC certificate, each not more than 3 years old) — and, for firm-fixed-price contracts containing spare parts, PGI 217.204-170 requires cost or price analysis of the spares before any option is exercised.

cite.quote: After reviewing price and other factors, the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and exercise of the option is in the Government's best interest

sat.q: What does the Anti-Deficiency Act prohibit?
sat.a: Creating or authorizing an obligation in excess of available funds, or in advance of appropriations, unless otherwise authorized by law.

cite.quote: No officer or employee of the Government may create or authorize an obligation in excess of the funds available, or in advance of appropriations (Anti-Deficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341), unless otherwise authorized by law.

sat.q: May a severable services contract cross fiscal years?
sat.a: Yes. A contract, option, or order for severable services may begin in one fiscal year and end in the next as long as the period does not exceed one year, and the first year's funds may be obligated for the total amount. In DoD the authority sits with the contracting officer under R-DFARS 232.703-3(b) (10 U.S.C. 3133), rather than with the head of the executive agency as FAR 32.703-3(b) frames it.

cite.quote: for severable services for a period that begins in one fiscal year and ends in the next fiscal year if the period of the contract awarded, option exercised, or order placed does not exceed one year

sat.q: When is an invoice payment due under the Prompt Payment rules?
sat.a: The later of two dates: the 30th day after the designated billing office receives a proper invoice, or the 30th day after Government acceptance of the supplies or services. For computing any interest penalty, acceptance is deemed to occur constructively on the 7th day after delivery or performance absent a dispute. DoD note: the contracting officer may extend a constructive acceptance period, but shorter than the 7-day (or 14-day construction) period is not authorized.

cite.quote: The later of the following two events: (i) The 30th day after the designated billing office receives a proper invoice from the contractor (except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section). (ii) The 30th day after Government acceptance of supplies delivered or services performed.

sat.q: What has to be in place before the Government pays a contractor's invoice?
sat.a: Two things: receipt of a proper invoice and satisfactory contract performance. A proper invoice carries the contractor's name and address, invoice date and number, contract number, the description, quantity, and price of what was delivered, shipping and payment terms, and correct EFT banking data. A defective invoice goes back with the reasons within 7 days — but 3 days for meat, meat food products, or fish, and 5 days for perishable agricultural commodities, dairy, and edible fats or oils. Miss the clock and the payment-due date slips by the extra days taken.

cite.quote: Payment will be based on receipt of a proper invoice and satisfactory contract performance.

sat.q: Must a contractor ask for interest when the Government pays late?
sat.a: No. The designated payment office pays the interest penalty automatically, without any request from the contractor, once a proper invoice was received, the receiving report cleared with no disagreement over quantity or quality, and payment went out after the due date.

cite.quote: The designated payment office will pay an interest penalty automatically, without request from the contractor, when all the following conditions, if applicable, have been met:

sat.q: How must contractors submit payment requests on DoD contracts?
sat.a: Electronically — and Wide Area WorkFlow (WAWF) is the only acceptable electronic form; facsimile, email, and scanned documents do not count. The exceptions are narrow: classified work where electronic submission would compromise safeguarding; performance where electronic submission is not feasible (no internet connectivity); cases where DoD cannot receive or accept electronically; cases where the contractor asked in writing and the contracting officer put an alternative method in the contract; and purchase-card payments, where only the receiving report must be electronic.

cite.quote: The only acceptable electronic form for submission of payment requests and receiving reports is Wide Area WorkFlow (WAWF)

sat.q: What is the simplified acquisition threshold?

cite.quote: Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000

sat.q: What is the micro-purchase threshold?

cite.quote: Micro-purchase threshold means $15,000

5m.q: Which acquisitions are exempt from the part 6 competition requirements?
5m.a: Simplified acquisitions under part 13; procedures expressly authorized by statute; in-scope modifications (including exercising priced options evaluated in the original competition); orders under requirements and definite-quantity contracts; and orders against task- and delivery-order contracts entered into under part 16. Orders under indefinite-quantity contracts are exempt only conditionally: the contract must have been awarded under 6.101 or 6.102 with all responsible sources realistically permitted to compete for the order's requirements, or under 6.103 with a J&A that adequately covers the order. The IDIQ exemption is earned by the underlying award — it is not automatic. DoD adds one exemption of its own: contracts awarded to individuals under the 10 U.S.C. 1091 personal-services authority for health care (R-DFARS 237.201-170(b)) are exempt from part 6 (R-DFARS 206.001).

cite.quote: Orders placed under indefinite-quantity contracts that were entered into according to this part when— (1) The contract was awarded under 6.101 or 6.102, and all responsible sources were realistically permitted to compete for the requirements contained in the order; or (2) The contract was awarded under 6.103, and the justification and approval, if required, adequately covers the requirements contained in the order;

5m.q: May other than full and open competition be justified by a lack of planning or a shortage of funds?
5m.a: No. It must not be justified on the basis of a lack of planning by the requiring activity or concerns about the amount of funds available to the agency or activity.

cite.quote: Contracting without providing for full and open competition must not be justified on the basis of— (1) A lack of planning by the requiring activity; or (2) Concerns related to the amount of funds available to the agency or activity for acquisition.

5m.q: Which competition exceptions do not require a justification and approval?
5m.a: Under 6.104(a) there are two: authorized or required by statute (6.103-5) and public interest (6.103-7). But an Air Force reader has a third — 6.103-4(c) provides that contracts awarded by DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard under the international agreement authority do not require the written justifications and approvals described in 6.104, and R-DFARS 206.103-4(c) adds that the head of the contracting activity instead prepares a document describing the terms of the agreement, treaty, or written directions (such as a Letter of Offer and Acceptance) that require other than competitive procedures. Every other 6.103 authority requires the 6.104 justification and approval. Two carve-backs inside the statute lane: 6.103-5(e) restores the J&A requirement for sole-source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, and for DoD R-DFARS 206.104-70 moves that trigger to $100 million — no J&A up to $100 million, but above it the contracting officer must justify the sole-source award in writing under FAR 6.104-1, obtain approval, and make the justification public after award.

cite.quote: A justification and approval must support procedures under 6.103, except 6.103-5 and 6.103-7.

5m.q: Under the one-responsible-source exception, when may a follow-on for a major system be sole-sourced?
5m.a: When award to another source would result in substantial duplication of cost to the Government not expected to be recovered through competition, or unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements. The authority covers follow-ons for the continued development or production of a major system or highly specialized equipment — and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, for the continued provision of highly specialized services as well.

cite.quote: (2) When awarding a follow-on contract for the continued development or production of a major system or highly specialized equipment and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, for the continued provision of highly specialized services, would result in— (i) Substantial duplication of cost to the Government that is not expected to be recovered through competition; or (ii) Unacceptable delays in fulfilling the agency's requirements.

5m.q: Does the only-one-responsible-source authority ever reach more than one source?
5m.a: Yes — for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the authority extends to situations where only a limited number of responsible sources can satisfy the requirement. Civilian agencies get the one-source version only. The one-or-a-limited-number distinction tells a board whether you know which statute you operate under — 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(1) versus 41 U.S.C. 3304(a)(1).

cite.quote: Agencies may contract without providing for full and open competition when the supplies or services required by the agency are available from only one responsible source and no other type of supplies or services will satisfy agency requirements. For DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, this authority extends to situations where only a limited number of responsible sources can satisfy agency requirements.

5m.q: Does a brand-name purchase description restrict competition? What about brand-name or equal?
5m.a: A pure brand-name description (or attributes peculiar to one manufacturer) prevents full and open competition and must be justified and approved under 6.104. Under the RFO, brand-name-or-equal descriptions provide for full and open competition and need no justification — but DoD flips that second half: section 888(a) of the FY 2017 NDAA requires the 6.104 justification and approval to use brand-name-or-equal descriptions, and to use proprietary specifications and standards (R-DFARS 206.103-170).

cite.quote: use of brand-name descriptions, or specification of attributes peculiar to one manufacturer, prevents full and open competition and should only be used when justified and approved according to 6.104. This does not apply to “brand name or equal” descriptions as they provide for full and open competition.

5m.q: How long may a contract awarded under the urgency exception run?
5m.a: For a contract greater than the simplified acquisition threshold, no longer than needed to meet the urgent requirement and to competitively award a follow-on — and not more than one year including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply. That determination is separate from the J&A, goes in the contract file, and any later extension must be approved at the same level. Two traps: the cap is conditional on exceeding the SAT, not universal; and 6.103-2(d) lets the J&A and the exceptional-circumstances determination be made after award when making them before award would unreasonably delay the acquisition.

cite.quote: The total period of performance of a contract greater than the simplified acquisition threshold awarded or modified using this authority— (1) May not exceed the time necessary— (i) To meet the unusual and compelling requirements of the work to be performed under the contract; and (ii) For the agency to enter into another contract for the required goods and services through competitive procedures; and (2) May not exceed one year, including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply.

5m.q: Recite the justification approval ladder.
5m.a: Up to $900,000 — the contracting officer (the 6.104(a)(12) certification is the approval). Over $900,000 to $20 million — advocate for competition, not delegable. Over $20 million to $90 million ($150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard) — head of the procuring activity, who may delegate to a general or flag officer or a civilian above GS-15. Above that — senior procurement executive, not delegable except to USD(A&S) acting as the senior procurement executive for DoD. Include the estimated dollar value of all options when setting the level, and note that a higher-level official may always approve a lower-dollar justification.

cite.quote: $900,000 or below Contracting officer. Accomplished by certification required at 6.104(a)(12). >$900,000 - $20,000,000 Advocate for competition. Not delegable.

5m.q: When must a justification for other than full and open competition be posted publicly?
5m.a: Within 14 days after contract award — except urgency (6.103-2) justifications post within 30 days, and brand-name justifications post with the solicitation.

cite.quote: The justification must be made publicly available within 14 days after contract award, except— (1) Justifications under 6.103-2 must be posted within 30 days after contract award

5m.q: Does full and open competition after excluding sources (for example, a set-aside) require its own justification and approval?
5m.a: No. It still uses the competitive procedures of 6.101 among the narrowed field, and requires no separate justification and approval or determination and findings.

cite.quote: Acquisitions under this section do not require separate justification and approval or determination and findings.

5m.q: When may sealed bidding be used instead of competitive proposals?
5m.a: Only when all four conditions hold: time permits soliciting, submitting, and evaluating sealed bids; award will be made on price and price-related factors; discussions with bidders are unnecessary; and more than one sealed bid is reasonably expected.

cite.quote: (i) Time permits staff to solicit, submit, and evaluate sealed bids; (ii) The award will be made on the basis of price and other price-related factors; (iii) Discussion with bidders is unnecessary; and (iv) Contracting officers reasonably expect to receive more than one sealed bid.

5m.q: Competitive DoD solicitation, one offer received. What must the contracting officer do?
5m.a: If the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days for proposals: consult the requiring activity on revising the requirements document to promote competition, then resolicit for at least 30 more days. If resolicitation is not required, still establish a fair and reasonable price — obtaining additional cost or pricing data where needed, certified above the certified-cost-or-pricing-data threshold unless an exception applies. The resolicit rule does not apply to acquisitions at or below the SAT, contingency/disaster support, small business set-asides, science-and-technology and architect-engineer acquisitions, commercial solutions openings, or commercial part 12 acquisitions — and the head of the contracting activity may waive it, delegable no lower than one level above the contracting officer. No exception relieves you of seeking maximum practicable competition (R-DFARS 215.202-71).

cite.quote: (1) If only one offer is received when competitive procedures were used and the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days for receipt of proposals, the contracting officer must— (i) Consult with the requiring activity as to whether the requirements document should be revised to promote more competition (see FAR 6.003(a) and 11.102); and (ii) Resolicit, allowing an additional period of at least 30 days for receipt of proposals

5m.q: What is the baseline ordering rule on a multiple-award contract?
5m.a: Each awardee must be given a fair opportunity to be considered for every order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold, unless a sole-source order is justified and approved under 16.507-6. For DoD, ordering also carries two DFARS guardrails: the limitations on lowest-price-technically-acceptable source selection apply to orders under multiple-award contracts, and reverse auctions are prohibited for personal protective equipment and aviation critical safety items (R-DFARS 216.507-2).

cite.quote: The contracting officer must provide each awardee a fair opportunity to be considered for each order or BPA valued above the micro-purchase threshold according to paragraph (c) and 16.507-3 through 16.507-5, unless a sole source order or BPA is justified and approved according to 16.507-6.

5m.q: Are task orders subject to part 6 competition or the subpart 15.3 source selection rules?
5m.a: No. The ordering process is not subject to part 6, subpart 15.3, or part 14 — streamlined procedures are allowed, with no required evaluation plans, scoring, or competitive range. Streamlined is not unconstrained in DoD, though — the DFARS limitations on lowest-price-technically-acceptable source selection still reach orders placed against multiple-award indefinite-delivery contracts (R-DFARS 216.507-2).

cite.quote: The ordering process is not subject to the competition requirements in part 6 or the policies in subpart 15.3 or part 14.

5m.q: Name the exceptions that allow a sole-source order despite fair opportunity.
5m.a: Urgency causing unacceptable delays; only one awardee capable (unique or highly specialized); logical follow-on in the interest of economy and efficiency; satisfying a minimum guarantee; a statute authorizing a specified source (orders over the SAT); and, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the 6.103 exceptions — with the caveat that the public interest exception must not be used unless Congress is notified under 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(7). Setting an order aside under part 19 is a separate lane that is not subject to these justification, approval, and posting requirements at all (16.507-6(c)). DoD adds a tripwire: an over-SAT order that is a follow-on to an order previously justified under the only-one-capable or logical-follow-on exception requires the procedures at PGI 216.507-6(b) (R-DFARS 216.507-6).

cite.quote: (1) The agency need for the supplies or services is so urgent that providing a fair opportunity would result in unacceptable delays. (2) Only one awardee is capable of providing the supplies or services required at the level of quality required because the supplies or services ordered are unique or highly specialized. (3) The order must be issued on a sole-source basis in the interest of economy and efficiency because it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order. (4) It is necessary to place an order to satisfy a minimum guarantee.

5m.q: What condition is built into the logical-follow-on exception?
5m.a: All awardees must have been given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order — and the justification must describe why the relationship between the initial order and the follow-on is logical. And for DoD, serial follow-ons get extra scrutiny — an over-SAT order following one previously justified under exception (b)(2) or (3) must follow the PGI 216.507-6(b) procedures.

cite.quote: it is a logical follow-on to an order already issued under the contract, provided that all awardees were given a fair opportunity to be considered for the original order.

5m.q: Recite the approval ladder for a fair-opportunity exception justification.
5m.a: Above the SAT to $900,000 — the ordering activity contracting officer's certification serves as approval, unless agency procedures set a higher level. Above $900,000 to $20 million — the advocate for competition of the activity placing the order, not delegable. Above $20 million to $90 million ($150 million for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard) — the head of the procuring activity, a general or flag officer, or a civilian above GS-15. Above that — the senior procurement executive, not delegable except for DoD's USD(A&S). Below the SAT, documenting the basis for the exception suffices. This is the order-level ladder — do not confuse it with the 6.104-2 contract-level J&A ladder.

cite.quote: (1) For proposed orders valued above the SAT, but not valued above $900,000, the ordering activity contracting officer’s certification that the justification is accurate and complete to the best of the ordering activity contracting officer’s knowledge and belief will serve as approval, unless a higher approval level is established in accordance with agency procedures. (2) For a proposed order valued above $900,000, but not above $20 million, the justification must be approved by the advocate for competition of the activity placing the order, or by an official named in paragraph (e)(3) or (4). This authority is not delegable. (3) For a proposed order valued above $20 million, but not above $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, not above $150 million, the justification must be approved by— (i) The head of the procuring activity placing the order; (ii) A designee who— (A) If a member of the armed forces, is a general or flag officer; (B) If a civilian, is serving in a position in a grade above GS-15 under the General Schedule (or in a comparable or higher position under another schedule); or (iii) An official named in paragraph (e)(4) of this subsection. (4) For a proposed order valued above $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, above $150 million), the justification must be approved by the senior procurement executive of the agency placing the order.

5m.q: Who hears a contract holder's complaint about order placement?
5m.a: The agency's task-order and delivery-order ombudsman — a senior official independent of the contracting officer who reviews complaints and ensures awardees are afforded a fair opportunity consistent with the contract's procedures.

cite.quote: The head of the agency must designate a task-order and delivery-order ombudsman. The ombudsman must review complaints from contractors and ensure they are afforded a fair opportunity to be considered, consistent with the procedures in the contract.

5m.q: What must the fair notice include for orders above $7.5 million?
5m.a: A clear statement of the agency's requirements, a reasonable response period, and disclosure of the significant evaluation factors and subfactors — including cost or price — and their relative importance.

cite.quote: Orders valued above $7.5 million (a) Procedures . Provide a fair notice of the intent to place an order to all contractors offering the products or services according to 16.507-4. A fair notice must— (1) Include a clear statement of the agency’s requirements; (2) Allow for a reasonable response period; and (3) Disclose the significant factors and subfactors, as applicable, including cost or price, that the agency expects to consider in evaluating quotations, offers, or other responses to notices, and their relative importance;

5m.q: Do losing contract holders get a debriefing on large task orders?
5m.a: Yes — for orders in the above-$7.5 million tier, postaward notifications and debriefings follow part 15, and a summary of the debriefing goes in the order file.
