DoD hardens this with its own statutory trigger: a written or oral postaward debriefing of successful and unsuccessful awardees is required for task and delivery orders valued at $10 million or more (section 818, FY 2018 NDAA; R-DFARS 216.507-5). Know both numbers — $7.5 million is the RFO procedures tier; $10 million is the DoD debriefing mandate.

cite.quote: (c) Postaward notices and debriefings. Provide postaward notifications and debriefings according to part 15. A summary of the debriefing must be included in the task or delivery order file.

5m.q: When can a task or delivery order be protested?
5m.a: Only on grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract — or, at GAO only, for orders valued over $35 million (DoD, NASA, Coast Guard) or $10 million (other agencies).

cite.quote: (1) A protest on the grounds that the order increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract; or (2) (i) For agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $10 million (41 U.S.C. 4106(f)); or (ii) For DoD, NASA, or the Coast Guard, a protest of an order valued in excess of $35 million (10 U.S.C. 3406(f)).

5m.q: What makes an indefinite-quantity contract binding?
5m.a: The stated minimum quantity the Government must order — it must be more than a nominal quantity, but should not exceed the amount the Government is fairly certain to order.

cite.quote: The contract must require the Government to order and the contractor to furnish at least a stated minimum quantity of supplies or services. To ensure that the contract is binding, the minimum quantity must be more than a nominal quantity, but it should not exceed the amount that the Government is fairly certain to order.

5m.q: Single award or multiple awards on an indefinite-quantity solicitation?
5m.a: Multiple awards are preferred to the maximum extent practicable, with the decision documented — and a single-award task- or delivery-order contract estimated over $150 million (including options) requires a written head-of-agency determination. In DoD, that $150 million determination belongs to the senior procurement executive, who must find the expected orders so integrally related that only a single source can efficiently — not merely reasonably — perform the work; the congressional-notification requirement does not apply to DoD; and no determination is required at all if a 6.104 justification has been executed (R-DFARS 216.504-3).

cite.quote: No task or delivery order contract in an amount estimated to exceed $150 million (including all options) may be awarded to a single source unless the head of the agency determines in writing

5m.q: When does an advisory and assistance services IDIQ force multiple awards?
5m.a: When the indefinite-quantity contract is estimated to exceed 3 years and $20 million including all options, the solicitation must provide for multiple awards — unless a written determination finds more than one award impracticable because the services are unique or highly specialized or the tasks integrally related, the evaluation shows only one offeror capable at the required quality level, or only one offer is received. The preference does not apply when the head of the agency determines in writing during planning that A&AS is necessarily incident to, and not a significant component of, the contract.

cite.quote: if an indefinite-quantity contract for advisory and assistance services is estimated to exceed 3 years and $20 million (including all options), the solicitation must provide for multiple awards unless- (i) The contracting officer or other official designated by the head of the agency determines in writing- (A) It is not practicable to award more than one contract because the services required are unique or highly specialized or the tasks are so integrally related; or (B) After the evaluation of offers, that only one offeror is capable of providing the services required at the level of quality required; or (ii) Only one offer is received.

5m.q: Can an order under a multiple-award contract be set aside for small business?
5m.a: Yes — contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders for small business concerns, and that discretionary decision is not itself a basis for protest.

cite.quote: contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders placed under multiple-award contracts for any of the small business concerns identified in 19.000(a)(3).

5m.q: How long may a DoD task- or delivery-order contract run?
5m.a: Up to five years, extendable by option or modification — but the total period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless the head of the agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances require a longer period (R-DFARS 217.201-270(a) restates the same 5/10-year rule for DoD). One carve-out a board will probe: a task-order contract for advisory and assistance services is capped at a 5-year ordering period including all extensions (16.501-2(c)(2)), unless a longer period is specifically authorized by statute or the A&AS is determined incidental and not a significant component of the contract — plus a sole-source extension of up to 6 months when a follow-on award is delayed by circumstances not reasonably foreseeable and continuity of services requires it. DoD adds one more tripwire: senior procurement executive approval is required before issuing an order expected to extend more than 1 year beyond that 10-year (or extended) limit (R-DFARS 217.201-270(c)).

cite.quote: may provide for the contract to cover any period up to five years and may extend the contract period for one or more successive periods pursuant to an option provided in the contract or a modification of the contract. The total contract period as extended may not exceed 10 years unless such head of an agency determines in writing that exceptional circumstances necessitate a longer contract period.

5m.q: List the determinations required before exercising an option.
5m.a: Written notice within the contract's specified time; funds available; the option fulfills an existing Government requirement; it was synopsized unless exempt; no active SAM exclusion; acceptable performance on the current contract; the price is fair and reasonable under current market conditions and exercise is in the Government's best interest; and the exercise complies with part 6. DoD adds two more gates before exercise: the contractor's SAM record is active with the UEI, CAGE code, name, and physical address accurate in the contract document; and SPRS shows both a current NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment summary score (not more than 3 years old) for each covered contractor information system and a current CMMC certificate at the level the contract requires (R-DFARS 217.204-170).

cite.quote: (1) Providing written notice to the contractor of the Government’s intention to exercise the option, within the time specified in the contract; (2) Confirming that funds are available; and (3) Determining that– (i) The option fulfills an existing Government requirement; (ii) The option was synopsized as required, unless exempt (see part 5); (iii) The Contractor does not have an active exclusion record in the System for Award Management (see part 9); (iv) The contractor’s performance on the current contract has been acceptable

5m.q: Why does exercising an option not require a new competition?
5m.a: Because the exercise must comply with part 6 by having been evaluated as part of the initial competition and being exercisable at an amount specified in, or reasonably determinable from, the terms of the contract.

cite.quote: The option exercise complies with the requirements of part 6 for full and open competition, i.e., the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the terms of the contract.

5m.q: When are options prohibited?
5m.a: When the price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable — introducing significant option-pricing risk — or when market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

cite.quote: The contracting officer must not use options when- (1) Price or availability of necessary material or labor is not reasonably foreseeable, introducing significant risk into option pricing; or (2) Market prices for the supplies or services are likely to change significantly.

5m.q: How far can the Option to Extend Services clause stretch a service contract?
5m.a: It may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance may not exceed 6 months, at the rates specified in the contract.

cite.quote: The option provision may be exercised more than once, but the total extension of performance hereunder shall not exceed 6 months.

5m.q: After market research, in what order of priority must an agency source its requirement?
5m.a: (1) A commercial product or service on an existing governmentwide contract; (2) modify the requirement so an existing governmentwide contract can be used; (3) a commercial product or service from another source; (4) a commercial product or service that could be modified; and only then (5) a nondevelopmental item.

cite.quote: (1) A commercial product or commercial service on an existing governmentwide contract can meet the agency's requirements; (2) The requirements could be modified so the agency could use an existing governmentwide contract; (3) A commercial product or commercial service is available from another source; (4) A commercial product or commercial service could be modified to meet the agency's requirements; or (5) The requirement can only be satisfied by a nondevelopmental item.

5m.q: How much information may you ask potential sources to submit during market research?
5m.a: No more than the minimum information necessary to make the determinations required by 10.001(f). Market research is the Government doing its homework — not a vehicle for extracting free proposals from industry.

cite.quote: When conducting market research, agencies must not ask potential sources to submit more than the minimum information necessary to make the determinations required in paragraph (f).

5m.q: Can a requirement that is not commercial be bought as if it were?
5m.a: Yes — and for DoD there is more than one lane. The RFO lane: the head of the agency may determine that supplies or services used to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack are to be treated as commercial products or commercial services — though a sole-source award over $25 million under this treatment remains subject to Cost Accounting Standards and certified cost or pricing data requirements. R-DFARS 212.001-70 adds two statutory lanes of its own: supplies and services provided by nontraditional defense contractors may be treated as commercial (10 U.S.C. 3457), and supplies or services resulting from a commercial solutions opening are treated as commercial (10 U.S.C. 3458) — none of the three lanes requires a commercial product or commercial service determination. And remember part 12's rank: it takes precedence over other parts whenever there is an inconsistency.

cite.quote: Agencies may treat any acquisition of supplies or services that, as determined by the head of the agency, are to be used to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack, as an acquisition of commercial products or commercial services. However, if the contract is awarded on a sole-source basis for an amount greater than $25 million, the contract is not exempt from Cost Accounting Standards (CAS) (see 48 CFR chapter 99) or certified cost or pricing data requirements (see part 15).

5m.q: How are commercial acquisitions over $9 million solicited?
5m.a: Using the subpart 12.2 procedures in conjunction with part 15 (requests for proposals) or part 14 (invitations for bids) — with the RFP preferred because it considers past performance. Know the moving line underneath the number: $9 million is the ceiling for the simplified procedures at 12.201-1, and 12.001(c) raises that ceiling to $15 million when the head of the agency determines the supplies or services support a contingency operation, facilitate defense against or recovery from a cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack, support a State/USAID request for international disaster assistance, or support response to an emergency or major disaster. Do not divide requirements merely to stay under a threshold (12.001(d)).

cite.quote: For acquisitions valued at greater than $9 million, use the procedures in this subpart in conjunction with the procedures in part 15 for requests for proposals (RFPs) or part 14 for invitations for bids (IFBs), as appropriate.

5m.q: How detailed do commercial evaluation factors need to be?
5m.a: For most commercial acquisitions, no more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services to meet the need), price, and past performance — predetermined technical subfactors are not required. DoD adds one mandatory factor: supply chain risk, whenever acquiring information technology — as a service or as a supply — that is, is part of, or supports a covered system (R-DFARS 212.203).

cite.quote: For most acquisitions of commercial products or commercial services, evaluation factors need not be more detailed than technical (capability of the products or services offered to meet the agency’s needs), price, and past performance.

5m.q: Which termination machinery applies to commercial contracts?
5m.a: The termination paragraphs of clause 52.212-4 — not part 49. And before terminating for cause, send a cure notice unless the reason is late delivery.

cite.quote: Follow the procedures in this section and the termination paragraphs of the clause at 52.212-4, when terminating contracts for commercial products or commercial services. Do not use the procedures in part 49.

5m.q: Which contract types are the default?
5m.a: Fixed-price types are the default and preferred. If a fixed-price type is not appropriate for the entire contract, consider whether a portion of it can be established on a fixed-price basis. DoD draws a hard line at development work: for programs other than major defense acquisition programs, R-DFARS 235.170(b) forbids awarding a fixed-price type contract for a development program effort unless the level of program risk permits realistic pricing, the fixed-price type allocates program risk equitably and sensibly between the Government and the contractor, and a written determination to that effect is executed — by USD(A&S) when the contract is over $25 million and covers non-major-system R&D or development of a major system or its subsystem, otherwise by the contracting officer. Major defense acquisition programs run a different track: 235.170(a) sends you to 234.7202.

cite.quote: Fixed-price contract types are the default and preferred contract types. If a fixed-price contract type is not appropriate for an entire contract, consider whether a portion of the contract can be established on a fixed-price basis.

5m.q: When must firm-fixed-price be used, and what if a reasonable basis for firm pricing does not exist?
5m.a: FFP must be used when the risk involved is minimal or predictable with an acceptable degree of certainty. Without a firm pricing basis, select a type (or combination) that appropriately ties profit to contractor performance. DoD bounds that rule for development: under R-DFARS 235.170(b), and for programs other than major defense acquisition programs, a fixed-price type contract may not be awarded for a development program effort unless program risk permits realistic pricing and the fixed-price type permits an equitable and sensible allocation of risk — backed by a written determination, executed by USD(A&S) for covered development contracts over $25 million and otherwise by the contracting officer. For major defense acquisition programs, 235.170(a) routes you to 234.7202 instead.

cite.quote: A firm-fixed-price contract (see section 16.202) must be used when the risk involved is minimal or can be predicted with an acceptable degree of certainty.

5m.q: What gates must a cost-reimbursement contract clear before award?
5m.a: A written acquisition plan approved at least one level above the contracting officer; the agency-head justification for other than fixed-price if 16.104 requires it; a contractor accounting system that can segregate, accumulate, and allocate contract costs; and sufficient Government resources — including a designated COR — to manage it. And one absolute bar: cost-reimbursement is not allowed for the purchase of commercial products and commercial services (16.301-3(b)). DoD adds a statutory bar of its own: no cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-award-fee, or cost-plus-incentive-fee contracts in connection with military construction or military family housing — even under a declaration of war or national emergency (10 U.S.C. 3323; R-DFARS 216.301-3).

cite.quote: (1) A written acquisition plan has been approved at least one level above the contracting officer (see 7.102(d)); (2) The agency head approves a justification for other than fixed-price contracts, if required by 16.104. (3) The contractor’s accounting system can adequately segregate, accumulate and allocate costs specifically attributed to the contract or order during contract performance; and (4) Before award of the contract or order, sufficient Government resources are available to award and manage a contract other than firm-fixed-priced (see part 7). This includes designating a contracting officer’s representative to monitor contractor performance and cost controls (see part 1). (b) The use of cost-reimbursement contracts is not allowed for the purchase of commercial products and commercial services (see part 12).

5m.q: At what values does the Executive Order 14402 other-than-fixed-price justification apply?
5m.a: $100 million for DoD, $35 million for NASA, $25 million for DHS, and $10 million for all other Federal agencies — approved by the head of the agency before using a covered contract or order. Know the exceptions: multiple-award contracts are exempt — but task orders, delivery orders, and BPAs under them are not — along with contracts supporting an emergency, major disaster, or contingency operation; R&D contracts or orders; and pre-production development for a major system acquisition (16.104(e)).

cite.quote: a justification is required for covered contracts and orders valued at or above— (i) $100 million, for DoD; (ii) $35 million, for NASA; (iii) $25 million, for Department of Homeland Security; or (iv) $10 million, for all other Federal agencies.

5m.q: What distinguishes a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract?
5m.a: The fixed fee does not change with actual cost — it may be adjusted only as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that includes payment of an agreed upon fixed-fee. The fixed fee does not change with actual cost but may be adjusted as a result of changes in the work to be performed under the contract.

5m.q: What elements does a fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specify, and who absorbs cost above the price ceiling?
5m.a: A target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but no profit ceiling or floor), and a profit-adjustment formula. If final negotiated cost exceeds the price ceiling, the contractor absorbs the difference as a loss.

cite.quote: A fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract specifies a target cost, a target profit, a price ceiling (but not a profit ceiling or floor), and a formula for profit adjustments. When the final cost is less than the target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit greater than the target profit; conversely, when final cost is more than target cost, application of the formula results in a final profit less than the target profit, or even a net loss. If the final negotiated cost exceeds the price ceiling, the contractor absorbs the difference as a loss.

5m.q: What are the HUBZone sole-source dollar caps?
5m.a: $8.5 million for requirements in manufacturing NAICS codes and $5.5 million for all other NAICS codes — with no reasonable expectation of offers from two or more HUBZone concerns, a responsible contractor, and award at a fair and reasonable price.

cite.quote: The anticipated price of the contract, including options, will not exceed— (i) $8.5 million for a requirement within the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes for manufacturing; or (ii) $5.5 million for a requirement within all other NAICS codes

5m.q: When must an 8(a) acquisition be competed among 8(a) participants?
5m.a: When there is a reasonable expectation that at least two eligible, responsible 8(a) participants will offer at a fair market price, and the anticipated total value including options exceeds $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes or $5.5 million for all other acquisitions. Do not read that as license to go sole-source below the threshold: under 19.108-7(d)(1) a contracting officer below the competitive threshold must first try the acquisition as a competitive 8(a) order using the governmentwide contracts SBA has approved for competition among 8(a) contract-holders before proceeding to a sole-source 8(a) award. Splitting a requirement that exceeds the threshold into lesser amounts to reach 8(a) sole-source procedures is prohibited (19.108-7(c)). One DoD wrinkle: above the competitive threshold, SBA may still accept the requirement for a sole-source 8(a) award on behalf of a concern owned by a Native Hawaiian Organization (R-DFARS 219.108-7).

cite.quote: The anticipated total value of the contract, including options, will exceed $8.5 million for acquisitions assigned manufacturing North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and $5.5 million for all other acquisitions.

5m.q: Once SBA accepts a requirement into the 8(a) program, can the follow-on be competed outside it?
5m.a: Not unilaterally. Follow-on requirements stay in the 8(a) program unless there is a mandatory source, the follow-on is set aside under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, or WOSB programs, or SBA agrees in writing to release the requirement.

cite.quote: Once a requirement has been accepted by SBA into the 8(a) program, any follow-on requirements (see definition at 13 CFR 124.3) must remain in the 8(a) program unless

5m.q: You find the apparent successful small business nonresponsible. Can you just award to the next offeror?
5m.a: No — the COC program applies to all Government acquisitions except 8(a) sole-source awards. Withhold award and refer the small business to SBA for a possible Certificate of Competency, even if the next acceptable offer is also from a small business.

cite.quote: The COC program applies to all Government acquisitions except for 8(a) sole-source awards. If a contracting officer determines an apparent successful small business offeror to be nonresponsible, the contracting officer must refer that small business to SBA for a possible COC, even if the next acceptable offer is from a small business.

5m.q: How final is an SBA Certificate of Competency?
5m.a: Final as to all elements of responsibility — a certified concern must not be held to any other responsibility requirements, though award may still be withheld for reasons unrelated to responsibility. If SBA has not issued the COC within 15 business days of the referral, award goes to another appropriately selected, responsible offeror.

cite.quote: SBA COCs are final with respect to all elements of responsibility of prospective small business contractors. An SBA-certified concern must not be required to meet any other requirements of responsibility.

5m.q: Before consolidating or bundling requirements, what must the agency do?
5m.a: Conduct market research; identify alternative approaches involving less consolidation; coordinate with the agency's small business office; identify any negative impact on small business participation; take steps to include small businesses in the strategy; and, when triggered, make a written determination that the consolidation or bundling is necessary and justified. The determination triggers: consolidation above $2 million, any bundling, and substantial bundling at $8 million or more for DoD ($6 million for NASA, GSA, and DOE; $2.5 million for all other agencies) — thresholds that also apply to orders under multiple-award contracts and interagency vehicles.

cite.quote: (b) Unless excepted in paragraph (c), a written determination is required for— (1) Consolidation requirements above $2 million (15 U.S.C. 657q); (2) Bundling requirements; and (3) Substantial bundling requirements with a cumulative estimated dollar value (including options) of: (i) $8 million or more for the Department of Defense.

5m.q: When does a subcontracting plan become a condition of award?
5m.a: In acquisitions expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction of a public facility) with subcontracting possibilities, the apparently successful other-than-small offeror must submit an acceptable subcontracting plan or be ineligible for award. Plans are never required from small business concerns, for personal services contracts, or for contracts performed entirely outside the United States and its outlying areas (19.109(b)). DoD contracts pair the 52.219-9 plan clause with the DoD-unique clause at 252.219-7996 — or 252.219-7997 for contractors with comprehensive subcontracting plans approved under the Test Program (R-DFARS 219.109).

cite.quote: each solicitation of offers to perform a contract that is expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction of any public facility) and that has subcontracting possibilities, must require the apparently successful offeror to submit an acceptable subcontracting plan.

5m.q: Who approves a J&A at or below $900,000?
5m.a: The contracting officer.

cite.quote: $900,000 or below Contracting officer.

25m.q: Who is the source selection authority by default, and what team must the SSA establish?
25m.a: The contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual. The SSA must establish an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition with contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise. For DoD, R-DFARS 215.201 adds a step: for high-dollar value and other acquisitions, as prescribed by agency procedures, the SSA must approve a source selection plan before the solicitation is issued.

cite.quote: Agency heads are responsible for source selection. A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions. (b) The SSA must— (1) Establish an evaluation team tailored for the acquisition that includes appropriate contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of proposals;

25m.q: When is the tradeoff approach appropriate, and what must a higher-priced award show?
25m.a: When it may be in the Government's best interest to award to other than the lowest-priced or highest-technically-rated offeror. It permits tradeoffs among price and non-price factors — but the anticipated benefits of the higher-priced proposal must merit the additional cost. DoD bolts on one mandate: for fuel acquisitions supporting an overseas contingency operation above the SAT, R-DFARS 215.103-170 directs consideration of a tradeoff approach — with past performance, cost, anticorruption training, and anticorruption compliance as candidate factors — and if tradeoff is not considered, a written justification approved one level above the contracting officer goes in the contract file before the solicitation issues.

cite.quote: This process permits tradeoffs among cost or price and non-cost or non-price factors. The anticipated benefits of a higher priced proposal must merit the additional cost.

25m.q: What defines the lowest price technically acceptable approach, and what does it forbid?
25m.a: Award goes to the offeror with a technically acceptable proposal at the lowest evaluated price. It does not permit tradeoffs — technical superiority beyond acceptability buys nothing. Watch the limitations split: the RFO's own limitations at 15.103-2(c) open with "Except for DoD," so they do not bind an Air Force buyer. DoD's parallel limits are at R-DFARS 215.103-270, which permits the LPTA approach only when all of the conditions it lists are met — among them that minimum requirements can be described clearly and comprehensively, that no or minimal value would come from exceeding them, that the file contains a determination that the lowest price reflects full life-cycle cost, and that the contracting officer documents the justifying circumstances.

cite.quote: The lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) approach to source selection is appropriate when it is in the Government’s best interest to award to the offeror that submits a technically acceptable proposal with the lowest evaluated price. This approach does not permit tradeoffs.

25m.q: How does the highest-technically-rated-with-a-fair-and-reasonable-price approach work?
25m.a: All proposals are rated on the non-price factors; the highest technically rated proposal's price is then checked for fairness and reasonableness under subpart 15.4. If it fails, move to the next highest rated — no tradeoffs between price and non-price factors are considered.

cite.quote: The highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price approach to source selection is appropriate when the Government determines in advance that it would not be advantageous to consider tradeoffs between cost or price and non-cost or non-price factors; rather, the acquisition warrants paying any fair and reasonable price for the highest quality performance.

25m.q: Must price or cost be evaluated in every competitive source selection?
25m.a: Not always. For DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the contracting officer may choose not to include price or cost as an award evaluation factor when the RFP is above the SAT, will result in multiple-award contracts for the same or similar services, and states the Government intends to award to each and all qualifying offerors — price or cost then must be considered on every order placed under the contract instead, and the exception does not apply to RFPs for multiple-award contracts that provide for sole source orders under section 8(a) of the Small Business Act. Otherwise the baseline holds: price or cost in every competitive source selection, and quality through one or more non-cost factors. On past performance the two books split: the RFO requires it in every competitive source selection unless the contracting officer documents why it is not appropriate, but R-DFARS 215.104-70 applies in lieu of that direction for DoD — past performance is evaluated when the contract, task order, or delivery order exceeds the category thresholds: $5 million for systems and operations support (including fuels), $1 million for services (including health care), $1 million for information technology, and $500,000 for ship repair and overhaul.

cite.quote: for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard– (A) Contracting officers may choose not to include price or cost as an evaluation factor for award when an RFP– (1) Has an estimated value above the simplified acquisition threshold; (2) Will result in multiple-award contracts that are for the same or similar services; and (3) States that the Government intends to make an award to each and all qualifying offerors.

25m.q: What must the RFP say about how non-price factors weigh against price?
25m.a: At a minimum, whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when combined, are significantly more important than, approximately equal to, or significantly less important than cost or price.

cite.quote: whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when combined, are— (1) Significantly more important than cost or price; (2) Approximately equal to cost or price; or (3) Significantly less important than cost or price

25m.q: What can clarifications never do?
25m.a: Permit proposal revisions, cure deficiencies or material omissions, or materially alter the technical or cost elements of a proposal. They are discretionary — conducting clarifications with one offeror does not require them with any other.

cite.quote: Clarifications do not permit offerors to revise their proposal and cannot be used to cure proposal deficiencies or material omissions or materially alter the technical or cost elements of the proposal.

25m.q: How do you evaluate an offeror with no relevant past performance record?
25m.a: Neither favorably nor unfavorably — the absence of a record may not count for or against the offeror. DoD adds one step before the record is treated as absent: when the offeror is a small business concern, R-DFARS 215.202-70 requires the contracting officer to consider relevant past performance information provided for the offeror's affiliates.

cite.quote: An offeror without a record of relevant past performance or for whom information on past performance is not available may not be evaluated favorably or unfavorably on past performance.

25m.q: Define the competitive range. When is establishing one required?
25m.a: The group of evaluated proposals the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. One must be established whenever negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals — and it may be limited to the greatest number that permits an efficient competition.

cite.quote: A competitive range is the group of evaluated proposals that the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. Contracting officers must establish a competitive range if negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals.

25m.q: What is the minimum content of negotiations with each offeror in the competitive range?
25m.a: Negotiate with each responsible offeror in the range, tailored to its proposal — and at a minimum indicate to, or negotiate with, each offeror any deficiencies or significant weaknesses in its proposal. For DoD, R-DFARS 215.204-2 adds an expectation: for acquisitions with an estimated value of $100 million or more, contracting officers should conduct negotiations.

cite.quote: (i) Negotiate with each responsible offeror within the competitive range; and (ii) Tailor the negotiation to the offeror’s proposal, but at a minimum, indicate to, or negotiate with, each offeror any deficiencies or significant weaknesses in the proposal.

25m.q: What happens when a proposal is eliminated from the competitive range?
25m.a: No further revisions to that proposal can be accepted or considered. Elimination can happen at any time once the contracting officer concludes the offeror is unlikely to receive award, with written notice to the offeror.

cite.quote: (1) When a proposal is eliminated, no further revisions to the proposal can be accepted or considered. (2) Contracting officers may eliminate a proposal from the competitive range at any time upon concluding that the offeror is unlikely to receive an award.

25m.q: Negotiations are finished. What must every offeror still in the competitive range receive?
25m.a: An opportunity to submit a proposal revision, plus a notice requiring the revision in writing and stating that the Government intends to make award without obtaining further revisions. Every offeror still in the competitive range must get an equal amount of time to submit its revision.

cite.quote: (1) When negotiations with an offeror are finished, and that offeror has not been eliminated from the competitive range, contracting officers must provide the offeror with— (i) An opportunity to submit a proposal revision; and (ii) A notice requiring the proposal revision in writing and stating that the Government intends to make award without obtaining further revisions. (2) Each offeror with a proposal still within the competitive range must be given an equal amount of time within which to submit their proposal revision.

25m.q: When may a competitive award be made without negotiations?
25m.a: When the RFP states the Government intends to evaluate proposals and make award without negotiation. If the Government then finds it necessary to negotiate anyway, the rationale must be documented in the contract file.

cite.quote: Contracting officers may make competitive awards without negotiations if the RFP states that the Government intends to evaluate proposals and make award without negotiation. If the RFP includes such a notice and the Government determines it is necessary to negotiate, the rationale for doing so must be documented in the contract file

25m.q: What must the source selection decision document contain?
25m.a: The SSA's independent judgment based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all RFP criteria, with the rationale for any business judgments and tradeoffs — including benefits associated with additional costs — though the tradeoffs need not be quantified.

cite.quote: The source selection decision must represent the SSA’s independent judgement and be based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all source selection criteria in the RFP. The source selection decision must be documented and include the rationale for any business judgments and tradeoffs made or relied on by the SSA, including benefits associated with additional costs. The documentation does not need to quantify the tradeoffs that led to the decision.

25m.q: An offeror is excluded from the competitive range before award. What notice and debriefing rights does it have?
25m.a: Prompt written notice stating the basis for the determination and that proposal revisions will not be considered (15.206-1). The offeror may then request a preaward debriefing in writing within 3 days after receiving the exclusion notice — or ask to delay it until after award, in which case it must include everything a postaward debriefing would, and the delay could affect the timeliness of any later protest. Miss the 3-day window and the offeror need not be given either a preaward or a postaward debriefing; no offeror gets more than one debriefing per proposal. A preaward debriefing must never disclose the number, identity, content, ranking, or evaluation of other offerors.

cite.quote: (1) Offerors may request a preaward debriefing by submitting a written request for debriefing to the contracting officer within 3 days after receipt of the notice of exclusion from the competition. (2) At the offeror's request, this debriefing may be delayed until after award. If the debriefing is delayed until after award, it must include all information normally provided in a postaward debriefing. Debriefings delayed pursuant to this paragraph could affect the timeliness of any protest filed subsequent to the debriefing.

25m.q: How quickly must an offeror request a postaward debriefing, and how soon should it occur?
25m.a: The written request is due within 3 days after receipt of the award notice; the debriefing should occur within 5 days after receipt of the request, to the maximum extent practicable. For DoD the skeleton has a tail: a written or oral debriefing is required, when requested, for contract awards valued at $15 million or more (R-DFARS 215.301-170), and under the enhanced procedure at 215.301-270 the debriefed offeror has 2 business days to submit additional written questions, the agency must respond in writing within 5 business days, and the debriefing is not concluded until the later of its delivery or that written response.

cite.quote: within 3 days after receipt of the award notice in accordance with 15.207-2. Such offerors must be debriefed and furnished the basis for the selection decision and contract award. (2) To the maximum extent practicable, the debriefing should occur within 5 days after receipt of the written request.

25m.q: What must a postaward debriefing never include?
25m.a: Point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with other offerors' proposals — or any information prohibited from disclosure, such as trade secrets, confidential cost breakdowns, or the names of past performance references. DoD adds a third rail: when the withholding authority at R-DFARS 240.271-6 is exercised, notifications to unsuccessful offerors must not reveal information determined withheld under 10 U.S.C. 3252 (R-DFARS 215.301-170(c)). And do not confuse the never-include list with DoD's must-disclose floor — for awards over $15 million a small business or nontraditional defense contractor may request the agency's redacted source selection decision document, and over $150 million its redacted release is required (R-DFARS 215.301-170(b), which supersedes the $10 million/$100 million figures still printed in RFO 15.301-1(c)).

cite.quote: The debriefing must not include point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with those of other offerors.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Above what dollar value must certified cost or pricing data be obtained?
25m.a: For DoD: $10 million for prime contracts awarded after June 30, 2026, and $2.5 million for primes awarded on or before that date — R-DFARS 215.403-3(a), in lieu of the RFO baseline. Civilian agencies stayed at $2.5 million. Either way the duty yields to a 15.403-2 exception (DoD adds its own at 215.403-270), and a waiver remains worth requesting when the standards can be met.

cite.quote: In lieu of the requirements of FAR 15.403-3(a), obtain certified cost or pricing data when a prime contract is expected to exceed $10 million and is awarded after June 30, 2026, unless an exception at FAR 15.403-2 or DFARS 215.403-270 applies. The threshold is $2.5 million when the prime contract is awarded on or before June 30, 2026

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Name the exceptions that prohibit requiring certified cost or pricing data.
25m.a: Adequate price competition; prices set by law or regulation; commercial products or services; an HCA waiver; and modifications of commercial-product or commercial-service contracts (plus the flat prohibition at or below the SAT). For DoD the list is longer: R-DFARS 215.403-270 adds that certified data are not required to the extent the data relate to an indirect offset, and sets DoD's own standards for the adequate-price-competition and waiver exceptions.

cite.quote: (1) When the contracting officer determines that prices agreed upon are based on adequate price competition (see standards in paragraph (c)(1) of this subsection); (2) When the contracting officer determines that prices agreed upon are based on prices set by law or regulation (see standards in paragraph (c)(2) of this subsection); (3) When a commercial product or commercial service is being acquired (see standards in paragraph (c)(3) of this subsection); (4) When a waiver has been granted (see standards in paragraph (c)(4) of this subsection); or (5) When modifying a contract or subcontract for commercial products or commercial services

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: When is a price based on adequate price competition — and which route is closed to DoD?
25m.a: The core standard: two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submit priced offers that satisfy the Government's expressed requirement; award goes to the best-value offeror where price is a substantial factor; and there is no finding that the successful price is unreasonable — any such finding needs a statement of facts approved above the contracting officer. Everything in 15.403-2(c)(1)(ii) is reserved to "agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard," and it holds two alternatives: (A) a reasonable expectation, based on market research, that two or more responsible offerors would compete even though only one offer arrived, with approval above the contracting officer; and (B) price analysis clearly demonstrating the proposed price is reasonable against current or recent prices for the same or similar items from adequate competition, adjusted for market and quantity changes. Neither alternative is open to DoD. What DoD gets instead is R-DFARS 215.403-270(a)(3): for dual or multiple source programs, adequate price competition is determined case by case — it normally exists when prices are solicited across a full range of step quantities, normally including a 0-100 percent split, from at least two offerors individually capable of producing the full quantity, and the reasonableness of all awarded prices is clearly established by price analysis. And when a competitive solicitation draws only one offer, R-DFARS routes you to 215.202-71.

cite.quote: (ii) For agencies other than DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, a price is also based on adequate price competition when (A) There was a reasonable expectation, based on market research or other assessment, that two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, would submit priced offers in response to the request for proposal’s (RFP) expressed requirement, even though only one offer is received from a responsible offeror

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Who can waive the certified cost or pricing data requirement?
25m.a: The head of the contracting activity, without power of delegation, in exceptional cases — only if the price can be determined fair and reasonable without the data, with the authorization and rationale in writing. For DoD, R-DFARS 215.403-270(b)(1) makes it a three-part determination: the property or services cannot reasonably be obtained without a waiver, the price can be determined fair and reasonable without certified data, and there are demonstrated benefits to granting the waiver.

cite.quote: In exceptional cases, the HCA may, without power of delegation, waive the requirement for submission of certified cost or pricing data if the price can be determined to be fair and reasonable without submission of certified cost or pricing data.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: A modification deletes $1.5 million of work and adds $1 million — a net $500,000 change. Does it cross the certified-data threshold?
25m.a: Against the baseline $2.5 million threshold, yes — price adjustments count both increases and decreases, so this is a $2.5 million pricing adjustment even though the net change is $500,000. For DoD, R-DFARS 215.403-3 directs you to use the same criteria as the prime contract being modified: primes awarded after June 30, 2026 carry a $10 million threshold, so this adjustment would not trigger certified data there, while primes awarded on or before that date keep the $2.5 million threshold and it would.

cite.quote: Price adjustment amounts must consider both increases and decreases ( e.g. , a $500,000 modification resulting from a reduction of $1,500,000 and an increase of $1,000,000 is a $2,500,000 pricing adjustment exceeding the $2,500,000 threshold).

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Which modifications never require certified cost or pricing data?
25m.a: Modifications solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments, and exercising an option at the price established at award or initial negotiation.

cite.quote: Certified cost or pricing data are not required for modifications— (A) Solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments; or (B) To exercise an option at the price established at contract award or initial negotiation.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Does the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data guarantee the contractor's estimates, and does holding one excuse analysis?
25m.a: No and no. The certificate applies to the facts the judgment was based on, not the accuracy of the contractor's judgment about future costs — and possession of a certificate is not a substitute for examining and analyzing the proposal.

cite.quote: The certificate does not constitute a representation as to the accuracy of the contractor's judgment on the estimate of future costs or projections. It applies to the data upon which the judgment or estimate was based.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What is price analysis, and which techniques are preferred?
25m.a: Examining and evaluating a proposed price without evaluating its separate cost elements and proposed profit. The preferred techniques are comparison of the proposed prices received in response to the RFP and comparison to historical prices paid, by the Government or others, for the same or similar items — a prior price must be a valid basis and adjusted for differing terms, quantities, and market conditions. Only when those are unavailable or insufficient do the others come in: parametric estimates and rough yardsticks, published price lists and market prices, independent Government cost estimates, market research, or analysis of data other than certified cost or pricing data. A catalog listing does not, by itself, make a price fair and reasonable. For DoD the preference is stated differently: under R-DFARS 215.404-170, when there is no adequate price competition, pricing based on market prices is the preferred method, and price reasonableness must not be based solely on historical prices paid by the Government.

cite.quote: Price analysis is the process of examining and evaluating a proposed price without evaluating its separate cost elements and proposed profit.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What is cost analysis?
25m.a: The review and evaluation of separate cost elements and profit or fee in a proposal, applying judgment to determine how well the proposed costs represent what the contract should cost, assuming reasonable economy and efficiency.

cite.quote: Cost analysis is the review and evaluation of any separate cost elements and profit or fee in an offeror's or contractor's proposal, as needed to determine a fair and reasonable price or to determine cost realism, and the application of judgment to determine how well the proposed costs represent what the cost of the contract should be, assuming reasonable economy and efficiency.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: Define cost realism analysis.
25m.a: Independently reviewing specific elements of each offeror's proposed cost estimate to determine whether they are realistic for the work, reflect a clear understanding of the requirements, and are consistent with the offeror's own technical proposal.

cite.quote: Cost realism analysis is the process of independently reviewing and evaluating specific elements of each offeror's proposed cost estimate to determine whether the estimated proposed cost elements are realistic for the work to be performed; reflect a clear understanding of the requirements; and are consistent with the unique methods of performance and materials described in the offeror's technical proposal.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: On which contracts is cost realism analysis mandatory, and what number does it produce?
25m.a: On cost-reimbursement contracts — it determines each offeror's probable cost of performance, which may differ from the proposed cost and must be used for the best-value evaluation.

cite.quote: Cost realism analyses must be performed on cost-reimbursement contacts to determine the probable cost of performance for each offeror.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: May offered prices be adjusted when cost realism is applied to competitive fixed-price proposals?
25m.a: No. Realism results may inform performance-risk assessments and responsibility determinations, but proposals are evaluated on the RFP criteria and the offered prices must not be adjusted.

cite.quote: However, proposals must be evaluated using the criteria in the RFP, and the offered prices must not be adjusted as a result of the analysis.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What is unbalanced pricing, and what may it cost an offeror?
25m.a: Despite an acceptable total evaluated price, one or more line items are significantly over- or understated. The risks must be considered in the competitive range and the selection decision — and the offer may be rejected if the imbalance poses an unacceptable risk.

cite.quote: Unbalanced pricing exists when, despite an acceptable total evaluated price, the price of one or more line items is significantly over or understated as indicated by the application of cost or price analysis techniques.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What is the Government entitled to when certified cost or pricing data prove defective after award?
25m.a: A price adjustment, including profit or fee, of any significant amount by which the price was increased because of the inaccurate, incomplete, or noncurrent data — plus recovery of overpayments with interest, and penalties for knowing submissions.

cite.quote: the Government is entitled to a price adjustment, including profit or fee, of any significant amount by which the price was increased because of the defective data.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What are the statutory cost-plus-fixed-fee ceilings?
25m.a: 15 percent of estimated cost for experimental, developmental, or research work; 10 percent for all other CPFF contracts; and for architect-engineer services, 6 percent of the estimated construction cost — but that 6 percent is the civilian baseline. For the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, R-DFARS 236.202-371 sets the A-E design-fee limit at 10 percent of the project's estimated construction cost (10 U.S.C. 7540, 8612, and 9540).

cite.quote: (i) For experimental, developmental, or research work performed under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, the fee must not exceed 15 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee. (ii) For architect-engineer services for public works or utilities, the contract price or the estimated cost and fee for production and delivery of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications must not exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost of construction of the public work or utility, excluding fees. (iii) For other cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, the fee must not exceed 10 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What is the architect-engineer design-fee limit for the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force?
25m.a: 10 percent of the project's estimated construction cost — the military departments' statutory limit under R-DFARS 236.202-371, which displaces the 6 percent civilian baseline. It reaches modifications and redesign work too, but only the portion of the price attributable to preparing designs, plans, drawings, and specifications.

cite.quote: The statutes at 10 U.S.C. 7540, 8612, and 9540, for the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, respectively, limit the contract price (or fee) for architect-engineer services for the preparation of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications to 10 percent of the project's estimated construction cost.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: May you settle the fee first and negotiate cost later?
25m.a: No. Profit or fee is one of several interrelated variables — the contracting officer must not agree on profit or fee without concurrent agreement on cost and contract type. At a true impasse, refer the action to a level above the contracting officer.

cite.quote: Because profit or fee is only one of several interrelated variables, contracting officers must not agree on profit or fee without concurrent agreement on cost and type of contract.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: How does DoD develop its profit objective when certified cost or pricing data are obtained?
25m.a: With a structured approach, documented on DD Form 1547: the weighted guidelines method is mandatory, except that the modified weighted guidelines method applies to nonprofit organizations other than FFRDCs, and an alternate structured approach is allowed only for actions at or below the certified data threshold, architect-engineer or construction work, material mostly from subcontractors, or termination settlements — or when weighted guidelines cannot produce a reasonable objective and the HCA approves in writing. Cost-plus-award-fee contracts and FFRDCs are excepted entirely, never perform a profit analysis when assessing cost realism in competitive acquisitions, and document the profit analysis in the contract file.

cite.quote: Use a structured approach for developing a prenegotiation profit or fee objective on any negotiated contract action when certified cost or pricing data is obtained, except for cost-plus-award-fee contracts (see PGI 215.404-974, 216.402-4, and FAR 16.402-4) or contracts with Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) (see PGI 215.404-975).

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What must you establish before negotiating any pricing action?
25m.a: Prenegotiation objectives — the Government's initial negotiation position, built on the contracting officer's analysis of the offeror's proposal. The scope and depth of the supporting analysis should track the dollar value, importance, and complexity of the action, and when cost analysis is required you must document the pertinent issues to be negotiated, the cost objectives, and a profit or fee objective.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must establish prenegotiation objectives before negotiating a pricing action. The scope and depth of the analysis supporting the objectives should be directly related to the dollar value, importance, and complexity of the pricing action.

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: What goes in your price negotiation memorandum?
25m.a: The principal elements of the negotiated agreement, in the contract file: the purpose of the negotiation; a description of the acquisition; who represented each side; the status of contractor systems that affected the negotiation; if certified cost or pricing data were not required above the threshold, the exception used and its basis; if they were required, the extent you relied on them and any inaccurate, incomplete, or noncurrent data recognized; a summary of the proposal, field pricing recommendations, the Government's objective, and the negotiated position — each major cost element when based on cost analysis, or the source and type of data when based on price analysis; the most significant facts controlling the objectives and the agreement, with any significant differences between the two explained; the impact of higher-level direction; the basis for the profit or fee objective and what was negotiated; and documentation of fair and reasonable pricing.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must document in the contract file the principal elements of the negotiated agreement. The documentation ( e.g. , price negotiation memorandum) must include the following: (1) The purpose of the negotiation. (2) A description of the acquisition, including appropriate identifying numbers ( e.g. , RFP No.).

25m.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
25m.q: May another contract's prices or profits influence this negotiation?
25m.a: No. Each contract is priced separately and independently — no proposed price reductions under other contracts, no losses or profits realized or anticipated elsewhere, and no contingency amounts the contract already covers by adjustment.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must price each contract separately and independently and not— (1) Consider proposed price reductions under other contracts; (2) Consider losses or profits realized or anticipated under other contracts

25m.q: What happens when responsibility cannot be clearly established?
25m.a: No award — a contract requires an affirmative determination of responsibility, and without a clear indication of responsibility the contracting officer must determine the offeror nonresponsible. The prospective contractor bears the burden of affirmatively demonstrating its responsibility.

cite.quote: Do not award a contract award before making an affirmative determination of contractor responsibility. Without a clear indication of responsibility, make a determination of nonresponsibility.

25m.q: Recite the general standards of responsibility.
25m.a: Adequate financial resources (or the ability to obtain them); ability to meet the delivery or performance schedule given existing commitments; a satisfactory performance record — but never determine a contractor responsible or nonresponsible based solely on a lack of relevant performance history; a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; the necessary organization, experience, controls, and technical skills; the necessary production, construction, and technical equipment and facilities; and being otherwise qualified and eligible under applicable laws. For DoD, R-DFARS 209.104-1 adds more: on cost-reimbursement, incentive, or progress-payment contracts the contractor's accounting system and internal controls must give reasonable assurance that laws are complied with, cost data are reliable, misallocation risk is minimized, and charges match invoice procedures — and control by a state sponsor of terrorism, or by a foreign government where the contract requires access to proscribed information, bars award.

cite.quote: (a) Have adequate financial resources to perform the contract, or the ability to obtain them (see 9.104-3(a)); (b) Be able to comply with the required or proposed delivery or performance schedule, taking into consideration all existing commercial and governmental business commitments; (c) Have a satisfactory performance record (see 9.104-3(b) and part 42). Do not determine a prospective contractor responsible or nonresponsible based solely on a lack of relevant performance history

25m.q: What integrity database check precedes award above the SAT?
25m.a: Review the performance and integrity information in FAPIIS — including SAM exclusions and CPARS — and document in the file how it was considered in the responsibility determination.

cite.quote: Before awarding a contract exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold, review the performance and integrity information available in the Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System (FAPIIS)

25m.q: What two principles underlie the organizational conflict of interest rules?
25m.a: Preventing conflicting roles that might bias a contractor's judgment, and preventing unfair competitive advantage.

cite.quote: The two underlying principles are— (a) Preventing the existence of conflicting roles that might bias a contractor’s judgment; and (b) Preventing unfair competitive advantage.

25m.q: What are the contracting officer's OCI duties?
25m.a: Identify and evaluate potential conflicts as early in the acquisition process as possible, and avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before contract award — recommending a course of action to the HCA before issuing a solicitation that may involve a significant conflict.

cite.quote: (1) Identify and evaluate potential organizational conflicts of interest as early in the acquisition process as possible; and (2) Avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before contract award.

25m.q: Who approves an OCI waiver, and how far may that authority be delegated?
25m.a: The agency head or a designee, on a written request setting forth the extent of the conflict — and the authority must not be delegated below the head of a contracting activity. DoD carves out consulting services: under R-DFARS 209.503-70, notwithstanding the baseline rule, the waiver approval authority for consulting services (as defined at 209.572(b)) is the Secretary of Defense, the Under Secretary of Defense (Acquisition and Sustainment), or the assistant secretaries of the military departments — with no delegation below an official appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

cite.quote: Any request for waiver must be in writing, must set forth the extent of the conflict, and requires approval by the agency head or a designee. Agency heads must not delegate waiver authority below the level of head of a contracting activity.

25m.q: When does an unfair competitive advantage exist?
25m.a: When a competing contractor possesses proprietary information obtained from a Government official without proper authorization, or source selection information relevant to the contract that is not available to all competitors and would assist it in winning.

cite.quote: an unfair competitive advantage exists where a contractor competing for award of any Federal contract possesses- (1) Proprietary information that was obtained from a Government official without proper authorization; or (2) Source selection information (as defined in 2.101) that is relevant to the contract but is not available to all competitors, and such information would assist that contractor in obtaining the contract.

25m.q: An offeror contacts you about a job while you are working its source selection. What must you do — and what waits on the other side of Government service?
25m.a: Report the contact promptly in writing to your supervisor and the agency ethics official, then either reject the possibility of non-Federal employment or disqualify yourself from further personal and substantial participation in that procurement — the duty attaches to any official participating personally and substantially in a procurement over the SAT, and unsolicited approaches count. On the back end, a former official who served as the contracting officer, SSA, evaluation-board member, evaluation-team chief, program manager, deputy PM, or ACO on a contract exceeding $10 million to that contractor — or personally made certain $10 million-plus award, rate, payment, or claim decisions — may not accept compensation from that contractor as an employee, officer, director, or consultant for 1 year.

cite.quote: (i) Promptly report the contact in writing to the official's supervisor and to the agency ethics official; and (ii) Either reject the possibility of non-Federal employment or disqualify himself or herself from further personal and substantial participation in that Federal agency procurement

25m.q: Where does a procurement integrity violation go if it impacts the procurement?
25m.a: To the head of the contracting activity. The contracting officer first determines whether the violation affects the pending award or selection; if it does, all information goes promptly to the HCA, who decides what happens next.

cite.quote: (2) If the contracting officer determines the violation does impact the procurement, the contracting officer must promptly forward all information to the HCA.

25m.q: What can the HCA direct before award if a procurement integrity violation is confirmed?
25m.a: Cancel the procurement, disqualify an offeror, or take other appropriate actions to protect the Government's interests.

cite.quote: (1) If a contract has not been awarded— (i) Cancel the procurement; (ii) Disqualify an offeror; or (iii) Take other appropriate actions to protect Government interests.

25m.q: State the GAO postaward stay rule precisely.
25m.a: If the agency receives GAO's protest notice within 10 days after award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered under a required debriefing — whichever is later — the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance or terminate the contract, unless the HCA authorizes continued performance. [Note: the quoted reference to “15.505 or 15.506” is a stale cross-reference — in the RFO those sections cover unsolicited proposals; the operative debriefing sections are 15.206-2 (preaward) and 15.301 (postaward).] For DoD, R-DFARS 233.105-370 swaps in its own clock: suspend or terminate if GAO's notice arrives within the LATEST of — 10 days after contract award; 10 days after issuance of a task or delivery order exceeding $25 million; 5 days after a debriefing date offered under a timely request (even if the protester rejected the offered date, unless an earlier date is negotiated); or 5 days after a required postaward debriefing is concluded — and under the enhanced-debriefing rule the debriefing is not concluded until timely follow-up questions are answered in writing (R-DFARS 215.301-270).

cite.quote: If the agency receives notice of a protest from the GAO within 10 days after contract award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered to the protester for any debriefing that is required by 15.505 or 15.506, whichever is later, then the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance or terminate the awarded contract, unless the head of the contracting activity authorizes contract performance.

25m.q: Who can override a GAO protest stay, and on what bases?
25m.a: The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, upon a written finding that performance is in the best interests of the United States, or that urgent and compelling circumstances significantly affecting U.S. interests will not permit waiting for GAO's decision — and GAO must be notified before performance is authorized.

cite.quote: The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, may authorize contract performance, upon a written finding that— (i) Contract performance will be in the best interests of the United States; or (ii) Urgent and compelling circumstances that significantly affect the interests of the United States will not permit waiting for the GAO's decision.

25m.q: Who approves a J&A above $900,000 up to $20M, and is it delegable?
25m.a: The advocate for competition. Not delegable.

cite.quote: Advocate for competition.

unlimited.q: What two pieces make up the fee on a cost-plus-award-fee contract?
unlimited.a: A base amount fixed at inception (if used, at the contracting officer's discretion) and an award fee the contractor may earn in whole or in part to motivate excellence in cost, schedule, and technical performance — decided each evaluation period by the Fee-Determining Official on the Award-Fee Board's recommendations. DoD adds hard guardrails: base fee capped at 3 percent of the estimated cost exclusive of fee, at least 40 percent of the award fee held for the final evaluation (going lower takes nondelegable HCA approval), award-fee payments outside the end-of-period evaluation prohibited, and the FDO's rating due to the contractor within 45 calendar days of the end of the period.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-award-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that provides a fee consisting of (1) a base amount fixed at inception of the contract, if applicable and at the discretion of the contracting officer, and (2) an award fee that the contractor may earn in whole or in part to provide motivation for excellence in the areas of cost, schedule, and technical performance.

unlimited.q: By when must a UCA's definitization schedule provide for definitization?
unlimited.a: By the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal, or the date obligated funds exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. The 180 days runs from the qualifying proposal — not from award.

cite.quote: UCAs must contain definitization schedules that provide for definitization by the earlier of— (1) The date that is 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal.

unlimited.q: How much of a UCA's not-to-exceed price may be obligated before definitization?
unlimited.a: No more than 50 percent — raised to no more than 75 percent if the contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent has been obligated.

cite.quote: The Government must not obligate more than 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price before definitization. However, if a contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price has been obligated by the Government, then the limitation on obligations before definitization may be increased to no more than 75 percent

unlimited.q: What definitization schedule applies to a DoD letter contract?
unlimited.a: The UCA schedule at 217.7404-3(a): definitize by the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal (extendable up to 90 more days only by HCA-level written determination) or the point where obligations exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. R-DFARS 216.603-2(c) applies that schedule instead of the civilian baseline at 16.603-2(c) — 180 days from the letter contract or 40 percent of the work — so for a DoD contracting officer the baseline rule simply does not apply.

cite.quote: In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 3372, establish definitization schedules for letter contracts following the requirements at 217.7404-3(a) instead of the requirements at FAR 16.603-2(c).

unlimited.q: A UCA definitizes after the 180-day window from the qualifying proposal has run. What does that do to the contractor's profit?
unlimited.a: Normally the profit on a late-definitized UCA reflects the contractor's reduced cost risk for costs already incurred. But when the contracting officer definitizes after the 180-day period from the qualifying proposal, the allowed profit must accurately reflect the contractor's cost risk as it existed on the date the qualifying proposal was submitted — the Government's own delay cannot be used to ratchet profit down further. The HCA ensures it, and the risk assessment is documented in the price negotiation memorandum.

cite.quote: the profit allowed on the contract must accurately reflect the cost risk of the contractor as such risk existed on the date the contractor submitted the qualifying proposal

unlimited.q: R-DFARS splits its LPTA restrictions into limitations and prohibitions. What falls on each side of the line?
unlimited.a: Limitations — avoid to the maximum extent practicable: acquisitions predominantly for information technology, cybersecurity, systems engineering and technical assistance, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; personal protective equipment generally; and knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency or other overseas operations. Prohibitions — do not use, period: PPE or aviation critical safety items where quality failure could cause combat casualties; engineering and manufacturing development for a major defense acquisition program; and auditing services. Mixing the two lists is the classic board trap — "avoid" is judgment, "do not use" is absolute.

cite.quote: Avoid using the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach, to the maximum extent practicable, for acquisitions that are predominately for— (i) Information technology services, cybersecurity services, systems engineering and technical assistance services, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; (ii) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment (except see paragraph (b)(1) of this section); or (iii) Services designated by the requiring activity as knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency operations or other operations outside the United States. (b) Prohibitions. Do not use the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach to procure— (1) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment or as an aviation critical safety item, for which the level of quality or failure of the equipment or item could result in combat casualties.

unlimited.q: The Government decides it will pay any fair and reasonable price for the highest quality performance, with no tradeoffs. What source selection approach is that, and how does award actually work?
unlimited.a: Highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price. All proposals are evaluated on the non-price factors in the solicitation; the source selection authority identifies the highest technically rated proposal and only then evaluates that proposal's price for fair-and-reasonableness under subpart 15.4. If the price passes, that proposal is selected — no tradeoffs. If it does not, the SSA moves to the next highest technically rated proposal and repeats until award. The RFP must tell offerors up front that tradeoffs between price and non-price factors will not be considered.

cite.quote: If the highest technically rated proposal’s price is fair and reasonable, the proposal is selected for award. If the price is not fair and reasonable, the source selection authority must determine the next highest technically rated proposal and evaluate whether the price is fair and reasonable in accordance with subpart 15.4. This process continues until a contract is awarded to the highest technically rated responsible offeror with a fair and reasonable price.

unlimited.q: Who is the source selection authority by default, and what must the SSA lock down before the RFP goes out?
unlimited.a: The contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions. Before RFP release the SSA approves the source selection approach or acquisition plan, and establishes an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition with contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise. The SSA must ensure proposals are evaluated solely on the RFP's factors and subfactors, and may reject all proposals when that serves the Government's best interest. In DoD, high-dollar acquisitions also require SSA approval of a source selection plan before the solicitation issues.

cite.quote: Agency heads are responsible for source selection. A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions.

unlimited.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
unlimited.q: How are forward pricing rate agreement rates used once established?
unlimited.a: As the bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions performed during the period the agreement covers; conditions affecting the agreement's validity must be promptly reported to the administrative contracting officer. In DoD the rates are not optional: use FPRA rates whenever they are available unless the head of the contracting activity waives them on a case-by-case basis — and advise the ACO of each case waived.

cite.quote: Contracting officers will use FPRA rates as bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions to be performed during the period covered by the agreement.

unlimited.q: What are DoD's customary progress payment rates — and when should progress payments not be the first choice?
unlimited.a: 80 percent for large business concerns and 90 percent for small business concerns — the same rates apply to contracts carrying foreign military sales requirements.
